title: Open and Distance eLearning: New Dimensions in Teaching, Learning, Research, and Extension for Higher Education Institutions
abstract:
Open and Distance eLearning has helped evolve the idea of openness in education which expands to include the following(Alfonso, 2014):
Openness in admission policies; openness in credit recognition and accreditation; openness in delivery modes; openness in cost and affordability (some are free); opennessin choosing educationaltrack through multiple bridges and pathways, exits and entrances; openness in course design and evaluation; openness in strengthening digital literacies and e-pedagogies, emerging e-Research paradigms. The digitization of open and distance learning led to theOpen Educational Resources (OER) movement and popularity of Massive Open Online Courses(MOOCs).
Based on UP Open University’s experience in Open and Distance eLearmig (ODeL), new dimensions of openness in instruction, research, and extension are explored, including the use of analytics in research, teaching and learning particularly in the areas of assessment and evaluation; openness in the shift from faculty-centered to learner-centered teaching; openness in flexible, distributed, blended, technology-enhanced and active learning; openness in the use of new digital technologies for course materials and for being in the core of teaching and learning process; openness in sharing resources and linking digital repositories; and openness in the use of Massive Open Online eLearning Systems as free and accessible to all.
half:
In "Open and Distance eLearning: New Dimensions in Teaching, Learning, Research, and Extension for Higher Education Institutions," Grace Javier Alfonso and Primo G. Garcia examine the evolution of Open and Distance eLearning (ODeL) as a transformative framework for higher education. By integrating open learning, distance education, and e-learning, ODeL aims to promote social transformation and educational equity within a globalized, digital "network society." Using the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) as a case study, the authors trace the transition from print-based modules to fully online delivery models.

The study identifies several key dimensions of this shift. In instruction, teaching moves from faculty-centered to learner-centered, with instructors acting as facilitators rather than sole knowledge sources. Regarding resources, the use of Open Educational Resources (OER) and Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) democratizes knowledge through localized content. In research, digital environments allow for the use of learner analytics to study student behavior. In extension, ODeL enables universities to reach non-traditional learners, such as overseas workers, through scalable platforms.

The authors conclude that ODeL bridges the gap between academic rigor and accessibility by embracing mass participation and distributed expertise. To succeed, higher education institutions must establish legal frameworks, pursue industry and government partnerships, and utilize ICT infrastructure to become integrated knowledge hubs that foster lifelong learning.

two:
The article "Open and Distance eLearning: New Dimensions in Teaching, Learning, Research, and Extension for Higher Education Institutions" explores the evolution of Open and Distance eLearning (ODeL) as a transformative force in higher education. The authors, Grace Javier Alfonso and Primo G. Garcia, frame ODeL not merely as a mode of delivery, but as a comprehensive worldview that integrates the principles of open learning, distance education, and e-learning to foster social transformation and educational equity.

The problem addressed by the authors stems from the changing demands of the 21st-century global economy and the digital age. As the "network society" increases the mobility of professionals and the globalization of ideas, traditional higher education models face challenges in remaining relevant. Modern learners require lifelong learning, transnational education, and flexible pathways to acquire skills in dynamic environments. Furthermore, the authors note that while many conventional universities have attempted to adopt e-learning, many have struggled to adapt their teaching methods quickly enough to ensure quality, sustainability, and increased access. There is a pressing need for institutions to move beyond traditional "monopolies" on knowledge and embrace openness to remain significant in a landscape where information is ubiquitous and increasingly decentralized.

The context of this discussion is rooted in the historical evolution of open education, which traces back to public lectures in the 14th century and the rise of distance education in the 20th century. In the digital era, this has been accelerated by the transition from analog to digital, from tethered to mobile, and from closed to open systems. The authors specifically use the experience of the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) as a primary case study. UPOU, established in 1995, transitioned from print-based modules to a fully online delivery model in 2001, providing a unique vantage point to observe how ODeL functions within a national university system.

The method employed in this paper is a qualitative exploration and synthesis of the ODeL worldview, drawing on the institutional experiences of UPOU. The authors analyze how the integration of open learning (focusing on access and equity), distance education (focusing on learner-centeredness and flexibility), and e-learning (focusing on interactivity, ubiquity, and connectivity) creates a new framework for higher education. They examine specific applications of this framework in instruction, the use of Open Educational Resources (OER), the implementation of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs), and the roles of research and extension.

The findings of the article highlight several new dimensions of openness. In instruction, the shift from faculty-centered to learner-centered teaching is paramount. Through platforms like Myportal (powered by MOODLE), students engage in asynchronous discussions, wikis, and blogs, which transform the teacher from a sole source of knowledge into a facilitator. This environment encourages peer-to-peer learning and requires students to apply theoretical concepts to real-world problems. Regarding resources, the authors find that OERs and MOOCs—specifically UPOU’s "MODeL" (massive open and distance elearning) approach—allow for the democratization of knowledge. OERs enable the creation of localized, culturally relevant content that moves away from a "monologue" toward a participatory construction of knowledge. In research, the authors find that the digital environment allows for the use of learner analytics to better understand student behaviors and profiles. Finally, in extension, the authors note that ODeL allows universities to fulfill their social contracts by reaching non-traditional learners, such as overseas workers and out-of-school youth, through scalable digital platforms.

The authors conclude that ODeL is a vital framework for the future of higher education, offering a way to bridge the gap between academic rigor and widespread accessibility. They emphasize that ODeL is not a rigid normative framework but an expression of values—such as excellence, academic freedom, and service to society—that can be adapted by various institutions. The success of ODeL depends on the ability of universities to embrace "mass participation" and "distributed expertise," moving away from closed systems toward a more collaborative "knowledge commons."

The implications of this study are significant for policymakers and educational leaders. The authors point to the importance of legal frameworks, such as the Philippines' Republic Act 10650 (the Open and Distance Learning Act), which mandates that institutions assist in the design and management of ODL programs. For higher education institutions to thrive, they must move toward institutional exchanges and partnerships with industry, government, and media. The authors suggest that the future of the university lies in becoming an active knowledge hub that integrates with the community through ICT infrastructure. Ultimately, the paper implies that by mainstreaming ODeL, universities can foster a culture of lifelong learning and innovation, ensuring that higher education remains a powerful tool for social transformation in a digitized world.

title: Introduction to IJODeL Volume 1, Numbers 1&2
half:
The maiden issue of the International Journal on Open and Distance eLearning (IJODeL) introduces a platform dedicated to researching open learning, distance education, and eLearning. The editorial frames open and distance eLearning (ODeL) as a worldview for organizing research and practice. A lead article by Grace Javier Alfonso and Primo G. Garcia suggests that combining the philosophy of openness with distance education modalities can drive social transformation when integrated with university value systems. The journal advocates for using information and communication technologies, specifically open educational resources, to create a digital knowledge hub.

Several studies in this issue focus on mobile learning in Asia. Tuliao, Duldulao, Pagtaconan, and Galang present "iSuro," a mobile application designed for the Kindergarten curriculum to address the scarcity of learning materials. Miguel, Salvador, Guillen, and Nisperos explored mobile applications as supplementary tools for teaching Philippine history through "HiStorya," an interactive Android game. Findings indicated that the game's immersive and reward aspects motivated deeper study, while system-generated reports helped teachers evaluate student proficiency. Additionally, Ahmad Sobri Shuib and Muhammad Nidzam Yaakob found that pre-service teachers in Malaysia maintain positive attitudes toward using mobile technology for teaching and learning. Finally, Felix Librero provides a historical report on the 20-year development of the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU), detailing how the institution addressed online learning issues.

The maiden issue of the International Journal on Open and Distance eLearning (IJODeL) introduces a university-based academic journal dedicated to the study of open learning, distance education, elearning, mobile learning, and related concepts. The journal aims to advance the understanding of the theory and practice of open and distance elearning through research-based papers, conceptual papers, reviews, and commentaries.

The editorial frames open and distance elearning (ODeL) as a worldview that provides a framework for organizing research, theory, and practice. A lead article by Grace Javier Alfonso and Primo G. Garcia suggests that the philosophy of openness, combined with the affordances of distance education and elearning modalities, can drive social transformation when integrated with university value systems in a digitized world. This is particularly relevant to the functions of higher education institutions, as seen in the experiences of the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). The journal advocates for the use of information and communication technologies (ICTs), specifically open educational resources (OERs) and a culture of sharing, to create a digital knowledge hub.

Several studies in this issue focus on mobile learning within the Asian educational context. One study by Tuliao, Duldulao, Pagtaconan, and Galang presents "iSuro," a mobile learning application designed for the Kindergarten curriculum to address the scarcity of learning materials. This tool provides digital content and a user-friendly environment to integrate ICTs into early childhood learning.

A second study by Miguel, Salvador, Guillen, and Nisperos explores mobile applications as supplementary tools for teaching Philippine history. The researchers developed "HiStorya," an interactive Android mobile game, and evaluated it using the Digital Game-based Learning-Instructional Design Model. Findings indicated that the immersive, reward, and challenge aspects of the game motivated students to study history more deeply. Additionally, teachers found the system-generated statistics reports helpful for evaluating student proficiency levels.

A third study by Ahmad Sobri Shuib and Muhammad Nidzam Yaakob examines the perceptions of 120 pre-service teachers at the Institute of Teacher Education Campus Darul Aman in Malaysia. The findings show that these pre-service teachers maintain a positive attitude toward using mobile technology for teaching and learning.

Finally, a historical report by Felix Librero, former Chancellor of UPOU, chronicles the institution's 20-year journey. The report details the academic, socio-political, organizational, and technological events during UPOU’s development, illustrating how the institution addressed online learning issues through collective efforts to understand emerging ODeL concepts.

title: Development of a Mobile Learning Application for Kindergarten: Process, Issues, and Challenges
abstract: Mobile learning is now considered as a branch of ICT in education. Because it makes use of technology that is more affordable and more easily self-procured and managed than tethered computers, mobile learning requires reconceptualizing traditional models of technology use and implementation. This study aimed to develop a mobile learning application that provides new learning pedagogy and integrate ICT in the learning process of Kindergarteners. This study focused on the development of a mobile learning application for Kindergarten named iSuro. The contents of the application were based from the existing learning modules of kindergarten in mother tongue (Iloco). The application is implemented in android- based mobile devices. It provides a digital content of information, a user-friendly environment to kindergarteners that enables them to be more productive and engaged in classroom activities, and a one-size-fits-all learning. The system should be adopted by schools in the Province of Ilocos Norte for the Kindergarteners to have an additional material for learning as well as more fun and exciting learning experiences. Since the dialect used in the contents of the application is Iloco, a language selection feature should be incorporated so that other Regions could also use the application.
half:
The study "Development of a Mobile Learning Application for Kindergarten: Process, Issues, and Challenges" investigates integrating Information and Communication Technology into early childhood education. Researchers identified several challenges in current Kindergarten environments, such as large class sizes, difficulty engaging students through traditional methods, the physical burden of heavy textbooks, and a scarcity of Department of Education learning materials.

Conducted within the Philippines' K to 12 Program, the research focused on the Cognitive/Intellectual Development domain using Mathematics. The researchers developed "iSuro," an Android-based mobile learning application designed to be an affordable, portable, and user-friendly complement to existing infrastructure. Using the Mobile-D Development Methodology, the team followed five phases: Explore, Initialize, Productionize, Stabilize, and System Test and Fix. The final iSuro application, developed using Eclipse 4.2 and an SQLite database, features a Learning Module with digital flipbooks and voice-overs, an Activity Module for skill evaluation, and an Assessment Module with rewards and leaderboards. Content is based on Kindergarten modules in the Iloco mother tongue.

User Acceptance Testing involving teachers, Kindergarteners, and parents indicated high satisfaction levels, with mean scores of 4.54, 4.37, and 4.43, respectively. The researchers conclude that mobile learning offers potential for personalization and mobility, making learners more productive and engaged. They recommend that schools in Ilocos Norte adopt the system and suggest adding more lessons and a language selection feature to increase accessibility.

The study "Development of a Mobile Learning Application for Kindergarten: Process, Issues, and Challenges" examines the integration of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) into early childhood education. Researchers identified several challenges in current Kindergarten environments, including large class sizes that prevent individual attention, difficulty engaging students through traditional "chalk and board" methods, the physical burden of heavy textbooks, and a scarcity of Department of Education learning materials.

Conducted within the context of the Philippines' K to 12 Program, the research focused on the Cognitive/Intellectual Development domain using Mathematics as the subject. The researchers developed "iSuro," an Android-based mobile learning application designed to be an affordable, portable, and user-friendly complement to existing educational infrastructure.

The researchers utilized the Mobile-D Development Methodology, an agile approach consisting of five phases: Explore, Initialize, Productionize, Stabilize, and System Test and Fix. Using an Input-Process-Output (IPO) model, the study incorporated the Kindergarten curriculum and teacher strategies as inputs. The development process involved identifying challenges, selecting tools, designing the application, and conducting user acceptance testing. The final output was the functional iSuro application, developed using Eclipse 4.2 (Juno) with an SQLite database.

The iSuro application features three primary modules: a Learning Module with digital flipbooks and voice-overs, an Activity Module for skill evaluation, and an Assessment Module that provides rewards and saves scores to a leaderboard. The content is based on existing Kindergarten learning modules in the mother tongue, Iloco.

User Acceptance Testing (UAT) involved 20 teachers, 25 Kindergarteners, and 20 parents. Results indicated high levels of satisfaction across all groups. Teachers reported an overall mean of 4.54, noting that the lessons were well-organized and made the teaching process more permanent. Kindergarteners provided an overall mean of 4.37, and parents provided an overall mean of 4.43. These results suggest the application is an effective tool for engaging young learners and supporting educators.

The researchers conclude that mobile learning offers unique potential for personalization and mobility. iSuro serves as a successful digital content provider that creates a user-friendly environment, making Kindergarteners more productive and engaged. The study confirms that mobile technology can complement traditional tools to provide learning experiences that transcend classroom boundaries.

The researchers recommend that schools in the Province of Ilocos Norte adopt the iSuro system. To improve the application, they suggest adding more lessons and activities. Additionally, because the current content is in the Iloco dialect, they recommend incorporating a language selection feature to increase accessibility and utility for students in other regions.

The study titled "Development of a Mobile Learning Application for Kindergarten: Process, Issues, and Challenges" addresses the integration of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) into early childhood education. The researchers identify a significant problem in the current Kindergarten teaching environment, where teachers struggle to provide individual attention due to large class sizes and difficulty in engaging students in traditional classroom activities. Furthermore, Kindergarteners face physical burdens from carrying heavy textbooks and notebooks, and there is a noted scarcity of learning materials provided by the Department of Education. Traditional teaching methods, often limited to the "chalk and board" approach within classroom walls, are identified as needing modernization to better suit the needs of young learners.

The research was conducted in the context of the Philippines' K to 12 Program, which aims to develop lifelong learners through specific developmental milestones. The study specifically focused on the Cognitive/Intellectual Development domain, utilizing Mathematics as the subject matter. The researchers aimed to develop "iSuro," an Android-based mobile learning application designed to provide a new pedagogy that integrates ICT into the learning process. The application was designed to be an affordable, portable, and user-friendly complement to existing educational investments like textbooks and infrastructure.

To achieve these objectives, the researchers employed the Mobile-D Development Methodology, an agile approach consisting of five phases: Explore, Initialize, Productionize, Stabilize, and System Test and Fix. The study utilized an Input-Process-Output (IPO) model as its conceptual framework. The inputs included the Kindergarten curriculum, teacher teaching strategies, and identified challenges regarding policy, materials, and methods. The process involved identifying these challenges, determining development tools, designing the application, and conducting user acceptance testing. The output was the functional iSuro application. The development was carried out using the Eclipse 4.2 (Juno) tool on a Windows 7 operating system, with SQLite serving as the database.

The findings of the study demonstrate the successful development and high acceptability of the iSuro application. The application features three primary modules: a Learning Module, which provides digital flipbooks and voice-overs; an Activity Module, which presents questions to evaluate skills; and an Assessment Module, which provides rewards and saves scores to a leaderboard. The contents of the application were based on existing Kindergarten learning modules in the mother tongue, Iloco.

User Acceptance Testing (UAT) was conducted with three groups of respondents: 20 teachers, 25 Kindergarteners, and 20 parents. The results showed high levels of satisfaction across all groups. Teachers reported an overall mean of 4.54, indicating they strongly agree with the system's functionality, usability, and performance, noting that the lessons were well-organized and made the teaching process more permanent. Kindergarteners provided an overall mean of 4.37, also signifying strong agreement. Parents provided an overall mean of 4.43, also indicating strong agreement. These results suggest that the application is an effective tool for engaging young learners and supporting educators.

The researchers conclude that mobile learning provides a unique ability to support teaching and learning through its mobility and potential for personalization. The iSuro application serves as a successful digital content provider that offers a user-friendly environment, making Kindergarteners more productive and engaged. The study confirms that mobile technology can complement traditional educational tools and provide exciting, fun learning experiences that transcend the physical boundaries of a classroom.

Based on these findings, the researchers offer several implications and recommendations. They suggest that the iSuro system should be adopted by schools in the Province of Ilocos Norte to provide students with additional, engaging learning materials. To improve the application, the researchers recommend adding more lessons and activities. Furthermore, because the current content is specifically in the Iloco dialect, they recommend incorporating a language selection feature to allow the application to be used by students in other regions, thereby increasing its accessibility and utility.

title: HiStorya: a Game Based Mobile Learning Application
abstract:
In mobile learning approach, game-based learning techniques have been popular to engage learning while still enjoying. This study sought to design and develop a mobile game application for Araling Panlipunan (AP) that could be used as a supplementary tool in learning the subject by Grade 8 students under the K-12 Curriculum of the Department of Education (DepEd) in the Philippines. The researchers identified the topics, teaching methods and evaluation techniques used by the AP teachers and the game preferences of the AP students by conducting interviews and surveys. HiStorya, an interactive mobile game, was developed using the Android platform and the Digital Game-based Learning-Instructional Design Model. An evaluation survey of the application was also accomplished by the AP teachers and students.
HiStorya is relevant to the current state of technology today where smart devices are very popular. It is beneficial to the Grade 8 students taking up AP, the teachers of AP and the current education system of the Philippines. The students who used the application played and learned AP during or outside ofschool hours. The immersive, challenge and reward aspects of the game motivated the students to study and learn more about AP. The application was also utilized by AP teachers as a supplementary tool in teaching the subject. With the game statistics report generated by the system, HiStorya demonstrated it could help the teacher evaluate the subject proficiency level of his students. Moreover, HiStorya emphasized the significance of using games for student learning and introduced itself as another tool for teaching AP in the Philippines.
half:
The study "HiStorya: a Game Based Mobile Learning Application" addresses low student engagement in the Araling Panlipunan (AP) subject within the Philippine K-12 curriculum, where heavy emphasis on memorization often leads to boredom. Researchers aimed to develop an interactive Android mobile application as a supplementary tool for students and teachers, specifically focusing on Asian geography, history, culture, society, government, and economy.

Using an input-process-output model and the Digital Game-based Learning-Instructional Design (DGBL-ID) model, researchers gathered data through interviews with educators and surveys of Grade 8 students. Findings revealed that 90% of students own smart devices, 63% use Android, and 89% play games for one to two hours daily, with a preference for analogy, quiz, and memory games.

The resulting application, HiStorya, features three game categories aligned with curriculum assessment levels: a Quiz game for knowledge, a Memory game for process/skills, and an Analogy game for understanding. The app is organized into four levels corresponding to curriculum units, requiring correct answers to unlock new content. HiStorya includes a synchronization feature that uploads statistics to an online database, enabling a web-based module for teachers to monitor progress and administrators to manage content. A leaderboard was also implemented to foster competition. Researchers concluded that HiStorya is a motivating, relevant tool for both learning and instructional planning.

The study "HiStorya: a Game Based Mobile Learning Application" addresses the lack of student engagement in the Araling Panlipunan (AP) subject within the Philippine K-12 curriculum. Grade 8 teachers reported that students often find the subject boring due to a heavy emphasis on memorization. To address this, researchers sought to develop an interactive Android mobile application that serves as a supplementary learning tool for both students and teachers, specifically focusing on Asian geography, history, culture, society, government, and economy.

The research objectives were to gather information regarding the AP curriculum, teaching methods, and evaluation techniques; to determine student gaming preferences; and to design and develop an interactive application based on these findings. Using an input-process-output model, the researchers collected data through unstructured interviews with Department of Education personnel and AP teachers, as well as surveys administered to Grade 8 students. The development process followed the Digital Game-based Learning-Instructional Design (DGBL-ID) model, which includes analysis, design, development, quality assurance, and implementation and evaluation.

Findings indicated that the Grade 8 AP curriculum covers four main units: Asian geography, ancient Asian civilizations, and the transitional and modern eras of West, South, East, and Southeast Asia. Assessment in the curriculum is categorized into knowledge, process/skills, understanding, and products/performances. Regarding student habits, 90% of respondents owned a smart device, 63% used Android, and 89% played games for one to two hours daily. The most popular game types identified were analogy, quiz, and memory games.

Based on these findings, the researchers developed HiStorya, which features three game categories designed to match the curriculum's assessment levels: a Quiz game for the knowledge level, a Memory game for the process/skills level, and an Analogy game for the understanding level. The application is organized into four levels corresponding to the curriculum units. To maintain engagement, players must answer a specific number of questions correctly to unlock subsequent levels.

HiStorya includes a synchronization feature that allows students to upload statistics to an online database. This enabled the creation of a web-based module for teachers and administrators. The teacher module allows educators to monitor student progress and identify specific topics where students struggle, while the administrator module allows for database management and the addition of new content. A leaderboard was also implemented to foster competition. The researchers concluded that HiStorya is a relevant tool that provides a motivating way to engage students, serving as an effective supplementary tool for both learning and instructional planning.

The study titled "HiStorya: a Game Based Mobile Learning Application" addresses the challenge of student engagement in the Araling Panlipunan (AP) subject within the Philippine K-12 curriculum. Teachers reported that Grade 8 students often find the subject boring due to the heavy emphasis on memorization. While the rapid growth of smart devices offers opportunities for mobile learning, there was a need for a specialized tool that could transform the study of Asian geography, history, culture, society, government, and economy into an engaging experience. The researchers sought to bridge this gap by developing a mobile application that serves as a supplementary learning tool for both students and teachers.

To address this problem, the researchers aimed to design and develop an interactive mobile game for the Android platform that aligns with the Grade 8 AP curriculum and student preferences. The study had three specific objectives: to gather information regarding the AP curriculum, teaching methods, and evaluation techniques; to determine the gaming preferences of students; and to design and develop an interactive application based on these findings.

The methodology employed an input-process-output model. The inputs consisted of the K-12 AP Curriculum for Grade 8 and user game preferences. To gather these inputs, the researchers conducted unstructured interviews with Department of Education personnel and AP teachers at MMSU Laboratory High School to understand teaching strategies and assessment guidelines. They also collected curriculum modules and assessment artifacts. Additionally, a survey was administered to Grade 8 students to identify their familiarity with Android technology and their preferred game types. For the development phase, the researchers utilized the Digital Game-based Learning-Instructional Design (DGBL-ID) model, which involves five phases: analysis, design, development, quality assurance, and implementation and evaluation.

The findings revealed significant data regarding both the curriculum and student habits. The Grade 8 AP curriculum covers four main units: Asian geography, ancient Asian civilizations, and the transitional and modern eras of West, South, East, and Southeast Asia. Assessment in this curriculum is categorized into knowledge, process/skills, understanding, and products/performances, with proficiency levels ranging from "Beginning" to "Advanced." Regarding student preferences, the survey showed that 90% of respondents owned a smart device, 63% used Android, and 89% played games for one to two hours daily. The most popular game types among students were analogy, quiz, and memory games.

Based on these findings, the researchers developed HiStorya, an Android application featuring three distinct game categories designed to match the curriculum's assessment levels: a Quiz game for the knowledge level, a Memory game for the process/skills level, and an Analogy game for the understanding level. The game is organized into four levels corresponding to the four units of the AP curriculum, with sub-levels for specific topics. To maintain engagement, the game includes a requirement to answer a certain number of questions correctly to unlock subsequent levels, creating an immersive experience through challenge and reward.

HiStorya also includes a synchronization feature that allows students to upload their statistics to an online database. This led to the development of a web-based module for teachers and administrators. The teacher module allows educators to manage classes and monitor student progress through detailed statistics. This system tracks the number of attempts per question, helping teachers identify specific topics or questions where students struggle, thereby informing the need for remedial instruction. The administrator module allows for the management of the online database, including the ability to add new questions and categories. To foster a sense of competition, a leaderboard was also implemented to display top scorers.

The researchers concluded that HiStorya is a relevant tool in the current technological landscape of widespread smart device usage. By integrating the curriculum's assessment levels and student gaming preferences, the application provides a way to engage students in a fun and motivating manner. The study demonstrates that HiStorya can serve as an effective supplementary tool for both students, who can learn inside or outside school hours, and teachers, who can use the generated data for assessment and instructional planning. The researchers recommend further studies to compare the effectiveness of HiStorya against traditional teaching approaches to formally assess its impact on student performance.

title: Perception and Readiness of Pre-service Teachers on Mobile Learning
abstract:
Developments in mobile technology have changed the way people learn. Learning is not confined in the classroom alone; it could also occur beyond the boundaries of the classroom and can happen anytime and anywhere. The current generation of students has greater access to knowledge through their mobile devices. Thus, innovation on pedagogy must change along with the changes in technology. The ability of mobile learning to deliver knowledge should be fully utilized by teacher educators when implementing teaching and learning in the classroom. The purpose of this study was to identify the perceptions and willingness of pre service teachers on the use of equipment and mobile technology in learning.
Preliminary data obtained in this study provide useful information for the implementation of teaching and learning at the Institute of Teacher Education Campus management. The sample in this study was a randomly selected group of 120 pre-service teachers studying Bachelor of Teaching at the Institute of Teacher Education, Darul Aman Campus. Data were analyzed using descriptive analysis using SPSS 19. The study found that pre- service teachers have a positive attitude towards the use of mobile technology in learning. The findings of this study provide teacher educators with useful information when it comes to diversifying their teaching by integrating mobile devices in teaching and learning at the institute.
half:
The study "Perception and Readiness of Pre-service Teachers on Mobile Learning" by Ahmad Sobri Shuib and Muhammad Nidzam Yaakob investigates how future educators in Malaysia view and prepare for integrating mobile technology into teaching. The research addresses the gap between the widespread use of smartphones and the limited formal mobile learning initiatives within teacher education institutes.

Using a quantitative design at the Institute of Teacher Education, Darul Aman Campus, the study surveyed 120 eighth-semester Bachelor of Teaching students. Data were collected through a validated 20-item Likert scale questionnaire. The findings indicate that pre-service teachers possess a high level of readiness and a positive perception toward mobile learning. Respondents showed a high willingness to use mobile devices for learning, specifically expressing very high willingness to use laptops and tablets to access the internet for information. They also showed high willingness to use smartphones to access the internet and download educational materials.

The authors conclude that implementing mobile learning in Malaysia is highly feasible and can serve as a cost-effective alternative to traditional methods by reducing expenses related to electricity, laboratories, and cabling. They recommend that institutions develop formal training modules and integrate mobile learning into the mainstream curriculum. Furthermore, the Ministry of Education should improve technological infrastructure and provide teachers with more devices and specialized training to support this shift.

The study "Perception and Readiness of Pre-service Teachers on Mobile Learning" by Ahmad Sobri Shuib and Muhammad Nidzam Yaakob examines how future educators view and prepare for integrating mobile technology into their teaching practices. The research addresses the gap in understanding whether pre-service teachers in Malaysia are ready to utilize mobile tools effectively, given that formal mobile learning initiatives in teacher education institutes remain limited despite the widespread use of smartphones.

Conducted at the Institute of Teacher Education, Darul Aman Campus, the study utilized a quantitative research design. The sample included 120 randomly selected eighth-semester Bachelor of Teaching students, representing 86% of the population at the campus. Data were collected via a validated 20-item questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale. A pilot study confirmed the instrument's reliability with a Cronbach Alpha value of 0.86.

The findings reveal that pre-service teachers possess a high level of readiness and a positive perception toward mobile learning. The sample was predominantly female (69.2%) and Malay (83.3%), with Special Education being the most common major. Nearly all respondents (99.2%) used their devices for SMS, and Samsung was the most frequent brand. Regarding readiness, the study found a high mean score (4.1) for the willingness to use mobile devices for learning. Specifically, students expressed a very high willingness to use laptops (mean 4.7) and tablets (mean 4.5) to access the internet for information, and a high willingness to use smartphones to access the internet (mean 4.4) and download educational materials (mean 4.1). The results suggest students are eager to use mobile devices for educational purposes rather than just entertainment or social networking.

The authors conclude that implementing mobile learning in Malaysia is highly feasible due to existing infrastructure and student enthusiasm. They suggest mobile learning can serve as a cost-effective alternative to traditional methods by reducing expenses related to electricity, specialized laboratories, and network cabling.

The study offers several implications for stakeholders. Teacher educators and institutions should develop formal training modules for various mobile devices and create specialized mobile learning materials. The authors suggest integrating mobile learning into the mainstream curriculum by incorporating it into course prospectuses, ensuring affordable tuition, maintaining standard assessment methods, and achieving formal accreditation. For the Ministry of Education, the findings imply a need to improve technological infrastructure and provide teachers with more devices and specialized training. Additionally, the authors recommend developing academic literature and textbooks specifically focused on mobile learning to support this technological shift.

The authors note that while students are increasingly connected via smartphones, formal mobile learning initiatives in teacher education institutes remain limited, and there is a need to understand whether pre-service teachers are ready to utilize these tools effectively in their future careers.

The context of the research is the Malaysian education system, which possesses a stable internet infrastructure and widespread mobile device usage across various demographics. The study focuses on the Institute of Teacher Education, Darul Aman Campus, where the authors seek to provide preliminary data to help campus management and teacher educators implement mobile learning strategies.

To investigate this, the researchers employed a quantitative research design. The sample consisted of 120 randomly selected pre-service teachers studying for a Bachelor of Teaching, representing 86% of the total population of eighth-semester students at the campus. Data were collected using a questionnaire adapted from existing research, consisting of demographic information and 20 items regarding preparedness and perceptions. The instrument utilized a five-point Likert scale. To ensure the quality of the tool, a pilot study was conducted with 30 students, yielding a high Cronbach Alpha value of 0.86, indicating high reliability. The questionnaire's validity was confirmed through reviews by experienced lecturers and students. Data were analyzed using descriptive analysis via SPSS 19.

The findings indicate that pre-service teachers possess a high level of readiness and a positive perception toward mobile learning. Demographically, the sample was predominantly female (69.2%) and Malay (83.3%), with Special Education being the most common major. Regarding device usage, almost all respondents (99.2%) used their devices for SMS, and Samsung was the most common brand.

Regarding specific perceptions, students expressed a very high willingness to use laptops (mean 4.7) and tablets (mean 4.5) to access the internet for finding information. They also showed high willingness to use smartphones to access the internet (mean 4.4) and download educational materials (mean 4.1). Overall, the results suggest that students are prepared to learn anytime and anywhere and are eager to use mobile devices for educational purposes rather than just entertainment or social networking.

The authors conclude that the implementation of mobile learning in Malaysia is highly feasible given the existing infrastructure and the enthusiastic attitude of students. They suggest that mobile learning should be encouraged within classroom settings, similar to how e-learning has been integrated into the education system. The study highlights that mobile learning can be a cost-effective alternative to traditional methods, potentially saving money on electricity, specialized laboratories, and network cabling.

The implications of this study are significant for various stakeholders. For teacher educators and institutions, the findings suggest a need to develop formal training modules for various mobile devices, such as smartphones and tablets, and to create specialized mobile learning materials. The authors suggest that mobile learning should be integrated into the mainstream curriculum, which requires meeting specific criteria: incorporating mobile learning into course prospectuses, ensuring affordable tuition, maintaining standard assessment methods, and achieving formal accreditation. For the Ministry of Education, the study implies a need to improve technological infrastructure and provide teachers with more mobile devices and specialized training. Finally, the authors suggest that the development of academic literature and textbooks specifically focused on mobile learning is necessary to support this technological shift in education.

title: ODeL at UPOU: Some Historical Antecedents: (How Did We Get Here, Anyway?)
half:
In "ODeL at UPOU: Some Historical Antecedents: (How Did We Get Here, Anyway?)", Felix Librero traces the evolution of distance education at the University of the Philippines, from radio-based initiatives to the establishment of the U.P. Open University (UPOU). The development was driven by the need to provide quality higher education to underserved populations, address resource constraints in traditional campus-based instruction, and provide professional upgrading for teachers without requiring them to leave their jobs.

The history is rooted in two precursors at the University of the Philippines Los Baños: the "school on the air" (SOA) format via Radio DZLB, which provided systematic instruction to farmers and homemakers, and the Science Teaching Using Distance Instruction (STUDI) project, which addressed the shortage of qualified science teachers. Librero organizes this evolution into three stages: radio-based non-formal education, pilot distance instruction projects like STUDI, and the formal institutionalization of the UP Distance Education Program in 1992, which led to the creation of UPOU in 1995.

Findings indicate that SOA was effective for millions of learners, and STUDI proved distance education could successfully upgrade teacher competence. UPOU was designed to provide technical assistance and quality control across the UP system, targeting remote areas and non-traditional students. This evolution culminated in the transition from printed modules and radio to Open Distance e-Learning (ODeL), a model integrating open learning, distance education, and e-learning.

The article "ODeL at UPOU: Some Historical Antecedents: (How Did We Get Here, Anyway?)" by Felix Librero provides a historical overview of the development of distance education at the University of the Philippines, culminating in the establishment and evolution of the U.P. Open University (UPOU). The author traces the lineage of Open Distance e-Learning (ODeL) from early radio-based educational initiatives to a sophisticated, internet-mediated institutional worldview.

The problem addressed by the text is the challenge of providing quality higher education to a growing population across the Philippine archipelago, particularly for those underserved by conventional campus-based instruction. The author notes that the University of the Philippines faced limited absorptive capacity due to resource constraints, and that traditional admission processes, such as the UPCAT, often inadvertently discriminated against students from less endowed backgrounds. Furthermore, there was a critical need to provide professional upgrading for teachers—specifically in science—without requiring them to leave their jobs or families.

The context of this development is rooted in two major historical precursors at the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB). The first was the rise of rural educational broadcasting, specifically the "school on the air" (SOA) format. Beginning in the 1960s, Radio DZLB implemented systematic, research-oriented radio programs designed to teach farmers and rural homemakers. These programs were characterized by well-defined instructional objectives and progressive subject matter. The second precursor was the Science Teaching Using Distance Instruction (STUDI) project, an action research project initiated in 1964. STUDI was designed to address the alarming lack of qualified science teachers in the Philippines by providing content mastery through distance instruction, allowing teachers to earn while they studied.

The method of the article is a historical narrative and descriptive analysis. The author organizes the evolution of distance education into three distinct stages: the era of radio-based non-formal education, the implementation of pilot distance instruction projects like STUDI, and the formal institutionalization of the UP Distance Education Program in 1992, which eventually led to the creation of UPOU in 1995.

The findings regarding these historical stages reveal several key successes and observations. The "school on the air" format proved highly effective, with some programs benefiting millions of farmers through systematic, non-formal instruction. The STUDI project demonstrated that distance education was a viable way to upgrade teacher competence, resulting in highly successful degree programs like the Diploma in Science Teaching. The author notes that the success of these programs relied on learner motivation, the availability of instructional materials, and a supportive environment.

The establishment of UPOU was driven by the need to harness the University's vast expertise to reach a wider spectrum of learners, including "late bloomers," non-academic personnel, the disabled, and those in remote areas. The author highlights that UPOU was designed not as a separate entity to compete with conventional campuses, but as an academic support unit to provide technical assistance and quality control for distance courses across the entire UP system.

The conclusions drawn by the author emphasize the transition from traditional distance education to Open Distance e-Learning (ODeL). While early efforts relied on printed modules and radio broadcasts, the UPOU eventually transitioned to fully online delivery. The author posits that UPOU’s unique contribution was the conceptualization of ODeL as a distinct worldview. Unlike standard distance education, ODeL integrates the affordances of open learning (access and equity), distance education (learner-centeredness and flexibility), and e-learning (ubiquity, interactivity, and connectivity). This specific focus on electronic learning processes is what distinguishes the UPOU approach.

The implications of this history are codified in Philippine law through Republic Act No. 10650, also known as the Open Distance Learning Act. The law recognizes the UPOU’s role in providing leadership, best practices, and technical assistance to national agencies like CHED and TESDA. The article concludes by noting that the UPOU has moved from a small coordination office to a major player in the digital learning landscape, with its future likely involving increasingly sophisticated forms of e-learning and mediated instruction.

title: Design, Development, and Testing of an Indigenous Knowledge Management System Using Mobile Device Video Capture and Web 2.0 Protocols
abstract: This study attempted to answer the following research questions: How can mobile devices be used by rural communities to document indigenous knowledge? How can Web 2.0 protocols be employed in an indigenous knowledge management system? How will indigenous peoples (IPs) respond to the use of mobile technology in the documentation of their local knowledge? The theoretical basis for proposing that mobile devices may lead to the active participation of rural communities and indigenous peoples as ICT4D Web content providers is founded on three concepts: social capital; the network effect; and critical mass theory. The primary technological intervention was the mobile device. GPRS enabled mobile phones, with audio-video capture and Internet browsing functionalities were provided to focal persons from three IP groups. The Principal Investigator trained the focal persons on mobile phone video capture of indigenous or local knowledge. A content management system was designed to contain indigenous or local knowledge in agriculture in the form of rituals, practices, and others. The Principal Investigator and his assistants observed the knowledge capture and utilization process. During the conduct of the study, however, the researcher observed a marked reluctance from organized indigenous people’s groups to participate in the initiative. It soon became apparent that interfacing indigenous knowledge with Web 2.0 and open access concepts held complicated issues. The intervening variables observed and deduced by the Principal Investigator were: indigenous belief systems; privacy of indigenous peoples; indigenous knowledge system (IKS) protocols; the significance of context in IKS; prejudice and value judgments among non-IP users; and misrepresentation of indigenous knowledge.
half:
This study investigates using mobile devices and Web 2.0 protocols to document and manage the indigenous knowledge systems (IKS) of rural communities in the Philippines. The research aimed to determine how mobile technology can empower marginalized groups to become active content providers, thereby increasing their social capital. Using a quasi-experimental action research design involving six indigenous communities, the researchers provided participants with GPRS-enabled mobile phones and training in mobile videography. A Web Content Management System was developed to serve as a secure repository for rich media.

The findings revealed a significant disconnect between technological potential and social realities. Although training provided technical proficiency, the participation rate in content submission was low. Several intervening variables hindered the implementation of an open-access system, including the need to honor indigenous belief systems that involve secrecy and ritual. Privacy concerns were paramount, as certain cultural practices are not intended for public viewing. Additionally, removing video clips from their original context can lead to inaccurate knowledge. The study also highlighted risks of prejudice from non-IP users and the potential for exploitation through bioprospecting and patenting.

The researchers concluded that while mobile technology can facilitate the capture of indigenous knowledge, "open access" cannot be applied universally. They proposed a conceptual model that incorporates inhibiting factors—such as belief systems, privacy, context, prejudice, misrepresentation, and legal protocols—into the framework of ICT4D.

This study investigates the potential for using mobile devices and Web 2.0 protocols to document and manage the indigenous knowledge systems (IKS) of rural communities in the Philippines. The research was driven by the premise that mobile technology can empower marginalized groups to become active content providers, thereby increasing their social capital through participatory development. The study addressed how mobile devices can document indigenous knowledge, how Web 2.0 protocols can be integrated into an IKS management system, and how indigenous peoples respond to such technology. The theoretical framework combined social capital, the network effect, and critical mass theory.

The researchers employed a quasi-experimental action research design involving six indigenous communities. Twelve focal persons from the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) and the IP communities participated in capacity building. The technological intervention provided participants with GPRS-enabled Nokia 5230 mobile phones capable of audio-video capture and internet browsing. Training modules on mobile videography and ethnovideography were provided, and a Web Content Management System (WCMS) was developed using PHP and MySQL to serve as a secure repository for rich media.

The findings revealed a significant disconnect between technological potential and social realities. While training successfully provided technical proficiency in mobile videography, the participation rate in content submission was low, with only one-third of participants complying with video submission requests during the testing phase.

Several intervening variables were identified that hindered the implementation of an open-access knowledge system. These included the necessity of honoring indigenous belief systems, which often involve secrecy and ritual regarding knowledge transfer. Privacy concerns were paramount, as certain cultural practices are not intended for public viewing. Additionally, removing video clips from their original context can lead to inaccurate or incomplete knowledge. The study also highlighted risks of prejudice and value judgments from non-IP users, who might misinterpret practices as "backward," as well as the ongoing issues of misrepresentation and the exploitation of indigenous knowledge through bioprospecting and patenting.

In conclusion, while mobile devices and Web 2.0 protocols are technically capable of facilitating the capture and sharing of indigenous knowledge, the concept of "open access" cannot be applied universally to IKS. Indigenous knowledge is often governed by strict protocols and a desire for privacy that conflicts with the open nature of the World Wide Web. The researchers proposed an alternative conceptual model that incorporates inhibiting factors—such as belief systems, privacy, context, prejudice, misrepresentation, and legal protocols—into the framework of ICT4D. Future initiatives must design systems that are culturally sensitive and legally aligned with specific indigenous protocols.

This study investigates the potential for using mobile devices and Web 2.0 protocols to document and manage the indigenous knowledge systems (IKS) of rural communities in the Philippines. The research was driven by the premise that mobile technology can empower marginalized groups to become active content providers, thereby increasing their social capital through participatory development.

The research problem centered on three primary questions: how mobile devices can be used by rural communities to document indigenous knowledge; how Web 2.0 protocols can be integrated into an indigenous knowledge management system; and how indigenous peoples (IPs) respond to the use of mobile technology for this purpose. The study was grounded in a theoretical framework combining social capital, the network effect, and critical mass theory, suggesting that mobile connectivity can create a reinforcing loop of knowledge sharing and community empowerment.

The methodology employed a quasi-experimental action research design, specifically a treatment-then-observation (XO) design. The study involved six indigenous communities across several provinces in the Philippines. Twelve focal persons from the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) and the IP communities were selected for capacity building. The technological intervention included providing participants with GPRS-enabled mobile phones (specifically the Nokia 5230) capable of audio-video capture and internet browsing. The researchers developed training modules on mobile videography and ethnovideography to teach participants how to capture and assemble video clips of local practices. Additionally, a Web Content Management System (WCMS) was designed using open-source software (PHP and MySQL) to serve as a secure repository for the captured rich media.

The findings revealed a significant disconnect between the technological potential of mobile devices and the social realities of indigenous communities. While the training successfully equipped participants with the technical proficiency to use mobile videography, the actual participation rate in content submission was low, with only one-third of participants complying with the video submission request during the testing phase. 

The study identified several critical "intervening variables" that hindered the implementation of an open-access knowledge system. These factors included the necessity of honoring indigenous belief systems, which often involve secrecy and ritual regarding the transfer of knowledge. Privacy concerns were also paramount, as certain cultural practices are not intended for public viewing. Furthermore, the researchers noted that removing video clips from their original context can lead to inaccurate or incomplete knowledge. The study also highlighted the risk of prejudice and value judgments from non-IP users, who might misinterpret indigenous practices as "backward," and the ongoing issue of misrepresentation and the exploitation of indigenous knowledge through bioprospecting and patenting.

In conclusion, while mobile devices and Web 2.0 protocols are technically capable of facilitating the capture and sharing of indigenous knowledge, the concept of "open access" cannot be applied universally to indigenous knowledge systems. The study found that indigenous knowledge is often governed by strict protocols and a desire for privacy, which conflicts with the open nature of the World Wide Web. The researchers proposed an alternative conceptual model that incorporates these inhibiting factors—such as belief systems, privacy, context, prejudice, misrepresentation, and legal protocols—into the framework of ICT4D.

The implications of this research suggest that future ICT4D initiatives must move beyond mere technical provision. Developers and researchers must design systems that are not only user-friendly and affordable but also culturally sensitive and legally aligned with the specific protocols of indigenous groups. The study recommends that further research should utilize critical theory to explore the tension between open-access knowledge commons and the protection of indigenous intellectual property and cultural sanctity.

title: Augmenting Learning Space in Post Graduate Courses in Literature Studies Through ODeL: A Critical Overview of NSOU Learning Praxis
abstract: Literature studies at an advanced level require open space for dialectical deliberations, which alone can provide benchmark quality assurance; but its horizontal expanse must perforce factor the vertical depth of the discipline with specific learning objectives. The analytics of learner responses while conducting Post-Graduate literature programmes fruitfully within the domain of ODL posits blended learning - a conjunction of direct interaction and ODL praxis, as a pre-requisite. This paper is premised on the proven results of an experiment at augmenting learner super structured upon the existing SIM’s and exhaustive Personal Contact Programmes (PCP), by means of basic ODeL, through ICT enabled social networking support services adopted by Netaji Subhas Open University (NSOU).The support is aimed for more than 8,000 learners of Post Graduate English(PGEG) and Post Graduate Bengali(PGBG) courses, enrolled in various Study Centres located far and wide from the University Headquarters. In its search for enhanced learner support services with a view of constructive academic feedback, the School of Humanities experimentally added a module of direct e-interaction between faculty and learners of Post Graduate literature courses through platforms like Facebook and Google chat. This empirical paper shows how the learner has availed this service to resolve their curricular academic issues on weekdays during University working hours. Concerned faculty on their part have, by way of answering queries mainly evolving out of existing study materials provided to learners, been able to dynamically identify areas that require development. This paper carries the authorial conviction that ODeL is best seen as an extension of the classical pedagogy of ODL, wherein a graded system of blended learning can be the panacea to reach out to the heterogeneous learner community.
half:
In "Augmenting Learning Space in Post Graduate Courses in Literature Studies Through ODeL: A Critical Overview of NSOU Learning Praxis," Manan Kumar Mandal examines the implementation of Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) within the School of Humanities at Netaji Subhas Open University (NSOU) in West Bengal, India. The study addresses the challenges of teaching advanced literature through distance education, which requires interactive spaces for dialectical deliberation, and the social skepticism regarding open university degrees.

Using an empirical analysis of NSOU's "blended learning" model, the author evaluates a system that combines traditional Open and Distance Learning (ODL) methods, such as Self-Instructional Materials (SIM) and Personal Contact Programmes (PCP), with ICT-enabled support via social networking platforms like Facebook and Google Chat. Findings indicate that this model significantly enhances learner engagement. SIMs serve as substitutes for face-to-face instruction, while PCPs maintain high attendance rates between 50% and 75%. Notably, virtual interaction via social media increased by approximately 50% between the 2014-15 and 2015-16 academic periods; for example, learners supported through online interaction in the Bengali course rose from approximately 500 to 1,200.

The author concludes that ODeL should extend rather than replace classical ODL pedagogy. By utilizing social media and existing resources to create interactive "learning spaces," open universities can improve academic accountability and provide inclusive higher education to diverse populations.

The article "Augmenting Learning Space in Post Graduate Courses in Literature Studies Through ODeL: A Critical Overview of NSOU Learning Praxis" by Manan Kumar Mandal examines the implementation and effectiveness of Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) within the School of Humanities at Netaji Subhas Open University (NSOU) in West Bengal, India.

The problem addressed by the author is the inherent difficulty of teaching literature at an advanced level through traditional distance education models. Literature studies require dialectical deliberation, interactive space, and the ability to share diverse interpretative arguments to upgrade a learner's self-understanding. Conventional distance learning often lacks this "polemic environment" of learning found in face-to-face classrooms. Furthermore, the author notes a social psyche in West Bengal where degrees from open universities are sometimes viewed with skepticism compared to conventional institutions, necessitating a more robust and interactive pedagogical approach to ensure quality and social acceptance.

The context of the study is the specific socio-educational landscape of West Bengal. The region has a high demand for higher education in humanities, particularly in Bengali and English, due to historical and cultural factors. While internet penetration in India has been growing, access in rural and suburban areas remains a challenge. NSOU, as a state-funded open university, serves a large, heterogeneous learner community, including those in remote areas, who require flexible but high-quality academic support to compete in the job market.

The methodology employed is an empirical analysis of the learning praxis at NSOU. The author uses a quantitative and qualitative approach to evaluate the "blended learning" model adopted by the university. This model combines traditional Open and Distance Learning (ODL) methods—such as Self-Instructional Materials (SIM) and Personal Contact Programmes (PCP)—with modern ICT-enabled support services. The study specifically analyzes learner engagement through online social networking platforms like Facebook and Google Chat to determine how these tools augment the learning space for Post Graduate (PG) students in English and Bengali.

The findings demonstrate that the blended learning model significantly enhances learner support and engagement. The study identifies four major components of the Student Support Service (SSS) at NSOU: printed Self-Instructional Materials (SIM), Personal Contact Programmes (PCP), online support via social networking, and internal assessment through assignments. The SIMs are designed to be lucid and purpose-based, acting as a substitute for a face-to-face teacher by covering reading, conceptual, and analytical needs. The PCPs, held on Sundays at various study centers, show high attendance rates (between 50% and 75%), proving that learners value the opportunity for interactive counseling.

Crucially, the experiment with online e-interaction via Facebook and Google Chat showed substantial success. The data indicates that learner engagement in virtual interactions increased by approximately 50% between the 2014-15 and 2015-16 academic periods. For example, in the Bengali course, the number of learners supported through online interaction rose from approximately 500 to 1,200. This digital intervention allows students to resolve curricular academic issues in real-time during university working hours, bridging the geographical gap between the faculty at the main campus and the learners at distant study centers.

The author concludes that ODeL should be viewed as an extension of classical ODL pedagogy rather than a replacement. A graded system of blended learning—integrating technology-enhanced pedagogy with traditional methods—serves as a "panacea" for reaching a heterogeneous learner community. The study proves that even in environments where digital infrastructure is still developing, a hybrid model can effectively facilitate the complex, non-linear process of studying literature.

The implications of this research suggest that for humanities disciplines, which rely heavily on interpretation and discussion, ODeL must move beyond mere content delivery toward creating interactive "learning spaces." By utilizing existing human resources (such as college teachers for PCP) and accessible social media platforms, open universities can improve academic accountability and build trust within the social psyche. The NSOU model provides a blueprint for how state-funded institutions can use ICT to augment curricula and provide high-quality, inclusive higher education to remote and diverse populations.

title: A Thematic Analysis of UPOU’s Virtual Roundtable Discussions (VRTDs) on the University of the Future
abstract: The impact of the Industrial Revolution 4.0 (IR 4.0) on education has been widely discussed in recent literature. Referred to as Education 4.0, teaching and learning in the future is seen to be largely influenced by advances in technology brought about by IR 4.0. This has prompted the education sector to evaluate the educational system and envision its future. Like most other educational institutions, Philippine higher education institutions (HEIs) are challenged to rethink and retool themselves for the “new normal” and future scenarios. University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) embarked on a participative, reflective, and forward-thinking discussion series through virtual roundtable discussions (VRTD) on the University of the Future (UoF). This study presented the collective thinking of UPOU’s constituencies as captured in the VRTDs conducted from November 2020 to January 2021. A thematic analysis was conducted to surface themes arising from the transcript of five (5) VRTDs on the UoF conducted by UPOU with its faculty, students, staff, and alumni as participants. To contextualize the emerging themes, these were superimposed on the Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) subsystems. The two arising themes were radical transformation and peripheral adjustments. Both refer to the different ways in which the UPOU can transform into a UoF, emanating from the VRTD discussions. An overarching theme of seamlessness was further abstracted. In becoming a UoF, a seamless UPOU is envisioned to be permeable and porous enough to be equal in prestige and purpose with its surroundings.

The research conducted by Ortiguero et al. (2021) explores the conceptualization of the University of the Future (UoF) through the lens of the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). As the Fourth Industrial Revolution (IR 4.0) introduces disruptive technologies like artificial intelligence, big data, and cloud computing, the educational sector faces the necessity of transitioning toward Education 4.0. This new paradigm shifts the focus toward personalized, lifelong learning and requires universities to become more agile to meet the needs of a rapidly changing global landscape.

The problem addressed by the study is the need for higher education institutions (HEIs), particularly those operating in Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL), to rethink and retool their existing systems to remain relevant in a future characterized by technological disruption and socio-political uncertainty. While much of the existing literature focuses on isolated aspects of education, such as pedagogy or structure, there is a lack of holistic research that views the university as an integrated system capable of navigating these shifts.

To address this, the researchers employed a qualitative approach using thematic analysis. The data source consisted of transcripts from five Virtual Roundtable Discussions (VRTDs) conducted between November 2020 and January 2021. These discussions included a diverse group of UPOU constituencies, including faculty, students, staff, and alumni. The researchers used an interpretive and inductive approach to identify patterns within the transcripts. To provide a structured interpretation, the emerging themes were superimposed onto the five established ODeL subsystems: course design, course delivery, instruction, student support, and management.

The findings are organized into sub-themes within the ODeL subsystems and culminate in two primary themes and one overarching theme. Within the course design subsystem, participants emphasized the need for "integrated" curricula that offer choice and customization through menu-type curricula, micro-credentials, and stackable credits. They also advocated for pluridisciplinary and transdisciplinary approaches to create "future-proof" degrees. In the course delivery subsystem, the focus was on the use of emerging technologies (AI and automation) to enable flexible modalities and personalized learning experiences.

The instruction subsystem findings highlighted the need for "innovative functions," such as mentoring and an "unbundled" structure where industry practitioners and academic staff collaborate. This includes a shift toward more open pedagogies and the use of "academic genealogy" to inform future disciplines. The student support subsystem was characterized by a need for responsive, analytics-based support to facilitate personalized learning. The management subsystem, acting as the integrator, was seen as needing a "malleable structure" that is open, collaborative, and capable of providing responsive quality assurance (QA) that is "fit-for-purpose" rather than merely process-oriented.

From these findings, the researchers abstracted two major themes: "Radical Transformation" and "Peripheral Adjustments." Peripheral adjustments refer to the strengthening of existing functions, such as improving digital literacy for staff and enhancing current QA systems. In contrast, radical transformation involves a fundamental overhaul of traditional academic dogmas, such as restructuring faculty tenure to accommodate short-term expert engagements and moving away from rigid, residential-based administrative models. These two paths represent the different scales of change required to achieve the ultimate goal.

The overarching theme identified is "Seamlessness." A seamless UPOU is envisioned as a university that is permeable and porous, meaning it has no rigid boundaries between itself and its environment (industry, society, and other institutions). This seamlessness implies a state of continuity and harmony where knowledge and resources flow effortlessly. It also suggests a need for an agile and resilient system that can respond to unexpected disruptions, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, by being minimally structured and highly adaptive.

The study concludes that for UPOU to become a UoF, it must embrace flexibility, sustainability, and collaboration. The authors recommend that the university begin by assessing its current priorities, policies, and structures to determine the necessary path toward seamlessness. They note that UPOU has already begun this journey through initiatives like the Independent Learning Track and the implementation of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs).

The implications of this research extend beyond UPOU. It provides a roadmap for other educational institutions to conceptualize their own futures. The authors suggest that for any institution to successfully transition to a UoF, its strategic direction must be aligned with its unique mission, contextualized within its specific operating model, and developed through a participative process that engages all stakeholders. Ultimately, the study posits that the university of the future must move away from "privileged seclusion" and instead become a responsive, adaptive system that is deeply integrated with the evolving needs of the global society.

title: Teacher Readiness for Online Teaching: A Critical Review*
abstract: Online teaching is not only a trend but also a must at most of universities and colleges in many countries. The changes from conventional teaching to online teaching requires good preparation for faculty to adapt to the paradigm shift. Although online teaching has been popular in the world over the last two decades, it is new to faculty at universities in Vietnam, typically Ho Chi Minh City Open University (HCMCOU). Within the context of HCMCOU who is about to launch their online programs, it is essential to prepare the readiness for the faculty in online teaching (e-readiness). Conducting a research-based set of content and criteria is an initial step in this process. Hence, this literature review examines the prior empirical and case study research studies about teacher e-readiness including teacher attitudes, teacher training, and technical skills. The findings provide a foundation for HCMCOU in enhancing the preparation quality.
half:
The article "Teacher Readiness for Online Teaching: A Critical Review" examines the challenges higher education institutions face when transitioning from conventional to online teaching models. Focusing on Ho Chi Minh City Open University (HCMCOU) as it prepares to launch online programs, the study addresses a lack of scholarly literature regarding teacher e-readiness within the Vietnamese context. Through a qualitative critical literature review of empirical studies, the authors synthesized several critical factors into a conceptual framework consisting of five elements: attitudes, technology competency, pedagogy, training, and time constraints.

The findings indicate that while teachers generally hold positive perceptions of e-learning, institutional pressures can cause resistance. Technology competency, specifically familiarity with ICT tools and learning management systems, is vital to readiness. Furthermore, successful online teaching requires a pedagogical shift from teacher-centered models to student-centered approaches. While training is necessary, many existing programs focus too heavily on basic ICT skills and fail to address the pedagogical aspects of online instruction. Additionally, time constraints act as an impediment as faculty struggle to balance course development with existing workloads.

The authors conclude that teacher e-readiness is a multi-dimensional construct requiring psychological, technical, and pedagogical readiness. For institutions like HCMCOU, administrators should implement strategic plans that assess faculty attitudes and skill levels and provide professional development that includes specialized pedagogical training for online environments.
