Specifically, the study focuses on Ho Chi Minh City Open University (HCMCOU), which is preparing to launch online programs using an instructor-led model. The authors identify a significant problem: while many academic leaders view online education as a strategic necessity, there is often a gap between institutional goals and faculty acceptance. At HCMCOU, the transition requires more than just technological infrastructure; it requires the readiness of faculty members, who must adapt to a new paradigm that demands expertise in content, technology, and online pedagogy.

The search spanned the period from 2002 to 2017. Although the initial search yielded 41 relevant articles, the authors applied strict selection criteria, ultimately focusing on seven empirical studies that specifically addressed teacher e-readiness rather than institutional readiness.

The findings of the literature review identify several critical factors that influence teacher e-readiness. Success in transitioning to online education depends on addressing the psychological, technical, and pedagogical readiness of the faculty. title: New Media Usage and Its Perceived Effects on Classroom Communication and Learning Behavior
abstract: The study delves on how new media tools have impacted classroom communication and learning behavior. Conducted at the Assumption College among college students and professors, the study showed that there is no relationship between new media tools usage with learning behaviors of self-efficacy and motivation. However, it was found that there’s a strong relation between technological competence and motivation and self- efficacy. Further, it was also shown that the ubiquity of technology has not been fully utilized in classroom communication.
half:
In the study "New Media Usage and Its Perceived Effects on Classroom Communication and Learning Behavior," Patricia Ann E. Vera examines the gap between technologically familiar students and professors who often rely on traditional instructional methods. Conducted at Assumption College in the Philippines with 97 students and 22 professors, the quantitative research utilized structured questionnaires to measure the frequency of use for 13 new media tools and their relationship to student learning behaviors, including technological competence, self-efficacy, and motivation.

Findings indicate that students most frequently use mobile devices, social networking sites, and video-sharing sites, while QR codes and mashups are the least utilized. A perceptual discrepancy exists: students believe professors do not use new media tools as frequently as necessary, while professors perceive students to be highly active on mobile and social platforms. While students reported high levels of technological competence, motivation, and self-efficacy, the study found no direct relationship between new media usage and student self-efficacy or motivation. However, a strong positive correlation was found between technological competence and self-efficacy, and a moderate correlation was found between motivation and self-efficacy.

The study concludes that technology adoption remains superficial, often used for entertainment rather than deep academic engagement. To bridge the communication gap, the research recommends that institutions provide targeted instructional technology training and invest in both infrastructure and the redesign of pedagogical skill sets.

In the study "New Media Usage and Its Perceived Effects on Classroom Communication and Learning Behavior," Patricia Ann E. Vera examines the intersection of technological advancement and educational practice. The research addresses the gap between "digital native" students, who possess high technological familiarity, and professors who often rely on traditional, verbal-heavy instructional methods. The study seeks to understand the usage levels of new media tools, their relationship to student learning behaviors—specifically technological competence, self-efficacy, and motivation—and the readiness of professors to integrate these tools into their teaching.

Conducted at Assumption College in the Philippines, the research utilized a quantitative design with a sample of 97 students and 22 professors. Data were collected via structured questionnaires measuring the frequency of use for 13 new media tools, perceptions of technology use, and learning behaviors. Analysis was performed using frequency tests and Pearson’s r correlation coefficient.

The findings reveal that students most frequently use mobile devices, social networking sites, and video-sharing sites, while QR codes and mashups are the least utilized. A discrepancy exists in perception: students believe professors do not use new media tools as efficiently or frequently as necessary, while professors perceive students to be highly active on mobile and social networking platforms. Regarding learning behavior, students reported high levels of technological competence, motivation, and self-efficacy. The study found no direct relationship between the usage of new media tools and student self-efficacy or motivation. However, a strong positive correlation was found between technological competence and self-efficacy, and a moderate correlation was found between motivation and self-efficacy. This suggests that being technologically competent is closely linked to a student's sense of efficacy, even if media usage itself does not inherently boost motivation.

Among faculty, openness to training varied by experience. Professors with more than six years of experience expressed higher interest in training for online collaboration, mobile usage, blogs, and video sharing, while younger professors preferred training in webinars and online collaboration.

The study concludes that technology has not yet been fully integrated into classroom communication to maximize meaningful learning. Adoption remains "superficial," with tools often used for entertainment rather than deep academic engagement. The research suggests that the mere presence of gadgets does not guarantee improved outcomes; benefits are realized only when technology fosters active, constructivist learning environments. To bridge the communication gap and prepare students for a globalized economy, the study recommends that institutions provide targeted instructional technology training and invest in both infrastructure and the redesign of pedagogical skill sets.

The study titled "New Media Usage and Its Perceived Effects on Classroom Communication and Learning Behavior" by Patricia Ann E. Vera explores the intersection of technological advancement and educational practice. The research addresses the growing challenge faced by educators as "digital natives" (Generation Z) enter classrooms with high levels of technological familiarity, while many professors continue to rely on traditional, verbal-heavy instructional methods. The central problem identified is a potential gap in classroom communication and learning effectiveness caused by the differing levels of technological adoption and competence between students and teachers. Specifically, the researcher seeks to understand the usage levels of new media tools, how these tools relate to student learning behaviors—defined as technological competence, self-efficacy, and motivation—and the perceived readiness of professors to integrate these tools into their teaching.

The research was conducted at Assumption College in the Philippines, utilizing a convenience sample of 97 students and 22 professors from various academic departments. The study employed a quantitative research design using two sets of structured questionnaires. The student questionnaire measured the frequency of use for 13 different new media tools (such as mobile devices, social networks, and video sharing sites), students' perceptions of their professors' technology use, and their own learning behaviors through a self-constructed scale based on learner empowerment. The professor questionnaire measured their own usage levels, their perceptions of student technology use, and their openness to receiving training in new media tools. Data analysis was performed using frequency tests and Pearson’s r correlation coefficient to determine relationships between variables.

The findings reveal several key insights into the current state of technology in the classroom. Among students, the most frequently used tools are mobile devices, social networking sites, and video-sharing sites, while QR codes and mashups are the least utilized. There is a notable discrepancy in perception: students feel their professors do not use new media tools as efficiently or as frequently as they should, whereas professors perceive students to be highly active on mobile and social networking platforms. Regarding learning behavior, students reported high levels of technological competence, motivation, and self-efficacy. Crucially, the study found no direct relationship between the usage of new media tools and the dimensions of student learning behavior, specifically self-efficacy and motivation. However, a strong positive correlation was found between technological competence and self-efficacy, as well as a moderate correlation between motivation and self-efficacy. This suggests that while using new media does not inherently boost motivation or efficacy, being technologically competent is closely linked to a student's sense of efficacy.

Regarding faculty, the study found that professors' openness to training varies by their years of experience. Professors with more than six years of teaching experience expressed a higher interest in training for online collaboration, mobile usage, blogs, and video sharing. Conversely, younger professors (those with less than six years of experience) showed a preference for training in more sophisticated tools like webinars and online collaboration.

The study concludes that while technology is ubiquitous, it has not yet been fully integrated into classroom communication to maximize meaningful learning. The research suggests that the mere presence of technological gadgets does not guarantee improved learning outcomes; rather, the benefits are realized when technology is used to foster active, constructivist learning environments. The findings highlight a "superficial" adoption of technology, where tools are often used for entertainment or socialization rather than deep academic engagement. Furthermore, the perceived gap between student and teacher technology use may contribute to communication barriers, as professors may feel intimidated by the digital fluency of their students.

The implications of this research are significant for educators, policymakers, and the broader educational system. For professors, the study emphasizes the importance of developing 21st-century technological competence to remain relevant and to bridge the communication gap with students. For educational institutions, the findings suggest a need for targeted, specialized training for faculty—specifically focusing on instructional technology—to move beyond traditional lecture-based models. The study also highlights the necessity of investing in both "hardware" (infrastructure and connectivity) and "software" (the redesign of pedagogical skill sets and instructional materials). Ultimately, the researcher suggests that to prevent a widening digital divide and to prepare students for a globalized economy, the educational system must move toward a "new culture" of teaching that embraces new media as a tool for meaningful, active, and collaborative learning.

The study titled "Simulation-Based Instructional Materials on Central Dogma of Molecular Biology" by Cano, Olvis, Disca, and Docena addresses the inherent difficulties in teaching complex, abstract biological processes. The central problem identified is that the Central Dogma of Molecular Biology—the process by which DNA information is used to produce functional proteins—is notoriously difficult for secondary learners to visualize and understand. Because these mechanisms occur at a molecular level and are not available for direct observation, they are frequently cited as being among the least mastered topics in genetics. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic necessitated a shift toward technology-based instructional modalities, creating a need for effective digital tools to mitigate educational constraints and address the downward trends in scientific literacy observed in standardized assessments.

The researchers sought to examine the effectiveness of simulation-based instructional materials on the learning performance of Grade 12 STEM learners. Specifically, the study aimed to determine the mastery levels of students in three key areas—DNA replication, transcription, and translation—before and after the intervention, to identify if significant differences existed between pretest and posttest scores, and to explore student attitudes toward the use of these simulations.

To address these objectives, the researchers employed a mixed-method research design. The quantitative phase utilized a one-group pretest-posttest design, where a single sample of Grade 12 STEM students from Notre Dame of Marbel University was assessed before and after the intervention. The qualitative phase involved semi-structured interviews to capture the learners' attitudes. The researchers developed session plans validated by experts in content, technical, and instructional quality. The instructional materials integrated several existing digital tools, including LabXchange® simulations, PhET® Gene Expression simulations, DNA Interactive simulations from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, and Holt’s Central Dogma simulations. Data were analyzed using mean and percentage for mastery levels, paired-samples t-tests for significant differences, and thematic content analysis for the qualitative interview data.

The findings revealed a significant improvement in student performance. In the pretest, learners were generally "approaching proficiency," with a mean score of 57.55%. Specifically, they were proficient in DNA replication but only approaching proficiency in transcription and translation. Following the implementation of the simulation-based instructional materials, the posttest results showed a significant increase in mastery, with the overall mean score rising to 83.59%, placing the learners in the "advanced" category. The paired-samples t-test confirmed that the increases in scores for DNA replication, transcription, and translation were all statistically significant (p < 0.05).

Qualitatively, the thematic content analysis revealed that the learners were "Engaged in Experiential Learning." The students reported that the simulations allowed them to move beyond mere imagination to a state of "experiencing" the biological processes. They emphasized that the visual and interactive nature of the tools helped them better understand complex concepts and provided a clear view of how processes occur. Additionally, the simulations encouraged evaluative thinking, as students noted they could observe the consequences of their actions and reflect on their errors within the virtual environment.

The study concludes that simulation-based instructional materials are highly effective in teaching the Central Dogma of Molecular Biology. The transition from "approaching proficiency" to "advanced mastery" suggests that these tools successfully bridge the gap between abstract theory and conceptual understanding. The researchers conclude that the simulations provide a safe, interactive, and visual environment that facilitates the experiential learning necessary to grasp molecular-level mechanisms.

title: Talk to Them not at Them: A Teacher-Initiated Model of Engagement (TIME) in Online Learning
abstract: This paper proposes that limited teacher-student interaction in large online classes can lead to a higher attrition rate. TIME as an e-learning pedagogy can avert the situation. TIME is a cyber classroom management style comprising of student engagement techniques used to address attrition and ensure quality education. This model has been found to increase student participation in a research class in the Master of Development Communication program of the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). Guided by the Theory of Interaction and Communication (Holmberg 1995), the study employed a quasi-experimental research design. From February to May 2018, submission bins were carefully tracked. A spreadsheet was prepared to document students’ submissions in the portal to include the date submitted to find out if TIME can decrease the attrition rate. The “treatments” include output affirmation; active “listening” to questions raised; quick responses to queries; student alerts or notifications; providing direct instructions on what needs to be done instead of leaving responses to chance; providing transitions to encourage continuous conversation by posting questions that will require further thinking, action, and revert; conducive learning environment; and, coaching and mentoring. Results were compared with the performance of students enrolled in the same subject from previous years, where TIME was not employed. Indeed, a difference was observed in terms of completion rates. Hence, it can be concluded that a responsive teacher encourages students to complete their tasks thus decreasing attrition rates in online learning. As independent learners, students can experience cognitive dissonance as a result of teachers’ delayed responses to their questions. Teachers, on the other hand, have to beat time to meet expectations. However, with MOODLE on mobile, a simple “I’ll get back to you shortly” is consolation enough for students to know that they are being attended to, which could lengthen their patience. A volatile learning environment where the teacher is separated from the learner could be compensated by a click of a button with a smiley at the end of the phrase to say, “I’m here to lend an ear.”

This issue is particularly significant for part-time and external students balancing various responsibilities. To combat this, the author proposed the Teacher-Initiated Model of Engagement (TIME), grounded in Holmberg’s Theory of Interaction and Communication. The model emphasizes "guided didactic conversation" through eight techniques, including output affirmation, active listening, quick responses, deadline alerts, clear instructions, the use of emoticons to encourage conversation, maintaining a conducive ICT environment, and providing coaching via online meeting platforms.

Using a quasi-experimental design, the study tracked submission bins in the MOODLE Learning Management System for a course at the University of the Philippines Open University. Results were compared against student performance from the previous three academic years when the TIME model was not used. Findings indicate that implementing TIME significantly improved completion rates. For the first assignment, completion rose from less than 10% to 88.24%. While subsequent assignments showed varying rates, the overall course completion rate was 60%, whereas it would have been only 38% without TIME interventions and flexible deadlines. The study concludes that responsive teachers who "talk to" students through a personal tone and timely feedback can mitigate isolation and improve student retention.

This is particularly problematic for part-time and external students who must balance academic requirements with professional and personal responsibilities.

The study focused on the Master of Development Communication (MDC) program at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU), specifically the DEVC 204 course during the second semester of the 2017-2018 academic year. To combat attrition, the author proposed the Teacher-Initiated Model of Engagement (TIME). Grounded in Holmberg’s (1995) Theory of Interaction and Communication, the model emphasizes "guided didactic conversation" to foster feelings of belonging and cooperation. The TIME model utilizes eight techniques: output affirmation, active listening to questions, providing quick responses to queries, sending deadline alerts, providing clear instructions, using transitions like emoticons to encourage conversation, maintaining a conducive ICT environment, and providing coaching through online meeting platforms.

The results were compared against student performance in the same subject during the previous three academic years (2014-2017) when the TIME model was not used.

The author notes that without TIME interventions and flexible deadlines, the completion rate would have been only 38%. The data suggests that constant interaction, such as answering inquiries and sending reminders, helped decrease attrition.

By "talking to" students rather than "at" them through a friendly, personal tone and timely feedback, teachers can mitigate the isolation of distance education and build a "screen relationship." The article "Talk to Them not at Them: A Teacher-Initiated Model of Engagement (TIME) in Online Learning" addresses the critical problem of high attrition rates in online education. The author posits that limited teacher-student interaction in large online classes can lead to student disengagement and subsequent dropout. This issue is particularly acute for part-time and external students who must balance academic requirements with professional and personal responsibilities. The study identifies that while online learners are often viewed as fully autonomous, the physical separation and the "volatile" nature of the digital learning environment can lead to feelings of isolation and cognitive dissonance, especially when teacher responses are delayed.

The context for this research is the Master of Development Communication (MDC) program at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). The specific subject studied was DEVC 204 (Communication Research and Evaluation), a course where students must master complex research skills. The students in this program are online learners studying on a part-time basis, making them susceptible to the attrition factors mentioned previously. The study was conducted during the second semester of the 2017-2018 academic year.

To address these challenges, the author proposes the Teacher-Initiated Model of Engagement (TIME), a cyber classroom management style designed to increase student participation and completion rates. The theoretical framework for this model is Holmberg’s (1995) Theory of Interaction and Communication, also known as "guided didactic conversation." This theory suggests that teaching effectiveness is linked to the feelings of belonging and cooperation fostered through mediated communication, including the exchange of questions, answers, and arguments.

The TIME model consists of eight specific student engagement techniques: output affirmation (providing positive and constructive comments), active "listening" to questions, providing quick responses to queries (even if only to acknowledge receipt), sending student alerts or notifications regarding deadlines, providing direct and clear instructions to reduce uncertainty, using transitions (such as follow-up questions or emoticons) to encourage continuous conversation, maintaining a conducive learning environment through ICTs, and providing coaching and mentoring through online meeting platforms.

The researcher employed a quasi-experimental research design to test the effectiveness of the TIME model. The study tracked submission bins in the MOODLE Learning Management System (LMS) from February to May 2018. The researcher used a spreadsheet to document the dates of student submissions to determine if the TIME interventions influenced the completion rate. The results from the 2017-2018 semester were compared against the performance of students enrolled in the same subject during the previous three academic years (2014-2015, 2015-2016, and 2016-2017), during which the TIME model was not employed.

The findings indicate that the implementation of TIME significantly improved student completion rates. For the first assignment (TMA1), the completion rate increased from less than 10% on the indicative due date to 88.24% by the final deadline, a change attributed to output affirmation and reminders. While subsequent assignments showed varying completion rates—ranging from approximately 61% to 67%—the overall completion rate for the course was 60%. The author notes that without the TIME interventions and the flexibility of extended deadlines, the completion rate would have been a much lower 38%. The data suggests that constant interaction, such as answering inquiries and sending reminders, helped decrease the attrition rate.

The study concludes that a responsive teacher is essential for encouraging students to complete their tasks in an online setting. The author emphasizes that while online learners are independent, they still require a sense of connectivity and support. The TIME model demonstrates that by "talking to" students rather than "at" them—using a friendly, personal tone and providing timely feedback—teachers can mitigate the isolation of distance education. The research suggests that digital communication tools, such as emoticons and quick mobile responses, can compensate for the lack of physical presence and build a "screen relationship" based on mutual respect.

The implications of this research suggest a necessary paradigm shift for online educators. Rather than acting solely as distant authorities, teachers should adopt a more engaging, accommodating, and proactive role. The study implies that the use of ICTs should be leveraged not just for content delivery, but for fostering a sense of community and continuous dialogue. For educational institutions, the findings suggest that investing in teacher-led engagement strategies and providing flexible submission windows can be vital tools for improving student retention and ensuring the successful completion of online degree programs.

title: Creating Virtual Corridors: Social Network Discovery and Landscape Patch Connectivity of Permaculture Projects and Initiatives on Facebook
abstract: Permaculture is a design system conceptualized in Australia in the 1970s in response to urgent environmental issues at that time. Mainstreamed via social media in recent years, permaculture is being practiced around the world on diverse landscapes. The study aimed to discover socio-spatial permaculture landscape networks based on a permaculture designer’s Facebook social network. Using social network theory and landscape ecology, the study simulated and predicted how permaculture designers would be able to create invisible landscape corridors called “virtual corridors.” Virtual corridors are determined by computing for the Percentage Linkage Strength (%LS) metric derived from data obtained from two scoring systems developed for the study: the Social Score (SS) and the Permaculture Score (PS). Two hundred eighty six network nodes were initially discovered to be potential permaculture designers via Facebook Group membership. The two scoring systems revealed the top ten network nodes with the highest computed %LS that created virtual corridors. A Meerkat Lite-generated sociogram overlayed on a Google Earth topographic map animated in Camtasia Studio were used to illustrate the discovered network. Then NetLogo was used to simulate and predict the virtual corridor creation process. In the future, the methodology could be used to determine potential study sites for transdisciplinary permaculture research and study the environmental impact of permaculture projects and initiatives on landscape patches. It would also provide practitioners and researchers a framework to better understand how a network of individual solutions could lead to macro-scale landscape patch management.

The study "Creating Virtual Corridors: Social Network Discovery and Landscape Patch Connectivity of Permaculture Projects and Initiatives on Facebook" examines the connection between social media discourse and real-world ecological impacts. The researchers introduce the concept of "virtual corridors" to describe intangible digital links that facilitate the movement of permaculture knowledge, technology, and energy between individuals. This research suggests that social relationships in digital spaces can act as precursors to physical landscape management.

Focusing on the Philippines, the researchers identified potential network nodes by analyzing Facebook friends of a focal node. From 1,267 friends, 286 were identified as potential practitioners based on their membership in eighteen Facebook groups related to agriculture and food. To measure connection strength, the researchers developed a Percentage Linkage Strength (%LS) metric, combining a Social Score based on online interactions with a Permaculture Score accounting for offline activities like formal training and projects.

The findings revealed that 14 nodes met the criteria for "virtual corridors," with ten respondents identified as highly significant virtual corridors possessing a %LS of 90% or higher. These top ten individuals, including organic farmers and urban gardeners, were characterized by high online activity and tangible offline commitment. NetLogo simulations predicted that the spread of permaculture information would increase significantly over a two-year period. The researchers concluded that online social networks serve as a functional equivalent to spatial networks, connecting individual landscape patches through shared values and practices.

The study "Creating Virtual Corridors: Social Network Discovery and Landscape Patch Connectivity of Permaculture Projects and Initiatives on Facebook" addresses the disconnect between the rising popularity of permaculture on social media and the lack of scientific research regarding its real-world ecological impacts. While permaculture is a design system used to manage small-to-large scale landscapes for sustainability, its dissemination often occurs through "feral ecology"—discourse happening outside traditional academic circles via digital platforms. The researchers sought to understand how online social interactions on Facebook might translate into physical landscape connectivity, proposing the concept of "virtual corridors" to describe the intangible links that facilitate the movement of permaculture knowledge, technology, and energy between individuals.

The research context is rooted in the intersection of social network theory and landscape ecology. The authors argue that social systems and ecological systems are co-evolving; therefore, the social relationships formed in digital spaces can be viewed as precursors to physical landscape management. The study specifically focuses on the Philippines, where permaculture practices remain largely undocumented by scientific research despite their potential impact on food security and landscape heterogeneity.

To investigate this, the researchers employed a multi-stage methodology. They first identified potential network nodes by analyzing the Facebook friends of a focal node (a researcher who is a permaculture designer). From a pool of 1,267 friends, 286 were identified as potential permaculture practitioners based on their membership in eighteen specific Facebook groups related to agriculture and food. To measure the strength of the connection between the focal node and these respondents, the researchers developed a unique metric called Percentage Linkage Strength (%LS). This metric is composed of two scoring systems: the Social Score (SS), which accounts for online interactions such as social distance (based on common group memberships), "likes," and "comments," and the Permaculture Score (PS), which accounts for offline activities like actual permaculture projects and formal training.

The study utilized several computational tools to analyze the data. Meerkat Lite was used to construct sociograms to visualize the social linkages (dyads and triads) within the network. Google Earth and Camtasia Studio were used to create GIS animations that mapped the geographic distribution of nodes and their chronological appearance on a topographic map. Finally, NetLogo was used to run a "rumor mill" simulation to predict how permaculture information might spread through the network over time.

The findings revealed that out of the 286 potential nodes, 14 met the criteria to be classified as "virtual corridors" (requiring an SS of at least 30 and a %LS of at least 75%). Among these, ten respondents were identified as highly significant virtual corridors, possessing a %LS of 90% or higher. These top ten individuals were a diverse group, including young organic farmers, urban gardeners, entrepreneurs, and students. The data showed that these high-performing nodes were characterized by high levels of online activity (averaging 280 likes and 43 comments per month) and tangible offline commitment, as all ten had both a permaculture project and formal training. The sociogram analysis showed a network density of 0.118, while the NetLogo simulation predicted that the spread of permaculture "rumors" (information) would increase significantly over a two-year period, particularly when considering 4-neighborhood and 8-neighborhood connectivity.

The researchers concluded that online social networks serve as a functional equivalent to spatial networks for permaculture practitioners. While the sample size is small, the study demonstrates that "virtual corridors" can exist as invisible linkages that connect individual landscape patches through shared values and practices. The study suggests that the social connectivity found on Facebook can theoretically translate into physical landscape connectivity, as these digital ties represent a network of sites that consciously transform landscapes.

The implications of this research are two-fold, affecting both social and ecological perspectives. Socially, the study identifies that virtual corridors are dependent on the online activity and real-world experience of a focal node, and that these nodes can act as powerful channels for information dissemination. Ecologically, the discovery of these corridors suggests that socio-spatial homophily—the tendency of similar people to connect—can lead to the creation of "energy zones" where permaculture practices like organic agriculture and microclimate creation are concentrated. Ultimately, the authors suggest that this methodology could be used to identify potential sites for transdisciplinary research and to study the macro-scale environmental impacts of individual permaculture initiatives on the broader landscape.

title: Reflection on Learner Support Services and Scope of Web-based Services under Distance Education: A Case Study
abstract: Quality learner support system (LSS) is one of the important components for successful completion of an educational programme under the open and distance learning (ODL) system. The use of Web-based technologies is encouraged to supplement LSS as it provides an important link between the teachers and students for knowledge and skills transfer and enhances interaction between teachers and learners and amongst learners themselves. This paper examined the types and extent of learner support services used by learners of a distance education programme along with difficulties encountered by the learners in completion of the programme. Awareness about the Web-based learner support services and perception on the utility of the Web-based LSS were included in the paper. The paper presented the opinion of the learners about requisite Web-based learner support services and their willingness to pay (WTP) for such support system under the ODL system. The study was conducted using an online survey method. The data were collected from the learners of the Post Graduate Diploma in Food Safety and Quality Management (PGDFSQM) programme which is being offered by the School of Agriculture, Indira Gandhi National Open University, New Delhi, India. The study revealed that LSS helped in successful completion of the programme under the ODL system. Further, those learners who used the Web-based support services were more successful in completing their studies. The study found that considerations for laptops and smart mobile phones should be made in the design of the Web-based support system since most of the learners had access to these devices. The expenditure on development of Web-based LSS could be met by charging the learners additional fees. The Web-based LSS, as suggested by the learners, has potential to resolve the constraints in completion of the programme under the ODL.
half:
The article "Reflection on Learner Support Services and Scope of Web-based Services under Distance Education: A Case Study" examines the role of Learner Support Services (LSS) in the success of Open and Distance Learning (ODL) programs. Focusing on the Post Graduate Diploma in Food Safety and Quality Management at Indira Gandhi National Open University, the study surveyed 112 learners to analyze demographic profiles, service usage, and awareness of web-based services.

Findings indicate that LSS is vital for program completion. Successful learners utilized support services at a higher rate (72.97%) than those who did not complete the program (62.69%). Common services included assignment submission and study material availability, peer interaction, and assignment feedback, while 71.67% of learners attended face-to-face counseling for content clarification and motivation.

Regarding digital services, 57% of learners were aware of web-based LSS, and 56.67% of those aware utilized them. Perceptions were positive, with 89.80% believing these services aid timely completion and 94% finding online materials helpful. Most learners used smartphones, laptops, or desktops, with laptops being the most preferred device. Furthermore, 49% of learners expressed a willingness to pay an additional fee, averaging approximately 29.32%, for enhanced web-based LSS. The authors recommend an integrated model combining conventional approaches with digital tools like virtual classes and smartphone-compatible applications.

Learners who utilized support services showed higher success rates, with 72.97% of successful learners using LSS compared to 62.69% of those who did not complete the program. Common services included assignment submission and study material availability (82%), peer interaction (66.67%), and assignment feedback (54.35%). Face-to-face counseling was also a core component, attended by 71.67% of learners to clarify content and gain motivation.

Regarding digital services, 57% of learners were aware of available web-based LSS, and 56.67% of those aware utilized them. Perceptions were overwhelmingly positive: 89.80% believed these services aid timely completion, and 94% found online materials helpful. Key benefits included 24/7 availability, flexibility, and ease of content updates. In terms of hardware, most learners possessed smartphones (89.19%), laptops (83.75%), and desktops (65.71%), with laptops being the most preferred device (72%). Additionally, 49% of learners expressed a willingness to pay an additional fee for enhanced web-based LSS, with an average additional cost of approximately 29.32%.

The authors conclude that web-based technologies offer significant potential to resolve constraints in program completion. They recommend that ODL institutions move toward an integrated model combining conventional study center approaches with advanced digital tools. Suggested features include online project management, virtual classes, digital repositories for audio-video content, online examinations, 24/7 query management, and smartphone-compatible applications. The study suggests that institutions can potentially offset the costs of developing these mobile-friendly and laptop-optimized platforms through the additional fees learners are willing to pay.
two:
The article "Reflection on Learner Support Services and Scope of Web-based Services under Distance Education: A Case Study" examines the critical role of Learner Support Services (LSS) in the success of Open and Distance Learning (ODL) programs. The authors investigate how web-based technologies can supplement traditional support structures to enhance interaction and facilitate knowledge transfer between teachers and learners.

The problem addressed by the researchers is the inherent challenge of distance education, where learners are often geographically dispersed and lack physical interaction with instructors. In ODL systems, learners rely heavily on self-learning materials, occasional face-to-face counseling, and assignment feedback for motivation and guidance. The study seeks to understand the types and extent of LSS currently used by learners, the difficulties they face in completing programs, their awareness of web-based services, and their willingness to pay for enhanced digital support.

The context of the study is the Post Graduate Diploma in Food Safety and Quality Management (PGDFSQM) program offered by the School of Agriculture at Indira Gandhi National Open University (IGNOU) in India. The learners in this program are primarily professional adults, with 88% being employed and an average work experience of approximately seven years. This demographic necessitates flexible support systems that can accommodate professional workloads.

The researchers employed an online survey method using a structured questionnaire administered via Qualtrics. The survey targeted 550 learners of the PGDFSQM program, resulting in 112 analyzed responses. The questionnaire covered demographic profiles, program completion status, types of LSS used, awareness of web-based platforms, digital device usage, and willingness to pay (WTP) for additional web-based services.

The findings reveal that LSS is vital for successful program completion. Learners who utilized support services were more successful than those who did not. Specifically, 72.97% of successful learners used LSS, compared to 62.69% of those who did not complete the program. Among those using LSS, the most common services included assignment submission and the availability of study materials (82%), followed by peer interaction (66.67%) and assignment feedback (54.35%). Face-to-face counseling was a core component, attended by 71.67% of learners, primarily to clarify subject content and provide motivation.

Regarding web-based services, 57% of learners were aware of the available web-based LSS, and of those aware, 56.67% utilized it. The perception of web-based LSS was overwhelmingly positive; 89.80% of learners believed these services help in timely and successful program completion, and 94% found online learning materials helpful. Key benefits identified by learners included the 24/7 availability of materials, flexibility, and the ease of updating online content.

The study also analyzed the digital landscape of the learners. Most learners possessed smart mobile phones (89.19%), laptops (83.75%), and desktop computers (65.71%). Laptops were the most preferred device (72%), followed by smartphones (56%) and desktops (52%). This indicates that any future web-based LSS must be optimized for laptop and smartphone interfaces to meet learner needs. Finally, the study found that 49% of learners were willing to pay an additional fee for enhanced web-based LSS, with an average additional cost of approximately 29.32%.

The authors conclude that LSS is essential for ODL success and that web-based technologies offer significant potential to resolve constraints in program completion. They suggest that ODL institutions should move toward an integrated model that combines conventional study center approaches with advanced web-based technologies. The findings suggest that web-based services should include features such as online project management tools, virtual classes, digital repositories for audio-video content (like podcasting), online examinations, 24/7 query management systems, and smartphone-compatible applications.

The implications of this research suggest that ODL institutions should prioritize the development of mobile-friendly and laptop-optimized digital platforms. Since learners are willing to pay for improved services, institutions can potentially offset the development costs of these technologies through additional fees. Ultimately, integrating robust web-based support can bridge the gap between teachers and learners, providing the flexibility and interaction necessary for professional learners to succeed in distance education.

title: Augmented Reality in Nursing Education: Addressing the Limitations of Developing a Learning Material for Nurses in the Philippines and Thailand
abstract: The application of Augmented Reality (AR) in nursing education is relatively new. When used as a learning tool, AR provides new digital media that result in teaching and learning enhancement. However, there seems to be a gap in the development and use of AR tools between the learners in the developed world and those who are in the developing world. Most, if not all, of the existing AR initiatives in nursing originated from economically and financially advanced countries. There is a limited number of researches and case studies done in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) where a majority of the countries are developing. For this reason, this exploratory study aims to provide a proof of concept for budget constrained and technologically challenged implementers from developing countries such as the Philippines and Thailand. An appropriate AR tool was chosen among the reviewed authoring tools. Utilizing the selected tool, a learning material prototype on English nursing communication was developed to aid nurses in potentially improving their English competency. The prototype, a talking comic strip that consists of a clinical scenario, was well-received. A majority of the respondents agreed that the AR-enhanced material was better than the printed material alone and that it enhanced their learning experience. It was also found to be usable, receiving a system usability score of 68.5937, which is higher than the mean global score of 68.
half:
The application of Augmented Reality (AR) in nursing education offers significant potential for interactive learning, yet a gap exists between development in wealthy nations and implementation in developing regions like the ASEAN area. In countries such as the Philippines and Thailand, budget constraints hinder the adoption of high-tech medical simulations. This exploratory study sought to address this by reviewing existing AR initiatives, identifying affordable development tools, and creating an AR prototype containing Open Educational Resources (OER) for English nursing communication.

The researchers developed a "talking comic strip" prototype using CraftAR, a tool selected for its free license and drag-and-drop interface suitable for non-programmers. The prototype integrated nursing-written scripts, illustrated comic strips, and recorded audio. Evaluation via a usability survey yielded an average System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 68.5937, which exceeds the global mean of 68, indicating relative usability. Students responded favorably, providing high average ratings for the material being better than printed media alone, the enhancement of their learning experience, and the recommendation of the material to training institutions.

The study concludes that AR is accessible to budget-constrained implementers in developing ASEAN countries through free, user-friendly tools. The research suggests that the digital divide in nursing education can be bridged using OER and accessible authoring tools. Future studies should evaluate new AR tools and focus on improving usability, sustainability, and accessibility.

two:
The application of Augmented Reality (AR) in nursing education presents a significant opportunity to enhance teaching and learning through interactive digital media. However, a notable gap exists between the development of AR tools in economically advanced nations and their implementation in developing regions. Most existing AR initiatives in nursing originate from wealthy countries, leaving a scarcity of research and case studies within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). This lack of localized resources is particularly problematic given the ASEAN Mutual Recognition Arrangement (MRA) on Nursing Services, which aims to facilitate the mobility of nursing professionals across member states. To participate effectively in this integrated market, nurses must achieve competency in English, the official working language of ASEAN.

The problem addressed by this study is the difficulty faced by budget-constrained and technologically challenged implementers in developing countries, such as the Philippines and Thailand, when attempting to adopt advanced educational technologies like AR. There is a clear need for a proof of concept that demonstrates how AR can be utilized effectively without the massive financial investments typically associated with high-tech medical simulations.

To address this, the researchers conducted an exploratory study with several specific objectives: to review existing AR initiatives in nursing, to identify affordable AR development tools, to develop an AR prototype containing Open Educational Resources (OER) for English nursing communication, and to evaluate the perceptions of Filipino and Thai nursing students regarding the prototype.

The methodology followed a structured approach beginning with a general literature review of published materials regarding AR in nursing services and education. Following the review, the researchers moved into the prototype development phase. They created a "talking comic strip" designed to aid English language learning. The process involved a nursing professional writing a script focused on basic patient care, an artist drawing the comic strip, and voice actors recording the audio. The researchers then used a selected AR tool to integrate the physical comic strip with the digital audio. Finally, the prototype was evaluated using a usability survey. This evaluation included the System Usability Scale (SUS) to measure effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction, as well as additional survey items to gauge student perceptions of the material's value compared to traditional printed media.

In the selection of technology, the researchers compared three cloud-based AR tools: Wikitude, Vuforia, and CraftAR. The selection criteria included the availability of a free license, the ease of content creation for both programmers and non-programmers, and the tool's widespread use. While Wikitude was noted for its popularity, it was less preferred due to a distracting watermark on free content. Vuforia was recognized for its widespread use but required programming knowledge via an SDK. Ultimately, CraftAR was selected because it offered a free license, a drag-and-drop interface suitable for those without programming experience, and a trusted reputation.

The findings of the study provided a successful proof of concept. The literature review confirmed that while AR is used in various healthcare settings—such as visualizing blood flow in veins or assisting in surgeries—most nursing-specific AR applications are found in developed nations. Regarding the prototype, the usability results were positive. The 17 respondents provided an average SUS score of 68.5937, which exceeds the mean global score of 68, indicating that the application is relatively usable. Furthermore, the students responded very favorably to the learning experience. On a scale where higher numbers indicate stronger agreement, the respondents gave an average rating of 4.5294 to the statement that the AR-enhanced material was better than printed material alone. They also gave an average rating of 4.3529 regarding whether AR enhanced their learning experience, and 4.3529 for whether they would recommend the material to training institutions.

The study concludes that despite being a relatively new and seemingly expensive technology, AR is accessible to budget-constrained implementers in developing ASEAN countries. By selecting appropriate, free, and user-friendly tools like CraftAR, educators can develop effective learning materials, such as the talking comic strip, to improve essential skills like English communication. The research proves that AR can be successfully implemented in a way that is both functional and well-received by students in the region.

The implications of this research suggest that the digital divide in nursing education can be bridged through the strategic use of Open Educational Resources and accessible AR authoring tools. For educators in developing nations, the study provides a roadmap for creating interactive, low-cost instructional materials. The researchers recommend that future studies focus on evaluating newly released AR tools to address evolving technological limitations. Additionally, they suggest that future iterations of the prototype should focus on improving usability, ensuring long-term sustainability, and increasing accessibility to further enhance the learning outcomes for nursing professionals.

title: Indispensable Innovations in an English Listening and Speaking Class at an E-Learning Training System at Ho Chi Minh Open University (HOU)
abstract: The core value of the e–learning training system at Ho Chi Minh Open University (HOU) is being open to all learners who are interested in developing their knowledge, sharpening their practical skills under flexible learning conditions, and following quality training procedures. In some learning environments, e-learning courses using web-based learning, online exercises, media broadcast lectures, and the like are applied to encourage learners to access knowledge and promote improved learning performances. However, in English listening and speaking classes, learners with strong preferences, interests, determination, and personalization mechanisms can attain great achievements, but the rest do not perform at a high level. Hence, to improve the quality of this training model and meet the preferences and requirements of the learners, a survey questionnaire was administered to 120 sophomores in two listening and speaking classes at HOU. The results show that most learners expect some indispensable innovations, including increasing the class time to help learners gain more confidence and sociolinguistic competence in speaking in the target language; providing supplementary online exercises to support learner autonomy and improvement of listening skill; and maintaining the teacher-learner relationship to provide learners with opportunities for consultation and assessment.
half:
Tuyen Nguyen Chau Bich investigates the challenges of teaching English listening and speaking skills within the e-learning system at Ho Chi Minh Open University (HOU). While the e-learning model offers flexibility and success in subjects like Economics and Finance, it remains ineffective for oral and aural skills due to the communicative needs of English majors, technological limitations, and cultural preferences for traditional instruction.

Using a qualitative methodology, the study surveyed 104 sophomore English majors to examine their perspectives on online versus face-to-face models. The findings reveal that while learners are highly motivated, they strongly prefer hybrid elements. Specifically, 76.92% of respondents believe the system should incorporate face-to-face speaking classes, and 71.15% agree these classes provide greater benefits. Learners perceive in-person interaction as essential for improving pronunciation, fluency, and listening skills across accents, noting that physical classrooms build confidence, facilitate self-correction, and foster better teacher-student relationships.

Learners identified three areas for innovation: increasing face-to-face hours for listening and speaking, implementing structured online listening exercises that progress from simple to complicated, and maintaining consistent teacher-student contact. The study concludes that technology cannot entirely replace the communicative benefits of face-to-face interaction. The author recommends that HOU adopt an integrated approach by increasing contact hours, designing tiered online exercises, and ensuring maintained teacher-learner relationships to improve training quality.
one:
Tuyen Nguyen Chau Bich investigates the challenges of teaching English listening and speaking skills within the e-learning training system at Ho Chi Minh Open University (HOU). While the e-learning model provides flexibility and has succeeded in subjects like Economics and Finance, its application to oral and aural skills remains ineffective. This failure is attributed to the specific communicative and psychological needs of English majors, technological limitations such as a lack of specialized program designers, and cultural preferences for traditional face-to-face instruction.

The study utilized a descriptive and qualitative methodology to examine the perspectives and expectations of English major learners. The sample consisted of 104 sophomore respondents selected from a population of 120. Data was collected through interviews and survey questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive simple analysis. The research aimed to determine learner preferences regarding online versus face-to-face models, the perceived benefits of in-person interaction, and desired innovations for the e-learning system.

The findings indicate that the majority of respondents are females aged 25–35 living in Ho Chi Minh City, suggesting the model primarily serves working-age individuals seeking professional development. While these learners are highly motivated and interested in English skills, their attitudes toward the current digital model reveal a strong preference for hybrid elements. Specifically, 76.92% of respondents believe the system should incorporate face-to-face English speaking classes, and 71.15% agree that such classes provide greater benefits. Learners perceive face-to-face interaction as essential for improving pronunciation, fluency, and listening skills across various accents. They also noted that physical classrooms help build confidence in public speaking, facilitate self-correction, and allow for better teacher-student relationships.

Learners identified three primary areas for innovation: increasing the number of face-to-face learning hours for listening and speaking, implementing a structured progression of online listening exercises that move from simple to complicated, and maintaining consistent contact between teachers and learners.

The study concludes that technology cannot entirely replace the communicative benefits of face-to-face interaction in language acquisition. The current HOU model requires adjustments to meet specific learner needs, as listening requires continuous practice through varied materials, while speaking benefits from the sociolinguistic competence provided by in-person instruction. The author recommends that HOU move toward an integrated approach by increasing face-to-face contact hours, designing robust, tiered online listening exercises to support autonomy, and ensuring maintained teacher-learner relationships. Implementing these changes could improve training quality and strengthen the university's reputation in distance education.
two:
The research conducted by Tuyen Nguyen Chau Bich addresses the challenges of teaching English listening and speaking skills within the e-learning training system at Ho Chi Minh Open University (HOU). While e-learning offers flexibility and accessibility, the author identifies a significant problem: the current application of technology in English listening and speaking classes is ineffective. This ineffectiveness stems from three primary factors: the specific communicative and psychological requirements of English majors, technological limitations such as a lack of program designers and an inexperienced online system, and cultural influences, including a traditional preference for face-to-face instruction and a reluctance to adopt new technologies.

The context of the study is the HOU e-learning system, which is designed as a distance learning model intended to be open to all learners seeking professional development and social mobility. While this model has been successful for other subjects like Economics and Finance, the complexity of developing oral and aural skills presents unique difficulties. Specifically, learners often struggle with a lack of confidence and language competence, and the "recording teaching and learning model" has not yet been successfully applied to these specific language skills.

To investigate these issues, the researcher employed a descriptive and qualitative methodology. The study focused on the perspectives, attitudes, perceptions, and expectations of English major learners. The population consisted of 120 sophomores, from which 104 respondents were selected for data collection. The researcher utilized interviews and survey questionnaires to gather data, which was then analyzed using descriptive simple analysis. The study sought to determine whether learners preferred online or face-to-face models, the perceived benefits of face-to-face interaction, and what specific innovations learners expected from the e-learning system.

The findings revealed several key insights regarding the learner demographic and their attitudes. The majority of respondents were females aged 25–35 living in Ho Chi Minh City, suggesting that the e-learning model is primarily utilized by working-age individuals seeking to improve their professional standing. Most learners expressed a strong interest in English listening and speaking skills and were highly motivated, with many attending classes to support their majors or obtain degrees.

Regarding attitudes and perceptions, the results showed a strong preference for hybrid elements. While learners were attentive to their online studies, 76.92% of respondents believed the system should incorporate face-to-face English speaking classes, and 71.15% agreed that such classes provide greater benefits. Learners perceived that face-to-face interaction is essential for improving pronunciation, fluency, and listening skills across various accents. Furthermore, they noted that physical classrooms help build confidence in public speaking, facilitate self-correction, and allow for better relationship-building between teachers and students.

When asked about specific innovations, the learners' expectations were clear. The top three suggestions included increasing the number of face-to-face learning hours for listening and speaking, implementing a structured progression of online listening exercises (from simple to complicated), and maintaining consistent contact between teachers and learners.

In conclusion, the study concludes that while technology is a valuable tool, it cannot entirely replace the communicative benefits of face-to-face interaction in language acquisition. The current e-learning model at HOU requires significant adjustments to meet the specific needs of English language learners. The author emphasizes that listening skills require continuous practice through varied materials, while speaking skills benefit immensely from the sociolinguistic competence and social interaction provided by in-person instruction.

The implications of this research suggest that HOU should move toward a more integrated approach. The author recommends implementing "indispensable innovations" such as increasing face-to-face contact hours, designing more robust and tiered online listening exercises to support learner autonomy, and ensuring that teacher-learner relationships are maintained despite the distance. By adopting these recommendations, the university can better satisfy learner requirements, improve the quality of its training, and strengthen its reputation as an effective provider of distance education.

title: Social Presence among Distance Learners: Portrait of Online Communication at Universitas Terbuka*
abstract: One of the main challenges faced by both distance education institutions and distance education students is how to maintain the spirit of students’ learning processes which is often felt solely. In providing services to students, Universitas Terbuka (UT) develops a variety of online services which are summarized in the facility of UT Online. Through this facility, students can communicate with UT and with other students, both for academic and non-academic purposes. Social presence, the ability to relatively feel proximity and intimacy in online interaction, becomes an important factor in disposing of the solitude sense of distance education students. This study explores various social presence indicators articulated by UT students in online interaction. By using the qualitative approach and implementing discourse analysis method, this study shows that social presence is quite minimum occurs in academic online interactive activities. As for the non-academic online interaction, social presence is more visible articulated. Social presence indicators emerging in online interactions are in the form of sharing stories and personal experiences, using informal hail, using emoticons, putting pictures as personnel identity, using informal everyday language, and motivating each other. One finding that should be highlighted is that distance learners are extending their online communication through social media.
half:
The study "Social Presence among Distance Learners: Portrait of Online Communication at Universitas Terbuka" investigates student isolation in Indonesian distance education, where the self-learning nature of the curriculum may conflict with social cultural needs. The research examines how social presence—the feeling of proximity and intimacy in digital spaces—manifests within the online services of Universitas Terbuka (UT). Using qualitative discourse analysis, the researcher examined interactions in academic online tutorials and non-academic Community Forums, supplemented by focus group discussions and tutor interviews.

Findings reveal a significant difference between these environments. In academic online tutorials, social presence is minimal, characterized by formal language and a strict focus on subject matter. While students use emoticons and profile pictures, "chattering about small things" and sharing personal stories are nearly non-existent. In contrast, social presence is much higher in the non-academic Community Forum, where communication is relaxed and informal. This forum serves as a vital space for students to share experiences, motivate one another, and extend social connections to platforms like WhatsApp or Facebook.

While the forum facilitates student-to-student interaction, institutional responsiveness remains minimal. Working students reported feeling alone due to low response rates from tutors and authorities, while tutors cited busy schedules as a barrier to interaction. The study recommends integrating social presence training into tutor guidance and increasing participation from academic advisors and faculty leadership in forums to mitigate isolation.
one:
The study "Social Presence among Distance Learners: Portrait of Online Communication at Universitas Terbuka" investigates the challenge of student isolation in distance education. In the Indonesian context, where culture is highly social, the self-learning nature of distance education can create tension between individualistic study requirements and the social needs of learners. The research examines how social presence—the feeling of proximity and intimacy in digital spaces—is manifested within the online services provided by Universitas Terbuka (UT).

Using a qualitative approach and discourse analysis, the researcher examined interactions in two environments: academic online tutorials and non-academic Community Forums. The study utilized established indicators of social presence, such as active involvement, humor, and sharing personal stories, while also identifying new indicators like the use of emoticons, profile pictures, informal language, and motivational support. Data was further enriched through Focus Group Discussions (FGD) with students in Surakarta and Pekanbaru and interviews with online tutors.

The findings reveal a significant difference between the two online environments. In academic online tutorials, social presence is minimal. Interactions are characterized by formal language and a strict focus on subject matter. While some female tutors used informal addresses, "chattering about small things" and sharing personal stories were nearly non-existent unless directly related to the course. However, students did use emoticons and profile pictures in these settings.

In contrast, social presence is much more visible in the non-academic Community Forum. Communication here is relaxed and informal, featuring informal addressing, abbreviations, and frequent use of emoticons. This forum serves as a vital space for students to share experiences regarding grades or registration, motivate one another, and extend social connections by inviting peers to social media groups like WhatsApp or Facebook.

FGD results showed that students in Surakarta, who received face-to-face tutorials, were highly motivated and used social media to maintain connections. Conversely, working students in Pekanbaru reported feeling alone, noting that UT's online communication did not significantly aid their learning due to low response rates from tutors and authorities. Tutors acknowledged the importance of social presence but cited busy schedules as a barrier to maximizing interaction.

The study concludes that social presence is low in academic tutorials due to their formal nature but high in the Community Forum. While the forum successfully facilitates student-to-student interaction, institutional responsiveness remains minimal. The research recommends integrating social presence training into tutor guidance and increasing the participation of academic advisors and faculty leadership in the Community Forum to mitigate isolation and foster a supportive environment.
two:
The study "Social Presence among Distance Learners: Portrait of Online Communication at Universitas Terbuka" addresses the challenge of student isolation in distance education. A primary problem in distance learning is the sense of solitude experienced by students who primarily interact with learning materials rather than people. This isolation can negatively impact the learning process. At Universitas Terbuka (UT), while various online services are provided to facilitate communication, there is a need to understand how social presence—the ability to feel proximity and intimacy in online interactions—is actually manifested in these digital spaces.

The context of the research is the Indonesian distance education system, which emphasizes a self-learning culture. This culture can be difficult to implement, as many students struggle with the transition to self-directed learning. Furthermore, Indonesian culture is highly social and communal, creating a potential tension between the individualistic nature of self-learning and the social needs of the learners. While UT provides various online support services, including online tutorials and a Community Forum, the effectiveness of these tools in fostering social presence remains a critical area of investigation.

To investigate this, the researcher employed a qualitative approach using a constructivist paradigm. The study utilized discourse analysis to examine online interactions within two specific environments: academic online tutorials and non-academic Community Forum discussions. The researcher used indicators of social presence previously proposed by Aragon (2003), such as active involvement, chattering about small things, humor, sharing personal stories, and informal addressing. Additionally, the study identified new indicators emerging from the data, including the use of emoticons, attaching profile pictures, using informal language, and providing motivation. To enrich the findings, the researcher conducted Focus Group Discussions (FGD) with students in the Surakarta and Pekanbaru regional offices and interviewed online tutors.

The findings reveal a significant difference between academic and non-academic online interactions. In academic online tutorials, social presence is quite minimal. Interactions in these forums tend to be formal, with tutors and students using polite, formal language. While some female tutors used informal addresses like "teman-teman" (friends) or "Mbak" (elder sister), most communication remained strictly focused on the subject matter. The study found that "chattering about small things" and sharing personal stories were almost non-existent in academic tutorials, except when personal experiences were directly related to the course topic. However, some new indicators of social presence were observed in these academic settings, such as the use of emoticons (primarily by students) and the attachment of profile pictures.

In contrast, social presence is much more visible and articulated in the non-academic Community Forum. In this space, communication is more relaxed and informal. Students use informal addressing (such as "mas," "mbak," or "bro"), use more emoticons, and employ informal language and abbreviations. The Community Forum serves as a vital space for students to share experiences related to their studies, such as successes or frustrations regarding grades and registration. Notably, students often use this forum to motivate one another and to extend their social connections by inviting peers to join social media groups like WhatsApp or Facebook.

The FGD results provided further depth to these findings. Students in Surakarta, who were scholarship recipients receiving face-to-face tutorials, were highly motivated and used social media groups to maintain connections. Conversely, students in Pekanbaru, who were working individuals and more independent, reported feeling alone and stated that UT's online communication did not significantly contribute to their learning process, largely due to low response rates from tutors and university authorities. Tutors interviewed acknowledged the importance of social presence but noted that their own busy schedules acted as an obstacle to maximizing student interaction.

The study concludes that social presence is low in academic online tutorials due to the formal nature of the interactions, whereas it is much higher in the non-academic Community Forum where students feel free to express themselves. While the Community Forum is a successful space for student-to-student interaction and motivation, the response from UT authorities within that forum remains minimal. The research also highlights that social media plays a crucial role in helping distance learners bridge the gap of isolation by providing a platform for more personal and informal interaction.

Based on these conclusions, the study offers several implications and recommendations. First, it suggests that the ability to articulate social presence should be integrated into the official guidance and training for online tutors to help them build better relationships with students. Second, the university should maximize the function of the Community Forum by ensuring more active participation from academic advisors and faculty leadership. By improving the responsiveness of the institution and the social engagement of tutors, distance learning institutions can better mitigate the sense of isolation and foster a more supportive learning environment.

title: Developing a Multimedia Courseware Using Cognitive Load Theory
abstract: This study describes the application of cognitive learning theory in the development of a multimedia courseware to enrich the clinical experience of nursing students in a distance learning environment. The objectives of the study include: (1) describing the nature and organization of tasks needed by students to demonstrate the performance of selected competencies in an adult health nursing specialty course; and (2) identifying strategies and approaches in addressing the intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load in the development of the multimedia material. Content experts, instructional designers, and multimedia specialists were involved in key informant interview, focus group discussion and roundtable discussion to develop the multimedia courseware guided by the cognitive load theory. Students were likewise consulted by soliciting their comments on the content, learning activities and design elements of the courseware. Cognitive load theory was shown to help guide in the development of a multimedia courseware involving complex learning; such as in the clinical practicum of nursing students. By addressing the intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load in developing a multimedia courseware, course developers help students: (1) manage tasks more effectively, (2) reduce the time spent on unnecessary steps in understanding concepts; and (3) focus on learning and demonstrating the competencies needed by the course. This framework forces the content experts, instructional designer, and multimedia specialist to work together to achieve a well-balanced and interesting course that will address directly the needs of the students and at the same time achieve the objectives of the course.
