The study "Developing a Multimedia Courseware Using Cognitive Load Theory" by Sheila R. Bonito addresses the challenges of delivering nursing education through distance learning. While distance education offers convenience and flexibility, it faces significant hurdles in disciplines like nursing, where technical skills and personal qualities are traditionally acquired through face-to-face interaction. Specifically, distance learners may struggle with a lack of continuous interaction, the need for new technological competencies, and the difficulty of mastering complex clinical skills without immediate access to physical clinical preceptors. The problem addressed is how to create a multimedia courseware that enriches the clinical practicum experience for nursing students in a distance-learning environment, ensuring they can achieve professional competencies despite the absence of a traditional classroom setting.

The context of this research is the clinical nursing practicum, which requires "complex learning"—the integration of knowledge, skills, and attitudes, and the ability to transfer learning to real-world settings. Because clinical tasks are inherently complex, they pose a high cognitive load on students. To address this, the researcher utilized Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) as a theoretical framework. CLT categorizes cognitive load into three types: intrinsic load (the inherent difficulty of the material), extraneous load (the load generated by how information is presented), and germane load (the mental effort used to construct schemas or mental representations). The goal was to use this theory to design a virtual clinical practicum that manages these loads effectively.

The methodology employed a multi-stage qualitative and developmental approach. First, content experts were engaged through key informant interviews and focus group discussions to identify the specific tasks and competencies required for adult health nursing. Second, a roundtable discussion was held involving content experts, instructional designers, and multimedia specialists to determine design elements that could reduce extraneous cognitive load while maintaining engagement. Finally, a pilot review was conducted with ten students to evaluate the courseware's content, learning activities, and design elements.

The findings of the study outline a four-step development process: selecting necessary tasks, simplifying task complexity, reducing extraneous load, and refocusing learners on the subject matter. The researchers identified core competencies such as utilizing the nursing process, maintaining documentation, and applying bioethical principles. To manage the intrinsic load (complexity), the courseware utilized "learning scaffolds," such as sequencing sub-tasks from simple to complex and providing templates and guides. To reduce extraneous load, the multimedia environment was designed to mimic a real hospital setting (e.g., nurses' stations and patient rooms) but with minimal distracting interactivity. Case studies were "chunked" into short, realistic video clips to prevent cognitive overload. To enhance germane load and refocus learners, the courseware included short lessons, self-assessment questions, and hyperlinks to glossaries and references. The pilot review indicated positive student responses, with students rating the presentation, relevance, and multimedia mix as "very good," though they suggested improvements for navigation and the addition of a tutorial guide.

The study concludes that Cognitive Load Theory is an effective guide for developing multimedia courseware for complex learning environments like nursing clinical practicums. By strategically addressing intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive loads, developers can help students manage tasks more effectively, reduce time wasted on unnecessary processing, and focus more intensely on demonstrating required competencies. Furthermore, the study highlights that using this framework encourages a synergistic collaboration between content experts, instructional designers, and multimedia specialists, resulting in a more balanced and effective educational product.

The implications of this research suggest that instructional designers in healthcare education should move beyond simple content delivery and instead focus on the cognitive architecture of the learner. By integrating learning tasks, supportive information, just-in-time information, and part-task practice, multimedia tools can successfully bridge the gap between theory and clinical practice in distance education. The author recommends that future studies include students earlier in the conceptualization phase and focus on measuring the actual effectiveness of such courseware in terms of student performance and the achievement of specific clinical learning goals.

title: Evaluating the Use and Acceptance of eLearning for Tertiary Education among Senior High School Students
abstract: This paper sought to determine senior high school students’ preconceived notions about eLearning, as well as their behavioral intention to pursue tertiary education online. Generally, it aimed to evaluate the use and acceptance of eLearning technologies among senior high school students in a private high school in Los Baños, Laguna. Stratified sampling was used to identify respondents from five K-12 strands – accountancy, business and management (ABM); science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM); humanities and social science (HUMSS); information and communication technology (ICT); and general academic strand (GAS). Grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2), 200 respondents were surveyed. The moderating effect of UTAUT variables on the respondents’ behavioral intention was examined through correlation and regression analysis. Results showed that majority of the respondents had a positive behavioral intention to pursue tertiary education through eLearning. Of the UTAUT constructs, only performance expectancy was found to be a significant predictor of behavioral intention. A weak association was observed between sex and social influence; as well as between age and hedonic motivation.

The study "Evaluating the Use and Acceptance of eLearning for Tertiary Education among Senior High School Students" by Patricia O. Calora and Yrelle Mae R. Lleva examines eLearning and Open and Distance eLearning (ODeL) as solutions to resource challenges in Philippine higher education. Using a quantitative design grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2), researchers surveyed 200 senior high school students across five K-12 strands to assess their perceptions and intentions regarding online undergraduate studies.

Findings indicate that 71.2% of respondents intend to enroll in an online institution. Most participants were 17-year-old females who use smartphones to access the internet. While students perceive eLearning as flexible and affordable, they lack specific knowledge regarding the practical mechanics of online assessments and virtual collaboration.

Analysis of UTAUT constructs showed that performance expectancy was the only significant predictor of behavioral intention; students more likely to pursue online education were those who believed eLearning would help them achieve academic goals. Other factors, such as effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value, and habit, were not significant predictors. The authors conclude that intention is driven by perceived utility for academic success. They recommend that institutions implement communication campaigns to explain online system functions and suggest that developers prioritize resource accessibility, student support, and interactive environments.

Lleva addresses the need for flexible educational solutions in the Philippines. As the K to 12 program increases the number of potential college students, traditional universities face challenges regarding physical, financial, and human resources. The authors identify eLearning and Open and Distance eLearning (ODeL) as potential solutions to address infrastructure inadequacies and increase accessibility.

The study was grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2), examining constructs such as performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value, and habit. The goal was to determine the students' socio-demographic profiles, perceptions of eLearning, and behavioral intention to pursue online undergraduate studies.

Findings revealed that 71.2% of respondents expressed a positive behavioral intention to enroll in an online institution. Most participants were 17 years old, slightly more female (53.5%), had internet access, and primarily used smartphones. While students viewed eLearning as flexible and more affordable than traditional modes, they lacked specific knowledge regarding how online classes, assessments, and virtual collaborations are conducted.

Analysis of UTAUT constructs showed general agreement with most factors, though agreement regarding price value was more neutral. Regarding moderating effects, age had a weak association with hedonic motivation, and sex had a weak association with social influence. Logistic regression revealed that performance expectancy (PE) was the only significant predictor of behavioral intention; students who believed eLearning would help them achieve academic goals were more likely to intend to pursue online tertiary education. Other factors, including effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value, and habit, were not significant predictors in this sample.

The authors conclude that while senior high school students are open to online tertiary education, their intention is primarily driven by the perceived utility of the technology for academic success. Despite being technologically capable, students have a limited understanding of the practical mechanics of online learning. The researchers recommend that institutions use detailed information, education, and communication (IEC) campaigns to explain how online systems function and help students meet goals. They also suggest that course developers prioritize resource accessibility, student support, interactive environments, and visible teacher presence. Future research should examine actual use behavior, the influence of specific academic strands, and factors like computer self-efficacy and anxiety.

Lleva addresses the growing need for flexible educational solutions in the Philippines. As the country implements the K to 12 program, a surplus of potential college students is expected to enter tertiary education. This influx poses significant challenges for traditional residential universities regarding physical, financial, and human resources. The authors identify eLearning and Open and Distance eLearning (ODeL) as potential solutions to address infrastructure inadequacies and increase educational accessibility.

The research context is rooted in the Philippine government's efforts to improve human capital development and democratize education through initiatives like the Universal Access to Quality Education Act. Despite these efforts, the readiness of future learners to adopt online learning remains a critical area for investigation. The authors note a lack of existing research specifically exploring the acceptability of eLearning among senior high school (SHS) students in the Philippines.

To investigate this, the researchers employed a quantitative research design using stratified sampling to select 200 respondents from five K-12 strands: Accountancy, Business and Management (ABM); Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM); Humanities and Social Science (HUMSS); Information and Communication Technology (ICT); and General Academic Strand (GAS). The study was grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2), which includes constructs such as performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value, and habit. The researchers aimed to determine the socio-demographic profile of the students, their perceptions of eLearning, their behavioral intention to pursue online undergraduate studies, and the factors affecting that intention.

The findings revealed that the majority of respondents had a positive behavioral intention to pursue tertiary education through eLearning, with 71.2% expressing willingness to enroll in an online institution. Regarding socio-demographic characteristics, the majority of respondents were 17 years old, with a slightly higher female representation (53.5%). Most participants had internet access and primarily used smartphones for technology-related activities. While students generally had a positive perception of eLearning—viewing it as flexible and more affordable than traditional modes—there was a notable lack of specific knowledge regarding how online classes are conducted, how assessments are administered, and how students interact or collaborate in a virtual environment.

The analysis of UTAUT constructs showed that respondents generally agreed with most constructs, though agreement regarding price value was more neutral. In terms of moderating effects, the study found that age had a weak association with hedonic motivation (older students found eLearning more enjoyable), and sex had a weak association with social influence (males were more likely to report positive social approval of eLearning). However, when examining the predictors of behavioral intention through logistic regression, only performance expectancy (PE) was found to be a significant predictor. Specifically, students who believed eLearning would help them achieve their academic goals were more likely to intend to pursue online tertiary education. Other factors, such as effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value, and habit, were not significant predictors in this specific sample.

The researchers conclude that while senior high school students are generally open to the idea of online tertiary education, their intention is primarily driven by the perceived utility of the technology in achieving academic success. The study highlights that while students are technologically capable, they possess limited understanding of the practical mechanics of online learning environments.

The implications of these findings suggest that eLearning institutions and educators should focus on specific strategic areas to increase acceptance and success. The authors recommend that information, education, and communication (IEC) campaigns should be more detailed, specifically explaining how online learning systems function and how they can help students meet their academic goals. Furthermore, course developers should prioritize the accessibility of resources, student support, and the creation of engaging, interactive, and collaborative environments. The study also emphasizes the importance of a visible teacher presence to encourage student success. For future research, the authors suggest examining actual use behavior, the influence of specific academic strands, and indirect determinants such as computer self-efficacy and anxiety.

title: Role of Teachers in Technology-mediated Distance Education: A Preliminary Synthesis
abstract: Technological advances in distance education have transformed the teaching learning processes. It has been realised that there are innumerable possibilities of using educational technology as a crucial pedagogical resource during teaching and learning. Technology has expanded the opportunities for students to access higher education but on the other hand it has presented challenges before the teachers to devise creative methods of teaching. Distance education today demands a change in the role of teachers so that meaningful leaner-centric interactions and discussions take place. However, at several occasions it is feared particularly in distance education systems that technology would replace teachers. In this context, it is necessary that teachers in distance education make use of the latest educational technologies as a resource to carry out effective teaching. In view of this, an attempt has been made in the current paper to explore the role of teachers in technology mediated distance education. The paper finally asserts that effective faculty participation is the key driving factor towards the success of technology- mediated distance education.
half:
In "Role of Teachers in Technology-mediated Distance Education: A Preliminary Synthesis," Deeksha Dave examines how technological advancements have shifted educator responsibilities from traditional correspondence models to interactive digital platforms. This evolution from postal services to digital tools like blogs and social media has changed the learner profile, as students now seek flexibility and real-time collaboration. Because students have instant access to online resources, teachers can no longer function merely as dispensers of information.

Using a review-based approach of 50 research papers and primary data from interactions with teachers at various universities, the study identifies several emerging roles for educators. Instead of being the sole authority, teachers become team members, team coordinators, and partners in learning who participate in knowledge exchange. Other roles include trainers, technology-savvy mentors, content developers, and instructional designers.

However, significant challenges hinder implementation, including resource shortages, inadequate staff training, and a lack of expertise in course design. There is a notable gap between the availability of technology and its pedagogical application, as many teachers are trained to operate tools rather than use them specifically for teaching. The paper concludes that successful technology-mediated distance education requires effective faculty participation and a fundamental shift in how instructors view their relationship with students. Institutions must prioritize professional development that focuses on the intersection of technology and pedagogy to empower teachers as guides and collaborators.

The article "Role of Teachers in Technology-mediated Distance Education: A Preliminary Synthesis" by Deeksha Dave explores the evolving responsibilities of educators within distance learning environments shaped by technological advancement. The author addresses the shift from traditional correspondence-based models to modern, interactive digital platforms, examining how these changes impact the pedagogical relationship between instructors and students.

The problem addressed in the paper is the tension between the increasing integration of educational technology and the traditional roles of teachers. While technology offers immense possibilities for student-centered learning and expanded access to higher education, it presents significant challenges for faculty. There is a pervasive fear among educators that technology might eventually replace the teacher, leading to a loss of classroom authority. Furthermore, many distance education systems fail to fully utilize available technologies due to a lack of resources, inadequate training, and teacher resistance to changing established instructional styles.

The context of this study is the rapid transformation of distance education. Historically, distance learning relied on postal services and physical media, but it has evolved through e-mail, digital repositories, and now interactive tools like blogs, wikis, and social media. This evolution has changed the learner profile, attracting students who seek flexibility and real-time collaboration. The study situates the teacher's role within this digital shift, noting that as students gain instant access to vast online resources, the teacher can no longer function simply as a "dispenser of information."

The method employed is a review-based research approach. The author synthesized findings from 50 research papers to establish the impact of technology on the changing roles of distance education teachers. The synthesis drew inferences from conclusions within these papers to identify the motivating and preventing factors for faculty adoption of technology. Additionally, the author gathered primary data through informal interactions with distance education teachers at various state and national open universities.

The findings of the synthesis identify several emerging roles for the teacher in a technology-mediated environment. Rather than being the sole authority, the teacher becomes a "Team Member," working within a student-driven environment where they no longer hold total control over the learning space. The teacher acts as a "Team Coordinator," organizing collaborative activities and peer tutoring. As a "Partner in Learning," the instructor moves away from being a mere facilitator to an active participant in the exchange of knowledge, viewing students as contributors to content. Other identified roles include "Trainer," providing individual skill development; "Technology Savvy Mentor," guiding students who are often more digitally native than their instructors; "Content Developer," acting as scriptwriters and multimedia specialists; and "Instructional Designer," planning unique lessons that leverage digital tools.

The study also identifies significant challenges. Implementation is often hindered by a lack of monetary resources, insufficient staff training, and a lack of expertise in course design and delivery. Administrative and legal constraints can limit the freedom of educators to use emerging technologies. Furthermore, there is a noted gap between the availability of technology and the actual pedagogical application; many teachers are trained on "how to use the tools" rather than "how to use the tools to teach."

In conclusion, the paper asserts that effective faculty participation is the primary driving factor for the success of technology-mediated distance education. For distance learning to be successful, teachers must be trained not just in the technical operation of tools, but in the specific pedagogy required for digital environments. The transition from traditional teaching to technology-mediated instruction requires a fundamental shift in how instructors view their relationship with students and the learning process.

The implications of this research suggest that educational institutions must prioritize professional development that focuses on the intersection of technology and pedagogy. Designers and administrators must move beyond simply providing hardware; they must deliberately design learning environments that promote interaction and collaboration. The paper implies that to overcome resistance and the "transactional distance gap"—the communication gap caused by geographic separation—teachers must be empowered to act as guides and collaborators rather than mere transmitters of information. Ultimately, the success of digital education depends on the ability of faculty to embrace these multifaceted roles and adapt their instructional methods to meet the needs of the 21st-century learner.

title: Aggregating Attention, Emotion, and Cognition Load as Basis for Developing a Rule-based Pedagogy for Online Learner
abstract: The e-learning system offers an opportunity for educational strategists to monitor the learners' status and improve the teaching-learning outcomes. The study aims to analyze the electroencephalogram (EEG) signal of the learners' attention, emotion, and cognition as determining factors to recommend an appropriate learning pedagogy for every learner. The study analyzed 5,400 data signal datasets with the application of different algorithms to optimize and label the signal classification categories. The data signal components were aggregated as inputs to the regression model. Its resulting p-value determined the prioritization which significantly impacted the learners' learning process. Based on the initial simulation of signal analysis, the study recommends an individualized rule-based pedagogy for each learner, incorporating the EEG instrument to collect the affective and cognitive attributes that can help the learners to adjust better and follow their learning process with minimal supervision of the educational strategist. Likewise, implementing this study in the current e-learning system would provide tremendous learning benefits and improvements in the teaching-learning process.
half:
In the study "Aggregating Attention, Emotion, and Cognition Load as Basis for Developing a Rule-based Pedagogy for Online Learner," Anna Liza A. Ramos and Melvin A. Ballera address the challenges of maintaining engagement and optimizing outcomes in virtual learning environments. The researchers identify that learners often face distractions, negative emotions like anxiety or frustration, and high cognitive load due to poorly designed instructional materials. While attention, emotion, and cognition have been studied individually, the authors note a gap in using technology, such as electroencephalogram (EEG) signals, to integrate these three components into a cohesive pedagogical framework.

Using a quantitative experimental design, the researchers utilized an Emotiv EPOC+14 Channel Mobile Encephalogram (EEG) tool to record the brain signals of 20 respondents with backgrounds in C++ programming. Participants performed tasks involving reading e-learning materials and completing machine problem activities, generating 5,400 datasets. The researchers used MATLAB EEG tools and various algorithms, including Bandpass filters, Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filters, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and Independent Component Analysis (ICA), to process signals and remove noise. The final values for attention load (Al), emotion load (EL), and cognitive load (CL) were aggregated using weighted means and used in a regression model to predict performance scores.

The findings established a mapping system where expert judgment was used to prioritize pedagogies based on simulated analysis and signal classification. The study developed specific criteria for different load levels across all three domains. The simulation demonstrated that the combined values of attention, emotion, and cognition are significant predictors of the learning process. The authors suggest that this rule-based pedagogy offers insights for selecting appropriate learning strategies, moving e-learning toward more individualized, adaptive environments through real-time, data-driven assessments.

Ballera address the difficulties of maintaining engagement and optimizing outcomes in virtual learning environments. The research was prompted by the rapid transition to online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors argue that understanding the relationship between attention, emotion, and cognition is essential for improving teaching-learning outcomes. They highlight that while attention and cognition are linked to achievement and emotion affects motivation, few studies use technology to assess all three simultaneously for real-time diagnostic assessments of a learner's mental state.

Using a quantitative experimental design, the researchers utilized an Emotiv EPOC+14 Channel Mobile Encephalogram (EEG) tool to record the brain signals of 20 respondents with backgrounds in C++ programming. Participants performed two tasks: reading e-learning materials to capture attention and emotion, and completing machine problem activities to capture cognitive load and skills. This generated 5,400 datasets. The researchers used MATLAB EEG tools and various algorithms, including Bandpass filters, Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filters, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and Independent Component Analysis (ICA), to process signals and remove noise. The final values for attention load (Al), emotion load (EL), and cognitive load (CL) were aggregated using weighted means and used as independent variables in a regression model to predict learners' performance scores.

The findings, based on simulated analysis and signal classification (High, Normal, and Low mental load), established a mapping system where expert judgment was used to prioritize pedagogies. The study developed specific criteria for different load levels across all three domains. For example, the cognitive load domain provided a rule-based hierarchy to recommend pedagogies based on load levels, while emotions were categorized into positive (satisfaction), neutral (confusion), and negative (frustration and dissatisfaction) to guide pedagogical selection.

The study concludes that monitoring a learner's mental state is critical to understanding how they process information. The simulation demonstrated that the combined values of attention, emotion, and cognition are significant predictors of the learning process. The study titled "Aggregating Attention, Emotion, and Cognition Load as Basis for Developing a Rule-based Pedagogy for Online Learner" by Anna Liza A. Ramos and Melvin A. Ballera addresses the challenges of maintaining learner engagement and optimizing educational outcomes in virtual environments. The researchers identify a critical problem in e-learning: learners often face distractions from complex content, experience negative emotions such as anxiety or frustration due to task irrelevance, and struggle with cognitive load when instructional materials are poorly designed. While previous research has explored attention, emotion, and cognition individually, the authors note a gap in utilizing artificial intelligence and advanced technology, such as electroencephalogram (EEG) signals, to integrate these three components into a cohesive pedagogical framework.

The context of this research is the rapid transition to online learning necessitated by the COVID-19 pandemic. This shift required educational strategists to develop well-designed courses that balance theoretical and practical teachings. The authors argue that understanding the relationship between attention, emotion, and cognition is essential for improving teaching-learning outcomes. They specifically highlight that while attention and cognition are linked to academic achievement, and emotion is a significant factor in motivation and attention span, few studies have used technology to assess all three simultaneously to provide real-time diagnostic assessments of a learner's mental state.

To address this, the researchers employed a quantitative approach using an experimental design. The study utilized the Emotiv EPOC+14 Channel Mobile Encephalogram (EEG) tool to record the brain signals of 20 respondents (10 males and 10 females) who had a background in C++ programming. The participants performed two distinct tasks: reading e-learning materials to capture attention and emotion, and completing machine problem activities to capture cognitive load and skills. This process generated a total of 5,400 datasets. The researchers used MATLAB EEG tools and various algorithms, including Bandpass filters, Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filters, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and Independent Component Analysis (ICA), to process the signals and remove noise. The final values for attention load (Al), emotion load (EL), and cognitive load (CL) were aggregated using weighted means. These aggregated values served as independent variables in a regression model, with the learners' performance scores serving as the dependent variable.

The findings of the study were based on simulated analysis and signal classification categories: High, Normal, and Low mental load. Through the regression model, the researchers determined the significance of each component using p-values. The study successfully established a mapping system where expert judgment was used to prioritize pedagogies based on the levels of attention, emotion, and cognitive load. For instance, the researchers developed specific criteria for "High," "Normal," and "Low" loads across all three domains. For example, in the cognitive load domain, the study provided a rule-based hierarchy to recommend different priority pedagogies depending on whether the load was high, normal, or low. Similarly, for emotions, the study categorized responses into positive (satisfaction), neutral (confusion), and negative (frustration and dissatisfaction) to guide pedagogical selection.

The conclusions of the study emphasize that monitoring a learner's mental state is critical to understanding how they process and manage information. The simulation demonstrated that the combined values of attention, emotion, and cognition are significant predictors of the learning process. By integrating these affective and cognitive domains, the study provides a framework for a more comprehensive diagnostic assessment of academic competence. The authors conclude that the developed rule-based pedagogy offers essential insights for selecting the most appropriate learning strategies for individual students, thereby enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of e-learning systems.

The implications of this research are significant for the future of digital education. By incorporating AI and EEG technology, e-learning systems can move toward more individualized, adaptive learning environments. This approach allows for real-time assessments that can help learners adjust to their learning processes with minimal supervision from educators. Furthermore, the study provides a foundation for stakeholders to make data-driven decisions regarding the design and implementation of learning materials. It suggests that by understanding the specific mental loads a student experiences, educational strategists can redesign content and activities to minimize frustration and maximize engagement, ultimately improving overall teaching-learning outcomes in the digital age.

title: Reflective Writing of New Graduate Students: Their Challenges and Experiences in an Open and Distance Education
abstract: The study was conceptualized out of the program educators’ reflections on coping and adjustment experiences of new graduate students’ transition into their first year of learning in an open and distance education graduate program in nursing. This study explored the questions raised by students during their first year in the program and looked more closely into their experiences and coping that they did in the open and distance education mode in their written reflections during their first year in the program. The objectives of this research were to identify the challenges and learning experiences revealed in reflective assignments written by new graduate students undertaking an open and distance e-learning education in their first year in an open university in the Philippines and use the written reflections of the students to construct new strategies and practices for the development of the program for the future students.
half:
The study "Reflective Writing of New Graduate Students: Their Challenges and Experiences in an Open and Distance Education" by Queenie R. Ridulme and Rachel Anne Joyce C. Sales investigates the transition of first-year graduate nursing students into an open and distance learning (ODL) environment at an open university in the Philippines. Using a qualitative research design guided by Gibbs’ Reflective Cycle, the researchers collected data from 13 graduate nursing students via an online self-administered questionnaire.

The findings revealed a dichotomy of experiences. On the positive side, students valued the flexibility of studying at their own pace and from their workplaces, which fostered independence and responsibility. Many participants noted the ability to apply theoretical knowledge to their actual clinical practice, while support from professors and peers and the satisfaction of achieving high grades served as significant motivators.

Conversely, the study identified significant challenges. The most prominent issue was delayed feedback, which caused confusion and tension. Technical difficulties, including poor internet connectivity, power interruptions, and software errors, also emerged as major barriers. Furthermore, students struggled with time management while balancing work, social life, and academic responsibilities.

The authors recommend that instructors provide more frequent and timely feedback and establish clear guidelines for response times. They also advocate for the continuous enhancement of learning tools, regular updating of modules, and ongoing training for faculty in educational technology.

The study "Reflective Writing of New Graduate Students: Their Challenges and Experiences in an Open and Distance Education" by Queenie R. Ridulme and Rachel Anne Joyce C. Sales investigates the transition of first-year graduate nursing students into an open and distance learning (ODL) environment. Conducted at an open university in the Philippines, the research addresses a gap in existing literature regarding the specific lived experiences of ODL students. The researchers aimed to identify challenges and learning experiences through students' written reflections to inform program improvement strategies.

Using a qualitative research design guided by Gibbs’ Reflective Cycle, the researchers collected data from 13 graduate nursing students via an online self-administered questionnaire. The participant profile consisted primarily of females (69.2%) and individuals in the 21–40 age bracket (84.6%), with most specializing in Nursing Administration.

The findings revealed a dichotomy of experiences. On the positive side, students valued the flexibility of studying at their own pace and from their workplaces, which fostered independence and responsibility. Many participants noted the ability to apply theoretical knowledge to their actual clinical practice as a highlight of their first year. Additionally, support from professors and peers, along with the satisfaction of achieving high grades, served as significant motivators.

Conversely, the study identified significant challenges. The most prominent issue was delayed feedback; students expressed frustration when queries went unanswered for weeks or months, causing confusion and tension. Technical difficulties also emerged as a major barrier, including poor internet connectivity, power interruptions in provincial areas, and software or portal errors during critical periods like examinations. Furthermore, students struggled with time management, finding it difficult to balance work, social life, and academic responsibilities, particularly when assignments had overlapping deadlines.

In conclusion, while ODL provides essential flexibility and promotes independent learning, it is heavily impacted by communication delays and technical infrastructure issues. The biggest hurdle for students was the self-discipline required for effective time management, while the most significant grievance was the lack of timely instructor responses.

To address these issues, the authors propose several strategies for program development. They recommend that instructors provide more frequent and timely feedback through various online methods and establish clear guidelines for response times to manage student expectations. They also advocate for the continuous enhancement of learning tools and the regular updating of modules. Finally, the study suggests that faculty members should receive ongoing training in educational technology and recommends that future research expand these investigations to undergraduate programs.

The study titled "Reflective Writing of New Graduate Students: Their Challenges and Experiences in an Open and Distance Education" by Queenie R. Ridulme and Rachel Anne Joyce C. Sales investigates the transition of first-year graduate nursing students into an open and distance learning (ODL) environment. The research was prompted by educators' observations regarding the coping and adjustment experiences of these students. The primary problem addressed is the lack of focus in existing literature regarding the specific lived experiences of ODL students, despite the increasing demand for this mode of education. The researchers aimed to identify the specific challenges and learning experiences revealed in students' written reflections and to use these insights to develop new strategies for program improvement.

The context of the study is situated within an open university in the Philippines, where ODL is particularly pervasive at the graduate level. The authors note that while ODL offers significant advantages—such as flexibility in time and space, cost-efficiency, and the ability to study without relocating—it also presents unique hurdles. These include the need for high levels of self-regulation, technological proficiency, and the ability to communicate effectively through written words.

To explore these experiences, the researchers employed a qualitative research design using Gibbs’ Reflective Cycle as a framework. This model guided the formulation of questions to elicit detailed information regarding the participants' backgrounds, feelings, thoughts, and both positive and negative experiences. The participants consisted of 13 graduate nursing students recruited through convenience sampling. Data were collected via an online self-administered questionnaire and analyzed using qualitative methods to highlight significant themes. The participant profile revealed a majority of female students (69.2%) and a majority of those in the 21–40 age bracket (84.6%), with most specializing in Nursing Administration.

The findings of the study revealed a dichotomy of favorable and unfavorable experiences. On the positive side, students valued the flexibility of studying at their own pace and from their respective workplaces, which fostered independence and responsibility. Many participants reported that the ability to apply theoretical knowledge to their actual clinical practice was a highlight of their first year. Furthermore, the support from professors and peers, along with the satisfaction of achieving high grades, served as significant motivators.

However, the study also identified significant challenges. The most prominent issue was delayed feedback; students expressed frustration when queries went unanswered for weeks or even months, which caused confusion and tension. Technical difficulties also emerged as a major barrier, including poor internet connectivity, power interruptions in provincial areas, and software or portal errors during critical times like examinations. Additionally, students struggled with time management, finding it difficult to balance the demands of work, social life, and academic responsibilities, particularly when multiple assignments had overlapping deadlines.

In conclusion, the researchers found that while ODL provides essential flexibility and promotes independent learning, it is heavily impacted by communication delays and technical infrastructure issues. The biggest hurdle for students was the self-discipline required for effective time management, while the most significant grievance was the lack of timely instructor responses.

Based on these findings, the authors propose several strategies for program development. First, they recommend that instructors provide more frequent and timely feedback using various online methods, such as email, student portals, or digital polls. Second, they suggest establishing clear guidelines for instructor response times to manage student expectations and reduce frustration. Third, they advocate for the continuous enhancement of learning tools and the regular review and updating of modules to ensure they remain relevant and functional. Finally, the study suggests that faculty members should receive ongoing training in educational technology to better support students in a digital environment. The authors recommend that future research expand these investigations to undergraduate programs to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the ODL experience.

title: Identification of User-Friendly Bioinformatics Tools for Courses in Open and Distance Learning
abstract: Bioinformatics has become a vital offspring of biology with a wider spectrum of applications. Many fields of biology now rely on the analysis and interpretations of observations through the genomic scale data using bioinformatics. There is a considerable demand to learn bioinformatics, which can be easily offered in open and distance (e)learning (ODL/ODeL) systems due to its total reliance on information and computer technology (ICT). Generally, course design and content development for new courses in ODL demand substantial resources and time. Use of existing bioinformatics software tools and allied documents can drastically reduce these resource demands and time factors in course designing and updating. Given a large number of proliferating bioinformatics software tools available on the Internet, it requires comprehensive criteria to identify software tools and documentation that are user-friendly for open and distance learners, and needs multidisciplinary knowledge in ODL, Biology, and Bioinformatics. A criteria-based software evaluation was adopted in this study to evaluate the user-friendliness of bioinformatics software, particularly the plant genomic analysis software which was available in the Internet for free usage. Two main criteria used in this selection: Usability and Maintainability. These main criteria consisted of several sub-criteria such as understandability, documentation, installability, learnability, etc. A wider spectrum of Bioinformatics software tools designed for different stages of genomic data analysis, from simple sequence analysis to genome wide analysis, were used in this evaluation process. Based on the criteria, a series of user-friendly bioinformatics tools that can be used at different stages of genomic data analysis were identified. In addition to the criteria of selection, these tools and allied documentation can effectively be integrated with development of a comprehensive ODL-based bioinformatics courses. Further, this outcome facilitates offering hard science concepts through the minimum commitment of resources and time to meet the escalating demand for capacity development in Bioinformatics.
half:
Bioinformatics is a multidisciplinary field merging biology with computer science, mathematics, statistics, and physics. Because it relies on information technology rather than physical laboratories, it is well-suited for Open and Distance Learning (ODL). However, creating ODL bioinformatics curricula is difficult due to the time required for content creation and the rapid evolution of the field. While many free software tools and Integrated Bioinformatics Platforms (IBPs) exist, educators lack established criteria to determine which tools are suitable for distance learners.

To address this, researchers developed an evaluation method to identify software that can be integrated into ODL programs. In September 2016, they evaluated over 40 tools and IBPs, focusing on those cited in research, the Expasy portal, and plant genomic analysis tools. The evaluation used two categories: Usability (including understandability, documentation, learnability, installability, copyright/licensing, and community) and Maintainability (including supportability, evolvability, interoperability, and portability).

Findings showed a diverse usability landscape. While most tools indicated primary functions, only 60% provided comprehensive manuals, 44% included screenshots, and 15% offered audio-visual tutorials. Regarding maintainability, over 75% provided routine updates and platform compatibility, and more than 80% met criteria for evolvability and portability. The study concludes that integrating high-quality existing software is an effective strategy for ODL. Tools scoring higher than six can be integrated directly, while lower-scoring tools require additional instructional support.

The evaluation, conducted in September 2016, utilized two primary categories: Usability and Maintainability.

The usability category included sub-criteria such as understandability, documentation, learnability, installability, copyright/licensing, and community. The maintainability category included supportability, evolvability, interoperability, and portability. Each criterion was scored as either 1 (compliant) or 0 (non-compliant), with the total percentage determining the tool's user-friendliness.

The findings revealed a diverse landscape of usability. While most tools indicated their primary functions, only 60% provided comprehensive user manuals, and only 44% included screenshots in their documentation. Only 15% of tools offered audio-visual tutorials, which are highly beneficial for self-directed ODL learners. Additionally, there was a gap in peer-assisted resources; only 40% provided a dedicated user space and 42% included an FAQ section.

Results for maintainability were more positive, with over 75% of tools providing routine updates and compatibility with various PC platforms. More than 80% met criteria for evolvability and portability. However, many tools for large-scale data analysis are optimized for LINUX-based systems, suggesting students may need LINUX familiarity. Some specialized tools also had minimal documentation, requiring additional facilitator support.

The study concludes that integrating high-quality, existing software and open resources is an effective strategy for developing responsive ODL courses. The researchers recommend using their scoring system to screen software: tools scoring higher than six can be integrated directly, while those with lower scores require additional instructional support. This approach allows ODL institutions to meet the global demand for bioinformatics professionals efficiently and scalably.
two:
The rapid expansion of biological data through high-throughput experimental methods has established bioinformatics as a vital multidisciplinary field. This field merges biology with computer science, mathematics, statistics, and physics to analyze genomic-scale data. As the demand for bioinformatics expertise grows, there is a significant opportunity to deliver this training through Open and Distance Learning (ODL) systems. Because bioinformatics relies heavily on information and communication technology (ICT) rather than physical laboratory infrastructure, it is uniquely suited for the flexible, technology-dependent nature of ODL.

However, developing and updating bioinformatics curricula in an ODL context presents significant challenges. Designing new courses and developing content requires substantial time and resources. Furthermore, the field evolves so rapidly that keeping course materials current is a constant struggle. While the internet provides a vast array of free bioinformatics software tools and Integrated Bioinformatics Platforms (IBPs), the sheer volume of available tools makes it difficult for educators to select the most appropriate ones. There is a lack of established criteria to evaluate whether a specific software tool is "user-friendly" or compatible with the unique needs of distance learners.

To address this problem, the researchers aimed to develop evaluation criteria to identify bioinformatics software that is suitable for integration into ODL programs. The study sought to identify a series of tools that could be used directly as learning materials, thereby reducing the time and resources required for course development and content updates.

The researchers employed a criteria-based software evaluation method. They selected a sample of more than 40 bioinformatics software tools and IBPs, focusing on those commonly cited in published research and those listed on the Expasy bioinformatics resource portal. While the study considered various subjects, particular attention was given to tools specialized for plant genomic analysis. The evaluation was conducted in September 2016 and utilized two primary categories of criteria adapted from existing software evaluation guidelines: Usability and Maintainability.

The usability category was further divided into sub-criteria: understandability (whether the software's purpose and functions are clear), documentation (the quality, structure, and clarity of user manuals and step-by-step guides), learnability (the ease of learning basic and advanced tasks), installability (the simplicity of installation on supported systems), copyright/licensing (the presence of appropriate open-source licenses), and community (the existence of an active user community or support forums). The maintainability category included supportability (availability of developer support and email archives), evolvability (evidence of future development and funding), interoperability (use of open standards), and portability (compatibility with different operating systems like Windows and MacOSX). Each criterion was scored as either 1 (compliant) or 0 (non-compliant), and the total percentage was used to determine the tool's user-friendliness.

The findings revealed a diverse landscape of software usability. Regarding understandability, while almost all tools indicated their primary functions, only 60% provided comprehensive user manuals. Step-by-step instructions were also relatively uncommon, found in only 60% of the tools, and only 44% provided documentation that included screenshots. Only 15% of the tools, primarily IBPs, offered audio-visual tutorials, which are highly beneficial for self-directed ODL learners. Furthermore, the study found a gap in peer-assisted learning resources; only 40% of tools provided a dedicated user space, and 42% included a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) section.

In terms of maintainability, the results were more positive. Over 75% of the tools and IBPs provided routine updates and were compatible with various PC platforms. More than 80% of the tools met the criteria for evolvability and portability. However, a notable finding was that many free bioinformatics tools designed for large-scale data analysis are optimized for LINUX-based systems, suggesting that students may need to become familiar with LINUX to use them effectively. The study also noted that some highly specialized tools have minimal documentation because they are intended for experienced users, meaning ODL facilitators may need to provide additional support for these specific tools.

The study concludes that the integration of existing, high-quality software tools and open learning resources is an effective strategy for developing responsive and up-to-date bioinformatics ODL courses. The researchers recommend using the developed scoring system to screen software for ODL compatibility. Tools that score higher than six can be integrated directly into curricula, while those with lower scores can still be used if facilitators provide additional instructional support to bridge the usability gap.

The implications of this research are significant for the future of science education in distance learning environments. By utilizing pre-evaluated, user-friendly tools, ODL institutions can meet the escalating global demand for bioinformatics professionals with a minimum commitment of resources and time. This approach allows for a more flexible and scalable way to teach complex "hard science" concepts, making specialized biological training accessible to a wider range of learners, including those in the workforce seeking to upskill.

title: Teaching Presence in K-12 Blended Learning Classes under the Alternative Delivery Mode
abstract: Flexible learning options and blended learning programs continue to serve marginalized student populations under the Alternative Delivery Mode of the Philippine K-12 system. However, blended learning interactions in these programs remain hidden. This exploratory case study sought to capture the interactions and experiences in three blended learning classes through the elements of the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework espoused by Garrison, Anderson, and Archer (2000). Qualitative data were gathered through interviews, focus group discussions, class observations, stored data, and field notes to investigate teacher and student blended learning interactions. An adapted version of the survey instrument based on the framework was also utilized to validate qualitative findings. Using content analysis and descriptive statistics, the study indicated strong teaching presence demonstrated through the roles and actions of K-12 teachers and students which lead to learning community building. Students manifested teaching presence through directing and regulating their learning. Areas for improvement which relate to teaching presence were also revealed, particularly in the communication and the timeliness of feedback, and online facilitation of discourse. This study justifies the CoI as a practical framework to understand and guide teaching and learning in K-12 blended learning programs. To highlight the role of teachers in learning community building, a CoI framework for the K-12 and a self-reflection tool for teachers are being proposed. Changes to the categories and indicators of the presences are recommended to further affirm the framework’s applicability in the K-12 setting.

Juliet Aleta R. Villanueva’s study, "Teaching Presence in K-12 Blended Learning Classes under the Alternative Delivery Mode," investigates how teaching presence manifests within the Philippine K-12 system's Alternative Delivery Mode (ADM). Using an exploratory case study design, the researcher examined three blended learning classes from three urban public schools through interviews, focus group discussions, observations, and data from Learning Management Systems and Facebook Messenger. The study applied the Community of Inquiry (CoI) model, categorizing teaching presence into design and organization, facilitating discourse, and direct instruction.

The findings demonstrate that teaching presence is strongly manifested and contributes significantly to building learning communities. Teachers showed strength in design and organization by providing clear instructions and goals, and they effectively facilitated discourse using technology like Facebook Messenger. Notably, the study revealed that teaching presence is not exclusive to instructors; students exhibited "peer-facilitation" during collaborative tasks, suggesting a dynamic interaction between teaching presence and cognitive presence.

Despite these strengths, students reported challenges regarding the timeliness of feedback and communication issues caused by technical difficulties or platform bugs. Some students also perceived a lack of presence in teachers who lacked proficiency with educational technology. The researcher proposes a modified CoI framework for K-12 that adds a "Self-direction" category and suggests a "CoI Self-Reflection Tool for Teachers" to help educators become active members of a learning community.

The article "Teaching Presence in K-12 Blended Learning Classes under the Alternative Delivery Mode" by Juliet Aleta R. Villanueva investigates the manifestation of teaching presence within the Philippine K-12 system's Alternative Delivery Mode (ADM). These programs are designed to target potential school leavers, minimize youth dropouts, and provide educational access to students in unusual circumstances. While blended learning (BL) is a vital component of these programs, the specific interactions and experiences within these digital and hybrid environments have remained largely unexamined in the K-12 context, as most existing research focuses on higher education in international settings.

The study addresses two primary research questions: how teaching presence is manifested in K-12 BL classes and how these interactions reveal the emergence of learning communities. To explore this, the researcher employed an exploratory case study design, treating three blended learning classes from three different urban public schools as a single case. The sample included five teachers and a range of 24 to 40 students. Data collection was comprehensive, utilizing interviews, focus group discussions, classroom observations, field notes, and stored data from Learning Management Systems (LMS) and Facebook Messenger group chats. The researcher also used an adapted version of the Community of Inquiry (CoI) survey to validate qualitative findings.

The theoretical framework used is the Community of Inquiry (CoI) model, which posits that a fruitful online learning community requires the interplay of three "presences": teaching presence (TP), social presence (SP), and cognitive presence (CP). Teaching presence is further categorized into design and organization, facilitating discourse, and direct instruction.

The findings indicate that teaching presence is strongly manifested in these K-12 classes, contributing significantly to the building of learning communities. Students reported positive experiences regarding the teachers' roles as instructors responsible for content and activities. Specifically, teachers demonstrated strong design and organization by providing clear instructions, subject goals, and deadlines, which provided necessary structure for student work. Facilitating discourse was also a noted strength, particularly in how teachers used technology to encourage communication and engagement. For example, teachers used Facebook Messenger and polls to prompt discussion and manage language learning.

Interestingly, the study revealed that teaching presence is not exclusive to the instructor in the K-12 setting. The researcher found evidence of student-driven teaching presence, particularly during online group work and collaborative tasks. Students engaged in "peer-facilitation," where they would teach classmates who were struggling to understand content. This suggests an interaction between teaching presence and cognitive presence, where students take on regulatory roles to achieve shared learning goals.

However, the study also identified specific areas for improvement. Students noted challenges regarding the timeliness of feedback, which received the lowest mean rating in the survey. Additionally, communication issues arose due to technical difficulties, such as platform bugs or updates, and some students perceived a lack of presence in teachers who were not proficient with educational technology.

The implications of this research are significant for the professional development of K-12 educators, especially as schools shift toward remote and online learning. The study justifies the use of the CoI framework as a practical tool for understanding and guiding K-12 blended learning. Based on the findings, the author proposes a modified CoI framework specifically for the K-12 setting. This proposed modification includes a new category under teaching presence called "Self-direction," which includes indicators such as monitoring/knowledge of cognition and strategy use. This addition accounts for the self-directed behaviors observed in students during online learning.

Furthermore, the researcher proposes a "CoI Self-Reflection Tool for Teachers." This tool is intended to help educators reflect on their own contributions to the learning community, moving beyond just being content deliverers to becoming active members of a learning community. The author suggests that such tools be integrated into in-service teacher training to help educators improve their course design, pedagogy, and ability to build trust and mutual respect within digital environments.

In conclusion, the study affirms that teaching presence is a vital driver of learning community building in K-12 blended learning. While teachers provide the essential structure and facilitation, students also manifest teaching-like behaviors through peer support and self-regulation. The research calls for a reconsideration of the CoI framework's indicators to better reflect the unique dynamics of K-12 learners, emphasizing the need for improved feedback timeliness and technological proficiency among educators.

title: Exploring the Potential of a Ticketing-Based Student Support System for Open and Distance e-Learning Institutions
abstract: Quality assurance in higher education can be examined in multiple dimensions, one being effective student support. It is arguably one of the most important aspects of an educational institution. This paper argues for the potential benefits of a ticketing-based system as part of an open and distance e-learning (ODeL) institution’s quality assurance initiatives in student support. In order to determine the ticketing-based system’s potential benefits, various educational ticketing-based support systems are reviewed. Aside from document reviews, interviews with the program chair, students, and support staff were also conducted as a way to identify the primary student support challenges in ODeL. Some of the issues that arose had to do with personalized support and interaction; response times; consistent and accurate solutions; clearly defined academic processes and policies; record keeping; the bulk of queries; and information lost during staff turnover. Interview data also revealed a set of criteria used to qualify excellent student support services both from an institutional and student perspective. Lastly, ODeL student support challenges that can be addressed by a ticketing-based system were assessed by analyzing the experiences of students, support staff, and faculty.
half:
The article "Exploring the Potential of a Ticketing-Based Student Support System for Open and Distance e-Learning Institutions" investigates how automated ticketing systems can enhance quality assurance in student support services within Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) environments. Because face-to-face interaction is limited in ODeL settings, reliable and timely support is vital for student retention and success.

At the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) within the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) program, students previously relied on at least eight different formal and informal online sources for information. This fragmentation leads to confusion and the risk of following outdated information. Institutional challenges identified include inconsistent response times, difficulties in record-keeping, loss of information during staff turnover, and the difficulty of providing personalized support to a diverse online student body.

Using a qualitative methodology, the researchers conducted a literature review and performed stakeholder interviews with BAMS students, alumni, and support staff. Findings indicate that ticketing-based systems offer significant benefits, such as improved workflows through automation, 24/7 access to a knowledge base, and data analytics insights. The implementation of Freshdesk in the BAMS program showed positive results by providing a centralized knowledge base that allows students to find solutions via articles before filing a ticket. This ensures information is accurate and up-to-date, while the ticketing feature ensures queries are tracked until resolution.

The authors conclude that ticketing-based systems are a promising intervention to improve support quality by making processes more efficient and responsive. They recommend that ODeL institutions adopt such systems as part of quality assurance frameworks, prioritizing ease of use and staff training. Institutions should also inform students of correct support channels to prevent the use of informal ones.

two:
The article "Exploring the Potential of a Ticketing-Based Student Support System for Open and Distance e-Learning Institutions" investigates how automated ticketing systems can enhance quality assurance (QA) in student support services within Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) environments. The authors argue that effective student support is a critical dimension of higher education quality assurance, facilitating smoother learning experiences and improving student retention and success. In ODeL settings, where face-to-face interaction is limited, providing reliable and timely support is particularly vital.

The problem addressed by the researchers is the lack of a centralized, reliable source of information for students, which leads to confusion and inefficiency. At the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU), specifically within the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) program, students previously relied on at least eight different online sources—both formal and informal—to find information regarding enrollment, academic policies, and registration. This fragmentation makes students susceptible to following outdated or conflicting information. Furthermore, the study identifies several institutional challenges, including inconsistent response times, difficulties in record-keeping and document tracking, loss of information during staff turnover, and the difficulty of providing personalized support to a diverse online student body.

To investigate these issues, the researchers employed a qualitative methodology involving a literature review and stakeholder interviews. The literature review examined existing ticketing-based support systems used in other higher education institutions, such as Nottingham Trent University, Ohio Wesleyan University, and the University of Sydney, which utilize platforms like Zendesk and Freshdesk. The researchers used convenience sampling to conduct interviews with BAMS students, alumni, and support staff to capture diverse perspectives on the transition from traditional support methods to an experimental Freshdesk-based ticketing system. Data were analyzed using thematic content analysis to identify common patterns across the interviews.

The findings reveal that ticketing-based systems offer significant benefits for ODeL institutions. The literature review showed that these systems improve workflows through automation, provide remote 24/7 access to a knowledge base, and allow universities to gain insights through data analytics. The stakeholder interviews identified several primary challenges in ODeL student support, including student unawareness of available services, the "trial and error" nature of finding information, and inconsistent response times. From an institutional perspective, staff noted that tracking student issues and maintaining records during staff turnover were significant hurdles.

The study also identified the criteria that constitute "excellent" student support services. According to the participants, an effective system must be centralized and characterized by high response rates, issue-tracking capabilities, accurate and consistent solutions, clearly defined academic and administrative policies, adequately trained staff, and a degree of personalization. The implementation of the Freshdesk system in the BAMS program showed positive results, such as providing a centralized knowledge base that allows students to find solutions through articles before filing a ticket. This centralization ensures that information is accurate, up-to-date, and accessible, while the ticketing feature ensures that no query is overlooked and that issues are tracked until resolution.

In conclusion, the authors argue that a ticketing-based system is a promising intervention for improving the quality of student support in ODeL institutions. Such systems address the complexity and bulk of student queries by making the process more efficient and responsive. By utilizing automation, reporting, and a robust knowledge base, institutions can move toward a model of self-service that reduces the volume of repetitive queries while ensuring that complex issues are handled with accountability. The study concludes that these systems help bridge the gap between the institution and the student, ultimately supporting the university's mission of providing quality learning opportunities.

The implications of this research suggest that ODeL institutions should consider adopting similar technology-based support systems as part of their broader quality assurance frameworks. The authors recommend that when implementing such technology, universities must prioritize user ease of use and ensure that support staff receive adequate training. Additionally, institutions should engage in activities to inform students about the correct support channels to prevent them from using incorrect or informal channels. The researchers suggest that future studies should utilize larger, more diverse sample sizes and employ probability sampling to generalize findings across different programs. Further research is also recommended to examine the usability and acceptability of these systems and to investigate why students might continue to submit queries even when solutions are available in a knowledge base.

title: Use of Tracer Studies to Enhance the UPOU Environment and Natural Resources Management Graduate Program
abstract: Distance education has evolved and improved since the advent of the Internet. Open and distance e-learning (ODeL) for higher education has allowed ease of access to higher institutions of learning for professionals and adult learners. The University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) has been offering the Diploma and Master of Environment and Natural Resources Management (MENRM) since 1999 through open and distance learning. The current program now offers a ladderized program with two-exits: a Diploma and a Master’s degree. This paper presents the results of an analysis of the profile of MENRM applicants and a tracer study on graduates about their motivations for choosing to pursue graduate studies at UPOU. It also explored how having earned a postgraduate degree has affected their current jobs. The admission information showed that more than 90% of admission applicants were employees of private institutions and government offices occupying mid-level and senior management positions mostly based in the Philippines. The study has shown that their work schedule was an important consideration in pursuing a MENRM graduate program. The tracer study of 29 MENRM graduates also showed that the increase in their work responsibility and compensation can be attributed to their successful completion of the program. Moreover, it has contributed to their personal and professional development, particularly in their increased capacity for project and people management and policy making, as well as improved skills in research, technical, and critical thinking. However, the enrichment and development of communication skills as a required 21st century skill of MENRM graduates need to be better addressed in the program.
half:
The study "Use of Tracer Studies to Enhance the UPOU Environment and Natural Resources Management Graduate Program" by Consuelo Dl. Habito and Maripres U. Sarinas evaluates the effectiveness of the Diploma and Master of Environment and Natural Resources Management (MENRM) program at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). Using a mixed-methods approach, the researchers analyzed admission data from 534 applicants and conducted an online tracer study with 29 graduates from school years 2010-2014.

Applicant profiles showed that 91% were employed, with 48% in private institutions and 34% in government offices. Primary motivations for enrollment included the desire to enhance knowledge and skills, the flexibility of the ODeL format, and the program's relevance to current employment.

The tracer study revealed significant professional benefits. A majority of respondents (52%) experienced job changes during their studies, 62% reported a change in professional rank, 41% were promoted, and 55% reported higher salaries. The program successfully enhanced academic knowledge (79%), confidence in independent learning (72%), critical thinking (65%), research skills (62%), and learning efficiency (62%). Graduates also reported growth in technical responsibility (75%), people management (60%), and policy-making roles (55%).

However, only 38% of graduates felt the program "very much" improved their communication skills. The authors conclude that while the program successfully builds capacity and catalyzes career advancement, the curriculum should strengthen its focus on environmental communication to better prepare graduates to influence public perception and policy.
