The study titled "Use of Tracer Studies to Enhance the UPOU Environment and Natural Resources Management Graduate Program" by Consuelo Dl. Habito and Maripres U. Sarinas examines the impact and effectiveness of the Diploma and Master of Environment and Natural Resources Management (MENRM) program offered by the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU).

The problem addressed by the authors is the need to assess whether an open and distance e-learning (ODeL) graduate program effectively contributes to the capacity-building of professionals in the field of environmental and natural resources management. Because distance education serves a specific demographic of working professionals, the researchers sought to determine if the program meets its objectives of providing technical skills, critical thinking, and management competencies necessary for career advancement and environmental advocacy.

The context of the study is the evolving landscape of higher education through ODeL, which provides accessibility to adult learners. The MENRM program, established in 1998, utilizes a ladderized system allowing students to exit with either a Diploma (after 24 units) or a Master’s degree (after 27 units, research courses, and a capstone project). The study focuses on the period between school years 2010-2014 to evaluate the program's relevance to the professional needs of its students.

The researchers employed a mixed-methods approach to gather data. First, they analyzed admission data from 534 MENRM applicants to establish professional profiles, including employment status, sector, and geographic location. They also reviewed admission essays to identify the primary motivations for applying. Second, they conducted an online tracer study via Google Docs with 29 MENRM graduates. This tracer study aimed to capture post-graduation outcomes, including changes in employment, career advancement, salary increases, and the perceived impact of the curriculum on personal and professional skill sets.

The findings are divided into applicant profiles and graduate outcomes. Regarding applicants, the study found that 91% were employed, with the majority working in private institutions (48%) or government offices (34%). Most applicants were based in the Philippines (88%), particularly in Metro Manila and South Luzon. The primary motivations for applying were the desire to gain or enhance knowledge and skills, the flexibility offered by the ODeL format, and the direct relevance of the program to their current work.

The tracer study of graduates revealed significant professional benefits. A majority of respondents (52%) experienced job changes during their studies, and 62% reported a change in their professional rank during the program. Notably, 41% of graduates reported being promoted to higher positions after earning their degree. Economically, 55% of respondents reported receiving higher salaries after completing the program.

In terms of skill development, the MENRM program was highly successful in enhancing several key areas. Graduates reported significant improvements in academic knowledge (79%), confidence in independent learning (72%), critical thinking (65%), research skills (62%), and learning efficiency (62%). Furthermore, the degree contributed to increased professional responsibilities, with graduates reporting growth in technical responsibility (75%), people management (60%), and policy-making roles (55%).

However, the findings also identified a specific area for improvement. While the results for communication skills were generally favorable, they were notably lower than other competencies; only 38% of graduates felt the program "very much" improved their communication skills, compared to much higher percentages for research and technical skills.

The authors conclude that the MENRM program successfully fulfills its mission of capacity-building for environmental professionals through the ODeL modality. The program is particularly effective at supporting working professionals by providing the flexibility required to balance employment and education. The study confirms that the degree serves as a significant catalyst for career advancement, professional promotion, and increased technical and managerial responsibility.

The implications of these findings suggest that while the program is robust in technical and research training, there is a clear need to strengthen the curriculum's focus on communication skills. The authors emphasize that environmental communication is a vital 21st-century skill, necessary for translating scientific research into actionable information that can influence public perception and policy. By addressing this gap, the program can better prepare graduates to advocate for environmental sustainability and effectively communicate complex resource management issues to diverse stakeholders.

title: Smart Lecture Video Production: A Case Study with Philosophy and Media Literacy*
abstract: This paper describes a case study of a method of creating video lectures while reducing cost and improving quality. Since 1985, the Open University of Japan (OUJ) has provided TV and radio broadcast lectures, as well as face-to-face lectures. As an additional lecture style, full online courses were launched in 2016. I was appointed start-up project manager, so I developed the Smart Lecture Video Production method to prepare the online courses. Our mission was to develop six undergraduate courses and two graduate courses within a year. Because hiring a video crew is generally expensive, we decided to try the entire development process ourselves. However, the project faced many problems, such as a limited budget, tight deadlines and lack of staff. To solve these problems, I created the following philosophy: we will achieve this project for all learners, for lecturers and staff. In accordance with this philosophy, we also developed production tools and media literacy instructional materials. As a result, the project mission was accomplished. Currently, the Smart Lecture Video Production method is applied to not only online courses but also some TV broadcasting productions.
half:
In "Smart Lecture Video Production: A Case Study with Philosophy and Media Literacy," Tomotsugu Kondo describes how The Open University of Japan (OUJ) developed eight online courses in one year despite limited budgets, tight deadlines, and a lack of professional video crews. The project aimed to produce broadcast-quality content using non-professional staff by implementing a mission-driven philosophy focused on learners, lecturers, and staff.

To support learners, the institution prioritized accessibility by implementing strict audio loudness standards and a custom closed caption function for the Moodle video player. For lecturers, the project utilized renovated warehouse studios and a custom PowerPoint macro-based prompter tool that synchronized scripts with slide transitions to ensure fluent delivery. To assist staff, the author developed a "Script Sheet Generating Tool" using PowerPoint macros, which automatically generated production scripts and time predictions from presentation notes. Technical staff were further supported through video manuals and a television lecture series.

The project was successful, launching the courses in April 2016 and attracting over 4,000 students in the first semester. The methodology allowed for various video formats, including on-location interviews and hand-drawn explanations, with much of the production completed in-house. Kondo concludes that while technical skills are necessary, success depends on a shared philosophy and trust between lecturers and staff. Institutions can overcome resource constraints by investing in custom-built digital tools and a clear organizational mission.

The article "Smart Lecture Video Production: A Case Study with Philosophy and Media Literacy" by Tomotsugu Kondo details a strategic approach to developing high-quality online courses at The Open University of Japan (OUJ). Faced with the challenge of launching a full suite of online courses within a single year, the author developed a specialized production method designed to overcome significant resource constraints.

**Problem and Context**
The Open University of Japan has a long history of providing educational content through television and radio broadcasts. In 2016, the institution aimed to expand this by launching eight full online courses. Unlike traditional classroom or broadcast settings, these online courses required students to engage with video lectures, documents, and discussions via a Learning Management System (LMS). 

The project faced several critical obstacles: a limited budget, tight deadlines, and a lack of specialized staff. Hiring professional video crews was deemed too expensive, necessitating a solution where non-professional staff could produce broadcast-quality content. The core problem was how to achieve high production standards for diverse lecture styles—ranging from straight talk to experiments—without the financial or human resources typically required for professional media production.

**Method**
To address these challenges, the author established a guiding philosophy: "we will achieve this project for all learners, for lecturers and staff." This mission-driven approach dictated the development of specific tools and training methods categorized by the three groups identified in the philosophy.

For learners, the focus was on accessibility and quality. This included developing a custom closed caption function for the Moodle video player to comply with Japanese disability legislation and implementing strict audio loudness standards (within -24LKFS ±1dB) to ensure a consistent listening experience. To ensure pedagogical quality, the project utilized Instructional Designers (IDers) selected from the faculty, including peer reviewers from different fields to ensure clarity.

For lecturers, the goal was to create a comfortable and efficient environment. The project utilized renovated warehouse spaces as studios and developed a custom PowerPoint macro-based prompter tool. This tool allowed lecturers to read scripts synchronized with their slide transitions, enabling fluent delivery without the need for manual page-turning.

For staff, the focus was on skill development and efficiency. The author developed a "Script Sheet Generating Tool" using PowerPoint macros. This tool allowed staff to input tags into the notes section of a presentation to automatically generate detailed production scripts (including camera work and telop instructions) and provided a time prediction function based on character counts. Additionally, the project provided video manuals for equipment and a television lecture series on "Creative Technologies for Digital Content" to motivate and train non-professional technical staff.

**Findings**
The implementation of the Smart Lecture Video Production method yielded successful results. In April 2016, the eight online courses were launched, attracting a cumulative enrollment of over 4,000 students in the first semester. The project successfully produced a wide variety of video formats, including on-location interviews, straight talk lectures, and hand-drawn explanations. 

The author notes that while some parts of the production were outsourced, a significant portion was completed in-house by the internal team. The use of automated tools, such as automatic speech recognition for closed captioning and the macro-based script generator, proved essential in meeting the tight deadlines and managing the workload of a small staff.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The author concludes that the project was a success, meeting the original objective of producing high-quality e-learning content under strict constraints. A key finding is that while technical skills can be acquired through training, the success of such a project relies heavily on a shared philosophy and a relationship of trust between lecturers and staff. The author emphasizes that collaboration between professionals and non-professionals is a viable pathway to creating high-quality educational content.

The implications of this study suggest that educational institutions can overcome budget and staffing limitations by investing in custom-built digital tools and a clear organizational mission. The "Smart Lecture Video Production" method has since been applied beyond online courses to assist in some television broadcasting productions, demonstrating its versatility in various media contexts.

title: Perceptions of Students to Open and Distance Learning of Review Classes in a Review Center in the Philippines
abstract: The Commission on Higher Education (CHED, 2007) defined review centers as hubs offering programs or courses of study intended to refresh and enhance knowledge, competencies, and skills of students who have already studied in any formal school to prepare them for upcoming licensure examinations given by any license-giving body such as those given by the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC). There were several review centers that offered open and distance learning aside from their brick-and-mortar classes in several locations in the Philippines. This had been possible due to technological advances that led to the distribution of knowledge using internet-enabled services. Review for Global Opportunities (RGO) Review Center, a CHED-accredited review center, was one of the leading review centers in the field of psychometrician review in the Philippines with having over 10 awards for the past 3 years and it has been offering the face-to-face classes in their review program for aspiring psychometricians. This 2018, RGO offered a home-based study program and delivered online. The study examined the perception of students enrolled in the said distance learning review program for aspiring psychometricians by RGO Review Center using a survey questionnaire partially adopted from Alam, Waqar, Zaman, Shehzadi, and Mehmood (2012) to provide a better understanding to predict student satisfaction, especially in online learning environments.
half:
The study "Perceptions of Students to Open and Distance Learning of Review Classes in a Review Center in the Philippines" by Aaron Bryan A. Lopez investigates student perceptions of a pilot distance education program at the Review for Global Opportunities (RGO) Review Center. The research focuses on the psychometrician review program, which transitioned to a home-based, online format in 2018 to accommodate students facing geographical or time constraints. The RGO Review Center utilized print-based materials and online delivery via Facebook, including live and recorded video lectures, review notes, mock examinations, and answer keys.

Findings indicated that respondents were predominantly female and aged 20–29. The primary motivation for choosing distance education was flexibility of time and location (69.6%), followed by work commitments (52.2%) and family commitments (34.8%). Regarding teaching, students generally agreed that the instructional medium was relevant and content met expectations, though feedback on examinations often arrived months after completion. Most students found learning materials self-explanatory, though some experienced workload congestion due to a lack of structured study schedules.

The study concludes that converting offline materials to online formats is insufficient for success. A comprehensive systems approach is required, including structured scheduling, interactive elements, and robust support services. Recommendations include establishing weekly learning schedules, providing prompt feedback through self-grading assessments, facilitating formal asynchronous group discussions, and providing clearer support regarding registration and the transition to home-based modes.

The study "Perceptions of Students to Open and Distance Learning of Review Classes in a Review Center in the Philippines" by Aaron Bryan A. Lopez investigates student perceptions of a pilot distance education program at the Review for Global Opportunities (RGO) Review Center. Specifically, the research examines the psychometrician review program, which transitioned to a home-based, online format in 2018 to accommodate students facing geographical or time constraints. The researcher addresses a gap in existing literature, as most research on distance education focuses on formal higher education institutions rather than the specific context of Philippine review centers.

The RGO Review Center utilized a combination of print-based materials and online delivery via Facebook, including live and recorded video lectures, review notes, mock examinations, and answer keys. Using a survey research method, the study targeted students enrolled in the program between August and October 2018. The research aimed to identify demographic characteristics, reasons for choosing distance learning, and student perceptions regarding teaching, learning materials, and learner support services.

Findings indicated that the respondents were predominantly female and aged 20–29. The primary motivation for choosing distance education was the flexibility of time and location (69.6%), followed by work commitments (52.2%) and family commitments (34.8%). Regarding teaching, students generally agreed that the instructional medium was relevant and content met expectations. However, feedback on instructor promptness was mixed; many students noted that feedback on examinations often arrived months after completion.

In terms of learning materials, most respondents found the materials self-explanatory and noted an increased use of the internet. While some found group discussions useful, formal discussions were not an explicit part of the program, with interactions mostly limited to student-prompted questions in comment sections. Regarding workload, most students did not find the workload excessive, though some experienced "workload congestion" due to a lack of structured study schedules.

The study concludes that simply converting offline materials to online formats is insufficient for a successful distance education program. A comprehensive systems approach is required, including structured scheduling, interactive elements, and robust support services. To increase satisfaction, the researcher recommends establishing clear weekly learning schedules, providing prompt feedback through self-grading assessments, allowing for downloadable materials in secure formats, facilitating formal asynchronous group discussions, and providing clearer support regarding registration and the transition to home-based modes. Future research should explore management, quality assurance, and comparative implementation across different educational contexts.

The research specifically focuses on the psychometrician review program, which was transitioned to a home-based, online format in 2018 to accommodate students with geographical or time constraints.

The problem addressed by the researcher is the lack of existing literature regarding the effectiveness of distance education within the specific context of review centers in the Philippines. While review centers are defined by the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) as hubs to enhance knowledge for licensure examinations, most existing research focuses on formal higher education institutions. As review centers adopt technological affordances like the internet to offer distance learning, there is a need to understand student satisfaction and the effectiveness of these programs to ensure they meet the rigorous demands of professional licensure preparation.

The context of the study is the RGO Review Center, a CHED-accredited institution known for its psychometrician review program. In 2018, the center launched a pilot distance education program utilizing a combination of print-based materials (books and examinations) and online delivery via Facebook. The online component included live and recorded video lectures, review notes, mock examinations, and answer keys. The study was conducted between August and October 2018, targeting students who were already halfway through the program.

The researcher employed a survey research method, utilizing a questionnaire partially adopted from Alam et al. (2012). The survey was distributed through an exclusive Facebook group containing the enrolled students. The study aimed to answer five specific research questions regarding the demographic characteristics of distance learners, the reasons for choosing distance learning, and student perceptions regarding teaching, learning materials, and learner support services.

The findings revealed that the respondent group was predominantly female and aged 20–29, reflecting a demographic of recent graduates. The primary motivation for choosing distance education was the flexibility of time and location (69.6%), followed by work commitments (52.2%) and family commitments (34.8%). Regarding teaching, students generally agreed that the instructional medium was relevant and that the content met their expectations. However, feedback on the promptness of instructor feedback was mixed; while some agreed, many were neutral or disagreed, noting that feedback on exams often arrived months after completion.

In terms of learning materials, most respondents agreed that the materials were self-explanatory and that their use of the internet increased. However, there were conflicting views regarding group discussions; while some found them useful, the study noted that formal group discussions were not explicitly part of the program, with interactions mostly limited to student-prompted questions in comment sections. Regarding workload, most students did not feel the workload was excessive, though a small number strongly disagreed, potentially due to a lack of a structured study schedule which led to "workload congestion."

The study concludes that while distance education offers significant flexibility for students with various life commitments, there is a distinct difference between simply making materials accessible online and providing a comprehensive distance education system. The pilot program demonstrated that simply converting offline materials to online formats is insufficient. A successful distance education program requires a systems approach, including structured scheduling, interactive elements, and robust support services, rather than just the digital distribution of content.

The implications of this research suggest that review centers must move beyond a "trial and error" approach when implementing distance learning. To increase student satisfaction, the researcher provides several recommendations: establishing a clear weekly learning schedule to manage cognitive load, providing prompt feedback through self-grading assessments, allowing students to download materials in secure formats (like PDF), facilitating formal asynchronous group discussions to bridge the gap between instructors and students, and providing clearer learner support regarding registration and the transition from face-to-face to home-based modes. Finally, the researcher suggests that future studies should explore the management, quality assurance, and comparative implementation of distance education across different educational contexts.

title: Using Facebook Metrics to Measure Student Engagement in Moodle
abstract: Facebook uses engagement rates as a metric for social media managers and marketers to measure how effectively a page, a post, a comment, a brand, or a topic is able to engage the target audience. Studies have proposed the use of these metrics for other types of online measurements in applications and industries other than social media. This concept paper proposes the use of a modified Facebook engagement rate formula to (i) measure students’ engagement with forum posts using virtual learning environments such as Moodle and (ii) get data from students regarding which topics or posts engage them more in the learning process. While virtual learning environments have their own logs and learning analytics software, and studies have explored the use of Facebook as a discrete and supplementary platform to traditional learning management systems, this paper fills the research gap by applying Facebook’s engagement rate formula to Moodle itself. Applying an existing social media audience engagement formula to an online course may provide instructors and educational institutions valuable feedback on what types of posts, comments, or topics make students interact and engage more in online learning sessions. Such an exercise may lead to new metrics which distance learning institutions could use to calibrate their content with the objective of improving students’ interaction and engagement with instructors, fellow students, and the online course in general.

The concept paper "Using Facebook Metrics to Measure Student Engagement in Moodle" by Leonardo Magno addresses the challenge of accurately measuring student engagement within virtual learning environments (VLEs). While learning management systems like Moodle and Blackboard possess built-in analytics and data logs to track student behavior, these tools often focus on usage data rather than the depth of interaction. Previous research has explored using Facebook as a supplementary platform to complement Moodle, but these studies typically treat the two as separate entities. Magno identifies a research gap: the lack of application of social media engagement formulas—specifically Facebook’s engagement rate—directly to the data generated within a learning management system.

The context of this research is situated within the growing field of learning analytics and the increasing popularity of social media among university students. While social media metrics are widely used in marketing to measure how effectively content engages an audience, their application in the distance learning sector remains under-explored. The author notes that while data mining is already used to study student behavior, there is an opportunity to marry Moodle’s data logs with social media calculation methods to provide more meaningful feedback to instructors regarding which specific topics or posts effectively drive student interaction.

To address this gap, the author proposes a methodology centered on a modified version of the Facebook Post Engagement Rate (PER) formula. The standard Facebook formula calculates engagement by taking the sum of clicks, comments, shares, and likes, and dividing that sum by the "reach" (the number of people who saw the post). Magno proposes a modified Moodle Post Engagement Rate (MPER) formula: MPER = (CL + C + L) / R. In this adaptation, "Shares" are removed because content in a self-contained online course is typically restricted to class members and not shared publicly. "Clicks" (CL) represent how many times a post was visited, "Comments" (C) represent the number of replies, and "Likes" (L) represent student approval. To facilitate this, the author suggests implementing Facebook-like features in Moodle, such as a "thumbs-up" or "Like" widget, to replace or supplement the standard rating feature.

The "Reach" (R) in this model is defined not as the total number of students enrolled in a course, but as the unique number of students who actually viewed the specific forum post. This distinction is crucial because, as the author argues, a high number of views does not necessarily equate to high engagement if those views do not result in further interaction.

Because this is a concept paper, the findings are based on a hypothetical application of the MPER formula using dummy data. The author presents a scenario involving two forum posts in a class of 30 students. Post A reaches only 10 students, but those students interact heavily by clicking, commenting, and liking the post multiple times. Post B reaches all 30 students, but the students only click the post once and offer no comments or likes. When processed through the MPER formula, Post A yields an engagement rate of 7%, while Post B yields only 1%. The results of this simulation suggest that the MPER formula successfully identifies Post A as the more engaging piece of content, despite it having a much lower "reach" than Post B. This demonstrates that the formula can distinguish between passive viewing and active, meaningful engagement.

The paper concludes that it is indeed possible to aggregate data using social media formulas and apply them to online courses to gain insights into student interaction. By using the MPER, instructors can move beyond simple usage logs to understand the qualitative impact of their content. The author suggests that identifying posts with high engagement rates could allow educators to predict student behavior and identify which types of topics or discussion prompts are most effective at eliciting interaction.

The implications of this research are significant for the design and management of distance learning. For educational institutions, adopting such metrics could provide a way to calibrate course content to improve student interaction with instructors and peers. Rather than measuring academic performance or grades, this metric focuses on the vitality of the learning community. The author recommends that future research involve applying this modified formula to actual Moodle courses over an entire academic term to test its real-world utility. Furthermore, the author suggests that once high-engagement content is identified, a content analysis could be performed to codify the specific characteristics of successful posts, potentially allowing for the predictive design of highly engaging online curricula. While the proposal is specific to Moodle, the concept is applicable to any learning management system.

title: Developing Facebook as an Accessible and Inclusive Online Personal Learning Platform: Ubiquity is Key
abstract: A myriad of online personal learning (OPL) platforms has been developed over the past few years in order to address the burgeoning demand for avant-garde learning environments. These online learning portals have been developed to engage 21st century learners through interactive media, advanced study tools, and other innovative applications. In the Philippines, however, the use of these popular learning platforms is not fully realized. The challenge lies in the accessibility and inclusivity concerns of these OPL platforms and other related issues such as application restrictions. With this, learners especially from marginalized and differently-abled communities have difficulty accessing popular learning portals. Therefore, this study proposed that Facebook be developed as an accessible and inclusive OPL platform as its impact as a collaborative learning space was greatly realized. This was further supported by related studies and personal experiences of the author as an educator and as an open and distance learner. Facebook, as the most popular online medium today, had undoubtedly become a pervasive global informational hub and thus this study posited that it may be considered as a breeding ground for collaborative learning and knowledge creation. Since educational professionals and system developers were focused on constructing new learning platforms, the potential of Facebook as an OPL platform was deemed overlooked. This paper argued that developing an existing ubiquitous social media platform such as Facebook, can better address accessibility and inclusivity issues rather than building new learning systems which posed more constraints to different types of educators and learners in the Philippine context.

In the article "Developing Facebook as an Accessible and Inclusive Online Personal Learning Platform: Ubiquity is Key," Hannah Kimberly I. Obar addresses the digital divide in the Philippines, specifically regarding the accessibility of Online Personal Learning (OPL) platforms. While Learning Management Systems (LMS) like Moodle and Blackboard facilitate modern learning, they are often inaccessible in the Philippines due to high costs, connectivity issues, and device storage constraints. This leaves marginalized communities and differently-abled learners at a disadvantage.

Using qualitative research methods based on personal observations and the management of 21 Facebook Groups used as makeshift LMS platforms since 2015, the author identifies a gap between sophisticated LMS tools and actual accessibility for the average Filipino learner. The findings reveal that while traditional LMS platforms offer advanced tracking tools, students engage more quickly via Facebook Groups because the application is already installed and the interface is familiar. Facebook Messenger also proved more efficient for communication than traditional discussion forums.

The author proposes "Facebook Classroom," a specialized mode within Facebook that incorporates essential LMS features like gradebooks, assignment bins, and test administration. This proposed platform would include specific modes to assist learners with visual, hearing, navigation, or overstimulation issues. The study suggests that multi-sectoral collaboration is needed to provide discounted data access for this platform, leveraging Facebook's ubiquity to bridge the digital divide.

The article "Developing Facebook as an Accessible and Inclusive Online Personal Learning Platform: Ubiquity is Key" by Hannah Kimberly I. Obar addresses the critical issue of the digital divide in the Philippines, specifically regarding the accessibility and inclusivity of Online Personal Learning (OPL) platforms. While various Learning Management Systems (LMS) like Blackboard, Moodle, and Edmodo exist to facilitate 21st-century learning, the author argues that these platforms are often not fully realized in the Philippine context due to high costs, application restrictions, and connectivity issues.

The problem is centered on the fact that many popular OPL platforms are designed for technologically advanced communities. In the Philippines, access to high-speed internet and expensive data packages is often limited to privileged urban areas, leaving marginalized communities and differently-abled learners at a disadvantage. The author notes that a significant portion of Philippine public schools lack internet connectivity, and even when connectivity is available, students often face the dilemma of having to choose between downloading educational applications or other essential apps due to limited device storage and data constraints. Furthermore, existing LMS platforms may present compatibility issues with various mobile gadgets and lack the seamless, multi-modal inclusivity required for students with different learning needs.

The context of this study is rooted in the Philippine educational landscape, characterized by a growing demand for open and distance learning, as seen in the work of the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). Despite the prestige of institutions using Moodle, the author identifies a gap between the availability of these tools and their actual accessibility for the average Filipino learner. The study is framed by the concept of "ubiquity," noting that Facebook is a pervasive global informational hub and is used extensively by Filipinos, who are among the most active social media users globally.

To investigate this, the author employed qualitative research methods. The study relied on the author's personal observations and experiences as both an educator and an online learner. Specifically, the author utilized data gathered from managing 21 Facebook Groups used as makeshift LMS platforms for college courses since 2015. This practical application served as a foundation for analyzing how social media features can be repurposed for formal education. The research also incorporated a review of related studies to support the potential of social networking sites as pedagogical tools.

The findings reveal that while established LMS platforms like Blackboard, Moodle, and Edmodo offer sophisticated tools for tracking progress and facilitating discussion, they face significant hurdles in the Philippine setting regarding ease of access and user experience. The author's observations from using Facebook Groups showed that students were more likely to engage quickly and without technical objection because they already had the application installed and were familiar with its interface. Facebook Messenger proved to be a more efficient medium for quick communication than the discussion forums of traditional LMSs. The study found that the "ubiquity" of Facebook—its presence on almost every student's device and its low barrier to entry—makes it a superior candidate for reaching a wider, more diverse demographic of learners.

The author concludes that rather than attempting to build new, resource-heavy learning systems that pose more constraints to educators and students, the focus should shift toward developing an existing, ubiquitous platform. The author proposes the creation of "Facebook Classroom," a specialized mode within Facebook that incorporates essential LMS features such as calendar notifications, to-do lists, test administration, assignment submission bins, gradebooks, and discussion forums. This proposed platform would be designed to be both accessible and inclusive, featuring specific modes to assist learners with visual impairments, hearing impairments, navigation difficulties, and overstimulation issues.

The implications of this study suggest a need for a multi-sectoral collaboration. The author recommends a partnership between the Philippine government, major telecommunication networks (such as Smart and Globe), Facebook management, and application developers. Such a collaboration would aim to provide free or discounted data access specifically for "Facebook Classroom," thereby mitigating the financial barriers to online learning. While the author acknowledges potential challenges—such as security risks like hacking, the potential for student distraction by personal social media content, and the psychological stress of constant notifications—the study posits that the benefits of increased engagement and accessibility far outweigh these drawbacks. title: Computer Self-Efficacy and Attitude Towards e-learning: A Study Among Graduate Students in Nursing in an Open University in the Philippines
abstract: With the advent of computer technologies and Internet, the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) has adopted online teaching and learning making education more accessible to students using the Internet. This study investigated the computer self-efficacy and attitudes of Master of Arts in Nursing graduate students towards e-learning. Results showed that the students’ computer self-efficacy skills were high in their beginning skills and rated fairly in their advanced skills. The students were also very confident in using their computers and had a positive attitude towards their learning through the Internet. The findings also revealed that there was no significant relationship between the students’ computer self-efficacy skills and attitude towards e-learning with a p-value of 0.902. This means that the students’ positive attitude towards e-learning does not affect their computer self-efficacy skills. It was concluded that even if the students have beginning skills in using their computers, they still feel positive in their studies.
half:
Queenie Roxas-Ridulme’s study investigates computer self-efficacy (CSE) and attitudes toward e-learning among 33 Master of Arts in Nursing (MAN) students at the University of the Philippines Open University. Using an online survey, the research analyzed how these students perceive their computer abilities and their views on online learning environments.

The findings indicate that students possess high computer self-efficacy at a "beginning" level, though they rated "fairly" in the "advanced" category. While confident in basic tasks like moving a cursor, they showed lower confidence in complex tasks such as troubleshooting hardware or software. Additionally, these students do not extensively use the Internet for educational research, potentially because they are in a non-computer-related discipline.

Regarding attitudes, students demonstrated a highly positive view of e-learning, yielding a total mean score of 4.01. They perceive e-learning as a useful, efficient, and flexible tool for continuing education that facilitates communication and offers equal opportunities for different personality types.

Statistical analysis revealed no significant relationship between computer self-efficacy and attitudes toward e-learning (p-value = 0.902), suggesting that a positive attitude does not depend on a student's level of computer confidence. The researcher recommends encouraging students to use academic databases more extensively and suggests implementing e-counselling to support students facing study difficulties.

The study "Computer Self-Efficacy and Attitude Towards e-learning: A Study Among Graduate Students in Nursing in an Open University in the Philippines" by Queenie Roxas-Ridulme investigates how Master of Arts in Nursing (MAN) students at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) perceive their ability to use computers and their attitudes toward online learning environments. The research seeks to describe the computer self-efficacy (CSE) and attitudes toward e-learning among these students and to determine if a correlation exists between these two variables.

The methodology employed an online survey to collect data from 33 MAN students. The participants were primarily female (70%), mostly aged 21–40 (82%), and a majority were single (76%) and residing offshore (61%). To measure the variables, the researcher used the Computer Self-Efficacy Scale for Adults created by Murphy (1989) and a questionnaire regarding attitudes toward e-learning. Data were analyzed using descriptive analysis and SPSS.

The findings revealed that the students' computer self-efficacy skills were high in the "beginning" category and rated "fairly" in the "advanced" category. While students showed high confidence in basic tasks like handling USB discs or moving a cursor, they showed lower confidence in more complex tasks, such as troubleshooting computer problems or understanding the intricacies of computer hardware and software. The study noted that these students are not utilizing the Internet extensively for educational purposes, such as researching via databases, which may be due to the fact that they are in a non-computer-related discipline.

Regarding attitudes, the students demonstrated a highly positive attitude toward e-learning, with a total mean score of 4.01. They viewed e-learning as a useful tool for continuing education, an efficient supplement to traditional classrooms, and a method that offers flexibility by delivering material anytime and anywhere. They also felt that e-learning provides equal opportunities for both shy and extroverted students and facilitates communication with teachers.

Crucially, the statistical analysis showed no significant relationship between the students' computer self-efficacy skills and their attitude toward e-learning, yielding a p-value of 0.902. This indicates that a student's positive attitude toward e-learning does not necessarily depend on or affect their level of computer self-efficacy.

The study concludes that MAN students possess a high level of beginning-level computer self-efficacy and a high level of positive attitude toward e-learning. The researcher recommends that students be encouraged to use the Internet and academic databases more extensively for their studies and suggests that the program could implement e-counselling to support students who encounter difficulties with their studies.

title: Association Between Nursing Students’ Self-Regulation and Online Learning Self-Efficacy
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has caused the suspension of face-to-face classes worldwide, which resulted in a shift to online learning. This presented a new challenge to students to improve their ability to complete tasks successfully and to direct their focus on acquiring knowledge and skills actively. Self-regulation (SR) and online learning self-efficacy (OLSE) are two important factors in online learning environments. SR allows learners to actively initiate and direct themselves, while OLSE refers to one’s beliefs and confidence in their abilities to complete or engage in a specific task required of online learners. Several studies conducted in Asia revealed that college students have low to moderate SR. Meanwhile, there is little known information about self-efficacy (SE) in an online learning environment. Similarly, limited literature supports the results; however, other studies suggest a positive and significant relationship between SR and SE for learning. The objectives of the study were to determine and describe the association between nursing students’ SR and OLSE Snowball sampling through social networking sites within Pampanga resulted in a sample of 166 nursing students. The results revealed that nursing students have moderate levels of SR (x = 54.75; SD = 10.60) and OLSE (x = 93.01; SD = 25.03). Pearson correlation coefficient revealed a statistically significant and strong positive association between nursing students’ SR and OLSE (r = .60; p = < .00). Thus, the academic administration and nurse educators should explore the dynamics between the two variables and develop programs that may improve SR and OLSE.

In this context, self-regulation (SR)—the ability to initiate and monitor one's own learning—and online learning self-efficacy (OLSE)—the belief in one's ability to succeed in online tasks—became critical for academic success. title: Open Educational Resources and Cost Savings Efforts: Lessons from WOU
abstract: As is the case with many open universities, Wawasan Open University relies on course development of custom-designed course materials with self-instructional properties using commissioned writers. These course materials are usually developed as adaption of textbooks or licensed course materials from other institutions. This eventually took a toll on the finances of the university as it was becoming costly to develop course materials using this model. As it is, proponents of open educational resources (OER) claim that significant cost savings are possible when OER replaces traditional course development collaterals. With the increasing costs of content creation, there was a need to re-evaluate the course development model that WOU employs as well as define a more prudent financial management approach in dealing with escalating costs of course material development and delivery. In the last four years, attempts were made to replace textbooks and licensed coursewares with OER in the course development process to minimise the cost of the development of course materials and make them more accessible to all. There were obvious challenges as the acceptance among academics were low in the use of OER for course development or revision purposes. This paper is an account of the experiences of the School of Business and Administration in their efforts to re-develop (revise) all the courses, on offer, by using OER. There were two significant contributions of this effort; a refinement of the course development model used in the university as well as the tremendous savings in the cost of course development. This little project saved the university a total of RM1.4 million (approximately US$350000) by mid-2016.
half:
Wawasan Open University (WOU) faced financial pressure due to the high costs and long timelines associated with its traditional "wrap-around" course development model. This method relied on expensive textbooks, external writers, graphic designers, and editors, often requiring 12 to 18 months to complete a single course. To address this, the School of Business and Administration investigated integrating Open Educational Resources (OER)—materials available at zero cost under open licenses or in the public domain—to reduce costs and improve accessibility.

Using a descriptive case study of a Microeconomics course, the study compared the traditional model against a revised model utilizing OER. The traditional model incurred costs totaling RM97,103 over four semesters, driven by external writer fees, textbook purchases, and licensing fees. In contrast, the OER model drastically reduced expenses by using full-time academic staff instead of external writers and eliminating textbook and licensing fees. The total cost for the Microeconomics course revision dropped to RM6,987.50, with a "real" cost to the university of approximately RM2,000 when accounting for internal academic time. This transition resulted in total savings of approximately RM1.4 million by mid-2016.

The study concludes that OER supports the mission of keeping tuition fees low and education accessible. However, OER introduces challenges regarding quality assurance. The author suggests the need for a standardized quality assurance framework and recommends future research into OER sustainability and its impact on student learning.

As an open and distance learning (ODL) institution, WOU's original "wrap-around" method relied on expensive textbooks, commissioned external writers, graphic designers, editors, and instructional designers. This approach was both costly and time-consuming, often requiring 12 to 18 months to complete a single course development cycle.

To address these challenges, the School of Business and Administration at WOU investigated integrating Open Educational Resources (OER)—materials available at zero cost under open copyright licenses or in the public domain. The objective was to determine if replacing traditional textbooks and licensed courseware with OER could minimize development costs and improve accessibility without compromising educational quality.

Using a descriptive case study methodology, the study analyzed the revision of a Microeconomics course. The researcher evaluated the roles of various stakeholders and compared the costs of the traditional model against a revised model utilizing OER, looking at both non-recurring costs, such as writer fees, and recurring costs, such as licensing fees and textbook purchases.

The findings revealed a dramatic difference in expenditure. Under the traditional model, the Microeconomics course incurred costs totaling RM97,103 over four semesters. These expenses included paying an external course writer (RM10,000), purchasing textbooks for every student (RM49,973), and paying licensing fees (RM33,880), alongside graphic design and external assessor fees.

In contrast, the revised model utilizing OER drastically reduced these expenses. The university internalized the role of the course writer by using full-time academic staff, eliminating external writing fees. By using OER, the need to purchase textbooks and pay licensing fees was removed. Additionally, because OER materials are often available in easily manipulated digital formats, the need for extensive graphic redesign was minimized. For the Microeconomics course, the total cost for the revision dropped to RM6,987.50, with the "real" cost to the university being approximately RM2,000 when accounting for the time spent by internal academics. This transition resulted in total savings of approximately RM1.4 million by mid-2016.

The study concludes that OER significantly reduces costs, supporting the ODL mission to keep tuition fees low and education accessible. While OER offers immense benefits, it introduces challenges regarding quality assurance, as determining the quality of resources created by various contributors can be difficult. The author suggests the need for a standardized quality assurance framework and recommends that future research focus on the sustainability of OER and its direct impact on student learning capabilities.

Wawasan Open University (WOU) faced significant financial pressure due to the escalating costs associated with its traditional course development model. As an open and distance learning (ODL) institution, WOU aims to make education accessible, but the costs of purchasing textbooks, paying commissioned external writers, hiring graphic designers and editors, and employing instructional designers created a heavy financial burden. The university’s original model relied on "wrap-around" methods using expensive textbooks or licensing proprietary materials from other institutions. This approach was not only costly but also time-consuming, often taking 12 to 18 months to complete a single course development cycle.

To address these financial challenges, the School of Business and Administration at WOU sought to re-evaluate its development model by integrating Open Educational Resources (OER). OER refers to educational materials available at zero cost under open copyright licenses or in the public domain. The goal was to determine if replacing traditional textbooks and licensed courseware with OER could minimize development costs and improve accessibility without compromising educational quality.

The study employed a descriptive case study methodology, focusing on the revision of a specific course, Microeconomics, as a representative example. The author analyzed the course development process by evaluating the roles of various stakeholders and comparing the costs of the traditional model against a revised model utilizing OER. The analysis looked at both non-recurring costs (such as writer fees and graphic design) and recurring costs (such as licensing fees and textbook purchases per student).

The findings revealed a dramatic difference in expenditure between the two models. Under the traditional model, the Microeconomics course incurred significant costs over four semesters, totaling RM97,103. These costs included paying an external course writer (RM10,000), purchasing textbooks for every student (RM49,973), paying licensing fees (RM33,880), and paying for graphic design and external course assessors.

In contrast, the revised model—which utilized OER—drastically reduced these expenses. The university internalized the role of the course writer by using full-time academic staff, thereby eliminating external writing fees. By using OER, the need to purchase textbooks and pay licensing fees was removed. Furthermore, because OER materials are often available in digital formats that are easy to manipulate, the need for extensive graphic redesign was minimized. For the Microeconomics course, the total cost for the revision dropped to just RM6,987.50, with the "real" cost to the university being approximately RM2,000 when accounting for the time spent by internal academics. This transition resulted in a total savings of approximately RM1.4 million (roughly US$350,000) for the university by mid-2016.

The study concludes that the use of OER in course development and delivery has a significant positive impact on reducing costs, aligning with the mission of ODL institutions to keep tuition fees low and education accessible. The transition from outsourcing to internalizing the development process, combined with the use of open resources, proved to be a highly effective strategy for financial sustainability.

However, the author notes several implications and challenges for the future. While OER offers immense cost benefits, it introduces challenges regarding quality assurance. Because OER can be created by various contributors, determining the quality of the resources can be difficult. The author suggests the need for a standardized quality assurance framework that can be implemented by institutions. Additionally, while much research has focused on the impact of OER on student learning, there is a lack of studies regarding student feedback on the learning experience when using fully localized OER. The author recommends that future research should focus on the sustainability and viability of OER and its direct impact on student learning capabilities.

title: Group Flow States of Intergenerational Networks Within Age-Friendly Academic Settings
abstract: This paper proposes a theoretical framework for investigating group flow within intergenerational networks. The framework is based on preliminary observations of intergenerational engagement among faculty members of an online open university. In describing, explaining and predicting group flow dynamics, the framework borrows heavily from autopoietic theory (Maturana & Varela, 1987), systems theory (Bateson, 1972), and flow theory (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990; Kotler & Wheal, 2017). A flow state is described as “an optimal state of consciousness where we feel our best and perform our best” (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990, p.5) Technically defined, it is the mental state of operation in which a person performing an activity is fully immersed in a feeling of energized focus, full involvement, and enjoyment in the process. Flow states may be experienced not only among individuals but among groups, the latter termed as group flow or communitas (Ibid). Autopoiesis, on the other hand, carries much intergenerational resonance since it is concerned with the renewal, regeneration, and evolution of living systems. A university, constituting different generations of academics, would represent such a living system engaged in a continuing effort of self-renewal and self-reinvention. Oftentimes, age, generational, and ideological chasms are wide enough to result in tensions that lead to system dysfunction even within open and online settings. During group flow states, intergenerational differences are diminished in a manner conducive to system renewal and reinvention.
half:
In the article "Group Flow States of Intergenerational Networks Within Age-Friendly Academic Settings," Alexander G. Flor examines how academic institutions maintain vitality during generational transitions. Using the Faculty of Information and Communication Studies at the University of the Philippines Open University as a case study, the research addresses potential systemic dysfunction caused by age and ideological gaps during leadership successions. The institution is considered age-friendly because it encourages the continued involvement of retirement-age faculty, creating a diverse demographic structure.

The author develops a theoretical framework integrating autopoietic theory, systems theory, and flow theory. The study explores "group flow" or "communitas," defined as collective joy shared during common experiences. Through qualitative observations of academic discussions, the research identifies specific triggers for these states, including subject novelty, a collegial atmosphere that suspends rigid social orders, and high levels of communication skills.

Findings indicate that group flow is facilitated by mutual respect for intergenerational expertise, where younger members provide technological authority and older members provide social impact expertise. During these episodes, participants experience effortless creativity and a distorted sense of time. The author concludes that these flow states diminish generational chasms and serve as indicators of autopoietic progression. Fostering environments conducive to group flow can mitigate systemic dysfunction and leverage intergenerational networks to drive continuous organizational evolution.

The article "Group Flow States of Intergenerational Networks Within Age-Friendly Academic Settings" by Alexander G. Flor addresses the complexities of maintaining organizational vitality during periods of generational transition. The central problem identified is the potential for system dysfunction within academic institutions when wide age, generational, and ideological chasms emerge. These tensions often arise during "liminal moments" of transition, such as the succession of leadership roles, which can redefine an institution's identity and create friction between different generations of academics.

The context for this investigation is the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU), specifically its Faculty of Information and Communication Studies (FICS). UPOU is described as a progressive, innovative, and "age-friendly" institution because it does not impose age limitations on students and encourages the continued involvement of retirement-age faculty. This unique demographic structure creates a living system composed of diverse generations. The FICS faculty, which clusters computer science, information systems, multimedia arts, and communication science, serves as the specific subject for observing how these diverse groups interact and evolve.

To investigate these dynamics, the author proposes a theoretical framework that integrates three major concepts: autopoietic theory, systems theory, and flow theory. Autopoiesis, drawn from Maturana and Varela, refers to the process of self-creation, self-organization, and self-maintenance within living systems. The author posits that a university is a living system that undergoes continuous renewal and regeneration through communication. Flow theory, based on the work of Csikszentmihalyi, describes an optimal state of consciousness characterized by energized focus, full involvement, and enjoyment. The author extends this to "group flow" or "communitas," which is the collective joy or pleasure shared during common experiences.

The method employed in this paper is the development of a theoretical framework based on preliminary observations of intergenerational engagement within the UPOU FICS. The author uses qualitative observations of academic discussions to identify the conditions under which individual and collective flow states occur among faculty members of different ages.

The findings suggest that group flow states (communitas) manifest during intense, engaged academic discussions. The author identifies several specific conditions that trigger these states: the novelty of the subject matter (such as cutting-edge innovations in communication studies); an atmosphere of collegiality that allows for a temporary absence of rigid social orders; the high level of communication skills among participants; a mutual respect for the unique expertise each generation brings to the table (e.g., younger generations providing technological authority while older generations provide social impact expertise); a shared recognition of conceptual relationships; and the spontaneous discovery of emerging patterns that lead to collective "Ah ha!" moments. During these episodes, participants experience a loss of self-consciousness, a distorted sense of time, and a feeling of effortless creativity.

In conclusion, the author asserts that communication is constitutive of social systems. The manifestation of individual and collective flow states during intergenerational exchanges serves as an indicator of autopoietic progression. When these flow states occur, the traditional generational and ideological chasms are diminished, facilitating the self-renewal and reinvention necessary for the organization to thrive.

The implications of this research suggest that fostering environments conducive to group flow can mitigate the risks of systemic dysfunction during leadership transitions. By encouraging collegial, high-level communicative exchanges that respect the diverse expertise of all age groups, academic institutions can leverage intergenerational networks to drive continuous renewal and evolution.

title: Special Report on Technology Application Design and Development of an Online Repository System for Thesis and Special Problem Manuscripts
abstract: It is vital to keep track of all the scholarly works undertaken by the students in research universities. As a premier research university,The University of the Philippines (UP) Mindanao has produced several scholarly works made by its students, such as thesis or special problem manuscripts. Similar to typical residential universities in the Philippines, UP Mindanao students submit both hardbound and digital copies of their thesis and special problem manuscripts to their respective departments. Problems such as duplication of work and missing manuscripts are rampant with the current method.This is because printed and electronic copies stored in optical discs can easily be misplaced and are difficult to track when borrowed. This paper describes the development of the UP Mindanao Manuscript e-library and Repository System (UPMERS), which is a web-based information system that provides administrators a tool to monitor and manage records of manuscripts by graduates of the University. This paper also describes the system’s user acceptance using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Furthermore, the study also discusses the result of the System Usability Scale survey.
half:
In the article "Special Report on Technology Application Design and Development of an Online Repository System for Thesis and Special Problem Manuscripts," Armacheska R. Mesa addresses challenges at the University of the Philippines (UP) Mindanao regarding the management of scholarly intellectual output. Existing manual storage methods, involving physical copies and optical discs, pose risks of loss, misplacement, and media degradation, which can lead to research works becoming obscured.

To resolve these issues, the author developed the UP Mindanao Manuscript e-library and Repository System (UPMERS). This web-based system provides a centralized digital archive for teachers, students, researchers, and alumni to search and retrieve titles, abstracts, and full manuscripts. It includes features to ensure compliance with Intellectual Property Rights by allowing administrators to restrict content access. Developed using the Rapid Application Development (RAD) framework, the system was built with PHP, MySQL, HTML, CSS, and Javascript.

Evaluation through black-box testing and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) showed that UPMERS successfully enables faster record retrieval and secure storage. The system achieved a System Usability Scale score of 85.5, indicating it is user-friendly. Furthermore, users reported high perceived usefulness in monitoring research and eliminating duplication. The author concludes that UPMERS is an effective tool but notes that future success depends on populating the database through departmental requirements.

Mesa addresses the challenges faced by the University of the Philippines (UP) Mindanao in managing its scholarly intellectual output. The institution's existing manual storage methods, which rely on hardbound physical copies and optical discs, present risks such as loss, misplacement, and issues regarding the longevity and durability of digital media. These problems lead to a lack of centralized tracking and can cause significant research works to fade into obscurity.

To address these issues, the author proposed the development of the UP Mindanao Manuscript e-library and Repository System (UPMERS). This web-based information system serves as a centralized digital archive that allows stakeholders—including teachers, students, researchers, and alumni—to access, search, and retrieve titles, abstracts, and full manuscripts. A key feature is its compliance with Intellectual Property Rights, allowing administrators to restrict content to specific users or make it available to the general public.

The development of UPMERS utilized the Rapid Application Development (RAD) framework within the System Development Life Cycle (SDLC). The project was completed in approximately five months through four phases: Requirements Planning, User Design, Rapid Construction, and Cutover. The system supports five user roles: system administrator, department chair, dean, faculty, and students. The software was built using PHP, MySQL, HTML, CSS, and Javascript, utilizing the Laravel 5.2 Model View Controller (MVC) framework and the Bootstrap front-end framework.

To evaluate the system, the study employed black-box testing and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), focusing on Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness. Perceived ease of use was measured via the System Usability Scale (SUS), while perceived usefulness was assessed through a customized six-item survey.

The findings indicate that UPMERS successfully met its objectives by enabling faster record retrieval and providing secure, centralized storage. The system achieved a SUS score of 85.5, interpreted as "more than satisfactory," indicating it is user-friendly. Regarding perceived usefulness, all survey items received average scores greater than 4, confirming that users believe the system assists in monitoring research, finding titles, and eliminating research duplication. The reliability of the usefulness survey was confirmed with a Cronbach alpha of 0.78.

The study concludes that UPMERS is a relevant and effective tool. While the technology is successful, the author notes that the primary future challenge is populating the database, which requires every department to make adding manuscript records a requirement. The author recommends future research include impact studies on research quality and post-implementation surveys to evaluate long-term assistance to students.

Mesa addresses the challenges faced by the University of the Philippines (UP) Mindanao in managing its scholarly intellectual output. As a premier research university, the institution produces a significant volume of theses and special problem manuscripts. However, the existing manual method of storage—relying on hardbound physical copies and digital copies stored on optical discs—presents several critical issues. These include the high risk of manuscripts being lost, misplaced, or not returned by borrowers. Furthermore, the author notes that optical discs face concerns regarding reliability, longevity, and durability. These problems lead to a lack of centralized tracking and can cause significant research works to fade into obscurity.

To address these issues, the author proposed the development of the UP Mindanao Manuscript e-library and Repository System (UPMERS). This web-based information system is designed to provide administrators with a tool to monitor and manage the records of manuscripts submitted by graduates. The system serves as a centralized digital archive that allows various stakeholders, including teachers, students, researchers, and alumni, to access, search, and retrieve titles, abstracts, and full manuscripts in various file formats. A key feature of the system is its compliance with Intellectual Property Rights, allowing administrators to specify whether content is available to the general public or restricted to specific users.

The methodology employed for the development of UPMERS was the Rapid Application Development (RAD) framework within the System Development Life Cycle (SDLC). This approach was chosen to facilitate faster development, as the project was completed in approximately five months. The RAD process followed four distinct phases: Requirements Planning, User Design, Rapid Construction, and Cutover. During the Requirements Planning phase, the developer conducted meetings and interviews with administrative staff to define the system scope and identify necessary functions. The system was designed to support five user roles: system administrator, department chair, dean, faculty, and students. The software was built using PHP, MySQL, HTML, CSS, and Javascript, utilizing the Laravel 5.2 Model View Controller (MVC) framework and the Bootstrap front-end framework.

The User Design and Construction phases involved iterative prototyping and coding based on continuous feedback from the primary users. The final phase, Cutover, involved installation, user testing, and evaluation. To ensure the system met user requirements, black-box testing was performed. To evaluate user acceptance, the study utilized the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), focusing on two primary factors: Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness. Perceived ease of use was measured using the System Usability Scale (SUS), a ten-item survey designed to determine if the system is user-friendly and easy to learn. Perceived usefulness was measured through a customized six-item survey designed to assess how the system benefits the productivity and research management of the university's stakeholders.

The findings of the study indicate that the development of UPMERS was successful in meeting its objectives. Upon deployment, the system enabled faster record retrieval and provided a more secure, centralized method for storing manuscript data. Stakeholders reported that the system allowed for easy searching of manuscripts via metadata such as titles and keywords. In terms of usability, the system achieved a System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 85.5, which is interpreted as being above average and "more than satisfactory." This indicates that users perceived the system as easy to use. Regarding perceived usefulness, all items in the survey received average scores greater than 4, demonstrating that users believed the system would effectively assist faculty in monitoring research, help students find research titles, provide centralized storage, eliminate research duplication, and solve the problem of unreturned hardbound copies. The reliability of the usefulness survey was confirmed with a Cronbach alpha of 0.78.

In conclusion, the study concludes that UPMERS is a relevant, helpful, and effective tool for the university. It provides significant benefits to administrators by securing digital copies and to students by providing a background for future research endeavors. The system was found to be user-friendly and met the functional requirements of its intended users. However, the author notes that the primary challenge moving forward is not the technology itself, but the task of populating the database. For the system to be fully effective, every department must make the addition of manuscript records a requirement.

The implications of this study suggest that while open-source software exists for journal and document management, bespoke systems like UPMERS are often necessary to meet the specific requirements of individual institutions. The author recommends that future research should include an impact study to determine how the system affects the quality of student research and the ease of acquiring research titles. Additionally, a post-implementation survey is suggested to further evaluate the long-term assistance the system provides to students during the thesis-writing process.

title: Ask Iska and IskOU: Analysis of UPOU's Chatbot for Information Support Services
abstract: In the educational domain, artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the information and communication technologies gaining popularity for its advantages in teaching and learning, especially in information support services. The University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU), as a leader of open and distance e-learning in the country, explored this technology and came up with its own tool to streamline its information support services. The UPOU chatbot, personified as Iska and IskOU, provides immediate and appropriate human-like conversations when prompted by users. The tool is able to deliver these conservations through its intelligence database or knowledge base, which is a result of a university-wide effort to collate relevant information. This chatbot intelligence influences user satisfaction as it is the basis of the tool’s performance. Therefore, the study aimed to evaluate the UPOU chatbot’s performance as an information support tool by determining the level of satisfaction of UPOU chatbot users. Data was collected through a post-interaction survey with the users and was analyzed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis. Results showed mixed experiences among UPOU chatbot users. It was mainly reported that the tool has issues in interpretations and addressing complex, multiple, and specific/unique queries. Nonetheless, users evaluated the UPOU chatbot as a satisfying and helpful tool. A number of areas and topics for future investigations were also listed.
half:
The study "Ask Iska and IskOU: Analysis of UPOU's Chatbot for Information Support Services" investigates the performance and user satisfaction of two AI chatbots, Iska and IskOU, developed by the University of the Philippines Open University. These tools aim to streamline information support for students, faculty, and the public via Facebook and the university website. Using a mixed-methods approach, researchers collected data from forty-one respondents and evaluated the chatbots based on response time, multi-thread conversation, maxim of quantity, perceived ease of use, and the recognition of user goals and intent.

Findings regarding performance were mixed. The chatbots performed exceptionally well in response time, with 100% of respondents reporting prompt answers and an average response time of 900 milliseconds. Users found the tools intuitive, reporting high levels of perceived ease of use and usefulness. However, significant limitations were identified regarding the chatbots' ability to interpret intent. While successful at answering frequently asked questions regarding application procedures and program lists, they struggled with complex or highly specific queries. Approximately 24.4% of users reported the chatbot "sometimes" answered completely, while 22% reported it "never" answered completely.

The study concludes that while the chatbots are successful for high-volume, repetitive tasks, they are not yet a complete replacement for human support. Researchers suggest expanding the knowledge base, improving the ability to provide direct answers rather than external links, and implementing monitoring schemes to track unresolved queries.

The research aimed to evaluate whether these chatbots effectively meet the information needs of the university community and to identify their strengths and limitations.

The researchers evaluated the chatbots based on five features: response time, multi-thread conversation, maxim of quantity, perceived ease of use, and the recognition of user goals and intent.
