title: Automated Student Advising: An App for Greater Efficiency
abstract: One of the attributes of open and distance e-learning (ODeL) is its adoption and deployment of ICTs. This attribute sits at the very core of ODeL. Thus, quality in ODeL means adequate augmentation of its academic and administrative processes with innovative applications. To administer the conduct of student thesis in the ODeL context where there are many students, an efficient system of assigning research topics to appropriate thesis advisers is required. This paper documents the development and application for academic advising developed by the Faculty of Information and Communication Studies (FICS).
half:
The article "Automated Student Advising: An App for Greater Efficiency" examines logistical challenges in academic advising within the Faculty of Information and Communication Studies (FICS) at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). In an open and distance e-learning environment, the transition to a one-time enrollment model rendered manual practices, such as face-to-face meetings for nominating advisers, insufficient. The lack of an automated system caused difficulties in record-keeping, managing faculty workloads, and reducing human error during committee designation for the DComm, MDC, and BAMS programs.

To resolve these issues, researchers developed the Online Advisory Committee (AdCom) App using an Iterative Incremental Model. The system features three user categories: Students, Advisers, and Administrators. Students can select committee members based on faculty names, photos, and research specializations, while a "quota" filter ensures equitable faculty workloads. Once a nomination is submitted, the system sends automated emails to faculty for acceptance or declination. Administrators can manage profiles, adjust quotas, and generate the official Nomination and Designation of Dissertation Committee Form.

Findings indicate that the AdCom App successfully enables students to formulate committees online. By displaying research interests, the app helps students make informed decisions to ensure committee members complement their research topics. The system streamlines administrative tasks through automated form generation and provides an efficient method for managing faculty loads. The researchers conclude that the app offers a more convenient, sustainable, and paperless method of student support compared to manual practices.

The article "Automated Student Advising: An App for Greater Efficiency" examines logistical challenges in academic advising within the Faculty of Information and Communication Studies (FICS) at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). In an open and distance e-learning (ODeL) environment, the transition to a one-time enrollment model for large unit blocks rendered previous manual practices, such as face-to-face meetings for nominating advisers, insufficient. The lack of an automated system led to difficulties in record-keeping, managing faculty workloads, responding to student needs, and reducing human error during committee designation for the DComm, MDC, and BAMS programs.

To resolve these issues, researchers developed the Online Advisory Committee (AdCom) App using an Iterative Incremental Model. The technical architecture utilizes PHP 7.0.30, the Laravel Framework 5.5, and a MySQL database, incorporating tools like Supervisor for email monitoring, Crontab for link expiration, and DomPDF for document generation. The system is designed to be user-friendly for a demographic ranging from Millennials to Baby Boomers.

The AdCom App features three user categories: Students, Advisers, and Administrators. Students can register and select committee members based on faculty names, photos, and research specializations. A "quota" filter ensures equitable faculty workloads. Once a student submits a nomination, the system sends an automated email to the faculty member to accept or decline. If an adviser accepts, the student is confirmed; if they decline, the system suggests an alternative. If an adviser reaches maximum capacity, the system automatically declines further nominations. Administrators can manage profiles, adjust quotas, and generate "Form 1," the official Nomination and Designation of Dissertation Committee Form.

Findings indicate that the AdCom App successfully enables students to formulate committees online. By displaying research interests, the app helps students make informed decisions to ensure committee members complement their research topics. The system streamlines administrative tasks through automated form generation and provides an efficient method for managing faculty loads via the quota system.

The researchers conclude that the AdCom App offers a more convenient, sustainable, and paperless method of student support compared to manual practices. Currently in its beta-testing phase, the app is subject to ongoing iterations. Future development suggestions include formal user evaluations, automated database maintenance, and automated quota computation. A significant recommendation is the potential integration of the Gale-Shapley "Stable Matching" algorithm to optimize the match between research topics and adviser specializations. Ultimately, the authors suggest this system can improve student-adviser relationships and serve as a model for other Higher Education Institutions.

The article "Automated Student Advising: An App for Greater Efficiency" addresses the logistical challenges of academic advising within the Faculty of Information and Communication Studies (FICS) at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). The system was designed to be user-friendly for a diverse demographic, ranging from Millennials to Baby Boomers. The technical architecture utilized PHP 7.0.30 for server-side operations, the Laravel Framework 5.5, and a MySQL database. Other tools included Supervisor for email monitoring, Crontab for link expiration, and DomPDF for generating official documentation.

The AdCom App categorizes users into three groups: Students, Advisers, and Administrators. Students can register and select their preferred advisory committee members from a list that includes faculty names, photos, and research specializations. The system includes a "quota" filter to ensure load equity among faculty members. Once a student submits a nomination, the system sends an automated email to the nominated faculty member, allowing them to either accept or decline the request. If an adviser accepts, the student receives a confirmation; if they decline, the system automatically suggests a new chair from the student's other choices or selects a random one. If an adviser reaches their maximum capacity, the system automatically declines further nominations. Administrators maintain oversight through a secure login, allowing them to perform CRUD (create, read, update, and delete) operations on student and adviser profiles, manage system access, adjust quotas, and generate "Form 1," which serves as the official Nomination and Designation of Dissertation Committee Form.

The findings indicate that the AdCom App successfully fulfills its primary function of enabling students to formulate their thesis or dissertation committees online. By providing faculty research interests and specializations within the interface, the app assists students in making informed decisions to ensure their committee is complementary to their research topics. The system provides a more efficient method for managing faculty loads through the quota system and streamlines administrative tasks by automating the generation of official forms and reducing manual record-keeping.

The researchers conclude that the AdCom App provides a more convenient and sustainable method of student support compared to previous manual practices. It promotes a paperless environment and maximizes available resources through technology-enabled advising. However, the application is currently in its beta-testing phase, meaning it is subject to ongoing iterations based on user feedback and encountered issues.

The implications of this study suggest that automated advising systems can significantly improve the quality of student support in ODeL contexts. The authors suggest several avenues for future development to further enhance the system. These include conducting formal user evaluations with students and faculty, developing automated database maintenance, and implementing automated computation for faculty quotas. A significant recommendation for future iterations is the potential integration of the Gale-Shapley "Stable Matching" algorithm to ensure the most apt matching between a student's research topic and an adviser's specialization. Ultimately, the authors posit that implementing such practices can improve the student-adviser relationship at UPOU and serve as a model for other Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) seeking to improve their academic advising efficiency.

title: Instructors’ Perceptions of Using Videos in Flipped Learning: A Reflective Study on Online Discussion Classes
abstract: Since most of the university courses in Tokyo shifted to online mode, instructors were forced to adapt to different teaching approaches and maintain quality education. This reflective paper investigates perceptions of instructors in using videos in flipped learning in online discussion classes. To maximize student speaking time and practice opportunities, they decided to implement flipped learning by creating videos explaining the target discussion skills for each lesson and posting them in an online learning management system (LMS). The students were required to complete their pre-learning in preparation for classroom activities with their instructors or their peers. Pre-learning involved having the students watch the video at any time in the week before the lesson and completing a connected task. When the students come to class, they could start to apply, analyze, evaluate, and produce meaningful, interactive, and rich discussions. After implementing flipped learning and pre-lesson tasks for one semester, the instructors reflect on and discuss their experiences and observations. This study analyzed and discussed the advantages and disadvantages of flipped learning. On one hand, it helped save time spent on online instruction, offered learners a chance to control their learnings, and helped students at different levels. On the other hand, learners and instructors also faced some challenges, such as time consumption and low motivation. The paper concluded with the study limitations and suggestions for future implementation in online, face-to-face, and hybrid settings.

The sudden shift to online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic forced university instructors in Tokyo to adapt their teaching methods. At Rikkyo University, instructors in English Discussion Classes implemented flipped learning (FL) to address the loss of face-to-face interaction and maximize student speaking time. By moving teacher-fronted instruction to individual learning spaces, instructors aimed to free up class time for interactive, student-centered activities.

Using a reflective research design, four instructors implemented the model over one semester through three stages: preparation, implementation, and reflection. Preparation involved creating instructional videos and pre-lesson tasks, such as pop quizzes and forum discussions, which students completed via a Learning Management System before online sessions.

Findings indicated several benefits, including saved in-class time for student-student interaction and increased student autonomy, as learners could replay videos at their own pace. The model also allowed for differentiated instruction and provided instructors with insights into specific student difficulties through pre-lesson assignments. However, challenges included decreased student motivation, increased workloads for both instructors and students, and difficulties transitioning from passive to active learning styles. Technical issues and communication barriers in virtual spaces also emerged. While limited by a small sample size and reliance on instructor observations, the study suggests flipped learning has significant potential for fostering independent, active learners in mixed-ability classrooms.

The sudden shift to online learning in April 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic forced university instructors in Tokyo to adapt their teaching methods. In English Discussion Classes (EDC) at Rikkyo University, instructors faced the loss of face-to-face interaction and the logistical difficulties of an online medium. To maximize student speaking time and practice, instructors implemented flipped learning (FL) to move teacher-fronted instruction to individual learning spaces, freeing up class time for interactive, student-centered activities.

The study utilized a reflective research design conducted over one semester by four instructors through three stages: preparation, implementation, and reflection. During preparation, researchers created five-minute instructional videos for various discussion skills and developed pre-lesson tasks, such as concept-checking pop quizzes and online forum discussions. During implementation, students watched these videos and completed tasks via a Learning Management System (LMS) before attending online sessions. In the final stage, instructors engaged in a recorded discussion to reflect on their experiences, which was coded and analyzed to identify recurring themes.

Findings revealed several benefits to the flipped learning model. Instructors noted that the method saved in-class time previously spent on lectures, allowing for more student-student interaction. The videos provided students with greater autonomy, as they could replay or slow down content to suit their individual proficiency levels, which was particularly beneficial for lower-level students. Furthermore, pre-lesson assignments provided insight into students' specific difficulties, allowing for more targeted feedback. The model also allowed instructors to differentiate instruction, providing more depth for advanced students through challenging forum tasks while offering simpler support for others.

However, implementation presented several challenges. A primary concern was student motivation; some students stopped watching videos or completed tasks too late to benefit during class. Instructors noted a significant increase in workload for both parties, involving time-consuming preparation for instructors and additional requirements for students. Additionally, many students struggled to transition from passive, teacher-centered learning styles to the active learning required by the flipped model. Technical issues and the difficulty of negotiating clear communication in a virtual space also created barriers.

The study acknowledges limitations, including the small sample size of four instructors at a single university and the reliance on instructor observations rather than quantified student surveys. It is also difficult to distinguish whether challenges were inherent to flipped learning or the sudden shift to online instruction. Ultimately, the study suggests that flipped learning has significant potential for creating independent, active learners, particularly in mixed-ability classrooms.

The sudden shift to online learning in April 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic forced university instructors in Tokyo to adapt their teaching methods to maintain educational quality. In English Discussion Classes (EDC) at Rikkyo University, instructors faced the challenge of losing face-to-face interaction time and the logistical difficulties of an online medium. To maximize student speaking time and practice opportunities, the instructors sought to implement flipped learning (FL) to move teacher-fronted instruction to individual learning spaces, thereby freeing up class time for interactive, student-centered activities.

The study utilized a reflective research design conducted over one semester by four instructors. The methodology involved three distinct stages: a pre-project preparation phase, an implementation phase, and a post-project reflection phase. During the preparation phase, the researchers created five-minute instructional videos for various discussion skills and developed accompanying pre-lesson tasks, such as concept-checking pop quizzes and online forum discussions. During the implementation phase, students watched these videos and completed tasks via a Learning Management System (LMS) before attending online sessions. In the final stage, the instructors engaged in a recorded discussion to reflect on their experiences, which was subsequently coded and analyzed to identify recurring themes regarding the benefits and challenges of the approach.

The findings revealed several significant benefits to the flipped learning model. Instructors noted that the method saved valuable in-class time that would otherwise have been spent on lectures, allowing for more student-student interaction and practice. The videos provided students with greater autonomy, as they could replay or slow down content to suit their individual proficiency levels. This was particularly beneficial for lower-level students. Furthermore, the instructors found that the pre-lesson assignments provided insight into students' specific difficulties, allowing for more targeted and specific feedback during class. The flexibility of the model also allowed instructors to differentiate instruction, providing more depth for advanced students through challenging forum tasks while offering simpler support for others.

However, the implementation also presented several challenges. A primary concern was student motivation; while some students engaged deeply, others stopped watching the videos or completed tasks too late to benefit from the content during class. The instructors also noted a significant increase in workload for both parties. Instructors faced time-consuming preparation in creating high-quality, concise videos and assignments, while students faced an increased workload due to the additional requirements of the online environment. Additionally, many students struggled to transition from the passive, teacher-centered learning styles they experienced in high school to the active learning required by the flipped model. The instructors also noted that the online medium itself created barriers, such as technical issues and the difficulty of negotiating clear communication in a virtual space.

In conclusion, the instructors found that flipped learning is a highly beneficial approach for online discussion classes, provided the preparation is manageable. It effectively shifts the classroom focus toward student-centered, interactive learning and allows for more efficient use of limited instructional time. While the transition can be demanding for both students and teachers, the ability to provide personalized instruction and maximize speaking opportunities makes it a valuable pedagogical tool.

The study acknowledges several limitations, including the small sample size of four instructors at a single university and the fact that the study was primarily based on instructor observations rather than quantified student surveys. Furthermore, because this was the first time these specific instructors taught online and used this specific FL model, it is difficult to distinguish whether the challenges were inherent to flipped learning or a result of the sudden shift to online instruction. 

The implications of this study suggest that flipped learning has significant potential across various settings, including face-to-face and hybrid models. It is particularly useful in mixed-ability classrooms where differentiation is necessary. The researchers suggest that future implementations could benefit from releasing videos closer to the lesson date to ensure content freshness, integrating videos and assignments into single platforms like Google Forms, and incorporating more direct student feedback to better align the materials with learner needs. Ultimately, the study positions flipped learning as a significant step toward creating more independent and active learners in the digital age.

title: Online Student Engagement and Sense of Community in a Philippine Online University
abstract: This study aimed to consider the correlation between student engagement and sense of community through the partial application of the online student engagement scale (OSE) and classroom community scale (CCS) as designed by Dixson (2015) and Rovai (2002), respectively. A total of 67 students from two classes in the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) program at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) participated in the study, whose input revealed a correlation coefficient of 0.442. This means that there is a moderate correlation between the two attributes. The study also revealed that, based on the two classes attended by different sets of students that as far as the participants are concerned, the level of engagement and sense of community stays the same over time. It is, however, important to note that there are underlying factors affecting respondents’ perceptions due to the COVID-19 pandemic as well as a series of natural calamities, which occurred during the academic year in which this study was conducted. The relatively low turnout of responses in the survey may also have affected the findings and subsequent analysis. Regardless of the underlying factors, certain areas can be improved in order to foster engagement, mainly through encouraging interaction through various communication and social media platforms. Data also suggests that official support from the university would also be of benefit. It is recommended that future studies build on the findings of this paper for a wider and deeper understanding of the issues that were discussed.
half:
In the study "Online Student Engagement and Sense of Community in a Philippine Online University," Al Francis D. Librero investigates the relationship between student engagement and sense of community among Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies students at the University of the Philippines Open University. Using a quantitative approach with the Online Student Engagement (OSE) scale and the Classroom Community Scale (CCS), the researcher surveyed 67 students from introductory and advanced courses to compare perceptions across different residency lengths.

The findings revealed a moderate positive correlation (r = 0.442) between student engagement and sense of community. While students exhibited fair to moderate levels of engagement regarding self-motivation and effort, engagement in interpersonal interactions, such as social chatting, was notably low. Regarding sense of community, students were largely neutral; they felt encouraged to ask questions but did not feel the course was "like a family" and reported a lack of interdependence. No statistically significant difference in engagement or community was found between first-year and third-year students. Notably, almost all respondents reported that the COVID-19 pandemic and natural calamities detrimentally affected engagement due to technical issues, such as poor internet and power failures, as well as mental and emotional stress. The researcher suggests that universities should design online experiences that encourage interaction through platforms like Zoom or Discord and establish student organizations to foster belonging.
one:
In the study "Online Student Engagement and Sense of Community in a Philippine Online University," Al Francis D. Librero investigates the relationship between student engagement and the sense of community within the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies program at the University of the Philippines Open University. The research addresses the challenges of fostering learning communities and maintaining engagement in a fully online environment, a problem intensified by the COVID-19 pandemic and frequent natural calamities in the Philippines.

The researcher employed a quantitative approach using the Online Student Engagement (OSE) scale and the Classroom Community Scale (CCS). The study involved 67 students from an introductory course (MMS 100) and an advanced course (MMS 175) to compare engagement and community perceptions across different lengths of residency. Data was collected via an anonymous Google Forms questionnaire.

The findings revealed a moderate positive correlation (r = 0.442) between student engagement and sense of community. Descriptive statistics showed that students exhibited fair to moderate levels of engagement, specifically regarding self-motivation and effort. However, engagement in interpersonal interaction, such as social chatting or getting to know peers, was notably low. Regarding the sense of community, students were largely neutral; while they felt encouraged to ask questions, they did not feel the course was "like a family" and reported a lack of interdependence.

The study found no statistically significant difference in engagement or sense of community between first-year and third-year students, suggesting residency length did not impact these attributes in this sample. A significant finding was the impact of external stressors: almost all respondents reported that the COVID-19 pandemic and natural calamities had a detrimental effect on their engagement, primarily due to technical issues like poor internet connectivity and power failures, as well as mental and emotional stress.

The author notes limitations including a relatively low and unbalanced response rate and the fact that the correlational nature of the study cannot determine causality. In conclusion, the study confirms that engagement and sense of community are linked, highlighting a gap between students' internal motivation to learn and their ability to connect socially. The researcher suggests that universities should use data to design better online experiences, such as encouraging interaction through platforms like Zoom or Discord and establishing sanctioned student organizations to foster belonging. Future research should utilize larger, more balanced samples and diverse data collection methods to validate these findings.
two:
The study "Online Student Engagement and Sense of Community in a Philippine Online University" by Al Francis D. Librero investigates the relationship between student engagement and the sense of community within a fully online academic environment. The research was conducted at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) specifically within the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) program.

The problem addressed by the author is the difficulty of fostering learning communities and maintaining student engagement in an online setting, a challenge exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic and various natural calamities in the Philippines. While educators often make adjustments to online teaching based on intuition, there has been a lack of comprehensive, data-driven analysis regarding how engaged students actually are and how they perceive their connection to their learning community at the university level.

The context of the study is unique due to the "new normal" brought about by the global pandemic, which forced an abrupt shift to online and blended learning. This shift increased anxiety and feelings of isolation among students. Furthermore, the study took place during a period of significant environmental instability in the Philippines, including storms and typhoons, which impacted the digital and physical realities of the learners.

To investigate these issues, the researcher employed a quantitative approach using two established instruments: the Online Student Engagement (OSE) scale by Dixson (2015) and the Classroom Community Scale (CCS) by Rovai (2002). The study involved 67 students from two specific classes: MMS 100 (an introductory course) and MMS 175 (an advanced course). This allowed the researcher to compare engagement and community perceptions across different lengths of residency in the program. Data was collected via an anonymous Google Forms questionnaire, which included Likert scales for the OSE and CCS, as well as additional items to account for the impact of external factors like the pandemic and natural disasters.

The findings revealed a moderate positive correlation (r = 0.442) between student engagement and sense of community, suggesting that as one increases, the other tends to increase as well. Descriptive statistics showed that students exhibited fair to moderate levels of engagement, particularly regarding self-motivation and effort. However, engagement in interpersonal interaction—such as having fun in chats or getting to know peers—was notably low. Regarding the sense of community, students were largely neutral; while they felt encouraged to ask questions, they did not feel the course was "like a family" and reported a lack of interdependence.

The study found no statistically significant difference in engagement or sense of community between the first-year students (MMS 100) and the third-year students (MMS 175), suggesting that residency length did not impact these attributes in this specific sample. A significant finding was the impact of external stressors: almost all respondents reported that the COVID-19 pandemic and natural calamities had a detrimental effect on their engagement, primarily due to technical issues like poor internet connectivity and power failures, as well as mental and emotional stress.

The author notes several limitations, including a relatively low and unbalanced response rate, particularly in the MMS 175 class, which may introduce response bias. Additionally, because the study was correlational, it cannot determine causality—specifically, whether engagement drives community or vice versa.

In conclusion, the study confirms that student engagement and a sense of community are linked in online learning environments. The results highlight a gap between students' internal motivation to learn and their ability to connect socially with peers and instructors. The researcher concludes that while students are motivated, the social and interpersonal dimensions of the online classroom require more intentional cultivation.

The implications of this research suggest that universities should move beyond relying on intuition and instead use data to design better online learning experiences. To improve engagement, the author proposes encouraging interaction through various communication and social media platforms, such as Zoom or Discord. There is also a noted need for official university support, such as the establishment of sanctioned student organizations, to help foster a sense of belonging. Finally, the study recommends that future research utilize larger, more balanced samples and more diverse data collection methods, such as teacher ratings and observations, to validate the findings and gain a deeper understanding of the complexities of online learning communities.

title: Student support in an open and distance electronic learning (ODeL) context: The experiences of students with disabilities in KwaZulu-Natal
abstract: The institutions of higher learning in South Africa and around the globe are under a lot of pressure to provide equal access to all students with diverse learning needs. It is important to realize that students come from diverse backgrounds, which leads to them experiencing the academic support services offered by open and distance e-learning (ODeL) institutions differently. The experiences of students with disabilities (SWDs) were studied through the adoption of the qualitative and interpretivism paradigm to produce data that is rich in insights. The exploratory research design was followed to achieve a better understanding of in-depth information. The research data was collected using the MS Teams platform, which was necessitated by adhering to the strict protocols demanded by the Covid-19 regulations. A small number of study participants were identified and recruited to provide the required in-depth information about the issues explored in the study. Using a purposive and snowball sampling method, 10 ODeL students were drawn as participants. The results revealed that the common denominator and the most important aspect of an ODeL institution is effectivestudent support. The qualitative findings revealed that institutions of higher learning must understand the needs and requirements of SWDs. This study contributes to the literature by providing a better understanding of SWDs’ needs and the proposed reviewed allocation of resources by the university to cater to the SWDs’ needs. The study recommended the development of disability-friendly technology and infrastructure and the strengthening of the safety program for students with albinism.
half:
In the study "Student support in an open and distance electronic learning (ODeL) context: The experiences of students with disabilities in KwaZulu-Natal," Zwelakhe Erick Cebisa examines inclusivity and equal access in higher education. While ODeL institutions aim for flexibility, a gap exists in understanding the lived experiences of students with disabilities (SWDs). Many SWDs face barriers such as inadequate physical infrastructure, a lack of assistive technologies, and systemic failures in specialized academic support, issues which were exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic's rapid shift to digital platforms.

Using a qualitative, exploratory design within an interpretivism paradigm, the researcher interviewed 10 participants with albinism, physical disabilities, and visual impairments via MS Teams. Thematic analysis revealed several critical findings. Participants reported significant discrimination and a lack of prioritization regarding their needs. Accessibility remains a major hurdle, as computer laboratories are often not disability-friendly and resource constraints lead to a lack of assistive devices or delays in receiving braille and large-print materials. Additionally, students with albinism reported safety concerns due to local myths and a lack of institutional support during transit. While disability forums were noted as a positive, the transition to online learning created inequities, such as the lack of extra time for online examinations.

The study concludes that institutions must move from reactive to proactive support. The author recommends active consultation with SWDs during policy design, developing disability-friendly technology, and implementing change management to ensure online transitions do not strip students of established accommodations.
one:
In the study "Student support in an open and distance electronic learning (ODeL) context: The experiences of students with disabilities in KwaZulu-Natal," Zwelakhe Erick Cebisa examines inclusivity and equal access in higher education. While ODeL institutions aim to be student-centered and flexible, a gap exists in understanding the lived experiences of students with disabilities (SWDs). Despite the theoretical promise of "anytime, anywhere" access, many SWDs face barriers such as inadequate physical infrastructure, a lack of assistive technologies, and systemic failures in specialized academic support. These issues were exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced a rapid shift to digital platforms that were often not designed with disability-friendly technology in mind.

The research focused on ODeL institutions in the KwaZulu-Natal region of South Africa. Using a qualitative approach within an interpretivism paradigm, the researcher employed an exploratory design to gain in-depth insights. Due to COVID-19 protocols, data collection was conducted via MS Teams. The study utilized purposive and snowball sampling to recruit 10 participants (seven females and three males) with albinism, physical disabilities, and visual impairments. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis.

The findings revealed several critical themes. First, participants reported significant discrimination and a lack of prioritization regarding their needs, often feeling undervalued or neglected. Second, accessibility remains a major hurdle; computer laboratories are frequently not disability-friendly, and resource constraints lead to a lack of assistive devices and delays in receiving materials like braille or large-print versions. Third, safety is a major concern, particularly for students with albinism, who reported feeling vulnerable due to local myths and a lack of institutional support or escort services when using public transport. Finally, while disability forums and approachable registration staff were noted as positives, the transition to online learning during the pandemic created inequity, specifically regarding the lack of extra time for online examinations compared to physical exams.

The study concludes that while ODeL provides beneficial flexibility, institutions are lagging in addressing the diverse needs of SWDs. Support systems are often reactive rather than proactive. The author recommends that being "student-centered" must include active consultation with SWDs during the design of policies and infrastructure. Recommendations include developing disability-friendly technology, strengthening safety programs for students with albinism, and providing mobility instructors. Furthermore, institutions must implement change management strategies to ensure that transitions to online modes do not strip SWDs of established accommodations, such as extended exam times. Ultimately, the study advocates for integrating the voices of SWDs into planning and budgeting to ensure academic success and social integration.
two:
The study titled "Student support in an open and distance electronic learning (ODeL) context: The experiences of students with disabilities in KwaZulu-Natal" by Zwelakhe Erick Cebisa addresses the critical issue of inclusivity and equal access in higher education. As institutions of higher learning face increasing pressure to meet the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals regarding the reduction of inequality, it is essential to examine how students with disabilities (SWDs) navigate the specific landscape of ODeL environments.

The problem identified by the author is that while ODeL institutions aim to be student-centered and provide flexible learning opportunities, there remains a significant gap in understanding the lived experiences of SWDs. Despite the theoretical promise of ODeL to provide "anytime, anywhere" access, many students with disabilities face substantial barriers to optimal performance. These barriers include inadequate physical infrastructure, lack of assistive technologies, and systemic failures in providing specialized academic support. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated these issues by forcing a rapid shift to online examinations and digital platforms that were often not designed with disability-friendly technology in mind.

The context of the research is centered on ODeL institutions in the KwaZulu-Natal region of South Africa. The study highlights that while ODeL is often chosen by SWDs due to its inherent flexibility and the ability to study from home, this choice is frequently driven by the need to avoid the social challenges or physical limitations associated with traditional campus life.

To investigate these issues, the researcher employed a qualitative approach using an interpretivism paradigm. This method was chosen to produce rich, in-depth insights into the personal experiences of the participants. The study utilized an exploratory research design, which was appropriate given the lack of existing research specifically focusing on the perspective of SWDs within the ODeL setting. Data collection was conducted via MS Teams, a necessity imposed by COVID-19 safety protocols that prevented face-to-face interviews. The researcher used purposive and snowball sampling to recruit 10 participants, including seven females and three males. The sample included students with albinism, physical disabilities, and visual impairments. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns in the participants' responses.

The findings of the study revealed several critical themes. First, the research identified significant discrimination and a lack of prioritization regarding the needs of SWDs. Participants reported feeling undervalued or neglected when institutions failed to address their specific requirements. Second, accessibility remains a major hurdle. Even when ODeL institutions provide computer laboratories, these facilities are often not disability-friendly. Furthermore, the study found that resource constraints lead to a lack of assistive devices and delays in receiving necessary study materials, such as braille or large-print versions.

Third, the study highlighted the specific issue of safety, particularly for students with albinism. These students reported feeling extremely vulnerable and targeted due to local myths, noting a lack of institutional support or escort services to ensure their safety when traveling to and from public transport. Finally, the findings indicated that while there are positive aspects—such as the existence of disability forums and approachable staff during registration—the transition to online learning during the pandemic was problematic. Specifically, the lack of extra time for online examinations, which is often granted during physical exams, created an inequitable testing environment.

The study concludes that while ODeL institutions provide a degree of flexibility that is beneficial to SWDs, they are currently lagging in their mission to effectively address the diverse needs of these students. The research emphasizes that being "student-centered" must include the active consultation of SWDs during the design of policies and physical/digital infrastructure. The findings suggest that the current support systems are often reactive rather than proactive, failing to account for the unique technological and physical requirements of students with various disabilities.

The implications of this research suggest a need for a fundamental shift in how ODeL institutions approach inclusivity. The author recommends the development of disability-friendly technology and infrastructure to ensure that digital learning environments are truly accessible. There is a specific call for strengthening safety programs for students with albinism and providing mobility instructors to assist those with physical disabilities on campus. Furthermore, the study implies that institutions must implement more robust change management strategies to ensure that during crises, such as a pandemic, the transition to online modes does not strip SWDs of their established academic accommodations, such as extended exam times. Ultimately, the study advocates for a more inclusive institutional culture where the voices of SWDs are integrated into the planning and budgeting processes to ensure academic success and social integration.

title: Applying the E-learning Framework: Evaluating an E-learning Course toward the Improvement of Quality of ODeL Programs
abstract: Anchored on Khan’s Eight-Dimensional E-Learning Framework, this cross-sectional study evaluated IH 213 (Health Promotion for Equity and Sustainable Development) course—an e-learning course under the Diploma in/Master of International Health Program of the Faculty of Management and Development Studies, University of the Philippines Open University. Guided by the Evaluation Dimension of the E-learning Framework, the core objective of the study was to evaluate the course through assessment of international health learners and evaluation of the instruction and the learning environment. Thirty-three (33) international health learners enrolled in the course during the 2nd semester of A.Y. 2016-2017 served as the respondents of the study. The study used the survey research design to gather data from the respondents. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Recommendations were also presented.
half:
In the study "Applying the E-learning Framework: Evaluating an E-learning Course toward the Improvement of Quality of ODeL Programs," Myra D. Oruga and Jelaine R. Bagos examine the complexities of evaluating Open and Distance E-learning (ODeL) environments. The researchers applied the "Evaluation Dimension" of Khan’s Eight-Dimensional E-Learning Framework to assess the course IH 213 (Health Promotion for Equity and Sustainable Development) at the University of the Philippines Open University. The study aimed to evaluate the course's relevance to learners, reflective thinking, interactivity, tutor support, peer support, and the interpretation of messages.

Using a survey research design, data were collected from thirty-three international health learners via an online questionnaire. The findings revealed that the e-learning course was perceived as highly effective in most dimensions. Students reported that the content was relevant to professional practice and that they engaged in critical thinking. Furthermore, tutor support, peer support, and the clarity of messages were rated highly.

However, interactivity was identified as a relative weakness, as students reported only "sometimes" asking classmates to explain ideas or responding to their ideas. This suggests that active interaction between learners is lower than other metrics. The authors conclude that while the course is effective in most areas, interactivity requires improvement. They recommend implementing graded discussion forums, incentives for participation, or activities like debates to enhance the quality of the ODeL program.

title: Online Facilitation of Field Instruction for the Social Work Programs of UP Open University
abstract: Experiential education refers to programs that are created to widen the learning experiences of individuals beyond the four walls of the classroom and extending to work and community context. Internship programs, in particular, are seen by studies as beneficial to graduate study programs and develop practice skills and enable the transition from theories to practice. The University of the Philippines Open University, a pioneer and advocate of online teaching and learning and distance e-learning in the Philippines, has the Social Work program under the Faculty of Management and Development Studies that requires its students to undergo internship inside reputable institutions. These courses are supervised and guided online by the faculty-in-charge via the MyPortal course site. However, there are few studies addressing the effectiveness of clinical preparation of students especially with online facilitated programs. The study aimed to identify emerging themes in the reflective outputs vis-à-vis the fieldwork experiences of Social Work students in UPOU given its online mode of facilitation. A review of relevant practicum and field instruction documents and records as well as an analysis of learner’s reflections based on twelve reflection videos and integrative papers of the social work students were conducted. Results of the study on students’ reflective outputs show that students went throzugh the cycle of concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization and active experimentation. Reflections of the students were also made in reference to the self (as a human being), the profession (as a social worker), and their multiple responsibilities (as an online learner).

The authors conclude that online facilitation is effective, as the open and distance e-learning framework allowed students to maximize experiential learning and integrate theory and practice through guided reflection.

The study titled "Online Facilitation of Field Instruction for the Social Work Programs of UP Open University" by Finaflor F. Taylan and Paula Grace Muyco investigates the effectiveness of online facilitation for field instruction (FI) within the Diploma in/Master of Social Work (D/MSW) program at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU).

The problem addressed by the authors is the lack of existing research regarding the effectiveness of clinical preparation for students in programs where internships are facilitated online. While experiential education is recognized as vital for transitioning theoretical knowledge into professional practice, the specific dynamics of managing these field experiences in a distance e-learning context require documentation and assessment. This is particularly relevant for UPOU, as its students are geographically dispersed across the Philippines and internationally, necessitating an effective online framework for fieldwork.

The context of the study is the UPOU’s Social Work program under the Faculty of Management and Development Studies. The program requires students to complete 320 hours of supervised field instruction in reputable agencies. Because the program is delivered via distance e-learning, the faculty-in-charge (FIC) supervises and guides these internships online through the MyPortal course site. The study specifically looks at the academic year 2016-2017.

To address the research objective of identifying emerging themes in students' reflective outputs, the researchers employed a qualitative design using thematic analysis. The data consisted of 12 final sharing outputs, which included both integrative papers and final sharing videos submitted by students. The researchers used Kolb and Fry’s (1974) Experiential Learning Cycle as a theoretical framework to analyze these outputs, focusing on four stages: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation.

The findings revealed that students successfully moved through all four stages of the experiential learning cycle. In the concrete experience stage, students provided detailed accounts of their agency profiles, organizational structures, and the specific activities and accomplishments completed during their placement. In the reflective observation stage, students identified several challenges, including emotional struggles (such as fear and doubt), the difficulty of managing multiple responsibilities (balancing work, school, and FI), and practice-related challenges like minimal training in specific interventions. However, these challenges led to significant realizations regarding the social worker's role in society, the development of professional competencies, the importance of self-awareness, and the application of theory to practice (praxis).

In the abstract conceptualization stage, students reported gaining new technical knowledge and life skills, such as a deeper understanding of social administration and the ability to develop practice frameworks. Finally, in the active experimentation stage, students provided recommendations for both the host agencies and the UPOU program, alongside personal plans to continue their work with clients or ensure the sustainability of their projects within the agencies. The analysis showed that students' reflections were multifaceted, addressing their identity as human beings, their roles as social workers, and their responsibilities as online learners.

The authors conclude that the online facilitation of field instruction is effective. The use of online strategies and the open and distance e-learning framework allowed students to maximize their experiential learning despite geographical limitations. The study confirms that the online mode of facilitation enables students to become better practitioners and contributors to social transformation by successfully integrating theory and practice through guided reflection.

Based on these findings, the authors offer several implications and recommendations. They suggest that student feedback should be integrated into regular program reviews to improve FI courses. They recommend further continuous studies to explore updated technologies and strategies for experiential learning. Regarding the curriculum, the authors suggest developing additional modules for specific specializations (such as Social Administration, Clinical Practice, and Community Organizing) using a Resource Based Course Package format. They also recommend that the university finalize a formal practicum guide for use by students, agencies, and faculty, and suggest that the program require students to propose agencies earlier to facilitate the timely completion of necessary bilateral agreements.

title: A Meta-Interpretation of Collaborative Learning Activities in an R&D Management Online Degree Program
abstract: Collaborative learning has been a commonly used instructional strategy in management education. To further understand the teaching and learning issues in adopting collaborative learning inOpen and Distance e-Learning (ODeL), this study adopted meta-interpretation to identify the themes that constitute learners’ views and experiences in the collaborative learning activities in two courses offered in the Diploma in Research & Development Management at UP Open University as reported in the literature, and from these, teaching and learning implications on collaborative learning in management in the ODeL environment were derived. The study also recommends some approaches to designing and delivering online collaborative learning in these contexts.
half:
The study "A Meta-Interpretation of Collaborative Learning Activities in an R&D Management Online Degree Program" investigates collaborative learning within Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) environments. Focusing on the Diploma in Research & Development Management at the University of the Philippines Open University, the researchers examined learner experiences through a mini-case study and a WebQuest. Using a meta-interpretive approach, the authors synthesized qualitative research into four themes: purpose, learner experience, teacher’s role, and format.

Regarding purpose, collaboration deepens learning through reflection and broadens perspectives by exchanging diverse professional experiences. While learners found activities enjoyable and socially interactive, they faced challenges such as geographical and time differences, difficulty scheduling meetings, and issues with co-learner responsiveness or missed deadlines. The teacher's role was described as a dual reality; while students valued informal interaction during the collaborative phase, they also highly valued the teacher's active presence as a facilitator who provides feedback and a "personal touch." Regarding format, students required flexibility in topics and resources, alongside clear structures like explicit objectives and well-timed assignments.

The study concludes that successful online collaboration requires a balance of structure and flexibility. To support students, instructors should design activities with specific timing, provide clear guidelines and scaffolding, and incorporate peer assessment to ensure individual accountability and the co-creation of knowledge.

While collaborative learning is a standard strategy in management education to improve problem-solving and critical thinking, empirical research on online collaborative learning in management programs is limited. The authors address this gap by examining learner experiences in two activities within the Diploma in Research & Development Management (DR&DM) program at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU): a mini-case study on organizational culture in R&DM220 and a WebQuest on technology evaluation in R&DM251.

Using a meta-interpretive approach, the researchers performed an interpretive synthesis of existing qualitative research, using previous interpretations of learner views as raw data. Through an iterative coding process, the authors organized the findings into four thematic points: purpose, learner experience, teacher’s role, and format.

Regarding purpose, the study found that collaboration deepens learning through in-depth discussion and reflection, broadens perspectives via the exchange of diverse professional experiences, and serves as a method of learning in itself. In terms of learner experience, activities were found to be enjoyable and provided social interaction similar to traditional school environments. However, collaboration was also challenging due to geographical and time differences, difficulty finding common meeting times, and co-learner behaviors such as lack of responsiveness or missed deadlines.

Regarding the teacher's role, the findings revealed a dual reality: the teacher's relative absence during the collaborative phase allows for informal student interaction, yet the teacher's active presence as a facilitator is highly valued. Students appreciated teachers who provided stimulating inputs, feedback, and a "personal touch." Regarding format, the study identified a need for flexibility in choosing topics and resources, alongside a need for clear structure, such as explicit learning objectives and well-timed assignments, to prevent confusion.

The study concludes that for DR&DM students, collaboration is fundamentally an act of learning that expands perspectives on complex R&D management issues. Successful online collaborative learning requires a "delicate balancing act" from educators: providing enough structure to ensure clarity and accountability while maintaining enough flexibility for student exploration. Implications suggest that instructors should design activities with specific timing in mind, ideally during the early to middle part of a term. To mitigate distance-related challenges, teachers should provide clear guidelines, scaffolding, and structured roles. The study titled "A Meta-Interpretation of Collaborative Learning Activities in an R&D Management Online Degree Program" addresses the need to understand teaching and learning issues associated with adopting collaborative learning in Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) environments. While collaborative learning is a standard instructional strategy in management education intended to enhance problem-solving, social skills, and critical thinking, empirical research specifically focused on online collaborative learning within management programs remains relatively scarce. The authors aim to fill this gap by examining learner experiences in two specific collaborative activities within the Diploma in Research & Development Management (DR&DM) program at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU).

The research context involves two distinct courses: R&DM220 (Organizational Structure, Relations, and Processes in R&D Systems) and R&DM251 (Technology Evaluation). In R&DM220, students participated in the "Alligator Story: An Exercise on Values," a mini-case study designed to help students understand the relationship between values, subcultures, and organizational culture. In R&DM251, students engaged in a WebQuest, an inquiry-oriented activity using internet resources and role-playing to synthesize learning regarding technology evaluation mechanisms.

To analyze the data, the authors employed a meta-interpretive approach. This qualitative method involves the interpretive synthesis of existing qualitative research, using the interpretations of other authors as raw data. The researchers analyzed texts from two previously published papers (written by the first two authors) that detailed the learners' views and experiences in these specific activities. The analysis involved an iterative coding process where texts were categorized into themes and sub-themes based on literature-derived concepts and the original authors' categories. The resulting themes were organized into four thematic points: purpose, learner experience, teacher’s role, and format.

The findings revealed several key themes regarding the learners' experiences. Regarding the purpose of collaboration, the study found that collaborative learning can deepen learning by allowing for in-depth discussion and reflection, broaden perspectives through the exchange of diverse professional experiences, and serve as a method of learning in itself. In terms of learner experience, the activities were found to be enjoyable, providing social interaction and personal contact that mimics a traditional school environment. However, collaboration was also described as challenging due to geographical and time differences, the difficulty of finding common meeting times, and issues with co-learner behavior, such as lack of responsiveness or failure to meet deadlines.

Regarding the teacher's role, the findings highlighted a dual reality: the teacher's relative absence in the collaborative phase creates a new space for informal, personal interaction among students, yet the teacher's active presence as a facilitator is highly valued. Students appreciated teachers who provided stimulating inputs, feedback, and a "personal touch." Finally, regarding format, the study identified a need for flexibility in how students choose topics and resources, as well as a need for clear structure, such as explicit learning objectives and well-timed assignments, to prevent confusion.

The study concludes that for students in the DR&DM program, the act of collaboration is fundamentally an act of learning. It provides essential opportunities to deepen understanding and expand perspectives on complex R&D management issues. While the social and cognitive benefits are significant, the online nature of the delivery introduces complexities that require careful management. The authors conclude that successful online collaborative learning requires a "delicate balancing act" from educators: providing enough structure to ensure clarity and accountability while maintaining enough flexibility to allow for student exploration and professional relevance.

The implications of this research suggest that instructors in ODeL environments should design collaborative activities with specific timing in mind, ideally scheduling them in the early to middle part of a term when student workloads are lighter. To mitigate the challenges of distance, teachers should provide clear guidelines, scaffolding (such as "hot lists" of resources), and structured roles to guide the process. Furthermore, the study suggests that incorporating peer assessment can serve as both a tool for co-creation of knowledge and a mechanism for ensuring individual accountability within groups. These findings are applicable to various management programs and can help optimize the design of collaborative tasks in distance education.

title: Assessing the Practices for the Conduct of Graduate Students’ Thesis at the Faculty of Management and Development Studies, UP Open University
abstract: Graduate student thesis practices are procedures and policies that are followed by graduate students, faculty members, and staff of higher education institutions. Since UP Open University (UPOU) is an Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) institution, the thesis practices that are implemented by its Faculty Offices must adhere to the principles of distance education. Appropriate implementation of graduate thesis production at UPOU requires closer coordination because of the time and space difference between and among advisers, students, staff, panel members, and program chair. The practices comprising graduate student thesis writing in the UPOU Faculty of Management and Development Studies (FMDS) Programs are here explored. The study examines the administrative practices followed by the programs of FMDS in the conduct of graduate thesis among its learners. Practices that contribute to quality thesis administration are suggested here. These suggestions follow those available in the literature and those uncovered from thesis students’ experiences. Finally, this inquiry presents recommendations that will promote good practices in administering the programs’ thesis courses in the distance mode.
half:
The study "Assessing the Practices for the Conduct of Graduate Students’ Thesis at the Faculty of Management and Development Studies, UP Open University" examines administrative practices for graduate thesis work within an Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) environment. The research addresses challenges caused by spatial and temporal gaps between students and faculty, which can complicate research supervision. Using a qualitative approach involving content analysis, interviews, and surveys, the researchers examined four Master’s programs: Master of ASEAN Studies, Master of Arts in Nursing, Master of International Health, and Master of Land Valuation and Management.

Findings reveal that the programs implement several ideal practices, such as establishing prerequisites like comprehensive exams and utilizing technology for orientations and communication via email, discussion forums, and social media. Support systems, including library services and monitoring task forces, are also in place. However, significant gaps exist between current practices and student needs. Students reported insufficient guidance, unclear expectations regarding thesis quality, and difficulties adhering to timelines. The "distance-ness" of the programs can magnify issues like scheduling consultation meetings and receiving consistent feedback.

The researchers concluded that while a foundation aligned with ODeL standards exists, implementation is inconsistent. Recommendations include explicitly defining high-quality thesis characteristics, providing advisers with training on online feedback technologies, offering online research skill courses, developing an automated learning management system for advising, and promoting learner interaction to reduce isolation.

title: Constraints on the Use of a Learning Management System in a Blended Learning Environment
abstract: This research investigated the blended learning environment constraints when academics use a learning management system (LMS). With the prevalent use of educational technologies including the LMS, a mix of traditional face-to-face and web-based technologies became an alternative mode of instructional delivery in higher education. However, despite of the reported benefits in many studies about the use of LMS, the uptake of using the system was not maximized by students and by academics. The problem this research sought to answer was: what were the constraints encountered by the academics in a blended learning environment? This investigation was conducted in a state university based in Mindanao, Philippines. Thirty-three academicsfrom different disciplines and professorial levels participated in this study. The LMS used in this university was Moodle and records of computer logs indicated that only 30% of academics used the LMS. Two major processes were carried out in this investigation. Firstly, a qualitative approach which employed a onehour, one-on-one in-depth interview with each participant was conducted. Data were then transcribed and coded in three stages: open, axial, and selective coding. Qualitative data were analyzed using a grounded theory approach. Secondly, a quantitative approach, using descriptive statistics was used in the analysis of the participants’ computer logs which were gathered and processed using a simple data mining procedure. The findings in this study suggested that academics had been experiencing difficulties in delivering courses in a technology-enhanced learning environment particularly with the use of LMS. Difficulties in time management, curriculum level, students' access, and economic viability were found to cause the constraints.
half:
Cenie M. Vilela-Malabanan and Nancy Q. Echavez investigated the constraints academics face when using a Learning Management System (LMS) in a blended learning environment at a state university in Mindanao, Philippines. Using a mixed-methods design involving interviews with thirty-three academics and analysis of Moodle computer logs, the study identified four major dimensions of constraints: time management, curriculum level, students' access and economic viability, and students' work and validity of control.

Regarding time management, academics reported that preparing digital materials is more time-consuming than traditional methods, increasing workloads as they manage both physical and online interactions. Curriculum constraints varied by subject; technology-driven courses struggled with laboratory availability, while non-technology courses faced limited student computer access. Additionally, computational subjects were harder to teach effectively online compared to descriptive subjects. Economic factors were a major concern, as students often lack personal computers or reliable internet. This leads to academic anxiety regarding teaching performance and the integrity of unsupervised online assessments.

Quantitative log analysis confirmed that while academics frequently use the LMS for uploading resources, the use of interactive features like forums and chats is significantly lower due to curriculum and economic limitations. The researchers conclude that LMS usage is heavily influenced by the socio-technological landscape, suggesting that administrators must address student technology access, improve infrastructure, and review teaching loads to support digital resource development.
one:
Cenie M. Vilela-Malabanan and Nancy Q. Echavez investigated the constraints faced by academics when using a Learning Management System (LMS) within a blended learning environment. Conducted at a state university in Mindanao, Philippines, the study focused on the use of Moodle, customized as the MSU-IIT Online Learning Environment (MOLE). The researchers employed a mixed-methods design, utilizing in-depth interviews with thirty-three academics across various disciplines and a descriptive statistical analysis of LMS computer logs.

The findings identified four major dimensions of constraints: time management, curriculum level, students' access and economic viability, and students' work and validity of control. Regarding time management, academics reported that preparing digital materials, such as multimedia content and lesson notes, is more time-consuming than traditional methods. The workload increases as instructors manage both physical contact hours and extensive online interactions, often without additional compensation.

Curriculum level constraints were tied to the nature of the subject matter. Technology-driven courses faced challenges regarding laboratory availability, while non-technology-driven courses faced difficulties due to limited student computer access. Additionally, descriptive subjects were perceived as more suitable for online delivery, whereas computational or problem-solving subjects were more difficult to teach effectively without face-to-face interaction.

Students' access and economic viability emerged as a major concern. Many students lack personal computers or reliable internet, forcing them to use internet cafés. These economic factors influence an academic's decision to use the LMS, as they fear the system may hinder teaching performance if students cannot access it. Furthermore, academics expressed anxiety regarding academic integrity and the veracity of student answers during online assessments conducted outside the classroom without direct supervision.

Quantitative log analysis supported these qualitative findings. While academics frequently used the LMS for non-interactive purposes, such as uploading resources and assignments, the usage of interactive features like chats, forums, and quizzes was significantly lower. This low interactive usage was strongly influenced by curriculum constraints and the economic limitations of students.

The study concludes that LMS usage is heavily influenced by the socio-technological landscape, and a "one-size-fits-all" approach to blended learning is inappropriate. External factors, such as student economic status and institutional infrastructure, are dominant drivers of academic engagement with the technology. The researchers suggest that administrators should address student access to technology, provide better infrastructure, and consider reviewing teaching loads to allow academics time to develop high-quality digital resources. Additionally, departments should develop guidelines for which courses are best suited for blended delivery based on their specific subject matter.
two:
The research conducted by Cenie M. Vilela-Malabanan and Nancy Q. Echavez investigates the constraints faced by academics when utilizing a Learning Management System (LMS) within a blended learning environment. Despite the growing prevalence of educational technologies and the shift toward learner-centered, web-based instructional delivery in higher education, the study notes that the uptake of these systems is often not maximized by either students or academics. The central problem addressed is identifying the specific constraints encountered by academics when delivering courses in a blended mode.

The study was conducted at a state university in Mindanao, Philippines, which utilizes Moodle, customized as the MSU-IIT Online Learning Environment (MOLE). The researchers employed a mixed-methods research design. The qualitative component involved one-on-one, in-depth interviews with thirty-three academics from various disciplines and professorial levels. These interviews were analyzed using a grounded theory approach involving open, axial, and selective coding. The quantitative component involved a descriptive statistical analysis of computer logs from the LMS, which were processed using a simple data mining procedure. To ensure validity, the researchers used two schemes: confirming interview transcripts with participants and presenting findings in workshops with both non-administrative academics and executive management.

The findings revealed that academics experience significant difficulties in delivering technology-enhanced courses. The researchers identified four major dimensions of constraints: time management, curriculum level, students' access and economic viability, and students' work and validity of control.

Regarding time management, academics reported that preparing learning materials and assessments for blended learning is more time-consuming than traditional methods. Tasks such as writing lesson notes, sourcing relevant links, and creating multimedia content like video recordings require significant effort. Furthermore, the time required to manage online discussions and the delays caused by connectivity issues add to the burden. The study also noted that the workload increases when academics must manage both physical contact hours and extensive online interactions, often without additional compensation.

Curriculum level constraints were linked to the nature of the subject matter. Technology-driven courses (such as Engineering and Computer Science) faced challenges regarding the availability of computer laboratories and facilities. Conversely, non-technology-driven courses (such as Arts and Social Sciences) faced difficulties in deciding whether to use the LMS due to limited student access to computers. Additionally, the study found that the type of subject matter matters; descriptive subjects were perceived as more suitable for online delivery, whereas computational or problem-solving subjects were more difficult to teach effectively without face-to-face interaction.

Students' access and economic viability emerged as a major concern for most participants. Many students are economically challenged and lack personal computers or reliable home internet connections. This creates an inequity in access and forces students to use internet cafés, which raises safety concerns for academics. These economic factors directly influence an academic's decision to utilize the LMS, as they fear the system may hinder teaching performance if students cannot access it.

The fourth dimension, students' work and validity of control, pertains to the issue of trust and academic integrity. Academics expressed anxiety regarding the veracity of student answers during online quizzes and assignments conducted outside the classroom. Without the ability to personally supervise students in a laboratory setting, academics struggle to ensure that students are performing tasks themselves, particularly when students must rely on external locations like internet cafés.

The quantitative log analysis supported these qualitative findings. The data showed that while many academics used the LMS for non-interactive purposes—such as uploading resources, assignments, and lesson notes—the usage of interactive features like chats, forums, and quizzes was significantly lower. The analysis indicated that low interactive usage was strongly influenced by curriculum constraints and the economic limitations of students. Many academics chose to use the LMS only for basic functions like posting notes rather than engaging in the full interactive potential of the system.

The study concludes that the usage of an LMS is heavily influenced by the socio-technological landscape of the learning environment. Academic discipline plays a crucial role in determining how a subject can be effectively delivered in a blended format, suggesting that a "one-size-fits-all" approach is inappropriate. The research confirms that external factors, such as student economic status and institutional infrastructure, are dominant drivers of how academics engage with the technology.

The implications of this research are significant for both academics and university administrators. For administrators, the findings suggest a need for institutional policies that address student access to technology and reliable internet. Providing better infrastructure and technical support could mitigate some environmental constraints. The study also suggests that universities might consider reviewing teaching loads; reducing the workload could allow academics the necessary time to develop high-quality digital learning resources. Furthermore, the findings imply that departments should develop specific guidelines for which types of courses are best suited for blended delivery based on their subject matter. Ultimately, the research serves as a guide for minimizing constraints to enhance the effectiveness of LMS usage in higher education.
