title: Computer-based Simulation and its Effects on Student’s Knowledge and Interest in Chemistry
abstract: Central to learning Chemistry is the development of fluency across various representations such as symbolic-, macroscopic-, and particulate-levels. “Simulations that support multi-representational fluency are considered critical (Moore, Chamberlain, Parson, & Perkins, 2014)” because of the inherent difficulty of Chemistry as a subject matter. This action research, aimed at analyzing the effects of computer simulation on students’ knowledge and interest in Chemistry, used a quasi-experimental research design. The participants of the study were three intact classes from different learning groups in a male boarding school in Southern Tagalog province. Four Physics Education Technology (PhET) interactive simulations were used in teaching the concepts of chemical reaction for three weeks. Pre- and post-test scores of the students showed that there is an increase in students’ knowledge and is highest in the advance group. The result of the interest survey showed that advance and proficient students were highly interested while students approaching proficiency were moderately interested in learning Chemistry using simulation. Students revealed that they enjoyed using the computer-based simulation while learning Chemistry because (1) of the stars that they virtually receive and the challenges posed in the game levels, (2) the material is easy to manipulate, (3) they perform the activity with minimal supervision, thus making them feel independent, and (4) the material contains practice exercises and a game after the topic introduction. The computer-based simulation is recommended to be employed in classroom instruction to increase students’ knowledge and interest in Chemistry.
half:
The study "Computer-based Simulation and its Effects on Student’s Knowledge and Interest in Chemistry" by Jhenly I. Asedillas and Maria Ana T. Quimbo investigates how computer-based simulation (CBS) impacts student learning and engagement. Prompted by the difficulty students face in mastering Chemistry, the researchers used a quasi-experimental design to study 143 students from a male boarding school in the Southern Tagalog province. Participants were divided into three homogeneous groups: advanced, proficient, and approaching proficiency. The intervention involved using Physics Education Technology (PhET) interactive simulations to teach chemical reaction concepts over three weeks.

Findings demonstrate that CBS effectively increased knowledge across all three learning groups. The advanced group showed the greatest increase in mean scores (10.980), followed by the proficient group (10.490) and the group approaching proficiency (4.614). Regarding interest, advanced and proficient students reported high interest, while those approaching proficiency reported moderate interest. Qualitative data indicated students enjoyed the simulations due to gamified elements, the ability to manipulate materials independently, the safety of making mistakes, and immediate feedback. Crucially, simulations helped students visualize abstract concepts like atomic movement.

The researchers concluded that CBS is an effective tool for increasing knowledge and interest by bridging the gap between abstract concepts and visual understanding. Because lower proficiency students showed lower interest, the authors suggest simulations may be more effective as reinforcement tools. They recommend integrating CBS into teaching guides and using simulations for topics that are difficult to visualize or unsafe for traditional labs.
one:
The study "Computer-based Simulation and its Effects on Student’s Knowledge and Interest in Chemistry" by Jhenly I. Asedillas and Maria Ana T. Quimbo investigates how computer-based simulation (CBS) impacts student learning and engagement. The research was prompted by the difficulty students face in mastering Chemistry, which requires fluency across symbolic, macroscopic, and particulate representations. This difficulty is reflected in low exam scores and declining science performance in the Philippines.

Using a quasi-experimental design, the researchers studied 143 students from a male boarding school in the Southern Tagalog province. The students were divided into three homogeneous groups based on their general weighted average: advanced, proficient, and approaching proficiency. The intervention involved using Physics Education Technology (PhET) interactive simulations to teach chemical reaction concepts over three weeks. Data were collected through pre-tests, post-tests, an interest survey adapted from the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory, and focus group discussions.

The findings demonstrate that CBS effectively increased knowledge across all three learning groups. The advanced group showed the greatest increase in mean scores (10.980), followed by the proficient group (10.490) and the group approaching proficiency (4.614). In terms of interest, advanced and proficient students reported high interest in learning through simulation, while those approaching proficiency reported moderate interest.

Qualitative data from focus groups indicated that students enjoyed the simulations due to gamified elements, such as virtual stars and levels. Students appreciated the ability to manipulate materials independently, the safety of making mistakes without real-world consequences, and the immediate feedback provided. Crucially, the simulations helped students visualize abstract concepts, such as the movement of atoms and molecules.

The researchers concluded that CBS is an effective tool for increasing both knowledge and interest by bridging the gap between abstract concepts and visual understanding. The simulations align with Gagne’s nine events of instruction by gaining attention and providing guidance. However, because students in the lower proficiency group showed lower interest levels, the authors suggest simulations may be more effective as reinforcement tools rather than primary instructional methods.

The authors recommend that science module developers integrate CBS into teaching guides and suggest that teachers use simulations for topics that are difficult to visualize or unsafe for traditional labs. They advise providing foundational lectures before using simulations to prevent frustration. Finally, the study emphasizes that the design of learning activities should take priority over the technology itself and recommends further research into the effects of computer-assisted activities on heterogeneous groups and varying levels of student engagement.
two:
The study titled "Computer-based Simulation and its Effects on Student’s Knowledge and Interest in Chemistry" by Jhenly I. Asedillas and Maria Ana T. Quimbo addresses the persistent challenge of teaching Chemistry, a subject often perceived as difficult due to the need for fluency across symbolic, macroscopic, and particulate representations. The authors note that traditional teaching methods, where the teacher remains the center of learning, may no longer be sufficient to meet modern educational needs. This problem is compounded by broader educational issues in the Philippines, including low student interest in school and declining performance in science and mathematics on international assessments like TIMSS. Specifically, the researchers observed that students in a male boarding school in the Southern Tagalog province struggled with Chemistry, as evidenced by low exam scores.

To address these issues, the researchers aimed to analyze how computer-based simulation (CBS) affects students' knowledge and interest in Chemistry. The study utilized a quasi-experimental research design involving 143 students from three intact classes, categorized into three homogeneous learning groups based on their general weighted average: advanced, proficient, and approaching proficiency. The intervention involved using Physics Education Technology (PhET) interactive simulations to teach chemical reaction concepts over a three-week period. Data collection included pre-tests and post-tests to measure knowledge gains, an interest survey adapted from the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory to measure enjoyment, value/usefulness, and perceived choice, and focus group discussions to gather qualitative insights.

The findings indicated that computer-based simulations effectively increased students' knowledge across all three learning groups. While the proficient group had the highest number of students passing the post-test, the advanced group demonstrated the greatest increase in mean scores. Specifically, the mean score increases were 10.980 for the advanced group, 10.490 for the proficient group, and 4.614 for the group approaching proficiency. Regarding student interest, the results showed that advanced and proficient students reported high interest in learning Chemistry through simulation, whereas students approaching proficiency reported moderate interest.

Qualitative data from the focus group discussions revealed that students enjoyed the simulations for several reasons. They appreciated the gamified elements, such as receiving virtual stars and navigating challenging game levels. Students also noted that the material was easy to manipulate and allowed them to work with minimal supervision, fostering a sense of independence. Furthermore, the simulations provided a safe environment to make mistakes and receive immediate feedback, which helped them master difficult concepts like balancing chemical equations. Students also highlighted the utility of the simulations in visualizing abstract concepts, such as the movement of atoms and molecules, which are otherwise difficult to imagine.

The study concludes that computer-based simulation is an effective tool for increasing both the knowledge and interest of students in Chemistry. The simulations help bridge the gap between abstract concepts and visual understanding, making learning more engaging and self-paced. The researchers noted that the simulations align with Gagne’s nine events of instruction by gaining attention, providing guidance, and eliciting performance. However, the study also found that students in the lower proficiency group had lower interest levels and suggested that simulations might be more effective as reinforcement tools rather than primary instructional methods.

Based on these findings, the authors offer several implications and recommendations. They recommend that science module developers integrate computer-based simulations into teaching and learning guides to enhance engagement and understanding. For classroom instruction, the researchers suggest that teachers use simulations to teach topics that are difficult to visualize or unsafe to perform in a traditional laboratory setting. They also recommend that teachers provide a foundational lecture before introducing simulations to ensure students have the necessary background knowledge to avoid frustration.

Furthermore, the study emphasizes the importance of monitoring all students, regardless of their proficiency level, to address individual differences, such as varying levels of computer literacy or language barriers. The authors suggest that the design of learning activities should take priority over the technology itself. Finally, they recommend further research to investigate the effects of computer-assisted activities on different learning groups, including heterogeneous groups, and to explore the impact of varying levels of student engagement with these digital tools.

title: Student co-creation in an online university: successes, failures and how to move forward
abstract:
I embarked on a Digital Collective project in 2018 to engage students and other stakeholders to co-create knowledge in a learning platform and tap the full potential of open educational practice at the University of the Philippines Open University. The project tried to co-create OERs with students and alumni to explore the idea of building an online learning community as the foundation over which co-creation was to be conducted. I recruited volunteers from UPOU’s Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) program to join me in the project, which ran for much of 2018. The purpose of this autoethnographic study is to assess and reflect on the strengths and weaknesses of how the project was conducted. These preliminary findings using autoethnography can hopefully help the university in drawing up a plan that can effectively build this online community.
Key themes were identified as factors for the project’s success. Through self-reflection, review of project notes, and a group discussion with some participants with respect to these themes, participation, and output can be attributed to setting clear goals for participants, level of incorporation into the curriculum, institutional support, and adopting an appropriate method of organization. The data suggest a more defined approach following a community of practice model rather than that of a learning community, as these may lead to not just improved project management and productivity, but also less dependency on any formal ties with the curriculum.
half:
In the article "Student co-creation in an online university: successes, failures and how to move forward," Al Francis D. Librero examines the 2018 Digital Collective initiative at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). The project aimed to move beyond faculty-centric Open Educational Resources (OERs) by engaging students and alumni to co-create multimedia learning materials, such as graphics, audio, and blogs, to support open educational practice and professional portfolio development.

Using an autoethnographic research method, the author analyzed personal experiences and data from over 30 students and alumni from the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies program. Findings indicate that while recruitment was successful, most participants remained passive, engaging only through social media "likes" rather than contributing content. This lack of productivity was attributed to competing priorities like work and family, the project's status as an extracurricular activity rather than a curricular one, and a lack of clear organizational hierarchy. Additionally, cultural factors like "hiya" (fear of scrutiny) and a conceptual mismatch—treating a voluntary project as a "learning community" rather than a "community of practice"—hindered progress.

The study concludes that student co-creation requires structural support to compete with other student responsibilities. To move toward productive co-creation, the author recommends clarity of goals, integration into the curriculum via academic credit, formal management structures, capacity building for junior students, and fostering a sense of community.
one:
In the article "Student co-creation in an online university: successes, failures and how to move forward," Al Francis D. Librero examines the 2018 Digital Collective initiative at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). The project sought to move beyond faculty-centric models of Open Educational Resources (OERs) by engaging students and alumni to co-create multimedia learning materials, such as graphics, audio content, and blogs. The objective was to build an online learning community that supports open educational practice (OEP) while allowing students to develop professional portfolios.

The study addresses the difficulty of transitioning students from passive content consumers to active collaborators. To investigate why the project struggled to maintain engagement and secure content contributions, the author utilized an autoethnographic research method. This involved analyzing personal experiences as project leader through self-reflection, project notes, and informal discussions. Data was gathered from over 30 students and alumni from the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) program, including a focused group discussion with the most active participants.

The findings indicate that while recruitment was successful, with nearly 60 people joining the project's Facebook group, most participants remained passive, engaging only through social media "likes" without contributing actual content. Several factors contributed to this lack of productivity. Participants faced competing priorities, including work, family, and primary academic studies. Additionally, because the project was not formally integrated into the university curriculum, it was viewed as an extracurricular activity. The author also noted that a lack of clear organizational hierarchy made it difficult to mobilize passive members.

Cultural and psychological barriers were also identified. Participants expressed a sense of "hiya" (a Filipino concept related to shame or sensitivity to criticism), suggesting a fear of public scrutiny from peers or instructors. Furthermore, the author realized the project was conceptually flawed; it was approached as a "learning community" focused on academic improvement, whereas its voluntary nature was better suited to a "community of practice" model.

The study concludes that student co-creation requires more than an open platform; it requires structural support to compete with students' other responsibilities. To move from social engagement to productive co-creation, the author recommends five key themes: clarity of goals, incorporation into the curriculum via academic credit, formal organization through a management structure, capacity building for junior students, and fostering a sense of community. Ultimately, formalizing the role of students within the academic structure is vital for the success of such initiatives.

The article "Student co-creation in an online university: successes, failures and how to move forward" by Al Francis D. Librero examines a 2018 initiative called the Digital Collective at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU). The project aimed to move beyond faculty-centric models of Open Educational Resources (OERs) by engaging students and alumni to co-create multimedia learning materials, such as stock photography, graphics, audio content, and blogs. The goal was to build an online learning community that would serve as a foundation for open educational practice (OEP) while allowing students to build professional portfolios.

The problem addressed by the study is the difficulty of transitioning from a model where students are merely consumers of content to one where they are active collaborators. Despite the potential benefits of student co-creation, the author encountered significant challenges in maintaining engagement and securing actual content contributions. The study seeks to understand why the project stalled and what structural or cultural factors influence the success of such community-driven initiatives in a distance education setting.

To investigate these issues, the author employed an autoethnographic research method. This approach allowed the researcher to systematically analyze his personal experiences as the project leader, using self-reflection, project notes, and informal discussions. Data collection included recruiting over 30 students and alumni from the Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) program. While many joined the project's Facebook group, the author conducted a focused group discussion with the most active participants to gather qualitative data regarding their motivations, the challenges they faced, and their perceptions of why the project failed to meet its immediate production goals.

The findings reveal several critical factors that influenced the project's trajectory. While recruitment was successful—with nearly 60 people joining the group—the majority of participants remained "passive," engaging through social media "likes" but failing to contribute actual content. The author identified several reasons for this lack of productivity. First, participants faced competing priorities, such as work, family, and their primary academic studies. Second, the lack of formal integration into the university curriculum meant that participation was viewed as extracurricular, placing it at the bottom of students' priority lists. Third, the author noted a lack of clear organizational hierarchy, which made it difficult for active members to mobilize passive ones.

The study also uncovered cultural and psychological barriers. Participants mentioned a sense of "hiya" (a Filipino concept related to shame or sensitivity to criticism), suggesting that students might have been hesitant to share their work publicly due to fear of scrutiny from peers or the instructor. Furthermore, the author realized that his conceptualization of the project was flawed; he had approached it as a "learning community" focused on academic improvement, whereas the project's nature—involving alumni and voluntary participation—was more aligned with a "community of practice" model.

The conclusions drawn from the study suggest that for student co-creation to be sustainable, it requires more than just an open platform. The author concludes that the project stalled because it lacked the necessary structural support to compete with students' other life responsibilities. The transition from a learning community to a community of practice is recommended to better accommodate voluntary participation and distributed leadership.

The implications of this research provide a roadmap for online universities looking to implement similar initiatives. The author identifies five key themes essential for success: clarity of goals (distinguishing between short-term tasks and long-term community building), incorporation into the curriculum (providing academic credit to incentivize participation), formal organization (establishing a structure or core group to manage operations), capacity building (providing skills development for junior students), and fostering a sense of community (building connectedness to sustain long-term interest). Ultimately, the study suggests that while online interaction is sufficient for maintaining social connections, formalizing the role of students within the academic structure is vital for moving from social engagement to productive co-creation.

title: Traditional e-Learning vs. Immersive Learning: A Perception Study among Maritime Students
abstract: e-Learning and immersive learning (i-Learning) are learning methods that focus on the use of technology in the field of education. e-Learning is a traditional learning that supports computer-based teaching while immersive learning is a new strategy that generates an inclusive and interactive learning environment in a virtual reality scene bringing students and trainees to a more experiential-learning workplace. The Philippines is struggling in the field of education because of the decreasing norms of education in the country’s education scheme. This research assessed the gap between traditional e-Learning and i-Learning through a questionnaire provided to the second-year maritime students of the Philippine Merchant Marine Academy (PMMA) under deck and engine departments. The data showed that there is a difference between e-Learning and i-Learning but it seems to be not statistically significant. The respondents had perceived that both e-Learning and i-Learning are most advantageous at time-efficiency and least advantageous at cost-effectivity and i-Learning seems to be more interactive and realistic than e-Learning. The results had also shown that the greatest disadvantage of e-Learning is that the method seems to be boring and noninteractive; however, both methods seem to be perceived as expensive. The Connectivism Theory emphasizes that learning is most effective when the learner is willing to learn. It was concluded that either method is supplemental to acquire knowledge and can be used to help create a fair and quality system.
half:
Dela Cerna, Ibias Jr., and Raymundo investigated maritime students' perceptions of traditional e-Learning versus immersive learning (i-Learning) to address technological gaps in the Philippine maritime education sector. Grounded in Connectivism Theory, the study utilized a quantitative design involving 192 second-year maritime students from the Philippine Merchant Marine Academy. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA) to compare the methods across five dimensions: risk reduction, interactivity, enjoyability, knowledge retention, and applicability to all subjects.

The findings showed that both methods were perceived as most beneficial for time-efficiency. i-Learning was viewed as more realistic and interactive, while e-Learning was considered more cost-effective. Regarding disadvantages, e-Learning was frequently described as boring and non-interactive, whereas i-Learning received much lower negative ratings in these areas. Both methods were perceived as expensive, though e-Learning was rated slightly higher in terms of cost-disadvantage.

MANOVA results indicated no statistically significant difference between traditional e-Learning and i-Learning regarding risk reduction, interactivity, enjoyability, retention, or applicability at an alpha level of 0.05. The researchers concluded that both methods serve as valuable supplemental tools and neither is a complete replacement for the other. They suggest integrating both methods for a balanced environment and recommend that future research include a wider variety of students and objective data on student performance.
one:
Dela Cerna, Ibias Jr., and Raymundo investigated maritime students' perceptions of two technological educational approaches: traditional e-Learning and immersive learning (i-Learning). The study addresses the need to bridge technological and knowledge gaps in the Philippine educational landscape, particularly as the maritime industry increasingly relies on simulators and advanced technology. Grounded in Connectivism Theory, the research explores the transition from computer-based teaching to experiential, virtual reality-based environments.

The researchers employed a quantitative research design using convenience sampling, involving 192 second-year maritime students from the Philippine Merchant Marine Academy (PMMA). The participants were predominantly male (96.4%), with 60% from the engine department and 40% from the deck department. The study noted that smartphones (98.4%) and laptops (74.5%) were the most common technological tools used by the respondents. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA) to compare the two methods across five dimensions: risk reduction, interactivity, enjoyability, knowledge retention, and applicability to all subjects.

The findings revealed that both e-Learning and i-Learning were perceived as most beneficial regarding time-efficiency (47.9%). However, i-Learning was viewed as more realistic (31.8%) and interactive (31.3%) than traditional e-Learning, while e-Learning was considered more cost-effective. Regarding disadvantages, e-Learning was frequently described as boring (41.7%) and non-interactive (39.6%), whereas i-Learning received much lower negative ratings in these areas. Both methods were perceived as being expensive, though e-Learning was rated slightly higher in terms of cost-disadvantage.

Crucially, MANOVA results indicated no statistically significant difference between traditional e-Learning and i-Learning regarding risk reduction, interactivity, enjoyability, retention, or applicability to all subjects at an alpha level of 0.05. This suggests that maritime students view both methods as relatively comparable in their educational utility.

The researchers concluded that both e-Learning and i-Learning serve as valuable supplemental tools for knowledge acquisition. While i-Learning offers a more interactive and realistic experience, neither method is a complete replacement for the other. The study suggests that educational institutions should consider integrating both methods to create a balanced learning environment. The authors recommend that future research expand the respondent base to include a wider variety of students and move beyond subjective perceptions by testing actual learning management systems to gather objective data on student performance and learning outcomes.
two:
The research conducted by Dela Cerna, Ibias Jr., and Raymundo investigates the perceptions of maritime students regarding two distinct technological educational approaches: traditional e-Learning and immersive learning (i-Learning). The study addresses a critical problem in the Philippine educational landscape, where declining educational standards and limited access to basic education have become significant socio-economic challenges. Specifically, the authors note that the Philippines has faced difficulties in international assessments, ranking low in mathematics and science. As the world enters the era of "Education 4.0," there is a pressing need to bridge technological and knowledge gaps to create a more effective and equitable learning system.

The context of this study is centered on the maritime industry, a field that increasingly relies on simulators and advanced technology to prepare students for life at sea. The researchers sought to understand how students perceive the transition from computer-based teaching to more experiential, virtual reality-based environments. The study is grounded in Connectivism Theory, which posits that learning is a network-based phenomenon and is most effective when the learner is engaged and willing to participate in the learning cycle.

To investigate these perceptions, the researchers employed a quantitative research design using a convenience sampling method. The participants consisted of 192 second-year maritime students from the Philippine Merchant Marine Academy (PMMA), comprising both deck and engine departments. The demographic profile of the respondents revealed a predominantly male population (96.4%), with 60% belonging to the engine department and 40% to the deck department. The study also identified the technological tools available to these students, finding that smartphones (98.4%) and laptops (74.5%) were the most commonly used devices.

The methodology utilized both descriptive statistics and Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA) to analyze the data. Descriptive statistics were used to determine the demographic profiles and the perceived advantages and disadvantages of both methods. MANOVA was applied to test for significant differences between e-Learning and i-Learning across five specific dimensions: risk reduction, interactivity, enjoyability, knowledge retention, and applicability to all subjects.

The findings of the study revealed several key insights into student perceptions. Regarding advantages, both e-Learning and i-Learning were perceived to be most beneficial in terms of time-efficiency (47.9%). However, i-Learning was perceived to be more realistic (31.8%) and interactive (31.3%) than traditional e-Learning. Conversely, e-Learning was viewed as being more cost-effective than i-Learning. In terms of disadvantages, e-Learning was frequently described as boring (41.7%) and non-interactive (39.6%), whereas i-Learning faced much lower negative ratings in these categories. Both methods were perceived by students as being expensive, though e-Learning was rated slightly higher in terms of cost-disadvantage.

Crucially, the MANOVA results indicated that while there were descriptive differences in how students viewed the two methods, there was no statistically significant difference between traditional e-Learning and i-Learning regarding risk reduction, interactivity, enjoyability, retention, or applicability to all subjects at an alpha level of 0.05. This suggests that, from the perspective of the maritime students, both methods are viewed as relatively comparable in their educational utility.

The researchers concluded that both e-Learning and i-Learning serve as valuable supplemental tools for acquiring knowledge. The study reinforces the idea that the effectiveness of these technologies is tied to the learner's willingness to engage, consistent with Connectivism Theory. While i-Learning offers a more interactive and realistic experience, neither method is a complete replacement for the other, and both can contribute to a high-quality, fair educational system if implemented correctly.

The implications of this study suggest that educational institutions should consider integrating both methods to create a balanced learning environment. The findings imply that while i-Learning provides a superior experiential quality that can mitigate the "boring" nature of traditional digital learning, the cost-effectiveness of e-Learning remains a practical consideration. The researchers recommend that future studies expand the respondent base beyond the PMMA to include a wider variety of students to achieve more generalizable data. Furthermore, they suggest that future research should move beyond subjective perceptions by testing actual learning management systems to gather more objective data on student performance and learning outcomes. Ultimately, the study advocates for the continued development of educational systems that align with the modern technological age while maintaining equity and quality.

title: Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) Readiness of Pangasinan State University – Open University Systems Students
abstract:
This study was conducted to determine the readiness of PSU-OUS students in Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) before its implementation in the institution. MOOC is an innovative online course available for anyone. It “provides an affordable and flexible way to learn new skills, advance student’s career, and deliver quality educational experiences” (Mooc.org, 2009; Veermata Jijabai Technological Institute (VJTI, n.d. p.1) being utilized by prestigious institutions like UPOU and SEAMEO INNOTECH. Hence, MOOC’s fusion to the different courses in PSU-OUS is promising and something to look forward to. The research used the descriptive method and the respondents were chosen through purposive sampling technique. To analyze and interpret the data gathered, the researcher used the weighted mean.
The majority of the students of PSU-OUS are female and are working in the government. Many of the respondents have less exposure to seminars relating to distance learning education while mostly of them are 21 – 30 years old, taking up Master of Arts in Education major in Educational Management and are receiving 21 – 30 thousand monthly.
The results reflected that students are slightly ready in downloading or installing programs or plugins such as Java, Adobe, Reader, Quick Time and etc., and they are also slightly ready in using Learning Management System like iFolio, SPIN, and Moodle. However, the results also showed that students are prepared on various aspects such as technology access, online skills, motivation, online audio/video and internet discussions. Therefore, the students of PSU-OUS are ready in the implementation of MOOC in the university.
half:
Phillip G. Queroda's study, "Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) Readiness of Pangasinan State University – Open University Systems Students," investigates student preparedness for MOOCs as institutions transition toward online delivery. Using a descriptive research method and purposive sampling, the study collected data from 141 respondents. The demographic profile showed that 72.3% were female, 73% were government employees, and most were aged 21 to 30. Notably, 73% of respondents had attended fewer than five seminars regarding online distance education.

Findings indicate varying levels of readiness. Students were considered very much ready in using hardware and standard software like web browsers and Microsoft Office. They demonstrated high readiness in online skills, such as email communication and clerical tasks, as well as in using audio and video media. However, they were only "slightly ready" regarding the use of Learning Management Systems (LMS) and installing specific programs or plugins.

Motivation and engagement levels were high, with students expressing confidence in completing work despite distractions. Students identified frequent participation, prior online experience, immediate application of materials, regular instructor contact, and technical support as vital to success. The study concludes that PSU-OUS students are ready for MOOC implementation. The researcher recommends increased participation in online learning seminars and suggests that the institution pursue MOOCs within the Open Distance Learning framework to support the transition to online delivery.
one:
The study "Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) Readiness of Pangasinan State University – Open University Systems Students" by Phillip G. Queroda investigates the preparedness of PSU-OUS students to engage with MOOCs. As educational institutions transition toward fully online delivery, understanding student readiness for these affordable and scalable learning experiences is essential. The research assesses readiness across technological and psychological dimensions to determine if the student body is prepared for such innovative delivery systems.

The study employed a descriptive research method using a two-part survey questionnaire distributed via written answers and Google Forms. Using a purposive sampling technique, the researcher collected data from 141 respondents. Data analysis was conducted using the weighted mean. The respondent profile revealed that 72.3% were female and 73% were employed in the government sector. Most respondents were between 21 and 30 years old, many were enrolled in the Master of Arts in Education major in Educational Management, and most earned a monthly salary between 21,000 and 30,000 pesos. Notably, 73% of respondents had attended fewer than five seminars related to online distance education.

Findings regarding readiness showed varying levels of preparedness. Students were considered very much ready in using hardware and standard software, such as Microsoft Office and web browsers. However, they were only "slightly ready" in using Learning Management Systems (LMS) and in installing specific programs or plugins like Java or Adobe Reader. Despite this, students demonstrated high readiness in online skills, specifically in clerical tasks, email communication, and using online technologies for discussion.

Motivation and engagement levels were high. Students reported being motivated when treated as unique individuals and when able to contribute relevant news to lessons. They expressed confidence in their ability to complete work despite home distractions or the absence of a physical instructor. Furthermore, students showed high readiness for using audio and video as learning media. Regarding internet discussions, students felt comfortable with online conversations, though the study noted a potential reliance on traditional instructor-centered models. Students identified frequent participation, prior online experience, immediate application of materials, regular instructor contact, and technical support as vital to their success.

The study concludes that PSU-OUS students are ready for MOOC implementation. While minor gaps exist regarding LMS use and plugin installation, overall readiness is high across all assessed aspects. The researcher recommends that students participate in more seminars and training related to online learning to bridge these gaps. For the institution, the study supports the pursuit of MOOCs within the Open Distance Learning framework to assist the university's transition toward fully online delivery models.
two:
The study titled "Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) Readiness of Pangasinan State University – Open University Systems Students" by Phillip G. Queroda investigates the preparedness of students at Pangasinan State University – Open University Systems (PSU-OUS) to engage with Massive Open Online Courses. As educational institutions increasingly transition from blended learning to fully online delivery, understanding student readiness for MOOCs—which offer affordable, flexible, and scalable learning experiences—is essential. The research aims to determine if the PSU-OUS student body is prepared for the implementation of such innovative online delivery systems.

The research was conducted within the context of the growing popularity of MOOCs, which were pioneered by researchers like Stephen Downes and George Siemens through the concept of connectivism. In the Philippines, institutions such as the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) and SEAMEO-INNOTECH have already begun utilizing MOOCs to provide free, accessible education. As PSU-OUS seeks to adjust its delivery models toward fully online formats, this study serves as a necessary assessment of student readiness across various technological and psychological dimensions.

To address the problem, the researcher sought to profile the respondents and measure their level of readiness regarding technological access, online skills, motivation, online audio/video usage, internet discussions, and the perceived importance of various factors to their academic success. The study employed a descriptive research method, utilizing a two-part survey questionnaire. The first part collected demographic and professional profiles, while the second part assessed readiness levels. Data collection was facilitated through written answers and a Google Form distributed via social media. A purposive sampling technique was used to select the respondents, and the gathered data were analyzed using the weighted mean.

The findings regarding the profile of the respondents revealed that out of 141 surveyed individuals, 72.3% were female and 73% were employed in the government sector. The majority of respondents were between 21 and 30 years old, many were enrolled in the Master of Arts in Education major in Educational Management, and most earned a monthly salary between 21,000 and 30,000 pesos. Notably, 73% of the respondents had attended fewer than five seminars related to online distance education.

In terms of readiness, the results showed varying levels of preparedness across different categories. Regarding technological access, students were considered very much ready in using hardware (such as computers and printers) and standard software (such as Microsoft Office and various web browsers). However, they were only "slightly ready" in using Learning Management Systems (LMS) like Moodle or iFolio and in installing specific programs or plugins like Java or Adobe Reader. Despite this, students demonstrated high readiness in online skills, specifically in clerical tasks, email communication, and using online technologies for discussion.

Motivation and engagement levels were also high. Students reported being motivated when treated as unique individuals and when able to contribute relevant news to lessons. They expressed confidence in their ability to complete work despite home distractions or the absence of a physical instructor. Furthermore, students showed high readiness for using audio and video as learning media, which is significant for course completion and engagement. Regarding internet discussions, students felt comfortable with online conversations, though the study noted a potential reliance on traditional instructor-centered models. Finally, students expressed that frequent participation, prior online experience, immediate application of materials, regular instructor contact, and technical support are all vital to their success in online coursework.

The study concludes that the students of PSU-OUS are ready for the implementation of MOOCs. While there are minor gaps in technical areas—specifically regarding the installation of plugins and the use of specific Learning Management Systems—the overall readiness across all assessed aspects is high. The students possess the necessary motivation, online communication skills, and technological access to succeed in a MOOC environment.

The implications of this research suggest that while the student body is prepared, there are specific areas for institutional support. The researcher recommends that students invest more time in participating in seminars and training specifically related to online learning education to bridge the identified gaps in LMS and plugin proficiency. For the institution, the study supports the pursuit of MOOCs within the Open Distance Learning framework of PSU-OUS, providing a foundation for the university's transition toward fully online delivery models.

title: Evaluation of Supplemental Interactive Learning Material for Teaching Physics in  University of the Philippines Los Baños
abstract:
With the advent of new technologies being infused in school curricula, educators and school leaders of higher education in the Philippines have embraced e-learning, which involves technology-mediated teaching strategies and a variety of tools to facilitate learning. In this regard, the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) through the Interactive Learning Center (ILC) started developing and producing online interactive educational materials known as Learning Objects (LOs), which are now being used by UPLB students as supplemental interactive learning materials in various courses in the university.
This study focused on the evaluation of the LO on Rotation of Rigid Bodies in terms of knowledge gain of the students and determine its effectiveness in terms of attractiveness, comprehensibility, applicability, interactivity, and assessment function. Students enrolled in PHYS 81 (Fundamental Physics 1) during the First Semester AY 2017-2018 were divided into control and treatment groups and subjected to pre-test-post-test for the LO evaluation. Using the t-test of significance, results showed that the treatment group had a significant increase in the mean scores after being exposed to the LO compared to the control group who did not view the LO, indicating that students aided with LO had greater knowledge gain than those without LO supplementation.
Additionally, the Likert scale of scores 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) was used to evaluate the treatment group’s responses on the different components of the LO. Computing for the weighted mean in each component, results showed that most respondents agreed that the LO was attractive (3.86) and that it was both comprehensible (4.38) and applicable (4.16). Similarly, most respondents in the treatment group agreed that the LO was interactive (4.14) and its assessment items were appropriate (4.28) to the program. Overall, the respondents agreed (4.27) and assessed the evaluated LO as an effective supplementary learning material for the physics topic on the rotation of rigid bodies.
half:
The rapid evolution of e-learning has increased the demand for high-quality digital materials, such as Learning Objects (LOs). This study evaluated a multimedia LO regarding the "Rotation of Rigid Bodies" in Physics developed by the Interactive Learning Center at the University of the Philippines Los Baños. The research aimed to determine the LO's effect on student knowledge gain and its effectiveness as a supplemental tool based on attractiveness, clarity, applicability, interactivity, and assessment function.

Using a quantitative approach, the study involved 150 students enrolled in a Fundamental Physics 1 course. Participants were divided into a control group receiving standard lectures and a treatment group receiving lectures supplemented by the LO. Findings revealed that the LO significantly enhanced knowledge gain. While both groups improved from pre-test to post-test, the treatment group achieved a significantly higher mean post-test score of 7.80 compared to the control group's 4.23. Socio-demographic characteristics did not significantly affect knowledge gain within the groups.

The LO received high ratings for clarity and comprehensibility (4.38), assessment function (4.28), applicability (4.16), and interactivity (4.14). It received a lower weighted mean for attractiveness (3.86), with suggestions to improve color schemes and graphics. Overall, respondents agreed the LO was an effective supplemental material (4.27). The study concludes that the LO effectively enhances physics knowledge and recommends using LOs to supplement classroom discussions.
one:
The rapid evolution of e-learning in higher education has created a need for high-quality digital materials and effective pedagogical models. One approach involves using Learning Objects (LOs), which are short, self-contained, reusable digital materials designed to meet specific learning objectives. At the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB), the Interactive Learning Center (ILC) has been developing multimedia LOs for undergraduate courses. This study evaluated a previously developed LO regarding the "Rotation of Rigid Bodies" in Physics to determine its effect on student knowledge gain and its effectiveness as a supplemental tool based on attractiveness, clarity and comprehensibility, applicability, interactivity, and assessment function.

The study utilized a quantitative approach involving 150 students enrolled in the PHYS 81 (Fundamental Physics 1) course during the first semester of the 2017-2018 academic year. Participants were divided into a control group of 72 students and a treatment group of 78 students using stratified random sampling. Both groups underwent a pre-test. Following regular classroom discussions, the control group received only the standard lecture, while the treatment group received the lecture supplemented by viewing the LO. Both groups then completed a post-test. To evaluate the quality of the LO, the treatment group used a Likert scale to rate the material based on the Learning Object Peer Review Rubric.

The findings revealed that the LO significantly enhanced student knowledge gain. While both groups showed significant improvement from pre-test to post-test scores due to regular classroom instruction, the treatment group achieved a much higher mean post-test score (7.80) compared to the control group (4.23). A z-test confirmed that this difference was statistically significant. Furthermore, socio-demographic characteristics, such as gender, classification, and college affiliation, did not significantly affect knowledge gain within the groups, though they did correlate with the differences observed between the control and treatment groups in the post-test.

The evaluation of the LO's components yielded positive results. The material was rated highly for clarity and comprehensibility (4.38), assessment function (4.28), applicability (4.16), and interactivity (4.14). Regarding attractiveness, the LO received a weighted mean of 3.86; while students found the layout interesting, feedback suggested improvements in color schemes, text animations, and the inclusion of more diverse graphics. Overall, respondents agreed (4.27) that the LO was an effective supplemental learning material. The study concludes that the LO is an effective tool for enhancing physics knowledge and recommends using LO viewing as a supplement to regular classroom discussions. Future development should focus on refining aesthetic elements and expanding the variety and difficulty of assessment items.
two:
The rapid evolution of e-learning in higher education has created a pressing need for high-quality digital materials and effective pedagogical models. As institutions embrace technology-mediated teaching, establishing standards for the creation and use of these tools is essential. One innovative approach involves the use of Learning Objects (LOs), which are short, self-contained, reusable, and digital teaching materials designed to meet specific learning objectives. These objects can be used in various instructional environments, including face-to-face and online settings, to support, supplement, or assess student learning.

At the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB), the Interactive Learning Center (ILC) has been developing multimedia LOs for undergraduate courses. This study specifically focuses on evaluating a previously developed LO regarding the "Rotation of Rigid Bodies" in Physics. The research aimed to determine the effect of exposure to this LO on student knowledge gain and to evaluate its effectiveness as a supplemental learning tool based on several quality components: attractiveness, clarity and comprehensibility, applicability, interactivity, and assessment function.

The study utilized a quantitative approach involving 150 students enrolled in the PHYS 81 (Fundamental Physics 1) course during the first semester of the 2017-2018 academic year. The participants were divided into two groups using stratified random sampling: a control group of 72 students and a treatment group of 78 students. Both groups underwent a pre-test to establish baseline knowledge. Following regular classroom discussions, the control group received only the standard lecture, while the treatment group received the lecture supplemented by viewing the LO. Both groups then completed a post-test. To evaluate the quality of the LO, the treatment group used a Likert scale to rate the material based on the Learning Object Peer Review Rubric. Statistical analyses included t-tests, z-tests, and the Mann-Whitney Test to examine differences in knowledge gain and the impact of socio-demographic characteristics.

The findings revealed that the LO significantly enhanced student knowledge gain. While both groups showed significant improvement from pre-test to post-test scores due to regular classroom instruction, the treatment group achieved a much higher mean post-test score (7.80) compared to the control group (4.23). A z-test confirmed that this difference was statistically significant, indicating that the LO provided superior supplemental support. Furthermore, the study found that socio-demographic characteristics, such as gender, classification, and college affiliation, did not significantly affect the knowledge gain between the pre-test and post-test within the groups, though they did correlate with the differences observed between the control and treatment groups in the post-test.

The evaluation of the LO's specific components yielded generally positive results. The material was rated highly for its clarity and comprehensibility (weighted mean of 4.38), as students felt it had a clear purpose and helped them understand the concepts. The LO also scored high in assessment function (4.28), with students agreeing that the assessments measured objectives and provided useful feedback. Applicability was also rated strongly (4.16), and interactivity received a high score (4.14), with students noting the material was easy to use and encouraged higher-order thinking. Regarding attractiveness, the LO received a weighted mean of 3.86. While students found the layout interesting and the text legible, some feedback suggested improvements in color schemes, the reduction of distracting text animations, and the inclusion of more diverse graphics or videos. Overall, the respondents agreed (4.27) that the LO was an effective supplemental learning material.

The study concludes that the Learning Object on the Rotation of Rigid Bodies is an effective tool for enhancing student knowledge in physics. It successfully meets the criteria for clarity, applicability, interactivity, and assessment. Based on these results, the authors recommend that LO viewing be encouraged as a supplement to regular classroom discussions to improve student assimilation of complex subject matter. Additionally, they suggest that future development of LOs should focus on refining aesthetic elements—such as simplifying visuals and improving font and color choices—and expanding the variety and difficulty of assessment items to further enhance the learning experience.

title: Developing Positive Climate and Behavior Management in a Flipped Classroom
abstract: This study aimed to examine the positive climate and behavior management aspects of the flipped classroom environment in a Grade 7 science class. Further, it determined the factors that contribute to the establishment of a positive learning classroom environment and management of student behavior in a flipped classroom. The students’ asynchronous pre-class activities included a science courseware developed by the Department of Science and Technology. Meanwhile, the synchronous face-to-face activities involved performing individual and group activities and answering concept questions through peer instruction. The classroom environment was described using the Classroom Assessment Scoring System. The scores obtained during the classroom observation were triangulated using the students’ and teacher’s daily journal entries, and student focus group discussions held at the end of the implementation. Findings showed that the flipped classroom experienced difficulty in establishing a positive climate and facilitating behavior management on the first few days of implementation. However, the scores in positive climate and behavior management gradually increased as the implementation of the flipped classroom progressed. It is worth noting that the flipped classroom exhibited high range scores in the following areas of positive climate – positive affect, relationship, and positive communication; and middle range score for respect. Towards the end of the implementation of the flipped classroom, middle range scores were obtained in the following areas of behavior management – clear behavior expectation, proactive, redirection of misbehavior, and student behavior. Based on the findings, this study discussed the ways of overcoming the challenges in developing a positive climate and behavior management.
half:
The study "Developing Positive Climate and Behavior Management in a Flipped Classroom" examines the implementation of a flipped classroom with peer instruction (FCPI) in a Grade 7 science class in Sta. Cruz, Laguna, Philippines. Using a one-group quasi-experimental design with 47 students, the research investigated how this model affects classroom climate and behavior management. The instructional approach involved asynchronous pre-class activities using DOST science courseware followed by synchronous face-to-face sessions utilizing the Plickers application for real-time formative assessment. Data was gathered through classroom observations, journal entries, and a focus group discussion.

Initial implementation faced challenges such as student disinterest, noise, and lack of engagement. However, as the study progressed, scores in both dimensions increased. The classroom achieved high-range scores in positive affect, relationship, and positive communication, while maintaining middle-range scores for respect. Regarding behavior management, the model reached middle-range scores in clear behavior expectation, proactive management, redirection of misbehavior, and student behavior. Researchers suggested initial unsettledness resulted from the shift from traditional lectures to active learning.

Success was attributed to communicating the model's benefits, arranging the physical layout for collaboration, matching pre-class and in-class activities, and encouraging cooperation. The study concludes that FCPI is an effective framework for 21st-century learning. Recommendations include specific teacher training in technology and activity-based management, providing pre-class materials in Filipino, and using diverse active learning strategies.

The study titled "Developing Positive Climate and Behavior Management in a Flipped Classroom" investigates the implementation of a flipped classroom with peer instruction (FCPI) in a Grade 7 science class. The research addresses the challenges faced by educators transitioning to blended learning modalities following the shift toward remote teaching in the Philippines. Specifically, the study seeks to examine how the FCPI model affects the classroom environment, focusing on two primary dimensions: the establishment of a positive learning climate and the effective management of student behavior.

The context of the research is an integrated national high school in Sta. Cruz, Laguna, Philippines, involving 47 Grade 7 students during the first quarter of the 2019-2020 school year. The researchers utilized a one-group quasi-experimental design. The instructional model involved asynchronous pre-class activities, where students used science courseware developed by the Department of Science and Technology (DOST), followed by synchronous face-to-face sessions. These in-class sessions utilized peer instruction facilitated by the Plickers application, a low-cost technology that allows teachers to collect real-time formative assessment data via smartphone scanning of printed cards.

The methodology employed a triangulation approach to ensure data validity. Classroom observations were conducted using the Classroom Assessment Scoring System (CLASS), which measures dimensions of positive climate (emotional support) and behavior management (classroom organization) on a scale of 1–7. This observational data was supplemented by daily journal entries from both the teacher and the students, as well as a focus group discussion (FGD) with students to capture their qualitative experiences and suggestions.

The findings indicate that the FCPI model experienced initial difficulties in establishing a positive climate and managing behavior during the first few days of implementation. Early lessons were marked by student disinterest, noise, and a lack of engagement. However, as the implementation progressed, scores in both dimensions gradually increased. In terms of positive climate, the classroom achieved high-range scores in positive affect, relationship, and positive communication, while maintaining a middle-range score for respect. Regarding behavior management, the implementation reached middle-range scores in clear behavior expectation, proactive management, redirection of misbehavior, and student behavior toward the end of the study. The researchers noted that the "unsettledness" observed in the classroom was likely a byproduct of high student engagement and the shift from traditional lectures to active, activity-based learning.

Several key factors were identified as contributors to the successful establishment of a positive climate and effective behavior management. First, the communication of benefits is essential; teachers must "sell" the concept of the flipped classroom to students to reduce resistance. Second, the physical layout of the classroom must be conducive to collaboration and monitoring. Third, there must be a close match between pre-class and in-class activities to ensure students feel prepared and motivated. Finally, encouraging students to work toward common goals—such as achieving high correct-answer percentages during peer instruction—promotes a cooperative atmosphere.

The study concludes that fostering a positive climate and managing behavior in an FCPI setting is achievable through strategic instructional design and proactive teaching. While the transition period presents challenges, the use of engaging, technology-integrated, and social learning activities helps students develop rapport with the teacher and their peers, ultimately leading to improved student behavior and engagement.

The implications of this research suggest that the FCPI model serves as an effective framework for transforming science classrooms into 21st-century learning environments. The authors recommend that teachers receive specific training on incorporating technology and managing the unique dynamics of an activity-based classroom. Furthermore, the study suggests that providing pre-class materials in the students' native language (Filipino) could alleviate comprehension difficulties. Educators are encouraged to use various active learning strategies, such as problem-based learning or debates, to maintain the momentum of the flipped classroom and ensure that the connection between asynchronous study and synchronous application remains seamless.

title: Design Research Approach in Developing Technology-Mediated Learning Modules in Practical Mathematics for Technical Vocational Education
abstract: Technical vocational education has become one of the four major tracks in the K to 12 curriculum in the Philippines (Ocampo, 2014). However, online learning technologies are not yet fully integrated into the core technicalvocational courses of this curriculum. Using the design research model of Mckenney and Reeves (2013) with two iterations, this study developed a set of technology-mediated learning modules in practical mathematics for the technical-vocational track of the K to 12 curriculum. From three researcher-made instruments, data were gathered from randomly selected samples from a private sectarian college. Results indicate that the design research modules were characterized by the following design principles: a) small-group collaborative learning through synchronous and asynchronous discussions based on simplified authentic problem-based tasks; b) online teaching roles as a facilitator, feedback giver, learning community mentor, course designer, and manager; c) use of Facebook and its online group chat; d) use of multimedia approach, behavioral objectives, simple language, and exercises in the presentation of the modules; and e) student context based on job skills specialization, motivation and interest in practical mathematics, familiarity with information and communication technology, and socio-economic status. Using the Mann-Whitney test at 0.05 significance level, the overall mean score of the second iteration group is significantly higher than the overall mean score of the first iteration group. This indicates that the technology-mediated learning modules facilitated the learning of practical mathematics concepts. This study recommends the design research approach because its iteration process has validated and put together effective design principles for online teaching and learning of practical mathematics. Further, it has involved both students and the teacher in developing these modules that yielded better student learning outcomes.
half:
The study "Design Research Approach in Developing Technology-Mediated Learning Modules in Practical Mathematics for Technical Vocational Education" addresses the lack of tailored online learning technologies for technical-vocational students in the Philippine K to 12 curriculum, specifically for subjects like Shielded Metal Arc Welding (SMAW). Using the design research model by McKenney and Reeves (2013), researchers employed an iterative methodology to develop and validate design principles for mathematics modules.

The research involved two iterations. The first iteration involved twelve Grade 11 students using modules on unit conversions, algebraic expressions, and ratios/percentages. Following feedback, modules were refined for a second iteration involving twelve Grade 12 students. Findings identified students as ICT-proficient learners who face socio-economic and connectivity challenges. Effective design principles included using small-group collaborative learning through synchronous and asynchronous discussions centered on simplified, authentic, problem-based tasks. Teachers were most effective when acting as facilitators, mentors, and course designers. Facebook was found to be the most effective technology due to its accessibility for messaging and file sharing. Successful module presentation utilized a multimedia approach, including video tutorials, clear text, and practical exercises.

Statistical analysis showed the second iteration group achieved significantly higher mean scores, moving evaluations from "good" to "excellent." The study concludes that technology-mediated modules developed through design research effectively facilitate learning for technical-vocational students.
one:
The study "Design Research Approach in Developing Technology-Mediated Learning Modules in Practical Mathematics for Technical Vocational Education" addresses the insufficient integration of online learning technologies within the technical-vocational track of the Philippine K to 12 curriculum. While online learning provides convenience, there is a specific need for technology-mediated modules tailored to the mathematical requirements of vocational students, such as those in Shielded Metal Arc Welding (SMAW).

Using the design research model by McKenney and Reeves (2013), the researchers employed an interventionist and iterative methodology to develop and validate design principles for these modules. The study focused on identifying effective characteristics regarding student context, online learning approaches, teacher roles, technology tools, and module presentation. The methodology consisted of two iterations. In the first iteration, twelve Grade 11 students used modules covering unit conversions, algebraic expressions, and ratios/percentages for seven weeks. Data were collected via evaluation rubrics, observation guides, and semi-structured interviews. Following feedback, the modules were refined for a second iteration involving twelve Grade 12 students.

The findings established several key design principles. Students were identified as ICT-proficient 21st-century learners who often face socio-economic and connectivity challenges. An effective online learning approach utilized small-group collaborative learning (groups of three to four) through synchronous and asynchronous discussions centered on simplified, authentic, problem-based tasks. Teacher effectiveness was highest when instructors acted as facilitators, feedback givers, mentors, course designers, and managers. Regarding technology, Facebook and its group chat features were most effective due to ease of access for messaging and file sharing. Module presentation was most successful when employing a multimedia approach, including video tutorials, clear text and pictures, measurable objectives, and practical exercises.

Statistical analysis using the Mann-Whitney test showed that the mean score of the second iteration group was significantly higher than the first. This indicates that the iterative process successfully improved the modules, moving student evaluations from a "good" to an "excellent" rating. Refinements included reducing group sizes, simplifying tasks, and replacing difficult-to-use tools like email and video calls with more accessible platforms like Facebook.

The study concludes that technology-mediated modules developed through design research effectively facilitate learning practical mathematics for technical-vocational students. Problem-based tasks contextualized in vocational settings and a social constructivist approach involving small group discussions and active facilitation foster productive environments. The researchers recommend that course designers use design research to create online mathematics curricula and suggest that future studies expand this approach to subjects like Geometry and Trigonometry.
two:
The study titled "Design Research Approach in Developing Technology-Mediated Learning Modules in Practical Mathematics for Technical Vocational Education" addresses the lack of full integration of online learning technologies within the technical-vocational track of the K to 12 curriculum in the Philippines. While online learning offers convenience and engagement for students facing time or distance constraints, there is a need for specialized, technology-mediated modules that cater to the specific mathematical needs of vocational students, such as those specializing in Shielded Metal Arc Welding (SMAW).

To address this, the researchers employed a design research approach based on the model by McKenney and Reeves (2013). This method is characterized as interventionist, iterative, and process-oriented, aiming to provide both a practical research-based intervention and a set of validated design principles. The study aimed to identify the characteristics of technology-mediated learning modules in terms of student context, online learning approach, teacher roles, technology tools, and module presentation. Additionally, the study sought to compare the effectiveness of the modules between a first iteration and a second iteration.

The methodology involved two iterations of development and implementation. In the first iteration, twelve Grade 11 students from a private sectarian college in the Southern Philippines used the initial modules for seven weeks. The modules focused on seven lessons covering unit conversions, algebraic expressions, and ratios/percentages. The researchers used an evaluation rubric, an observation guide, and semi-structured interviews to gather data. Based on the feedback from the first iteration, the modules were modified for the second iteration, which involved another twelve Grade 12 students. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, percentage scores, and the Mann-Whitney test to compare the mean scores of the two groups.

The findings revealed several key design principles. Regarding the student context, participants were identified as 21st-century learners proficient in ICT but often facing socio-economic challenges and internet connectivity issues. The online learning approach was characterized by small-group collaborative learning (specifically groups of three to four) using synchronous and asynchronous discussions centered on simplified, authentic, problem-based tasks. The roles of the online teacher were found to be highly effective when the instructor acted as a facilitator, feedback giver, learning community mentor, course designer, and manager. The technology tools used were most effective when utilizing Facebook and its group chat features, which provided easy access to instant messaging and file sharing. Finally, the presentation of the modules was most successful when employing a multimedia approach, including video tutorials, clear textual and pictorial information, measurable learning objectives, and practical exercises.

The results of the Mann-Whitney test indicated that the overall mean score of the second iteration group was significantly higher than that of the first iteration group. This statistical difference demonstrates that the iterative design process successfully improved the modules, moving student evaluations from a "good" rating to an "excellent" rating. The second iteration benefited from refinements such as reducing group sizes, simplifying problem-based tasks, and removing tools that were difficult to use due to poor internet, such as email and video calls, in favor of more accessible platforms like Facebook.

In conclusion, the study concludes that technology-mediated learning modules developed through design research effectively facilitate the learning of practical mathematics concepts for technical-vocational students. The findings show that problem-based tasks contextualized in vocational settings are highly relevant to students' career goals. Furthermore, the social constructivist approach, supported by small group discussions and active teacher facilitation, fosters a productive learning environment. The study also highlights that multimedia presentations and simplified language are crucial for helping students master mathematical concepts in an online setting.

The implications of this research suggest that the design research approach is a highly effective method for developing educational interventions because its iterative nature allows for the validation of design principles through direct involvement of both students and teachers. For course designers working within the K to 12 technical-vocational track, this study recommends using design research to create effective online mathematics curricula. The researchers also suggest that future studies could expand this approach to other mathematical subjects, such as Geometry and Trigonometry, while considering larger sample sizes and providing participants with more stable internet access to further validate these findings.
