title: Addressing the Needs of Distance Education Learners Based on their Perception of a Successful Student
abstract:
The study aimed at determining possible teaching and assessment practices in a general education course to better address a range of distance education learners’ needs based on a thematic analysis of their graded learning activity reports on students’ perception of success submitted by 147 learners of a general education course offered in an open education institution in the Philippines.
Analysis of data revealed that a huge majority (70%) of the students perceive success as the ability to “combine academic and non-academic life well,” while manifesting the following traits, “disciplined, great at time management, can apply what was learned in the classroom to real-life situations, an all-rounder, good character, and good social life.” Almost half of the students (49%) assessed themselves as not successful. Based on the students’ impression, majority (68%) of their parents define success as “excelling academically in a prestigious university and getting a high-paying job;” while most (68%) of their friends perceive success as the “ability to combine academic and non-academic initiatives well.” Almost all (95%) of the students said they were challenged by the views of their parents on student success.
Based on the results, the following teaching and assessment practices are recommended: (1) FICs should provide more engagement avenues to encourage socialization or interaction, e.g., conducting F2F synchronous interaction even on a limited basis, and should respond to emails or portal chats as soon as possible to help students strike a good balance between academic and non-academic achievements, their most popular definition of students’ success; (2) Learning assessments can be made more practical as these should prepare the learner to use classroom knowledge at work or can be applied in their daily lives; (3) Learning assessments can be made more doable and within a realistic time frame to help students fulfill course requirements; and (4) Module topics can be reexamined to assess if they can be streamlined for a more efficient and/or effective conduct of the course’s learning outcomes.
half:
In the study "Addressing the Needs of Distance Education Learners Based on their Perception of a Successful Student," Mabini DG. Dizon investigates how distance education learners define success and how these perceptions can inform teaching and assessment practices. Conducted at an open education institution in the Philippines, the qualitative study used thematic analysis of graded learning activity reports from 147 learners. The participant profile was predominantly young, female, and single, with 44% being employed.

The findings reveal a significant distinction between student-defined and parent-defined success. A majority of students (70%) define success as the ability to balance academic and non-academic life through discipline and time management, with only 6% equating success solely with high grades. Conversely, 68% of students believe their parents define success through academic excellence at prestigious universities and securing high-paying jobs. While 68% of students believe their friends share their "all-rounder" view of success, 95% of students report being affected by the views of parents and friends. This influence motivates 65% of students but leaves 35% feeling overwhelmed by pressure.

The researcher concludes that student success in distance education is a holistic phenomenon involving social, psychological, and professional dimensions. To support this, the study recommends that faculty provide more synchronous interaction, offer practical and authentic assessments that accommodate diverse circumstances, and streamline module topics to prevent overwhelming workloads.

two:
The study titled "Addressing the Needs of Distance Education Learners Based on their Perception of a Successful Student" by Mabini DG. Dizon investigates how distance education learners define success and how these perceptions can inform teaching and assessment practices. The research was conducted within a general education course, COMM 10 (Critical Perspectives in Communication), at an open education institution in the Philippines.

The problem addressed by the researcher is the potential disconnect between traditional academic measures of success and the actual needs and perceptions of distance learners. Distance learners often face unique challenges, such as balancing education with employment, family responsibilities, or being solo parents. The researcher suggests that if educators do not understand what students consider "success," they may fail to provide the necessary support or implement assessment methods that are meaningful to the learners' lives.

The context of the study is the Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) environment, which emphasizes flexibility, accessibility, and learner-centeredness. The participants consisted of 147 learners from a general education course. The profile of these learners indicates a predominantly young (63% aged 24 and below), female (63%), and single (93%) population, with 56% being full-time students and 44% being employed part-time or full-time.

The researcher employed a qualitative methodology using thematic analysis (TA) to identify patterns in the students' graded learning activity reports. The students were asked to reflect on their own image of a successful student, whether they considered themselves successful, how they perceived their parents' and friends' views of success, and how those views influenced them.

The findings reveal a significant distinction between student-defined success and parent-defined success. A large majority of students (70%) perceive success as the ability to "combine academic and non-academic life well," manifesting traits such as discipline, time management, good character, and the ability to apply classroom learning to real-life situations. Interestingly, only 6% of students equated success solely with academic excellence, such as Latin honors or high grades. In contrast, 68% of students perceived that their parents define success through academic excellence in prestigious universities and securing high-paying jobs. Furthermore, 68% of students believed their friends shared their own view of success as an "all-rounder" who balances various commitments.

The study also found that students are heavily influenced by these external perceptions; 95% of participants reported being challenged or affected by the views of their parents and friends. While 65% felt motivated or encouraged by these views, 35% reported feeling "crippled" or under overwhelming pressure. Regarding self-assessment, 49% of students did not consider themselves successful, while 41% felt they were successful.

Based on these findings, the researcher draws several conclusions. First, student success in a distance education context is a holistic phenomenon that extends far beyond grades to include social, psychological, and professional dimensions. Second, there is a tension between the academic-centric expectations of parents and the holistic, balance-oriented goals of the students themselves. Third, the current methods of measuring success (often through grades alone) may not fully capture the multifaceted nature of student achievement in an ODeL setting.

The implications of this research lead to several recommendations for Faculty-in-Charge (FICs) to better serve distance learners. Regarding teaching practices, the researcher suggests providing more engagement avenues, such as synchronous interaction or prompt responses to digital communications, to help students achieve the balance they value. For assessments, the study recommends making tasks more practical and authentic so that students can apply classroom knowledge to their daily lives or workplaces. Assessments should also be designed to be "doable" within realistic timeframes and should offer choices or alternatives to accommodate the diverse circumstances of learners (e.g., working students vs. full-time students). Finally, the researcher suggests streamlining module topics to prevent overwhelming workloads and to allow students more time for the non-academic growth they prioritize.

title: Change in Students’ Welfare during the COVID-19 Pandemic and the Shift to Remote Learning: The Case of BA in Business Economics Students at a State University Unit in Pampanga
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has forced schools in the Philippines and abroad to shift to remote learning even without ample preparation. This unwanted scenario begged two questions. Firstly, has the welfare of students changed for the worse due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the shift to remote learning? And secondly, is the shift to remote or flexible learning as ordered by the state university and the CHED sound? To address these questions, the study determined whether the consumer surplus as a welfare indicator of 25 Business Economics students at a state university unit in Pampanga has significantly changed during the COVID-19 pandemic and the shift to remote learning. The students were chosen through purposive sampling. They belong to a block that has experienced a semester each of face-to-face and remote classes under the same professor in academic years 2019-2020 and 2020-2021. The quantitative and qualitative data needed for the study were obtained through an online survey. The result of the paired samples t-test showed that the mean difference of Php 8,380.00 between the students’ consumer surplus during the pre-COVID-19 pandemic face-to-face modality and their consumer surplus during the COVID-19 pandemic and the shift to remote learning was not significant, with a standard deviation of 20,964.39442, confidence interval of 95%, t (24) = 1.999, and p = 0.057. This result suggests that: (1) the welfare of the 25 BA in Business Economics students, as indicated by their consumer surplus, has not significantly changed when the learning modality has shifted from face-to-face to remote during the COVID-19 pandemic; and (2) the shift to remote or flexible learning as ordered by the state university’s Memorandum No. OVPAA 2020-31 dated 09 March 2020 and the CHED Memorandum Order No. 4 Series of 2020 was sound.
half:
The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated an unplanned transition from face-to-face instruction to remote learning in the Philippines, raising concerns regarding student welfare and academic integrity. This quantitative study examined the welfare of 25 Bachelor of Arts in Business Economics students at a state university in Pampanga. Using the microeconomic concept of consumer surplus, the researcher treated education as a consumption good, where the "price" included tuition, fees, food, transportation, housing, and internet costs. The study compared students who experienced both face-to-face and remote learning modalities under the same professor during the 2019-2020 and 2020-2021 academic years.

Findings indicated that while willingness to pay and actual costs differed between modalities, the change in consumer surplus was not statistically significant. The mean difference in consumer surplus between face-to-face classes (Php 58,600.00) and remote classes (negative Php 2,520.00) was Php 8,380.00, yielding a p-value of 0.057. However, satisfaction ratings showed a significant difference; students reported a mean satisfaction rating of 4.520 for face-to-face classes, compared to 3.000 for remote classes. Qualitative data identified dissatisfaction due to unfavorable learning environments, lack of interaction, unstable internet, increased course requirements, and less thorough lesson discussions. The study concludes that the shift to remote learning did not significantly impact student welfare as measured by consumer surplus, though pedagogical and environmental challenges persist.
one:
The COVID-19 pandemic forced an unplanned transition from face-to-face instruction to remote learning in the Philippines, raising concerns regarding student welfare and the mandates issued by state universities and the Commission on Higher Education (CHED). This shift highlighted inequalities in internet access and introduced challenges such as mental health issues, home distractions, and increased academic dishonesty.

This quantitative study examined the welfare of 25 Bachelor of Arts in Business Economics students at a state university in Pampanga. Using the microeconomic concept of consumer surplus, the researcher treated education as a consumption good. The "price" of education included tuition, fees, food, transportation, housing, and internet costs. Through purposive sampling, the study compared students who experienced both face-to-face and remote learning modalities under the same professor during the 2019-2020 and 2020-2021 academic years. Data was collected via an online survey measuring willingness to pay and actual expenditures, alongside Likert-scale satisfaction ratings.

The findings indicated that while willingness to pay and actual costs differed between modalities, the change in consumer surplus was not statistically significant. The mean difference in consumer surplus between face-to-face classes (Php 58,600.00) and remote classes (negative Php 2,520.00) was Php 8,380.00, yielding a p-value of 0.057. At a 95% confidence interval, this difference is considered insignificant. The researcher noted that the result might have been significant if the confidence interval were lower or if pandemic-era inflation had not been higher.

In contrast, satisfaction ratings showed a significant difference. Students reported a mean satisfaction rating of 4.520 for face-to-face classes, while they were merely indifferent toward remote classes, with a mean rating of 3.000. Qualitative data identified five primary reasons for dissatisfaction with remote learning: unfavorable learning environments, lack of interaction between students and teachers or peers, unstable internet connections, an increased volume of course requirements, and the perception that lessons were not discussed as thoroughly as in-person sessions.

The study concludes that student welfare, as measured by consumer surplus, did not change significantly during the transition. Therefore, the researcher suggests the mandated shift to remote learning was a sound decision as it did not result in a significant loss of student welfare. However, pedagogical and environmental challenges remain. Recommendations include collaborative efforts to provide stable internet and quiet study spaces, increasing interaction during synchronous sessions, streamlining syllabi, ensuring thorough topic coverage, and investing in online proctored examinations and plagiarism detection software to maintain academic integrity.
two:
The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated an abrupt and unplanned shift from traditional face-to-face instruction to remote learning across educational institutions in the Philippines. This transition raised critical questions regarding student welfare and the soundness of the flexible learning mandates issued by state universities and the Commission on Higher Education (CHED). While the shift aimed to ensure continuity of education, it also highlighted significant inequalities, such as varying levels of internet access, and introduced new challenges including mental health issues, distractions in the home environment, and increased instances of academic dishonesty.

The study focused on the welfare of 25 Bachelor of Arts in Business Economics students at a state university unit in Pampanga. To measure welfare, the researcher utilized the microeconomic concept of consumer surplus, defined as the difference between what a consumer is willing to pay for a good or service and the price they actually pay. In this context, the study treated education as a consumption good, where the "price" included tuition and other school fees, as well as costs for food, transportation, housing, and internet. The research design was quantitative, employing a survey research method and purposive sampling to select a specific block of students who had experienced both face-to-face and remote learning modalities under the same professor during the 2019-2020 and 2020-2021 academic years.

The methodology involved an online survey where students reported their willingness to pay and actual expenditures for both learning modalities. The researcher then applied a paired samples t-test to compare the mean consumer surplus between the two periods. Additionally, students provided Likert-scale ratings regarding their satisfaction with each modality and offered qualitative reasons for their ratings. Ethical considerations were maintained by obtaining informed consent, ensuring respondent anonymity, and keeping the specific name of the university unit confidential.

The findings revealed that while students' willingness to pay and actual costs differed significantly between the two modalities, the change in consumer surplus was not statistically significant. Specifically, the mean difference in consumer surplus between face-to-face classes (Php 58,600.00) and remote classes (negative Php 2,520.00) was Php 8,380.00, which resulted in a p-value of 0.057. At a 95% confidence interval, this difference is considered insignificant. The researcher noted that this result might have been significant if the confidence interval were lower (such as 90%) or if the inflation rate during the pandemic had not been higher.

In contrast to the consumer surplus results, the satisfaction ratings showed a significant difference. Students reported a mean satisfaction rating of 4.520 for face-to-face classes, whereas they were merely indifferent toward remote classes, with a mean rating of 3.000. Qualitative data identified five primary reasons for this dissatisfaction with remote learning: an unfavorable learning environment (lack of quiet space and household interruptions), a lack of interaction between students and teachers or among peers, unstable internet connections, an increased volume of course requirements, and the perception that lessons were not being discussed as thoroughly as they were in person.

The study concludes that the welfare of the sampled Business Economics students, as measured by consumer surplus, did not change significantly during the shift from face-to-face to remote learning. Consequently, the researcher suggests that the mandated shift to remote or flexible learning by the state university and CHED was a sound decision, as it did not result in a significant loss of student welfare.

The implications of these findings suggest that while the policy was sound in terms of economic welfare, significant pedagogical and environmental challenges remain. To improve the remote learning experience, the study recommends a collaborative effort between parents, teachers, and the government to provide students with stable internet and quiet study environments. It also suggests that teachers should increase interaction during synchronous sessions, streamline syllabi to focus on essential requirements, and ensure thorough coverage of topics. Finally, to combat the rise in academic dishonesty during remote learning, the researcher recommends that institutions invest in online proctored examinations and plagiarism detection software to maintain academic integrity.

title: Technology-Mediated Teaching-Learning Process: From Developing of Learning Materials to Classroom Management and Practices to Students’ Welfare
half:
The COVID-19 pandemic forced a global transition from physical classrooms to remote learning in K-12 and tertiary education, requiring institutions to re-evaluate pedagogical frameworks and technology-mediated programs. This special issue examines this shift across various contexts, including technical-vocational, general education, and flipped classroom settings, using methodologies such as design-based research and empirical analysis.

Findings indicate that design-based approaches improve learning experiences in subjects like mathematics. This transition requires teachers to shift from traditional authority figures to facilitators, mentors, and providers of feedback. In online general education, student success is linked to socialization opportunities and timely faculty responses. Therefore, online assessments should prioritize the practical application of knowledge and provide realistic timelines to help students balance academic and non-academic responsibilities.

Regarding student welfare, empirical data suggests the shift to remote learning did not significantly affect welfare. In flipped classroom models, effective behavior management and a positive learning climate require transparency in technology use and face-to-face components that maximize student interaction. Research emphasizes that classroom behavior management is a shared responsibility between teachers and students.

Ultimately, pedagogical roles must adapt to technology-mediated modalities. Teachers must relinquish traditional control over the time and place of learning to empower students. Institutions should train educators to act as facilitators, prioritize practical application in curricula, and implement strategies that promote socialization and transparency to enhance educational quality.

title: A Case Study in Tablet-Based Augmented Reality Vocabulary Acquisition
abstract: Augmented Reality (AR) is a novel technology capable of embedding digital objects a user's experience of reality via a smartphone, tablet, or head-mounted display. AR offers interesting pedagogical applications and research possibilities in the field of SLA, particularly in the deliberate study of vocabulary. Such applications also offer implications for distance learning. This case study examined a 25-year-old Japanese language teacher in her deliberate acquisition of three sets of 15 vocabulary items selected from the first 1,000 most frequent words of Basque. A word card study method was compared with two AR vocabulary study methods. One AR study method involved the study of physical objects and their signifying Basque vocabulary items within a context-independent scene which was unknown to the participant. The second AR study method similarly involved the study of physical objects and their signifying Basque vocabulary items within a context-dependent scene which was known to the learner. In terms of vocabulary retention as measured with meaning recognition, form recognition, and form recall tests, both AR methods of study appeared to be as effective if not more so than word cards. The study of vocabulary items represented by physical objects in a contextualized environment with the use of a tablet-based AR application was beneficial in leveraging the recall of meaning and form of those items. During reflective interviews regarding the use of AR the participant indicated that she found the novel method of vocabulary study to be engaging and motivating. The findings of this study also indicate that mobile AR applications have potential pedagogical uses relevant to distance education practices.
half:
In "A Case Study in Tablet-Based Augmented Reality Vocabulary Acquisition," Adam Dabrowski investigates the efficacy of mobile-based Augmented Reality (AR) for deliberate second language vocabulary acquisition. The study explores whether AR, which overlays digital information onto the real world, facilitates learning more effectively than traditional paper-based word cards, specifically examining the impact of context-independent versus context-dependent scenes.

The methodology utilized a single-subject case study involving a 25-year-old Japanese language teacher with no prior knowledge of Basque. Using three sets of 15 concrete Basque nouns, the study compared three methods: traditional paper-based word cards, context-independent AR (items on a plain white table), and context-dependent AR (items within a familiar desk space). Testing included pretests, posttests, and delayed posttests measuring meaning recognition, form recognition, and form recall.

Findings revealed that both AR methods outperformed paper-based word cards in immediate posttests. The context-dependent AR group achieved the highest immediate score (87%), followed by context-independent AR (80%), while word cards scored 60%. However, in delayed posttests, the context-dependent AR group's scores decayed to 66%, whereas the context-independent AR group and word card group showed unexpected gains or stability, scoring 87% and 66%, respectively. Qualitatively, the participant found AR entertaining and motivating. The study concludes that tablet-based AR is an effective, practical tool for establishing form-meaning links, though further research is needed regarding long-term retention in physical environments.

The study addresses whether AR, which overlays digital information onto the real world, can effectively facilitate learning compared to traditional methods like paper-based word cards. Specifically, the research explores how different environmental contexts within AR—context-independent versus context-dependent scenes—impact the acquisition and retention of vocabulary.

The methodology utilized a single-subject case study involving a 25-year-old Japanese language teacher with no prior knowledge of Basque. The study used three sets of 15 concrete Basque nouns. The three study methods were a control group using traditional paper-based word cards, a context-independent AR group where items were placed on a plain white table, and a context-dependent AR group where items were placed within a familiar desk space. Testing included a pretest, posttest, and delayed posttest (24 hours later) measuring meaning recognition, form recognition, and form recall.

The findings revealed that both AR methods were more effective than paper-based word cards in immediate posttests. The context-dependent AR group achieved the highest immediate score (87%), followed by the context-independent AR group (80%), while the word card group scored 60%. However, results for the delayed posttests showed a different trend: the context-dependent AR group's scores decayed to 66%, while the context-independent AR group and the word card group showed unexpected gains or stability, with scores of 87% and 66%, respectively. This suggests that while a familiar, context-dependent environment may provide temporary scaffolding for immediate recognition, that benefit may decay more rapidly than in other methods.

Qualitatively, the participant reported that the AR method was interesting, entertaining, and felt like playing a game, expressing high levels of motivation and a desire to use the technology in her own teaching.

The study concludes that tablet-based AR is an effective method for establishing form-meaning links in second language vocabulary acquisition. While the immediate benefits of context-dependent AR may be temporary, the technology performs as well as or better than traditional word cards in the short term. The researcher notes that the use of ubiquitous mobile devices makes AR a practical, budget-friendly tool for classroom and distance education. The article "A Case Study in Tablet-Based Augmented Reality Vocabulary Acquisition" by Adam Dabrowski investigates the efficacy of Augmented Reality (AR) as a tool for deliberate second language vocabulary acquisition. While traditional methods like word cards are well-established, the rise of immersive technologies presents new pedagogical possibilities. The study specifically explores whether mobile-based AR, which is more accessible and cost-effective than expensive head-mounted displays, can effectively facilitate the learning of new vocabulary and how different environmental contexts within AR affect retention.

The research problem centers on the need to understand how AR technology—which overlays digital information onto the real world—compares to traditional study methods and how the environmental setting of the AR experience influences learning. The author notes a gap in existing research regarding how variations in AR study environments, specifically context-independent versus context-dependent scenes, impact the acquisition and retention of vocabulary.

The methodology employed a single-subject case study design involving a 25-year-old Japanese language teacher, referred to as Rachel. The participant had no prior knowledge of Basque, which was chosen as the target language due to its lack of cognates with English or Japanese. The study utilized three distinct vocabulary sets, each containing 15 concrete nouns selected from the 1,000 most frequent Basque words. The three study methods were: a control group using traditional paper-based word cards; a context-independent AR group where items were placed on a plain white table; and a context-dependent AR group where items were placed within a familiar desk space known to the participant.

The study used a pretest, posttest, and delayed posttest design for each set. Testing included three types of tasks: meaning recognition (multiple choice), form recognition (gap-fill sentences), and form recall (spelling). All tests were administered via Google Forms. Following the delayed posttests, the participant participated in a reflective interview to provide qualitative data on her experience.

The findings revealed that both AR methods were more effective than paper-based word cards in the immediate posttests. Specifically, the context-dependent AR group achieved the highest immediate posttest score (87%), followed by the context-independent AR group (80%), while the word card group scored 60%. However, the results for the delayed posttests (conducted 24 hours later) showed a different trend. The scores for the context-dependent AR group decayed to 66%, whereas the context-independent AR group and the word card group showed unexpected gains or stability, with scores of 87% and 66%, respectively. This suggests that while a familiar, context-dependent environment may provide temporary scaffolding that aids immediate recognition, that benefit may decay more rapidly than in other methods.

Qualitatively, the participant reported that the AR method was "interesting and entertaining" and felt "like playing a game." She expressed high levels of motivation and indicated a desire to use such technology in her own teaching practice.

The study concludes that tablet-based AR is an effective method for establishing form-meaning links in second language vocabulary acquisition. While the immediate benefits of context-dependent AR may be temporary, the technology overall performs as well as or better than traditional word cards in the short term. The researcher notes that the use of ubiquitous mobile devices like iPads makes AR a practical and budget-friendly tool for both classroom and distance education settings.

The implications of this research are significant for both pedagogy and distance learning. The study demonstrates that mobile AR can meet the pedagogical needs of learners in remote settings, providing an immersive experience without the need for expensive hardware. Furthermore, the findings suggest that educators can leverage the motivating and engaging nature of AR to increase student interest in language study. The author recommends further research into the relationship between physical environments and long-term vocabulary retention, as well as larger-scale studies to account for the limitations of a single-subject case study.

title: Alignment of Teachers’ Epistemic Understanding and Intended Dialogic Scaffolding of Classroom argumentation: Implications on Face-to-Face, Open and Distance Learning Environments
abstract: Dialogic scaffolding has the capacity to encourage and sustain students’ engagement in classroom argumentation. This study explored how the teachers’ levels of epistemic understanding were aligned with their intentions for dialogic scaffolding to encourage student's participation in classroom argumentation. Using varied data- gathering procedures such as surveys, classroom observation guides, and interview guides, results showed that the teachers’ varying levels of epistemic understanding are aligned with their dialogic scaffolding. Based on the criteria before the selection, each teacher was knowledgeable about the nature with significant exposure to inquiry-based teaching and learning, including classroom argumentation. Results showed that their rationale and nature of dialogic scaffolding were based on their levels of epistemic understanding. Results corroborate previous findings that explicit implementation of classroom argumentation depends on teachers’ strong intention and foundation of science content to challenge and stretch the capacities of their students in grasping the meaning of the subject matter. The study foregrounds the possibility of implementing classroom argumentation in any classroom, provided that the teachers can dialogically scaffold the class and lessen the immediate evaluative responses to students’ dialogues. The study, therefore, recommends teacher educators increase pre-service teachers’ exposure to inquiry approaches to science education, such as argumentation, as an investment for developing their dialogic scaffolding for classroom argumentation.
half:
In the study "Alignment of Teachers’ Epistemic Understanding and Intended Dialogic Scaffolding of Classroom Argumentation: Implications on Face-to-Face, Open and Distance Learning Environments," Sally B. Gutierez examines the relationship between teachers' epistemological beliefs and their use of dialogic scaffolding to support student argumentation in secondary science education in the Philippines. Using a qualitative methodology involving surveys, observations, and interviews with four teachers, the research compared the DepEd curriculum with the PSHS curriculum within biology instruction.

The findings indicate that teachers' levels of epistemic understanding align closely with their intended dialogic scaffolding. The study identified three teacher profiles: highly constructivist, constructivist, and transitional. Highly constructivist teachers utilized a "culture of negotiation," acting as facilitators who used open-ended, higher-level questions and socio-scientific issues to encourage students to defend opinions and build consensus. Conversely, transitional teachers expressed a desire to adopt constructivist practices but remained influenced by traditional, content-heavy approaches, often hindered by time constraints or content knowledge limitations.

The study concludes that epistemic understanding significantly shapes instructional decisions. Teachers who view knowledge as socially constructed are more likely to implement effective scaffolding that enhances student reasoning. The researcher recommends increasing pre-service exposure to inquiry-based approaches and providing continuous professional development to help in-service teachers refine their ability to facilitate classroom argumentation.

In the study "Alignment of Teachers’ Epistemic Understanding and Intended Dialogic Scaffolding of Classroom Argumentation: Implications on Face-to-Face, Open and Distance Learning Environments," Sally B. Gutierez explores the relationship between teachers' epistemological beliefs and their practical application of dialogic scaffolding to support student argumentation. The research addresses the potential disconnect between teachers' beliefs about science education and their facilitation of classroom discourse. Successful argumentation requires dialogic scaffolding, where teachers use questions, verifications, and elaborations to guide students through making claims, providing evidence, and offering justifications.

The study focused on secondary science education in the Philippines, comparing the Department of Education (DepEd) curriculum with the DOST-Philippine Science High School (PSHS) curriculum within biology instruction. Using a qualitative methodology and purposive sampling, the researcher examined four teachers through surveys, classroom observations, and interviews. Data were analyzed using the constant comparison method, involving iterative coding and theme development.

The findings revealed that teachers' levels of epistemic understanding align closely with their intended dialogic scaffolding. The study identified three distinct teacher profiles based on constructivist levels: highly constructivist, constructivist, and transitional.

Teachers with highly constructivist views and high knowledge regarding argumentation utilized a "culture of negotiation." These teachers acted as facilitators rather than transmitters of information, using socio-scientific issues to link scientific concepts to real-world scenarios. Their scaffolding was characterized by open-ended, higher-level questions that encouraged students to defend opinions and engage in collective consensus-building. These teachers viewed students as capable agents of their own learning, using dialogue to expand and clarify thinking rather than providing immediate evaluative responses.

Teachers in the "transitional" category demonstrated a desire to adopt constructivist practices but remained influenced by traditional or content-heavy approaches. Their scaffolding was less challenging, often focusing on conceptual-reflective questions to connect biology to daily life. Their ability to implement full argumentation was sometimes hindered by time constraints or perceived limitations in content knowledge.

The study concludes that epistemic understanding significantly shapes instructional decisions. When teachers view knowledge as something constructed through social negotiation, they are more likely to implement effective dialogic scaffolding, which enhances students' communication and reasoning skills. In face-to-face settings, these beliefs dictate responses to interactional needs, while in online and distance learning, the role shifts toward providing structured prompts and sustaining discussions. The researcher recommends that teacher educators increase pre-service exposure to inquiry-based approaches and that in-service teachers receive continuous professional development to refine their ability to facilitate classroom argumentation.
two:
The study titled "Alignment of Teachers’ Epistemic Understanding and Intended Dialogic Scaffolding of Classroom Argumentation: Implications on Face-to-Face, Open and Distance Learning Environments" by Sally B. Gutierez explores the relationship between teachers' epistemological beliefs and their practical application of dialogic scaffolding to support student argumentation.

The research problem centers on the potential disconnect between what teachers believe about science education and how they actually facilitate classroom discourse. While classroom argumentation is a vital tool for student engagement and knowledge construction, its success depends on a teacher's ability to provide dialogic scaffolding—using questions, verifications, and elaborations to guide students through the process of making claims, providing evidence, and offering justifications. The study seeks to understand how teachers' varying levels of epistemic understanding (their beliefs regarding the nature of knowledge and teaching) align with their intentions and practices regarding dialogic scaffolding. Furthermore, the study investigates the implications of these beliefs for different learning environments, specifically face-to-face versus online and distance learning.

The context of the study is the secondary science education curriculum in the Philippines, specifically comparing the Department of Education (DepEd) curriculum and the DOST-Philippine Science High School (PSHS) curriculum. The researcher focused on biology instruction, examining both content-based approaches and socio-scientific issue (SSI)-based approaches.

To investigate these dynamics, the researcher employed a qualitative methodology using purposive sampling to select four teachers representing different curricula and teaching methods. The data collection involved a multi-method approach, including surveys (the Teacher’s Beliefs on Teaching and Learning Questionnaire and the Teacher’s Knowledge and Beliefs on Argumentation Survey), classroom observation guides (the Teacher’s Dialogic Scaffolding on Argumentation Observation Checklist), and interview guides (the Teacher’s Beliefs on Teaching and Learning Interview and the Teacher’s Support for Classroom Argumentation Interview Guide). Data were analyzed using the constant comparison method, involving iterative coding and the development of themes through inductive and template coding.

The findings revealed that teachers' levels of epistemic understanding are closely aligned with their intended dialogic scaffolding. The study identified three distinct profiles of teachers based on their constructivist levels: highly constructivist, constructivist, and transitional.

Teachers with highly constructivist views and high levels of knowledge regarding argumentation (such as Teacher Loida and Teacher Carlo) utilized a "culture of negotiation." These teachers acted as facilitators rather than transmitters of information. They used socio-scientific issues to prompt students to link scientific concepts to real-world scenarios. Their dialogic scaffolding was characterized by open-ended, higher-level questions (such as "how" and "why") that encouraged students to defend opinions and engage in collective consensus-building. These teachers viewed students as capable agents of their own learning and used dialogue to expand and clarify student thinking rather than providing immediate evaluative responses.

Teachers in the "transitional" category (such as Teacher Don) demonstrated a desire to adopt constructivist practices but were still influenced by traditional or content-heavy approaches. Their dialogic scaffolding was less challenging, often focusing on conceptual-reflective questions to help students connect biology to daily life. Their ability to implement full argumentation was sometimes hindered by perceived limitations in content knowledge or time constraints.

The findings also highlighted that teachers with strong constructivist beliefs and high pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) were more successful at creating environments where students could exercise argumentative agency. In these settings, students moved from being passive recipients of facts to active participants who could critique, support, and evaluate one another's lines of thought.

The study concludes that teachers' epistemic understanding significantly shapes their instructional decisions and classroom management. When teachers view knowledge as something to be constructed through social negotiation rather than something to be transmitted, they are more likely to implement effective dialogic scaffolding. This scaffolding is a promising method for enhancing students' communication and reasoning skills. The study also notes that the success of classroom argumentation is heavily dependent on the teacher's ability to provide autonomy in discussion and to avoid the "recitation method" in favor of genuine dialogue.

The implications of these findings extend to different learning environments. In face-to-face settings, these beliefs dictate how teachers respond to moment-by-moment interactional needs. In online and distance learning environments, where interaction is often asynchronous, the teacher's role shifts toward providing structured prompts and sustaining discussions through occasional involvement, a process akin to the "fading" stage of scaffolding. The study suggests that the pedagogical beliefs held by teachers are relatively stable and can guide their transition between these different learning modalities.

Based on these results, the researcher recommends that teacher educators increase pre-service teachers' exposure to inquiry-based approaches and dialogic scaffolding strategies. For in-service teachers, continuous professional development focused on emerging inquiry-based teaching methods is suggested to help update their epistemic understanding and refine their ability to facilitate classroom argumentation.

title: Is the University of Makati e-Ready? An Evaluation of Its Faculty’s Technology Acceptance in LMS Utilization
abstract: The conduct of online classes has tremendously increased in the year 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic. In this regard, the education sector worldwide decided to conduct classes online which brought the birth of learning management systems (LMS) that allows a one-stop shop of essential online class tools for both teachers and students. The University of Makati introduced the Technology Based Learning Hub (TBL Hub) to its academe in the second semester of the school year 2020-2021. This study aims to analyze the perceived behavior of the UMak Academic community in utilizing the said LMS. The respondents of this paper are selected via purposive-total enumeration of the university’s College of Education. The quantitative-qualitative research analyzed the perception and evaluation of its respondents through a researcher-made questionnaire adapted from Alshorman and Bawaneh (2018) and Cunningham & Bradley (n.d.) based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) authored by Fred Davis (2018). The study titled "Is the University of Makati e-Ready? An Evaluation of Its Faculty’s Technology Acceptance in LMS Utilization" by April E. Leaño investigates the readiness and acceptance of the Technology-Based Learning (TBL) Hub, the official Learning Management System (LMS) of the University of Makati (UMak).

The problem addressed is the sudden and forced migration of academic institutions to online learning modalities due to the COVID-19 pandemic. While the Open Distance Learning Act of 2014 provided a legal basis for online education in the Philippines, the pandemic caught many educators unprepared. This transition created significant concerns regarding the practicality, validity, and reliability of online teaching, specifically concerning faculty members' access to devices, technical knowledge, and their ability to navigate required LMS platforms.

The context of the study is centered on the University of Makati, a locally funded institution that introduced the TBL Hub—a customized version of the Moodle open-source software—during the second semester of the 2020-2021 school year. The study focuses specifically on the faculty members of the College of Education (COE) who utilize the platform daily. The research is framed by Fred Davis’s Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which posits that technology acceptance is driven by two primary factors: perceived usefulness (the belief that the system will improve job performance) and perceived ease of use (the belief that the system is free of effort).

To investigate these factors, the researcher employed an explanatory-sequential mixed methods research design. Quantitative data were collected via a researcher-made questionnaire adapted from existing literature, utilizing a 4-point Likert scale to measure perceived efficiency and implementation. This quantitative phase was followed by a qualitative phase involving open-ended questions to gather personal experiences and recommendations from the respondents. The study utilized purposive sampling through total enumeration of the COE faculty members. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation, via SPSS version 25.

The findings indicate that the UMak-COE faculty are "e-ready," as they demonstrated positive technology acceptance. Regarding perceived usefulness, the TBL Hub received an overall mean score of 2.76, interpreted as "Somewhat Met Expectations." The platform was highly successful as a repository for teaching materials, with the ability to post syllabi, handouts, and modules exceeding expectations. However, the platform struggled in areas of interaction; both faculty and students reported that the system did not meet expectations regarding promoting interaction outside the classroom and learning online courses through the platform. Qualitative data revealed that while the TBL Hub serves its purpose, users experienced technical issues such as error messages, lagging, and difficulties with the Gradebook. Furthermore, poor internet connectivity was cited as a major barrier to seamless utilization.

In terms of perceived ease of use, the implementation of the TBL Hub received an overall mean score of 2.97, interpreted as "Agree." The faculty expressed high levels of confidence in the support systems provided, noting they knew whom to contact for technical issues. The administration was praised for providing necessary training and webinars. However, the respondents noted that the integration of the LMS still met some resistance and that the time required for instructional preparation increased.

The study concludes that the TBL Hub is an essential and effective tool for online teaching at UMak, having achieved positive acceptance in both perceived usefulness and ease of use. While the system is relatively new, it has successfully facilitated the transition to online pedagogy. However, the "e-readiness" of the institution is tempered by external factors like national internet connectivity issues and internal system limitations regarding file upload capacities and interactive features.

The implications of this research suggest several pathways for improvement. To maintain and improve technology acceptance, the researcher recommends that the university address technical limitations by increasing file upload capacities and upgrading the Moodle system to prevent lagging. To foster a positive "technology culture," the study suggests that the administration should implement policies that encourage the use of the TBL Hub for all official submissions and interactions, thereby normalizing its use. Additionally, the researcher recommends a behaviorist approach where college coordinators act as "ambassadors" to share best practices and acknowledge faculty who successfully integrate the LMS. Finally, the study suggests that future research should evaluate the technology acceptance of students to provide a holistic view of the university's e-readiness.

title: Technology-Based Support of Final Year Bachelor of Education Students in a South African Open Distance e-Learning Institution
abstract: Throughput rates are a cause for concern across South African universities. Acceptance at university does not guarantee success for students, particularly the historically and economically disadvantaged majority. This challenge is exacerbated in Open Distance e-Learning institutions such as the University of South Africa (UNISA). Through a case study, this paper discusses key issues affecting students who were on the brink of completion, requiring one or two modules to complete their Bachelor of Education qualification at UNISA. The two hundred students who were part of the study were enrolled in the second-level English module, Genres in Literature and Language: Theory, Style and Poetics. The sampling was voluntary and purposeful from students in this module, who either sought assistance with the module content via email or who qualified for the FI Concession, which is an additional assessment opportunity for final-year students. The study identifies existing barriers to successful study using Keller’s (1987) ARCS Model of Motivation. It offers a glimpse of support efforts provided to these students using the myUnisa Learning Management System in combination with the WhatsApp application, short video podcasts, and NoRedInk. The latter is an online learning site that seeks to develop writing skills through grammar and writing activities. These digital platforms and resources were used as part of the Lecturer-in-the-Pocket (LiP) approach, which underpins the intervention. The success of this cohort provides another approach to improving throughput rates in Open Distance e-Learning institutions.
half:
This study investigates the challenges faced by final-year Bachelor of Education students at the University of South Africa, a distance learning institution. The research focuses on students near completion who face high failure rates in the second-level English module, ENG2602. These failures cause despondence and financial strain, particularly for students relying on bursaries. Challenges include the digital divide, limited access to campus resources due to work and family commitments, and the limitations of existing institutional concessions.

Using a mixed-methods approach guided by Keller’s ARCS Model of Motivation, the researcher analyzed data from 200 students. Findings revealed barriers across all four ARCS dimensions: inconsistent internet access (Attention), low self-efficacy due to high-level critical analysis requirements (Confidence), and delayed or vague assignment feedback (Relevance and Satisfaction). Additionally, 36% of students identified the two-hour duration of venue-based examinations as a major barrier for intensive analysis.

To address these issues, the researcher implemented the "Lecturer-in-the-Pocket" (LiP) intervention, utilizing WhatsApp, NoRedInk, and the myUnisa platform to provide mobile-based support. A Portfolio of Evidence (PoE) was also used as a summative assessment to mitigate exam stress. Results showed significant improvement: while 81% of the cohort previously scored between 40% and 49% in traditional exams, 95% of those using the PoE passed the module. The study recommends improving feedback quality, ensuring device access, and allowing alternative assessment formats for students near graduation.

The research focuses on the low throughput rate among students "on the brink" of completion—those requiring only one or two modules to graduate. A specific problem identified is the high failure rate in the second-level English module, ENG2602. Many students repeat this module multiple times, leading to despondence and financial strain, particularly for those relying on bursaries like the National Student Financial Aid Scheme, where failure can result in a loss of funding.

The context is rooted in the unique challenges of distance education, where students often balance work and family responsibilities, leading to limited time for library or computer center access. This creates a digital divide regarding internet connectivity. Furthermore, existing institutional interventions, such as the Final Year (FI) Concession, have limitations as they do not apply to all modules and can only be used once.

Using a mixed-methods approach, the researcher sampled 200 students enrolled in ENG2602. The quantitative component analyzed performance statistics and baseline surveys, while the qualitative component utilized framework analysis of student reflections from myUnisa discussion forums and a summative Portfolio of Evidence (PoE). The study was guided by Keller’s (1987) ARCS Model of Motivation, focusing on Attention, Relevance, Confidence, and Satisfaction.

Findings revealed significant barriers across all four ARCS dimensions. Regarding Attention, students faced inconsistent internet access. Regarding Confidence, the module's requirement for high-level critical analysis lowered self-efficacy. Regarding Relevance and Satisfaction, students reported that assignment feedback was often delayed, vague, or focused solely on negative aspects. Additionally, 36% of students identified the two-hour duration of venue-based examinations as a major barrier for the intensive analysis required.

The researcher implemented the "Lecturer-in-the-Pocket" (LiP) intervention, a four-month approach using mobile technology to bridge the gap between academics and students. This utilized WhatsApp for immediate communication, NoRedInk for grammar tutorials, and the myUnisa platform for discussion forums and video podcasts. To mitigate examination stress, a PoE was used as the summative assessment. Results showed significant improvement: while 81% of the cohort had previously scored between 40% and 49% in traditional exams, 95% of those using the PoE passed the module.

The study concludes that the LiP approach successfully addresses motivation gaps by providing "face-to-face at a distance" support. Recommendations include negotiating bulk tablet purchases to ensure access, improving synergy between support services, enhancing the quality and speed of feedback, and amending assessment policies to allow for alternative formats like portfolios for students near graduation.
two:
The study investigates the challenges faced by final-year Bachelor of Education (BEd) students at the University of South Africa (UNISA), a Comprehensive Open Distance e-Learning (CODeL) institution. The central problem is the low throughput rate among students who are "on the brink" of completion—those requiring only one or two modules to graduate. Specifically, the researcher identifies a high failure rate in the second-level English module, Genres in Literature and Language: Theory, Style and Poetics (ENG2602). Many students repeat this module multiple times, sometimes up to eight times, which leads to despondence and financial strain. For students relying on bursaries like the National Student Financial Aid Scheme, failing a final module can result in a loss of funding, making it impossible to pay fees for subsequent attempts and ultimately leading to dropout.

The context of the study is rooted in the unique challenges of distance education in South Africa. Unlike contact universities, ODeL students often balance multiple identities as workers, parents, or spouses, leaving them with limited time to access physical libraries or computer centers. This creates a digital divide where underprivileged students struggle with meaningful internet connectivity. Furthermore, existing institutional interventions, such as the Final Year (FI) Concession, have limitations, as they do not apply to all modules and can only be used once.

To address these issues, the researcher employed a mixed-methods approach, utilizing both quantitative and qualitative data. The study used purposeful and voluntary sampling to select 200 students enrolled in the ENG2602 module, including those who had requested assistance via email and those qualifying for the FI Concession. The quantitative component involved analyzing performance statistics and baseline surveys to determine how many times students had repeated the module and their previous examination scores. The qualitative component involved framework analysis of student reflections collected via myUnisa discussion forums and a summative Portfolio of Evidence (PoE).

The theoretical framework used to guide the study was Keller’s (1987) ARCS Model of Motivation, which focuses on four components: Attention, Relevance, Confidence, and Satisfaction. The researcher hypothesized that gaps in these four areas were contributing to student failure.

The findings revealed significant barriers across all four ARCS dimensions. Regarding Attention, students faced challenges due to limited and inconsistent internet access. In terms of Confidence, the complexity of the module—which requires high-level critical analysis—lowered student self-efficacy. Regarding Relevance and Satisfaction, students reported that assignment feedback was often delayed, vague, or focused solely on negative aspects, which discouraged them from applying the feedback to improve. Additionally, 36% of students identified the two-hour duration of venue-based examinations as a major barrier, noting that the time was insufficient for the intensive analysis and writing required.

The intervention implemented was the "Lecturer-in-the-Pocket" (LiP) approach, designed to bridge the gap between academics and students through accessible mobile technology. The intervention lasted four months and was facilitated by five academics. It utilized WhatsApp to provide immediate communication, NoRedInk to offer targeted grammar tutorials that addressed specific errors found in student emails, and the myUnisa platform for discussion forums and video podcasts (vidcasts). To mitigate the stress of timed examinations, the researchers used a Portfolio of Evidence (PoE) as the summative assessment. The results showed a significant improvement in success rates; while 81% of the cohort had previously scored between 40% and 49% in traditional exams, 95% of the students who opted for the PoE passed the module.

The study concludes that the LiP approach successfully addresses gaps in student motivation by providing "face-to-face at a distance" support. By using affordable platforms like WhatsApp, academics can sustain student attention and provide the immediate feedback necessary for satisfaction. The study demonstrates that the ARCS model is a valuable tool not just for planning instruction, but for diagnosing existing instructional gaps in ODeL environments.

The implications of this research suggest several recommendations for ODeL institutions. To improve throughput, institutions should consider negotiating bulk purchases of tablets to ensure all students have access to learning materials. There is a need for greater synergy between various support services, such as e-tutors and lecturers, to prevent student confusion. The researcher also suggests that institutions should improve the turnaround time and quality of assignment feedback, emphasizing student strengths to build confidence. Furthermore, the study suggests that institutions should consider amending assessment policies to allow for alternative formats, such as portfolios, for students on the brink of graduation, and potentially lengthening examination durations to reduce anxiety and increase the "expectancy for success."

title: Online Laboratory Instruction as Alternative and Supplementary Mode: Students’ Assessment of the BS Agricultural Biotechnology Program
abstract: When the COVID-19 pandemic hit the education sector, the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) faculty started to tailor-fit their lectures and laboratory activities in the form of course packs to continue the delivery of various academic programs. The BS Agricultural Biotechnology (BS ABT) program is one of the courses in hard science that relies heavily on laboratory exercises. To assess the remote learning of the courses with laboratory exercises, BS ABT students were randomly surveyed to evaluate the effectiveness of their laboratory classes in the remote learning set-up. Based on the results, 94.5% of the BS ABT student-respondents were generally satisfied with the teaching style of the faculty, and implementation of the laboratory activities remotely. Experiments in all exercises were conducted synchronously and asynchronously through Google Classroom, and commonly accomplished with simplified experiments, simulations online, and supplemented by online videos via their personal laptops and smartphones. Regular synchronous meetings (96.4%) were religiously done every week with classes meeting once (49.1%), or twice (85.5%) a week. Ranking the three major courses of the ABT program that require laboratory exercises, ABT 104 (51%) obtained the highest satisfaction rating, followed by ABT 103 (47.3%), and ABT 106 (40%), respectively. Aside from ABT subjects with laboratory, Agriculture core subjects such as AGR21 (27.27%), AGR22 (27.27%), AGR31 (27.27%), AGR32 (27.27%), AGR41 (32.74%), AGR42 (23.64%), and AGR51 (20%) were the most enrolled courses. The findings of the present study serve as inputs in enhancing implementation of laboratory classes remotely in hard science particularly in the BS ABT program.
half:
The study "Online Laboratory Instruction as Alternative and Supplementary Mode: Students’ Assessment of the BS Agricultural Biotechnology Program" by Reniel S. Pamplona and Inero V. Ancho examines the effectiveness of remote laboratory instruction for BS ABT students at the University of the Philippines Los Baños during the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a descriptive research design, the researchers surveyed 55 randomly selected students regarding virtual learning access, teaching modes, lecture information, and remote laboratory instruction.

Findings revealed high student satisfaction with faculty teaching styles, course syllabi, learning outcomes, and curriculum coherence. Students also showed high approval for audiovisual presentations, handouts, and course packs. While Google Classroom, Zoom, and Google Meet were the primary tools for asynchronous and synchronous delivery, satisfaction specifically for remote laboratory instruction was low at 45.45%, with 34.55% of students expressing dissatisfaction. Qualitative feedback indicated that while do-it-yourself experiments using household materials allowed for some skill application, students felt a significant lack of hands-on experience with professional equipment, noting that relying on videos and written instructions felt like a waste of specialized training.

The study concludes that online instruction successfully maintained program continuity but serves better as an alternative or supplementary mode rather than a full replacement for physical laboratory work. Researchers recommend that future remote instruction utilize low-cost, accessible materials announced early, provide highly detailed instructions, and implement structured activity sequences.

two:
The study titled "Online Laboratory Instruction as Alternative and Supplementary Mode: Students’ Assessment of the BS Agricultural Biotechnology Program" by Reniel S. Pamplona and Inero V. Ancho investigates the effectiveness and student perceptions of remote laboratory instruction during the COVID-19 pandemic.

**Problem and Context**
The onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020 necessitated a drastic shift in educational modalities due to government-imposed lockdowns and quarantine restrictions. For science-based programs like the Bachelor of Science in Agricultural Biotechnology (BS ABT) at the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB), this transition presented significant challenges. The BS ABT program is heavily reliant on laboratory exercises to provide the hands-on experience and face-to-face interaction essential for student contentment and the retention of theoretical knowledge. Because remote learning is traditionally designed for lectures and recitations, applying it to laboratory instruction—where methodological and troubleshooting skills are developed—posed a major pedagogical problem.

**Method**
The researchers employed a descriptive research design using a survey method. A survey instrument consisting of close-ended, multiple-choice, and modified Likert Scale questions was distributed via Google Forms to a randomly selected group of BS ABT students. The sample included 55 respondents, representing approximately 10% to 14% of the total student population enrolled during the transition period (2nd semester 2020 to mid-year July 2022). The survey targeted students across different year levels, ages, and majors (Crop Biotechnology, Food Biotechnology, Animal Biotechnology, and Crop Protection Biotechnology). The research instrument focused on four key areas: access to virtual learning (technology and connectivity), the mode of teaching (platforms and frequency), lecture-related information (quality of activities), and remote laboratory instruction. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics for quantitative data and thematic analysis for qualitative student feedback.

**Findings**
The results indicated a high level of student satisfaction regarding the faculty's teaching style and the remote implementation of laboratory activities, with 94.5% of respondents expressing general agreement with the delivery of instruction. Students reported high satisfaction with the course syllabus (98.2%), the achievement of learning outcomes (96.4%), the breadth and depth of teaching (90.9%), and the coherence of the curriculum (96.3%). Regarding educational materials, students expressed high approval for audiovisual presentations (94.6%), handouts (90.9%), and course packs (90.9%), though satisfaction with revised laboratory manuals was slightly lower at 81.8%.

In terms of instructional delivery, Google Classroom was the most utilized platform for asynchronous activities (100%), while Zoom (100%) and Google Meet (83.6%) were the preferred tools for synchronous meetings. Most classes were held twice a week (85.5%). While students appreciated the use of DIY (do-it-yourself) experiments using household materials as substitutes for traditional lab work, the overall satisfaction for the implementation of remote laboratory instruction specifically was lower, at 45.45%, with 34.55% expressing dissatisfaction. Qualitative feedback revealed that while DIY experiments allowed for skill application, students felt a significant lack of hands-on experience with professional equipment. Many students expressed regret over the inability to perform actual laboratory work, noting that relying on videos and written instructions felt like a "waste" of their specialized training.

**Conclusions**
The study concludes that while online instruction and digital platforms like Google Classroom and Zoom successfully maintained the continuity of the BS ABT program, they serve better as alternative or supplementary modes rather than full replacements for physical laboratory work. The transition was successful in terms of maintaining engagement and delivering theoretical content, but it struggled to replicate the authentic, hands-on technical training required for biotechnology. The findings suggest that while digital tools can bridge the gap, the lack of physical laboratory access remains a primary concern for students in hard science programs.

**Implications**
The researchers propose several implications for improving future remote or hybrid laboratory instruction. First, they recommend the use of low-cost, easily accessible materials for home-based experiments, with early announcement to allow students time for procurement. Second, faculty should provide highly detailed instructions and maintain regular consultation to guide students through complex home-based procedures. Third, instructors should implement a structured sequence and strict timeframe for activities to help students manage their academic workload. Finally, the study emphasizes the need for equitable class requirements, ensuring that assessments reflect authentic learning without placing an undue burden on students' socio-economic status. For higher education institutions, the study suggests crafting policies that prioritize student welfare, resource availability, and the identification of essential competencies that can be realistically achieved in a remote setting.

title: A Conjoint Study and Segmentation on the Preferred Online Learning Attributes of Senior High School Learners
abstract: The educational systems have been disrupted due to the COVID-19 pandemic that has resulted in the sudden shift in the instructional implementation from face-to-face to fully online distance learning. This quantitative study examined the learners’ socio-demographic characteristics and access to technological resources, preferred online learning attributes, and their segmentation. The study employed a descriptive and exploratory research design. Using Cochran's formula and disproportionate stratified random sampling technique, 300 senior high school learners were identified as respondents of the study. Five online learning attributes consisting of delivery type, lecture, learning tasks, learning materials, and assessment methods were analyzed through the orthogonal plan component of SPSS 22.0. Respondents voluntarily answered 16 profiles with 2 holdouts generated by the orthogonal design using an online 5-point Likert scale. The conjoint analysis revealed that learners' most preferred online learning attributes were assessment methods using multiple-choice and multiple types of exams; synchronous online lectures with slides as the delivery type; individual tasks; and learning materials utilizing visual aids. Further analysis revealed that learners, considering their preferences and profiles, could be classified into two segments based on grade level. Grade 12 learners comprised segment one, and Grade 11 dominated segment two. The results provide insights for academic institutions that learners in different grade levels differ in their learning preferences in an online setup and to reconsider the appropriate pedagogical activities to be utilized in an online learning setup to ensure educational advantage. Therefore, it would be ideal to redesign the curricula and innovate pedagogical approaches based on learners’ preferences and segmentation (grade level) to leverage learning in online education.
half:
Junar S. Cano’s study, "A Conjoint Study and Segmentation on the Preferred Online Learning Attributes of Senior High School Learners," examines educational disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a quantitative, descriptive, and exploratory design, the researcher sampled 300 senior high school learners from Notre Dame of Marbel University to analyze preferences regarding delivery type, lecture, learning tasks, learning materials, and assessment methods.

Conjoint analysis revealed that assessment methods, specifically multiple-choice and multiple-type exams, were the most significant factor influencing preferences. Other highly valued attributes included synchronous delivery, individual learning tasks, and visual aids, while asynchronous delivery and recorded lectures were less preferred. Socio-demographic data showed most respondents were female, from low-income families, and owned smartphones or laptops, though many faced unreliable internet.

Cluster analysis identified two distinct segments. Segment 1 (54.2%), primarily Grade 12 learners, preferred recorded lectures with slides, individual tasks, hands-on materials, and multiple-choice exams. Segment 2 (45.5%), dominated by Grade 11 learners, preferred live online lectures with slides, reading materials, individual tasks, and multiple-type exams. Chi-square tests confirmed these segments differ significantly in gender, family income, grade level, and internet access. The study concludes that institutions should avoid a "one-size-fits-all" approach, instead prioritizing recorded content for Grade 12 and real-time interaction for Grade 11, while addressing logistical barriers like internet stability.

The study "A Conjoint Study and Segmentation on the Preferred Online Learning Attributes of Senior High School Learners" by Junar S. Cano examines the educational disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The shift to online distance learning highlighted challenges such as the digital divide, unstable internet connectivity, and the need for effective pedagogical strategies. The researcher identified a gap in literature regarding the segmentation of K-12 learners in online setups, suggesting that understanding specific preferences is vital for designing effective curricula.

Using a quantitative, descriptive, and exploratory research design, the study sampled 300 senior high school learners from Notre Dame of Marbel University-Senior High School Department.
