title: Learning Under the New Normal: Remote Learning Readiness among Students of a Philippine State University
abstract: With the outbreak of COVID-19, education shifted to a new norm with remote learning becoming the primary mode of instruction. This transition highlighted the need to understand students’ readiness for this new educational set-up. This study was conducted to assess students’ readiness for remote learning at a Philippine State University. It aimed to determine the expectations of the students on remote learning set-up, the challenges faced, and the assistance needed to propose recommendations and interventions to address the challenges and ensure an effective delivery of education through remote learning. The study was conducted through an online survey administered to 238 undergraduate and graduate students. The remote learning readiness survey was adapted from the Online Readiness Assessment by Vicki Williams (2014), which covers areas such as expectations, self-direction, learning preferences, study habits, learning strategies, language skills, technology skills, technology-mediated communication skills, and hardware/software requirements. Results showed that most of the respondents strongly agreed that remote courses are not easier than face-to-face courses. Moreover, a majority reported being self-directed to finish what they started and dedicated specific time to do their coursework. The majority also expressed confidence in navigating the internet and communicating via email and other synchronous platforms. Challenges encountered are poor or unstable internet connections, financial cost of study, heavy academic workload, time management difficulties, unavailability of gadgets and internet data, difficulty in managing distractions, and mental health issues concerns such as anxiety, In response to these challenges, the study proposes several interventions, including academic support, financial assistance, and mental health services.

The study "Learning Under the New Normal: Remote Learning Readiness among Students of a Philippine State University" by Beverly R. Pabro and Maria Ana T. Quimbo investigates student preparedness during the transition from face-to-face to remote learning caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a quantitative approach, researchers surveyed 238 undergraduate and graduate students to assess readiness across dimensions such as self-direction, technology skills, and learning strategies.

Findings indicate that students generally possess high readiness in several areas. Most respondents recognized that remote learning is not easier than traditional instruction and demonstrated strong self-direction, including the ability to set goals. Students expressed confidence in navigating the internet, using computer applications, and communicating via email or synchronous platforms. They also showed a preference for auditory and reading content, utilized adequate learning strategies, and possessed satisfactory language skills.

However, significant barriers were identified. The most prominent challenge was unstable or inaccessible internet connections. Other obstacles included technological problems, high financial costs, and a lack of necessary hardware. Students also reported difficulties with time management, heavy workloads, and distractions, alongside increased psychological burdens like anxiety, stress, and reduced social interaction. The authors conclude that while students are capable of self-directed learning, they are not fully prepared for systemic and personal challenges. They recommend that institutions provide financial, technological, and psychosocial support, including internet subsidies, gadgets, and counseling services.

The study "Learning Under the New Normal: Remote Learning Readiness among Students of a Philippine State University" by Beverly R. Pabro and Maria Ana T. Quimbo investigates the preparedness of students transitioning from traditional face-to-face instruction to remote learning environments. This shift was necessitated by the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced educational institutions to adopt remote modes of delivery to ensure safety and continuity.

The problem addressed by the authors is the sudden and disruptive transition to remote learning, which presents various challenges that can impede academic success. While remote learning offers flexibility and inclusivity, its effectiveness is heavily dependent on student readiness, technological infrastructure, and institutional support. The researchers sought to understand student expectations, identify the specific challenges encountered during this transition, and determine what forms of assistance are required to ensure effective education in a remote setting.

The research was conducted at a Philippine State University and utilized an online survey administered via Google Forms to 238 undergraduate and graduate students. The study employed a quantitative approach, using a 4-point Likert scale to assess readiness across several dimensions adapted from Vicki Williams’ Online Readiness Assessment. These dimensions included expectations, self-direction, learning preferences, study habits, learning strategies, language skills, technology skills, technology-mediated communication skills, and hardware/software requirements. Data were analyzed using frequency counts, percentages, and mean scores, while qualitative responses were examined for recurring themes.

The findings revealed that students generally possess a high level of readiness in several key areas. Most respondents agreed that remote learning is not easier than face-to-face instruction and demonstrated strong self-direction, with many reporting they are capable of setting goals, finishing tasks, and staying on track. In terms of technology, the majority of students expressed confidence in navigating the internet, using various computer applications, and communicating via email or synchronous platforms like Zoom and Messenger. Regarding learning preferences, students showed a strong inclination toward auditory content and reading. Additionally, most students reported having adequate learning strategies, such as note-taking and reflection, and possessed satisfactory language skills.

However, the study also identified significant barriers to remote learning. The most prominent challenge was unstable or inaccessible internet connections. Other major obstacles included technological problems, the high financial cost of studying, and a lack of necessary hardware, such as printers or reliable gadgets. Students also reported difficulties with time management, heavy academic workloads, and the inability to ignore distractions, such as social media or household responsibilities. Furthermore, the transition led to increased psychological burdens, including anxiety and stress, and a perceived reduction in social interaction compared to traditional settings.

The conclusions drawn from the study indicate that while students are largely capable of self-directed learning and possess the necessary digital communication skills, they are not fully prepared for the systemic and personal challenges posed by remote learning. The findings suggest that student readiness is not merely a matter of individual skill but is deeply intertwined with socio-economic factors, technological access, and mental health. The researchers concluded that for remote learning to be effective, institutions must provide comprehensive support that addresses financial, technological, and psychosocial needs.

Based on these findings, the authors propose several implications and recommendations for universities and educators. To address the identified challenges, the study recommends regular assessments of both student and faculty situations to facilitate timely interventions. Regarding financial and technological needs, the authors highlight the importance of programs like the University's Grants-in-Aid, which provides internet connectivity subsidies and gadgets to vulnerable students. For psychological well-being, the study suggests that counseling services should be proactive in addressing the rising prevalence of mental health issues among remote learners.

Furthermore, the authors recommend that the Center for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning (CATL) provide ongoing technical assistance and training for both faculty and students to improve the management of Learning Management Systems (LMS) and the creation of interactive digital materials. For faculty, the study suggests a need for continued support in developing innovative teaching strategies and digital capabilities. Finally, the authors suggest that future research should incorporate qualitative methods, such as interviews or focus groups, to gain deeper insights into student experiences and should explore the perspectives of instructors to create a more holistic understanding of remote learning readiness.

title: Identifying Learner Support Services Gaps In Distance Education: Case Study of A Federal Owned University In Nigeria
abstract: A distance education institution must have strategies for success in place, one of which should be the provision of effective learner support services. Compared to that of the traditional/face-to-face mode of teaching and learning, the learner support services needed for distance learning are more critical. The aim of the study was to identify the availability of the components of learner support services and gaps existing in any available system. The study also investigated the level of availability of different support services at the institution for distance learners. It further examined the challenges faced by the institution in the provision of support services. The case institution for this study is the Centre for Distance Learning, University of Benin, Benin City, Nigeria. The study applied qualitative and investigative methods to obtain knowledge by means of observation, interviews and study of official documents. A total of 43 stakeholders participated in the study. The population comprised of management staff, program coordinator, course adviser, E-tutors, technical and administrative staff and learners. The study identified the need for increased funding to upgrade the facilities and sustain the day-to-day operations of the institution. More training and engagements with the learners on how Open and Distance Learning (ODL) works and how to carry out the important tasks required of them on the learning application were also recommended. In order to reduce isolation created by the physical separation between learners and the Centre, there is a need for periodic face to face interaction between learners and the Centre.
half:
In the study "Identifying Learner Support Services Gaps In Distance Education: Case Study Of A Federal Owned University In Nigeria," Osaretin Aigbovo and Dorothy Akpon-Ebiyomare investigate support systems at the University of Benin's Centre for Distance Learning. Using a qualitative case study approach involving interviews with 43 stakeholders, observations, and document reviews, the researchers examined how support systems mitigate learner isolation and improve academic success in Open and Distance Learning environments.

The findings reveal a mixture of functional systems and significant service gaps. While the institution utilizes an automated admission portal and a Moodle-based Learning Management System, staff often rely on personal mobile devices for official communication, and counselors lack official devices. Library services are inadequate; the existing mini digital library is non-functional due to a lack of networking and internet connectivity, and the absence of physical study materials creates barriers for students without reliable internet or computers. Furthermore, academic support is limited to electronic formats, failing to accommodate diverse learning preferences or students with limited data and power.

Key challenges include poor quality ICT hardware and understaffed counseling services, with only one counselor for three offices. Financial constraints are the primary driver of these gaps. The authors recommend providing materials in multiple formats, upgrading ICT and library facilities, increasing funding, and implementing periodic face-to-face interactions to reduce learner isolation.
one:
In the study "Identifying Learner Support Services Gaps In Distance Education: Case Study Of A Federal Owned University In Nigeria," Osaretin Aigbovo and Dorothy Akpon-Ebiyomare investigate the effectiveness and availability of support systems at the Centre for Distance Learning, University of Benin. The research addresses the need for robust support in Open and Distance Learning (ODL) environments to mitigate learner isolation and improve retention and academic success. The authors note that without effective support, learners may lack the guidance necessary to navigate technology-enabled environments, potentially leading to attrition and poor performance.

Using a qualitative case study approach with a triangulation method, the researchers collected data through interviews with 43 stakeholders—including management, coordinators, e-tutors, staff, and learners—as well as direct observation and document reviews. The findings reveal a mixture of functional systems and significant service gaps. While the institution has implemented an automated admission process via a student portal and maintains communication through telephone, social media, and a Moodle-based Learning Management System, a gap exists because staff often use personal mobile devices for official communication, and counselors lack official devices to reach learners.

Library services were found to be inadequate. A mini digital library exists but is non-functional because the computer systems are not networked and lack internet connectivity. Additionally, the library lacks physical copies of study materials, forcing students to rely entirely on online platforms, which creates barriers for those without personal computers or reliable internet. Regarding academic support, study materials are prepared by experienced lecturers but are only available in electronic format. This lack of multimedia options, such as print or audio, fails to meet diverse learning preferences and creates barriers for students with limited data or power supply.

The study also identified significant challenges in ICT infrastructure and counseling. Physical ICT equipment is of poor quality and frequently suffers from hardware failures. Furthermore, counseling services are understaffed, with only one counselor employed for three counseling offices. Financial constraints were identified as a primary driver of these gaps, as insufficient funding limits the ability to produce hard-copy materials, upgrade equipment, and provide administrative resources.

The authors conclude that the Centre faces major challenges regarding space, funding, and communication. To make ODL sustainable, they recommend providing study materials in multiple formats, upgrading library and ICT facilities, and establishing a robust guidance and counseling system. They also suggest increasing financial allocations, motivating e-tutors through better compensation, and implementing periodic face-to-face interactions to reduce learner isolation.

The study titled "Identifying Learner Support Services Gaps In Distance Education: Case Study Of A Federal Owned University In Nigeria" by Osaretin Aigbovo and Dorothy Akpon-Ebiyomare investigates the effectiveness and availability of support systems at the Centre for Distance Learning, University of Benin. The research addresses the critical need for robust support services in Open and Distance Learning (ODL) environments to mitigate the inherent isolation of remote study and to improve student retention and academic success.

The problem addressed by the authors is the potential for significant gaps in learner support services which can lead to student attrition, delayed program completion, and poor academic performance. While distance education provides flexible access to education for diverse populations—including those with physical challenges or geographical constraints—it requires specialized support systems to be successful. The authors note that without effective support, learners may experience isolation and lack the necessary guidance to navigate technology-enabled learning environments.

The context of the study is a federal owned university in Nigeria, a country with a large population where regular tertiary institutions cannot accommodate all qualified candidates. The study focuses specifically on the Centre for Distance Learning at the University of Benin. The researchers employed a qualitative and investigative case study approach, utilizing a triangulation method to ensure data reliability. Data was collected through interviews with 43 stakeholders—including management, program coordinators, e-tutors, technical and administrative staff, and learners—as well as direct observation and a review of official institutional and regulatory documents.

The findings reveal a mixture of functional systems and significant service gaps. Regarding admission, the institution has successfully implemented an automated process via a student portal that handles applications, clearance, and fee payments. Communication is maintained through a two-way system involving telephone lines, social media, and a Learning Management System (LMS) using Moodle. However, a notable gap exists as staff members often use personal mobile devices for official communication, and counselors lack official devices to reach learners.

Library services were found to be inadequate. While a mini digital library exists, it is non-functional because the computer systems are not networked and lack internet connectivity. Furthermore, the library lacks physical copies of study materials, forcing students to rely entirely on online platforms, which is problematic for those without personal computers or reliable internet. Regarding academic support, while study materials are adequately prepared by experienced lecturers, they are only available in electronic format. This lack of multimedia options (such as print or audio) fails to meet the diverse learning preferences of students and creates barriers for those with limited data or power supply.

The study also identified significant challenges in ICT infrastructure and counseling. The physical ICT equipment at the Centre is of poor quality, frequently suffering from hardware failures such as hard disk and monitor issues. Additionally, the counseling services are understaffed; while the Centre has three counseling offices, it currently employs only one counselor, which is insufficient for the expected growth of the learner population. Financial constraints were identified as a primary driver of these gaps, as insufficient funding limits the ability to produce hard-copy materials, upgrade ICT equipment, and provide adequate administrative resources.

In conclusion, the authors conclude that the Centre for Distance Learning faces major challenges regarding space, funding, and communication. The shortage of space for e-libraries and computer labs, combined with inadequate financial resources, prevents the institution from providing a comprehensive support system. The reliance on personal devices for official communication and the lack of diverse learning formats further exacerbate the distance between the institution and its learners.

The implications of these findings suggest that for ODL to be sustainable and effective, institutions must move beyond providing mere digital access and invest in holistic support structures. The authors recommend several interventions: providing study materials in multiple formats (print, electronic, and audio); upgrading library and ICT facilities with high-powered, networked equipment; and establishing a robust guidance and counseling system that includes both academic and psychological support. Furthermore, the study suggests that increasing financial allocations and motivating e-tutors through better compensation and professional development is essential for maintaining educational quality. Finally, the researchers recommend periodic face-to-face interactions to reduce the sense of isolation among distance learners.

title: Student Evaluation of Blended Learning Implementation and Faculty Performance with Online Components: A Comparative Analysis Across Senior High School Grade Levels and Academic  Strands
abstract: Blended learning, which combines face-to-face instruction with online learning components, has become increasingly prevalent in Philippine senior high schools. This study examines student evaluations of blended learning implementation, with a specific focus on the effectiveness of its online components. Additionally, it explores faculty performance in delivering these online aspects across various grade levels and academic strands in a Philippine senior high school. Using a mixed-methods approach, this study surveyed 1,450 students from various academic strands (STEM, ABM, HUMSS, and GAS) in Grades 11 and 12. Quantitative data were analyzed using t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, and Kruskal-Wallis tests, while qualitative data underwent constant comparative analysis. Results showed no significant differences between grade levels but revealed variations across academic strands. STEM students reported more positive evaluations of online learning implementation, while GAS students viewed faculty performance most favorably. Common challenges identified by the students included excessive workload, unstable internet connections, and mental health concerns. Opportunities focused on better time management, diverse learning tools, and independent learning. These findings underscore the need for strand-specific customization in blended learning implementation and targeted faculty development. The study contributes to research on blended learning in secondary education and offers insights for enhancing technology-enhanced learning in diverse academic contexts.

Findings indicated moderate to positive evaluations for both implementation and faculty performance. Students valued relevant subject resources and the functionality of the Canvas Learning Management System. Regarding faculty, students praised feedback and clear rubrics, though they noted a lack of exact schedules for online activities. However, satisfaction was lower regarding how online modes aligned with personal learning preferences. Comparative analyses showed no significant differences between Grade 11 and Grade 12 students, but significant differences emerged across academic strands. STEM students reported more positive implementation evaluations than HUMSS students, while ABM students reported lower implementation evaluations than both GAS and HUMSS students. For faculty performance, GAS students expressed the highest satisfaction, while ABM students expressed the lowest.

Students identified excessive workloads, unstable internet, and mental health concerns as primary challenges. The study concludes that while resource provision and teacher interaction are effective, a mismatch exists between online delivery and student learning preferences. The author recommends strand-specific customization, particularly for ABM students, and faculty development focused on workload management and activity scheduling.

The research addresses whether grade levels and specific academic strands—STEM, ABM, HUMSS, and GAS—influence these perceptions.

Using a mixed-methods approach, the researcher surveyed 1,450 stratified students from a private senior high school. Quantitative data were collected via two 4-point Likert scales measuring implementation and faculty performance, while qualitative data were gathered through open-ended questions. Statistical analyses included independent t-tests and Kruskal-Wallis tests.

The findings indicated moderate to positive evaluations for both implementation and faculty performance. Students highly valued the relevance of subject resources and the functionality of the Canvas Learning Management System. Regarding faculty, students praised teachers' ability to provide feedback and use clear rubrics, though they noted a lack of exact schedules for online activities. However, students reported lower satisfaction regarding how online modes aligned with their personal learning preferences.

Comparative analyses showed no significant differences between Grade 11 and Grade 12 students, suggesting similar adaptation levels across both groups. Significant differences did emerge across academic strands. STEM students reported significantly more positive evaluations of online implementation than HUMSS students, while ABM students reported lower implementation evaluations than both GAS and HUMSS students. In terms of faculty performance, GAS students expressed the highest satisfaction, while ABM students expressed the lowest.

Students identified excessive workloads, unstable internet, and mental health concerns as primary challenges. Conversely, they noted opportunities for better time management, the use of diverse learning tools, and increased time with family. Qualitative feedback emphasized the need for reduced workloads, better scheduling, and enhanced teacher support.

The study concludes that while resource provision and teacher interaction are effective, a mismatch exists between online delivery and student learning preferences, potentially increasing extraneous cognitive load. The results suggest that blended learning effectiveness is highly dependent on the specific academic context.

The author recommends that schools move away from "one-size-fits-all" models in favor of strand-specific customization, particularly for ABM students. Additionally, faculty development should focus on structural online teaching aspects, such as workload management and activity scheduling. two:
The study titled "Student Evaluation of Blended Learning Implementation and Faculty Performance with Online Components: A Comparative Analysis Across Senior High School Grade Levels and Academic Strands" by Stephen Jay Co investigates how students perceive the online elements of blended learning and the performance of faculty in these digital spaces. The research is situated within the context of the Philippine senior high school system, where the integration of technology has been accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic and the implementation of the K-12 curriculum. While blended learning—combining face-to-face and online instruction—is a growing pedagogical strategy to address large class sizes and geographical barriers, the effectiveness of its online components and the variations in student experiences across different academic specializations remain under-researched.

The primary problem addressed is the need to understand the nuanced experiences of students in technology-enhanced environments, specifically looking at whether grade levels and academic strands influence perceptions of implementation and teacher effectiveness. The study aims to determine if significant differences exist between Grade 11 and Grade 12 students, and among the various academic strands: Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM); Accountancy, Business, and Management (ABM); Humanities and Social Sciences (HUMSS); and General Academic Strand (GAS).

To address these objectives, the researcher employed a mixed-methods approach. The quantitative component utilized a cross-sectional survey design targeting 1,450 students from a private senior high school in the Philippines. The sample was stratified by grade level and academic strand. The survey instrument consisted of two validated 4-point Likert scales: one measuring blended learning implementation and another assessing faculty performance. The qualitative component involved an open-ended question regarding suggestions for improvement, which was analyzed using the constant comparative method to identify emerging themes. Statistical analyses included independent t-tests for grade-level comparisons and Kruskal-Wallis tests for comparisons across academic strands.

The findings revealed moderate to positive evaluations for both implementation and faculty performance. Regarding implementation, students highly valued the relevance of subject resources and the functionality of the Learning Management System (Canvas). However, they reported lower satisfaction regarding how well online modes aligned with their personal learning preferences and expressed moderate overall satisfaction. In terms of faculty performance, students gave high marks to teachers' ability to accommodate questions and feedback and their use of clear rubrics. A notable weakness identified was the lack of exact schedules for online activities.

Comparative analyses yielded significant results. There were no significant differences in evaluations between Grade 11 and Grade 12 students, suggesting that both groups have adapted similarly to the blended learning environment. However, significant differences were found across academic strands. STEM students reported significantly more positive evaluations of the online implementation compared to HUMSS students. Conversely, ABM students reported lower evaluations for implementation than both GAS and HUMSS students. Regarding faculty performance, GAS students were the most satisfied, while ABM students were the least satisfied.

Students identified several key challenges and opportunities. The most prominent challenges were excessive workload/assignments, unstable internet connections, and mental health concerns. Conversely, the most recognized opportunities included better time management, the exploration of diverse learning tools, and increased time with family. Qualitative feedback from students emphasized the need for reduced workloads, improved time management through better scheduling, and enhanced teacher support.

The study concludes that while blended learning is being implemented effectively in terms of resource provision and teacher interaction, there is a clear mismatch between online delivery methods and student learning preferences. The findings suggest that the online components may impose a high extraneous cognitive load on students, particularly regarding workload and scheduling. The lack of difference between grade levels suggests a stabilization of the learning environment, while the differences across strands indicate that the effectiveness of blended learning is highly dependent on the specific academic context and curriculum.

The implications of this research are significant for educational policy and practice. The author suggests that schools should move away from a "one-size-fits-all" approach and instead adopt strand-specific customization for blended learning. For example, because ABM students reported lower satisfaction, targeted interventions may be needed for their specific subject areas. Furthermore, the study highlights the necessity for structured faculty development programs that focus on the structural aspects of online teaching, such as activity scheduling and workload management, rather than just content delivery. Finally, the study recommends that future research should integrate learning outcome assessments to validate whether these student perceptions correlate with actual academic performance and should expand studies to include public school settings to account for different resource availability.

title: Prospects of Open and Distance Learning at the Open University of Tanzania Post-COVID-19 Pandemic
abstract: The rise of the COVID-19 pandemic created a paradox in the continuity of education among students all over the world. Open and Distance Learning (ODL) has become a vital solution to overcome barriers to education access associated with the pandemic. This paper analyzed the prospects of ODL at the Open University of Tanzania (OUT) after the emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic to avail potential opportunities for learning irrespective of emerging challenges. The study employs a qualitative research approach and an exploratory case study design. A sample of fifteen participants was purposively selected, and five ODL technical staff were conveniently sampled for the study. Findings showed that, following the COVID-19 pandemic, future plans and prospects of the ODL at OUT focus on increasing community awareness towards ODL, increasing flexibility for learning, and expanding enrollment rates. Furthermore, the OUT strives to increase accessibility for ODL by strengthening internet bandwidth to sustain distance learning and engaging financial institutions in supporting students' learning at the OUT. Based on the findings, the study recommends government organizations including the Tanzania Commission for Universities (TCU) to establish ODL policies that will serve as guidelines for ODL operations and place equal promotion for learners' opportunities to education utilizing flexible ODL platforms at the OUT.
half:
In the article "Prospects of Open and Distance Learning at the Open University of Tanzania Post-COVID-19 Pandemic," Baraka Gaitan Luvanga and Philipo Lonati Sanga examine the future potential of Open and Distance Learning (ODL) at the Open University of Tanzania (OUT) following pandemic-related disruptions. Using a qualitative exploratory case study design, the researchers conducted interviews with academic and technical staff and performed a documentary review to understand how ODL can ensure educational continuity.

The findings identify six primary prospects for ODL at OUT. The institution aims to provide quality, flexible, and affordable online education while increasing community awareness through marketing efforts involving Regional Advisory Committees and Ward Educational Officers. To improve access, the university seeks to increase enrollment flexibility through more frequent intakes and flexible certification. Financial sustainability is addressed through potential partnerships with banks to provide student loans. Additionally, the study emphasizes the need for strengthened ICT integration, specifically through stable internet and tools like Moodle and Zoom, and the enrichment of curricula to include entrepreneurship and non-degree programs.

The authors conclude that successful implementation of these strategic areas can significantly promote educational access for remote populations and women. They recommend that the government establish specific ODL policies to ensure these platforms receive support equal to traditional modes. Furthermore, OUT should commit to strategic planning and continuous investment in connectivity, while financial institutions should prioritize loan provisions for ODL learners.

The article "Prospects of Open and Distance Learning at the Open University of Tanzania Post-COVID-19 Pandemic" by Baraka Gaitan Luvanga and Philipo Lonati Sanga examines the future potential of Open and Distance Learning (ODL) at the Open University of Tanzania (OUT) following the global disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The problem addressed by the authors is the crisis faced by higher education institutions (HEIs) during the pandemic, where traditional modes of education delivery—which rely on physical contact between instructors and students—were rendered impossible by lockdowns. While ODL is a long-standing solution to educational barriers such as geographical remoteness, time constraints, and personal responsibilities, the pandemic created an urgent need to strengthen these services to ensure educational continuity. The study seeks to identify the specific prospects and opportunities for ODL at OUT in this post-pandemic landscape to ensure sustainability and effective service delivery.

The context of the study is situated within the broader evolution of ODL globally and specifically in Africa. The authors note that ODL is gaining importance as a tool to meet the unmet demand for higher education. In Tanzania, OUT was established in 1994 to expand access for adult learners and currently serves a large student population through blended learning—a combination of online and face-to-face instruction. The study is theoretically underpinned by the constructivist framework, which posits that learning is a student-centered process where learners actively construct knowledge through interaction with technology and social environments.

To investigate the prospects of ODL at OUT, the researchers employed a qualitative research approach using an exploratory case study design. This allowed for an in-depth analysis of the phenomena within its natural setting. Data were collected through interviews with fifteen purposively selected academic staff members and five conveniently sampled ODL technical staff from OUT. Additionally, the researchers conducted a documentary review to enhance the triangulation of findings. The data were analyzed using a six-stage thematic analysis process.

The findings of the study identified six primary prospects for ODL at OUT:
First, the institution aims to deliberately execute its mission and vision, which focuses on providing relevant, quality, flexible, and affordable open online education. The authors found that daily operations are increasingly guided by these strategic goals.
Second, there is a significant opportunity to raise community awareness. The study found that OUT intends to increase its visibility through marketing efforts, such as involving Regional Advisory Committees and utilizing Ward Educational Officers to reach secondary school students.
Third, increasing enrollment flexibility is a key prospect. The institution plans to increase its student population significantly by offering more frequent intakes (such as adding an April intake) and providing more flexible certification processes to help students secure employment faster.
Fourth, engaging financial institutions is identified as a vital prospect. Because financial constraints limit enrollment, OUT seeks to partner with banks to provide student loans through specific contractual agreements.
Fifth, the strengthening of ICT integration is essential. The findings show that OUT has the infrastructure but needs to maximize its use through stable internet bandwidth and advanced tools like Moodle, Zoom, and On-Demand Examination (ODEX) systems.
Sixth, the institution aims to enrich its courses and programs to meet market demands. This includes developing curricula for entrepreneurship and non-degree programs that provide practical, job-related skills.

In conclusion, the authors state that the future of ODL at OUT is tied to the successful implementation of these strategic areas. The study concludes that OUT possesses a rich repertoire of prospects that, if fully utilized, can significantly promote educational access in Tanzania. As the population grows, the prominence of ODL will continue to increase as a means to provide higher education to a wider demographic, including those in remote areas and women with domestic responsibilities.

The study offers several implications and recommendations for stakeholders. For the government and regulatory bodies like the Tanzania Commission for Universities (TCU), the authors recommend the establishment of specific ODL policies to serve as guidelines and to ensure that ODL platforms receive equal promotion and support as traditional modes of education. For the Open University of Tanzania, the authors recommend a heightened commitment to strategic planning, increased use of social media for advertising, and continuous investment in internet connectivity to accommodate a growing student body. Finally, the study suggests that financial and monitoring institutions should prioritize student support and loan provisions for ODL learners to ensure equitable access to higher education.

title: Student Perception of Learning, Engagement, and Confidence in Research Skills Using Mobile Devices as an Active Learning Strategy in a Science Course
abstract: This study aimed to determine how tertiary students use their mobile devices for academic in-class activities and learning tasks. Specifically, it examined the students’ perceptions of their learning, engagement, and confidence in research skills in relation to their use of mobile devices. This study used an online survey which consisted of a four-point Likert scale and verbal interpretation. Data analysis was performed using frequency distribution, mean, and standard deviation to assess respondents’ views on the influence of mobile devices in their learning and confidence in conducting research. The findings showed that students agreed with the positive impact of mobile devices in their education. In addition, students reported greater confidence in their research skills when using mobile devices. Overall, the students felt that mobile technology improved their knowledge and engagement. Moreover, the study showed that gadgets and applications should only be used as learning tools because the outcomes should still depend on the pedagogical strategy and learning objectives. As the research used convenience sampling, the results may only partially represent undergraduate students' perceptions of engagement, learning, and confidence in their research skills using their mobile devices. However, the research’s findings still provide insights on the potential benefits of integrating mobile devices in the classroom. These results can guide the development and formulation of more effective instructional methods and materials to enhance the students' learning experience.

The study "Student Perception of Learning, Engagement, and Confidence in Research Skills Using Mobile Devices as an Active Learning Strategy in a Science Course" investigates how undergraduate science students utilize mobile devices for academic purposes during the transition back to face-to-face instruction at the University of the East Manila. Using a quantitative research design and an online survey, researchers collected data from 18 undergraduate biology students to measure perceptions regarding engagement, learning, and confidence in research skills.

The findings indicate that mobile devices positively influence student engagement by increasing participation in lecture discussions, helping students pay attention to instructors, and motivating them to learn course material. Regarding learning, students agreed that mobile devices helped them participate in activities that enhanced learning, developed academic and professional skills, assisted in problem-solving, allowed for connecting ideas in new ways, and boosted confidence in specific subject areas. The highest level of agreement was observed in the use of mobile devices to participate in learning-enhancing activities.

Students reported being "very confident" across all measured research skill variables, including using electronic bibliographic databases, accessing literature through search engines, and understanding how theory leads to specific research questions. The authors conclude that mobile technology positively impacts engagement, learning, and research skill development, though success depends on the underlying pedagogical strategy rather than the technology itself.

title: Instructors’ Coping Strategies for Effective Online Teaching at the Open University of Tanzania (OUT)
abstract: Online teaching, now widely regarded as an appealing method of instruction in higher learning institutions, is constrained by various factors, including technological, pedagogical, and financial challenges that hinder instructors' efficiency in teaching. This study explored the coping strategies employed by instructors to facilitate effective online teaching at the Open University of Tanzania. Employing a qualitative approach and a phenomenological design, the study involved ten (10) participants, comprising two instructors selected from each of the five faculties at OUT. These faculties include the Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences, the Faculty of Education, the Faculty of Business Management, the Faculty of Law, and the Faculty of Science, Technology, and Environmental Studies. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and document reviews, and were analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings revealed that instructors adopted various coping strategies to enhance the effectiveness of online teaching. These strategies included teaching in university premises, using alternative tools other than Zoom and Moodle, delivery pre-recording online lectures, distributing digital and printed copies of learning resources and using personal devices and internet bundles to support course delivery. The study recommends that instructors be trained in diverse coping strategies for effective online teaching. Additionally, they should be provided with essential tools such as personal laptops and provided with institutional bandwidth support. Furthermore, the university should establish mechanisms to motivate instructors engaged in online teaching.

The study titled "Instructors’ Coping Strategies for Effective Online Teaching at the Open University of Tanzania (OUT)" by Joseph Kabage and Lulu Simon Mahai explores how educators navigate the complexities of digital instruction. As higher education institutions increasingly adopt online and blended learning models to democratize access and provide flexibility for students balancing work and family, instructors face significant hurdles. At the Open University of Tanzania, which has transitioned from pure correspondence and face-to-face instruction to a blended learning model using platforms like Moodle and Zoom, these challenges are particularly acute.

The problem addressed by the researchers is that while online teaching offers convenience and inclusivity, it is constrained by various technological, pedagogical, and financial obstacles. Specifically, instructors at OUT face issues such as a lack of dedicated teaching spaces, unreliable internet connectivity, high bandwidth costs, insufficient pedagogical skills for digital environments, technical difficulties, low student attendance, and limited access to internet bundles. The study sought to understand how instructors manage to maintain effective teaching despite these systemic and environmental impediments.

To investigate this, the researchers employed a qualitative research approach utilizing a phenomenological design. This design allowed the authors to explore the lived experiences and specific strategies used by instructors to overcome obstacles. The study was conducted at the OUT headquarters in Dar es Salaam, a location chosen because it houses the heads of departments and instructional designers. The sample consisted of ten instructors—five male and five female—selected purposively from each of the five faculties at the university: Arts and Social Sciences, Education, Business Management, Law, and Science, Technology, and Environmental Studies. Data collection involved semi-structured interviews and document reviews, including the university's strategic plan and prospectus. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns in the instructors' responses. The study was theoretically grounded in Resilience Theory, which views resilience as an individual's capacity to adapt and maintain functional behavior despite experiencing hardships.

The findings revealed that instructors adopted several distinct coping strategies to ensure effective course delivery. First, to combat domestic distractions (such as family interruptions) and technical issues like power outages or unstable home internet, many instructors chose to teach from the university premises to utilize reliable electricity, standby generators, and institutional internet. Second, when the primary platforms of Moodle and Zoom proved unreliable or inaccessible, instructors utilized alternative communication tools. WhatsApp emerged as the most prominent tool, used for creating subject groups to share materials, conduct discussions, and provide announcements. Other tools included Telegram, email, and SMS.

Third, instructors utilized pre-recorded lectures to provide asynchronous learning opportunities. While the study noted that recorded lectures were primarily available for level one courses via the OUT ODL YouTube channel, this method allowed students to engage with content at their own pace and revisit difficult material. Fourth, to mitigate the impact of unreliable internet, instructors distributed both digital and printed copies of learning resources. Students were encouraged to download materials to their devices for offline reading, and the use of print materials helped bridge the digital divide. Finally, instructors relied heavily on personal resources, using their own laptops, smartphones, and private internet bundles to ensure that teaching sessions could continue even when institutional support was insufficient or delayed.

The study concludes that transitioning from traditional to online teaching is a complex process that requires significant adaptation in methodology and time management. Instructors at OUT are successfully navigating these challenges through various adaptive behaviors, but they are often doing so by utilizing their own personal resources and working around institutional limitations.

Based on these findings, the authors offer several implications and recommendations for the university and policymakers. They recommend that instructors receive formal training in diverse coping strategies specifically tailored for effective online pedagogy. To reduce the personal financial and logistical burden on staff, the university should provide essential hardware, such as personal laptops, and ensure reliable institutional bandwidth and internet support. Finally, the researchers suggest that the university should establish formal mechanisms to motivate instructors who are engaged in the demanding task of online teaching.

title: Students' Usage of Google Classroom as LMS during Covid-19
abstract: Both developed and developing nations have adopted online education in response to the difficulties posed by the Covid-19 pandemic. Learning Management Systems (LMS) have gained rapid popularity as a widely utilized method for teaching and learning in the blended learning environment of universities. In the context of Open and Distance Learning (ODL), Google Classroom has often been used as a substitute for LMS, either due to the constraints of traditional LMSs or the absence of any existing LMSs. This study investigates the students' reactions to the utilization of Google Classroom as a LMS during the Covid-19 pandemic, when traditional in- person instruction was suspended in universities in Bangladesh. The study employed various techniques to gather responses from the students. A mixed-methods approach was employed, incorporating both survey questionnaires and in-depth interviews to gather quantitative and qualitative data. A total of 152 pupils completed the survey, and five learners participated in interviews. The findings of the study revealed that majority of the students responded positively on the usage of Google Classroom as LMS. However, several problems were observed such as the need for formalization and concerns over privacy and safety. The study recommends that the respective university authority should provide constant monitoring, timely feedback, and regular updates. Moreover, having clear policy guidelines, online surveillance measures, and active facilitation role of teachers are essential for the effective use of Google Classroom in ODL settings.

The findings reveal a positive student response, with a total mean score of 3.88. Notably, 108 out of 152 students expressed a preference for using Google Classroom alongside traditional instruction in a blended learning model. The author concludes that while the platform was vital, institutions should provide constant monitoring, timely feedback, and clear policy guidelines to maximize its potential.

The article "Students' Usage of Google Classroom as LMS during Covid-19" by Md. Omar Faruk Bhuiyan investigates how students in Bangladesh utilized Google Classroom as a Learning Management System (LMS) during the COVID-19 pandemic. The study addresses the sudden shift from in-person instruction to online modalities necessitated by government-mandated lockdowns in March 2020. In the context of Bangladeshi higher education, which includes 50 public and 108 private universities, Google Classroom emerged as a popular alternative to traditional LMS platforms due to its free availability and integration with the Google Suite for Education. The researcher identifies a gap in existing literature, noting that while Google Classroom's effectiveness has been studied globally, there is limited research specifically addressing student responses to its use as an LMS within the Bangladeshi university context.

To investigate this, the study employed a mixed-methods research design to capture both quantitative and qualitative data. The quantitative component involved a survey of 152 students from both public and private universities, selected using Cochran’s formula to ensure a representative sample. The survey utilized a 5-point Likert scale across three sections: demographic information, utilization of the platform, and perceived problems and opportunities. The quantitative instrument demonstrated high internal consistency, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.855. The qualitative component consisted of semi-structured interviews conducted via Google Meet with five students selected through convenience sampling. These interviews lasted between 40 and 50 minutes and were transcribed and analyzed using thematic coding. Data triangulation was used to enhance the reliability and validity of the findings.

The findings indicate that the majority of students responded positively to the use of Google Classroom. Descriptive statistics revealed a total mean score of 3.88 for student responses, indicating moderate to positive reactions. The highest-rated aspect of the platform was the usefulness of shared videos and study materials (M = 3.99), followed by its convenience and user-friendliness (M = 3.89). Students also found the platform easy to navigate (M = 3.88) and appreciated the ability to receive quick feedback and interact (M = 3.88). Qualitative interview data supported these results, with one participant noting that the platform allowed for voluntary participation and the adoption of 21st-century technologies. Another participant highlighted the emotional value of the platform, stating that it facilitated social interaction and helped alleviate psychological strain during the pandemic.

However, the study also identified significant challenges. Regarding concentration, a majority of respondents (73 agreed and 33 strongly agreed) found it difficult to maintain focus during Google Classroom sessions. Environmental and technical barriers were also prominent; 114 students reported lacking an appropriate learning environment, which included difficulties with internet access, lack of digital devices, and the absence of a dedicated study space. Furthermore, many students experienced a perceived lack of interactivity and effectiveness compared to face-to-face instruction. Interviewees echoed these concerns, citing a lack of motivation, difficulty in communicating with peers, and the necessity of a reliable internet connection as primary obstacles.

Despite these challenges, the study found significant possibilities for the platform's future use. Most students agreed that faculty members used Google Classroom to organize classes effectively and found it easy to access learning resources. Notably, a large majority of students (108 out of 152) expressed a preference for continuing to use Google Classroom as part of their educational experience alongside traditional instruction in the post-pandemic era. This suggests that students view the platform as a viable component of a blended learning model.

The author concludes that while Google Classroom served as a vital tool for sustaining academic activities during the pandemic, its implementation in Bangladeshi universities faces distinct hurdles. The transition to a post-pandemic hybrid model requires careful integration of digital tools with face-to-face teaching. To maximize the potential of Google Classroom, the study recommends that university authorities provide constant monitoring, timely feedback, and regular updates. Furthermore, the author suggests that institutions should establish clear policy guidelines, implement online surveillance measures, and encourage the active facilitation role of teachers. The study also suggests that future research should include the perspectives of faculty members and university administrators to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the platform's role in higher education.

title: Level of Social Presence, Social Interaction, Collaborative Learning, and Satisfaction in a BAMS Course Discord Server
abstract:
The integration of Discord as a communication and collaboration platform in online learning has gained attention due to its interactive features that support real-time engagement. This study examines students’ perceptions of social presence, social interaction, collaborative learning, and overall satisfaction in a Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) course Discord server. Using survey data, activity logs, open-ended responses, and the Student Evaluation of Teaching (SET) data for the BAMS course, the study evaluates how Discord fosters a sense of community, facilitates peer interaction, and enhances the learning experience.Findings indicate a high level of social presence, with 84% of students agreeing that Discord helped them feel connected with peers and faculty-in-charge (FIC). Real-time chat, voice discussions, and multimedia sharing contributed to a stronger sense of community compared to traditional Learning Management Systems (LMSs). In terms of social interaction, 71% of students reported frequent engagement with classmates, with text chat (95%), voice discussions (60%), and direct messaging (50%) being the most utilized features. Additionally, collaborative learning was supported, with 65% of students acknowledging that Discord facilitated knowledge sharing, teamwork, and problem-solving. Students appreciated its structured organization, which helped them locate discussions and announcements efficiently.
 
Overall, 64% of students expressed satisfaction with Discord as a learning platform, citing benefits, such as enhanced faculty communication (86%), improved peer interaction (69%), and a relaxed yet productive learning environment (62%). However, challenges included unfamiliarity with the platform, underutilization of certain channels, and reliance on peer engagement for meaningful discussions.The study concludes that Discord serves as an effective supplementary learning tool, enhancing online learning experiences through real-time interaction and collaboration. Recommendations include onboarding tutorials, structured engagement activities, and periodic check-ins to improve student participation further and maximize the platform’s potential.

The study titled "Level of Social Presence, Social Interaction, Collaborative Learning, and Satisfaction in a BAMS Course Discord Server" by Blancaflor P. Arada investigates the effectiveness of Discord as a communication and collaboration tool within an online learning environment. Specifically, the research focuses on a Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) course at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU).

The problem addressed by the study is the challenge of fostering a sense of community, engagement, and interaction in entirely online programs. While asynchronous discussion forums are traditional tools for this purpose, they often lack the dynamic, real-time engagement found in other communication technologies. The researcher sought to understand how a dedicated Discord server could address these needs by facilitating social presence, social interaction, and collaborative learning, and whether these factors ultimately lead to higher student satisfaction.

The study was conducted within the context of the BAMS program, which is delivered entirely online. To explore this, the researcher employed a descriptive research design using a mixed-methods approach. This involved collecting quantitative data through structured Likert-scale surveys and qualitative data through open-ended responses, Discord activity logs, and Student Evaluation of Teaching (SET) data. The participants included 238 BAMS students who actively used the Discord server. The theoretical framework for the study integrated the Community of Inquiry (CoI) model, Social Presence Theory, and Collaborative Learning Theory to examine the relationships between social presence, interaction, collaboration, and satisfaction.

The findings revealed several positive outcomes regarding the use of Discord. Regarding social presence, 84% of students agreed that the platform helped them feel connected to their peers and faculty-in-charge (FIC). Students noted that real-time chat, voice discussions, and multimedia sharing created a stronger sense of community than traditional Learning Management Systems (LMSs). In terms of social interaction, 71% of students reported frequent engagement with classmates, with text chat being the most utilized feature (95%), followed by voice discussions (60%) and direct messaging (50%).

Collaborative learning was also supported, with 65% of students acknowledging that Discord facilitated knowledge sharing and problem-solving. Students specifically appreciated the organized structure of the server, which allowed them to locate announcements and discussions efficiently. Overall, 64% of students expressed satisfaction with Discord as a learning platform. The primary drivers of this satisfaction were enhanced communication with the faculty (86%), improved peer interaction (69%), and the creation of a relaxed yet productive learning environment (62%).

However, the study also identified several challenges. Some students were unfamiliar with the Discord interface and preferred using other platforms like Facebook Messenger or MyPortal. There was also evidence of underutilization of certain channels, such as the "off-topic" and "study lounge" areas, which could have fostered more informal social bonds. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the platform was heavily dependent on peer engagement; when students did not participate, meaningful discussions were limited, and some students felt the platform did not fully foster a sense of camaraderie.

The study concludes that Discord serves as an effective supplementary tool for online learning. It successfully enhances social presence and facilitates real-time interaction and collaboration, which are vital for reducing isolation in online education. While it is a powerful tool for communication and academic support, its full potential is often constrained by varying levels of student participation and technical familiarity.

Based on these conclusions, the researcher offers several implications and recommendations for educators using Discord. To maximize the platform's potential, the study suggests implementing onboarding tutorials or brief orientation sessions to assist students unfamiliar with the technology. To encourage more robust social interaction, the author recommends hosting informal activities such as "Kamustahan" (wellness check-ins), student-led discussion sessions, and informal study or co-working sessions in voice channels. Finally, instructors are encouraged to actively promote non-academic channels, such as "off-topic" spaces, to help build a stronger, more cohesive learning community.

title: A Pragmatic Discursive Culture Model for Global Teams
abstract: Cultural aspects affect the success of organizations as well as teams enormously. There are many well known barriers and challenges, but also mitigation strategies. This paper presents a pragmatic culture model for analyzing cultural aspects to identify differences and similarities, as well as a usage process for global teams. The model combines aspects of national and regional culture as well as contextual culture and pragmatic attributes. The model improves the weaknesses of current national culture models by extending context and pragmatic factors. These factors are essential for its practical application, in particular to facilitate global teams. The model has been used and validated in different Higher Education courses between German and Indonesian students in the field of Business Information Systems. It has shown that potential barriers can be identified in advance, leading to successfully working teams in a global work environment.

In "A Pragmatic Discursive Culture Model for Global Teams," Jan Pawlowski and Sinung Suakanto address the challenges of distributed teams, such as communication breakdowns and sociocultural barriers. The authors argue that existing frameworks like Hofstede’s dimensions are often too abstract for daily professional use, necessitating a model that provides actionable guidance for collaboration.

Using Action Design Research (ADR), the researchers developed the Pragmatic Discursive Culture Model (PDCM). This model consists of a culture-aware group work process and three layers of culture: national/regional, context-specific, and pragmatic factors focusing on concrete behaviors like trust-building and communication formality. The model was validated through three case studies in Higher Education settings in Germany and Indonesia, involving 70 students and six educators working on collaborative software projects.

Findings indicated significant improvements in student competencies, specifically in communication, collaboration, cultural, and teamwork skills. The most substantial increases occurred in students' ability to identify cultural similarities and differences, understand how culture influences work, and work effectively in multicultural teams. Participants rated the PDCM highly for its usefulness and applicability. Qualitative feedback highlighted that the "discourse" aspect—using the model to discuss and reflect on cultural attributes—was highly productive for resolving communication issues. The authors conclude that integrating cultural reflection directly into the work process bridges the gap between abstract theory and practical teamwork.

The article "A Pragmatic Discursive Culture Model for Global Teams" by Jan Pawlowski and Sinung Suakanto addresses the significant challenges faced by global organizations and distributed teams. The authors identify that while cultural aspects are crucial to organizational success, existing models often fall short of providing practical, actionable guidance for real-world teamwork.

**Problem and Context**
The authors note that global teams face numerous barriers, including geographical and temporal distance, communication breakdowns, difficulties in establishing trust, and sociocultural distance. While various culture models exist—such as Hofstede’s six dimensions or the GLOBE study—these are often criticized for being too abstract, limited in scope, or lacking practical application. Many models provide theoretical insights but fail to offer specific guidance for daily work behaviors or how to navigate specific professional domains. Consequently, there is a need for a model that moves beyond mere abstraction to facilitate actual cultural competence and effective collaboration in global work environments.

**Method**
The researchers employed Action Design Research (ADR) to develop and validate their approach. This methodology involved three distinct phases: problem formulation, artefact creation and implementation, and evaluation. The resulting "Pragmatic Discursive Culture Model" (PDCM) consists of two interconnected components: the model itself, which contains specific cultural attributes, and a "culture-aware group work process" designed to build cultural competencies.

The PDCM integrates three layers of culture: national/regional culture (using attributes like power distance and individualism), context-specific culture (which can be adapted to specific domains like energy or education), and pragmatic factors (focusing on concrete work behaviors such as communication formality, directness, and trust-building). To validate the model, the authors conducted three case studies within Higher Education settings in Germany and Indonesia. These studies involved 70 students and six educators working on collaborative software projects. The evaluation utilized a mixed-methods approach, combining qualitative observations with quantitative surveys using Likert scales to measure competence development and model effectiveness.

**Findings**
The results of the case studies demonstrated significant improvements in student competencies. Self-assessments showed that all measured areas—communication, collaboration, cultural, and teamwork competencies—improved after the culture-awareness process. The most substantial increases were observed in students' understanding of how culture influences work life, their ability to identify cultural similarities and differences, and their ability to work effectively in multicultural teams.

Regarding the PDCM itself, participants evaluated the model highly across all criteria, including comprehensibility, usefulness, extensibility, applicability, team building, and cultural understanding. Qualitative feedback indicated that students found the model easy to use and were able to successfully extend it by adding context-specific attributes. The study also revealed that the "discourse" aspect—the process of discussing and reflecting on these cultural attributes—was highly productive. For example, when communication issues arose (such as students failing to reply to emails), the group was able to use the model to reflect on the underlying cultural reasons and create new, agreed-upon communication guidelines.

**Conclusions and Implications**
The authors conclude that the PDCM successfully bridges the gap between abstract cultural theory and practical teamwork. By treating culture models as a starting point for discourse rather than a static set of rules, the model encourages continuous learning and adaptation. The research demonstrates that integrating cultural reflection directly into the project work process—rather than treating it as a separate, one-time training—is essential for managing the complexities of global collaboration.

The implications of this research are twofold. Theoretically, the study contributes to the field by proposing a multi-layered model that combines geographic, context-specific, and pragmatic dimensions, thereby avoiding the speculative reasoning often found in purely national culture models. Practically, the PDCM provides a "hands-on" tool for managers and educators. It offers a structured way to facilitate discussions about work habits, communication styles, and conflict resolution. The authors suggest that this model is particularly valuable in international learning and training contexts, such as Collaborative Online International Learning (COIL) programs, to help participants develop the necessary competencies for a globalized workforce. Future research is intended to test the model in different professional sectors and across a wider variety of countries.

title: Instructional Supervision Needs of Private Higher Education Institutions: Towards a Distinct Distance Learning Management Framework
abstract: This study examined the instructional supervision needs of private higher education institutions engaged in online distance learning to develop a unique framework for managing online distance learning effectively. Employing a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, quantitative data were collected from 301 teachers via surveys, followed by qualitative insights from five purposively selected school leaders through focus group discussion. Thematic analysis of qualitative data involved coding, theme development, and cross-referencing with existing literature to identify key supervisory practices. Results indicated that teachers demonstrated strong competencies in management, institutional, social, and communication skills, while pedagogical, design, and content skills were adequate. Technological skills, however, were the weakest and required focused improvement. In response, school leaders implemented tailored instructional supervision strategies addressing these needs. Based on these findings, the study proposes a distinct distance learning management framework comprising initiatives across six categories: pedagogical, technological, management and institutional, social and communication, design, and content. This framework provides a valuable tool for school leaders to effectively support and manage online teaching, particularly during crises or unexpected disruptions.

Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, the researcher assessed the online teaching competencies of 301 teachers and conducted focus group discussions with five school leaders.

The findings indicate that teachers possess a high overall proficiency in online teaching, with a grand mean of 3.26. Their strongest competencies are social and communication skills and management and institutional skills, both rated as "superior." However, competencies in pedagogical, content, design, and technological skills were rated as "satisfactory," with technological skills identified as the weakest area. Qualitative data revealed that school leaders address these competencies through capacity building for interactive strategies, adjusting learning plans, developing interactive modules, providing LMS training, and implementing policies for attendance and integrity. Social and communication practices prioritize wellness through mental health breaks and regular student dialogue.

The study proposes the Distinct Distance Learning Management Framework, organized into six categories: pedagogical, technological, management and institutional, social and communication, design, and content. The researcher recommends that institutions conduct regular assessments to develop individualized intervention plans, promote collaborative efforts like peer mentoring, and provide comprehensive training for school leaders to execute these new supervisory initiatives.
