two:
The study titled "Instructional Supervision Needs of Private Higher Education Institutions: Towards a Distinct Distance Learning Management Framework" by Cherry D. Dizon addresses the critical need for effective instructional supervision in private higher education institutions (HEIs) during shifts to online distance learning. The research was prompted by the global disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, natural disasters, and environmental hazards, which forced institutions to adopt remote learning to maintain educational continuity. While distance learning is an effective contingency strategy, the rapid transition exposed significant gaps in teacher preparedness, technological proficiency, and the ability of school leaders to supervise instruction in virtual environments.

The primary objective of the study was to propose a distinct distance learning management framework to assist school leaders in providing better support and guidance to teachers delivering online instruction. Specifically, the study aimed to identify teachers' instructional supervision needs by assessing their online teaching competencies, describe the supervision practices implemented by school leaders to address these needs, and propose a management framework.

To achieve these objectives, the researcher employed a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design. In the first phase, quantitative data were collected from 301 teachers at private HEIs using a survey instrument adapted from Albrahim (2020) to assess six domains: pedagogical, content knowledge, instructional design, technological, management and institutional, and social and communication skills. In the second phase, qualitative insights were gathered through focus group discussions with five purposively selected school leaders. The qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis, involving coding, theme development, and cross-referencing with existing literature to ensure data saturation and contextual accuracy.

The findings revealed that teachers demonstrated a high overall proficiency in online teaching, with a grand mean of 3.26. Their greatest strengths were in social and communication skills (3.41) and management and institutional skills (3.27), both of which were rated as "superior." However, competencies in pedagogical, content, design, and technological skills were rated as "satisfactory." Notably, technological skills were identified as the weakest area, with the lowest mean of 3.18.

Qualitative data from school leaders provided deeper insight into the supervision practices implemented to address these competencies. Regarding pedagogical skills, leaders focused on capacity building for interactive teaching strategies, the use of alternative assessment modes (such as performance-based tasks to prevent academic dishonesty), streamlining assessment tasks to manage student workload, implementing compressed schedules for laboratory classes, and providing extensive training for students to navigate the new modality. In terms of content skills, leaders emphasized the adjustability of learning plans to suit the virtual environment. For design skills, the focus was on promoting interactive learning modules. Technological support included training on Learning Management Systems (LMS) and providing assistance for internet access and digital devices. Management and institutional practices involved implementing academic policies regarding attendance and integrity, alongside online supervision of instruction through virtual observations. Finally, social and communication practices centered on prioritizing wellness through mental health breaks and regular dialogue with students.

Based on these findings, the study proposes the Distinct Distance Learning Management Framework. This framework is symbolized by a Wi-Fi image and is organized into six categories: pedagogical, technological, management and institutional, social and communication, design, and content. The framework is structured such that the pedagogical category contains the widest curve, reflecting the highest number of supervision initiatives, while the content category is the narrowest, as it serves as a preparatory phase. A unique feature of this framework is the inclusion of wellness and mental health initiatives, developed in response to the unprecedented challenges of the global health crisis.

The study concludes that while teachers in private HEIs possess superior online teaching competencies, they require specialized skills distinct from traditional classroom instruction, particularly in technological, design, and pedagogical areas. School leaders have proactively adapted their supervisory roles to meet these needs, but a formalized, distinct framework is necessary to ensure instructional quality and educational continuity during future disruptions.

The implications of this research suggest that instructional supervision must evolve beyond mere oversight to become a supportive coaching process tailored to digital environments. The researcher recommends that institutions conduct regular assessments of teachers' online competencies to develop individualized intervention plans. Furthermore, the study advocates for collaborative efforts among school leaders, teachers, and students, including peer mentoring and the co-design of learning materials. Finally, it is recommended that school leaders receive comprehensive training to execute these new supervisory initiatives with confidence and that the proposed framework be adopted and validated through further experimental research.

title: Evaluating the Implementation of Oral Examination (OREX) as an Alternative Assessment Method in Higher Learning Institutions
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated rapid shifts in higher education assessment practice, leading institutions like The Open University of Tanzania (OUT) to adopt Online Remote Oral Examinations (OREX) as an alternative evaluation method (Iglesias-Pradas et al., 2021). This study examines the implementation of OREX during the 2019/2020 academic year, where examiners and students engaged in real-time, interactive oral assessments via digital platforms. This modality showed potential for upholding academic integrity while adapting to remote learning constraints (Smith & Lee, 2020). Focusing on OUT’s experience, the paper evaluates OREX’s effectiveness in maintaining academic standards, credibility, and reliability, particularly in mitigating risks of academic dishonesty a key concern in online assessments (Nguyen et al., 2022). The study details the preparatory measures undertaken, including examiner and student training, technical setup, and procedural adjustments to ensure seamless execution. Findings indicate that despite initial challenges such as internet instability and digital literacy gaps (UNESCO, 2020), OREX provided a viable, flexible, and competency-based assessment approach, aligning with global trends in diversified evaluation methods (MoEST, 2021). The research suggests that OREX, initially a pandemic contingency, holds potential for long-term integration into higher education assessment frameworks. By combining interactive rigor with logistical adaptability, OREX could expand the toolkit for evaluating student learning outcomes beyond traditional written exams. This study contributes to the growing discourse on sustainable remote assessment models in African distance learning contexts, offering empirical insights for policymakers and educators.
half:
In the article "Evaluating the Implementation of Oral Examination (OREX) as an Alternative Assessment Method in Higher Learning Institutions," Raphael Tumaini O’maitarya examines the transition from traditional examinations to Online Remote Oral Examinations (OREX) at the Open University of Tanzania (OUT) during the 2019/2020 academic year. Driven by COVID-19 disruptions, the study utilizes Constructive Alignment Theory and the Task-Technology Fit framework to assess the effectiveness of OREX in an African distance-learning context. Through qualitative document analysis of institutional records, the research evaluates the planning, implementation, and evaluation stages of the process.

The findings show that OREX implementation was highly structured and operationally successful. Preparatory training via Zoom achieved staff participation rates exceeding 91%. The examination utilized a role-based system and a dual-authentication process involving OREX Visa Cards and national identity documents. Results indicate that 86% of the 1,240 sessions were conducted smoothly, with only 4% requiring rescheduling due to major disruptions and 10% experiencing minor technical issues. This performance exceeded regional comparators in Kenya and Uganda. Standardized digital rubrics and pre-uploaded model answers helped maintain validity and reliability.

However, challenges included digital inequity, as 14% of sessions were impacted by unstable internet or lack of devices. Other risks included "Zoom fatigue" and logistical hurdles regarding documentation. The study concludes OREX is a viable, flexible method for evaluating higher-order cognitive skills. Recommendations include developing digital assessment policies, investing in infrastructure to bridge the digital divide, and creating low-bandwidth alternatives to ensure equity.

The study addresses the disruption of conventional assessments caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, specifically focusing on the implementation and effectiveness of OREX within African distance-learning contexts. The research considers how this model addresses infrastructure limitations, academic integrity, equitable access, and long-term sustainability.

The study is grounded in Constructive Alignment Theory and the Task-Technology Fit (TTF) framework. Using a qualitative document analysis approach, the researcher analyzed institutional records, including OREX spreadsheets, attendance records, meeting minutes, and evaluation reports. Identity verification was managed through a dual-authentication system involving the OREX Visa Card and national identity documents.

However, challenges were identified, including digital inequity. Approximately 14% of sessions were impacted by unstable internet or lack of devices, particularly in rural areas. The dual-authentication process also presented logistical hurdles for students lacking specific documentation. Other noted risks included "Zoom fatigue" and the necessity for continuous ICT infrastructure investment.

The study concludes that OREX is a viable, flexible, and pedagogically valuable method that successfully maintained academic continuity. It demonstrates that when technology aligns with pedagogical tasks, it can effectively evaluate higher-order cognitive skills. The article "Evaluating the Implementation of Oral Examination (OREX) as an Alternative Assessment Method in Higher Learning Institutions" by Raphael Tumaini O’maitarya examines the transition from traditional examination models to Online Remote Oral Examinations (OREX) at the Open University of Tanzania (OUT) during the 2019/2020 academic year.

The problem addressed is the unprecedented disruption of conventional summative assessments caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. While many institutions globally shifted to remote modalities, there was a significant research gap regarding the implementation and effectiveness of OREX within African distance-learning contexts. Specifically, the study highlights concerns regarding how such a model addresses infrastructure limitations, academic integrity, equitable access, and long-term sustainability in resource-constrained environments like Tanzania.

The context of the study is the Open University of Tanzania, a flagship distance-learning institution serving approximately 50,000 students across diverse geographic and socioeconomic landscapes. The research is grounded in Constructive Alignment Theory, which posits that assessment tasks must align with intended learning outcomes, and the Task-Technology Fit (TTF) framework, which emphasizes the alignment between technological capabilities and pedagogical requirements.

To investigate this, the researcher employed a qualitative document analysis approach. Data were collected over a three-month period from various institutional records at OUT headquarters, including OREX information spreadsheets, attendance records for staff and student training, official meeting minutes, evaluation reports, and internal assessment protocols. A purposive sampling strategy was used to select documents from the planning, implementation, and evaluation stages of the OREX process. The analysis followed a five-step model involving skimming, reading, interpreting, thematic coding, and synthesis.

The findings reveal that the implementation of OREX at OUT was highly structured and operationally successful. Preparatory measures included three major online training sessions via Zoom, which saw exceptionally high academic staff participation rates, exceeding 91%. The examination process utilized a role-based system involving a Chief Examiner, a Second Examiner, and an Examination Observer to ensure rigor. Identity verification was maintained through a dual-authentication system involving the OREX Visa Card and national identity documents.

In terms of outcomes, 86% of the 1,240 examination sessions were conducted smoothly without major irregularities. Only 4% of sessions faced major disruptions requiring rescheduling, and 10% experienced minor technical issues such as login delays. This performance was notably higher than regional comparators in Kenya and Uganda, where disruption rates were significantly higher. The study found that the use of standardized digital rubrics and pre-uploaded model answers helped maintain assessment validity and reliability, reducing grading subjectivity.

However, several challenges were identified. Digital inequity remains a significant barrier, as approximately 14% of sessions were impacted by unstable internet connections or lack of appropriate devices, particularly for students in rural areas. Furthermore, the dual-authentication process presented logistical hurdles for students lacking specific documentation. The study also noted potential risks regarding "Zoom fatigue" and the need for continuous investment in ICT infrastructure to ensure long-term viability.

The study concludes that OREX is a viable, flexible, and pedagogically valuable assessment method that successfully maintained academic continuity during the pandemic. It demonstrated that when technology is well-aligned with pedagogical tasks—as seen through the use of Zoom, digital rubrics, and structured examiner roles—it can effectively evaluate higher-order cognitive skills like critical thinking and problem-solving. While successful as an emergency measure, the findings suggest OREX has the potential to be integrated into long-term, sustainable assessment frameworks in African higher education.

Based on these findings, the author offers several implications and recommendations for policymakers and educators. To transition OREX from a contingency measure to a permanent tool, institutions should develop comprehensive digital assessment policies that address ethical standards and contingency planning. There is a critical need for continued investment in digital infrastructure, particularly in rural areas, to bridge the digital divide. The study recommends strengthening capacity building through ongoing digital literacy training for both staff and students. Additionally, the author suggests that institutions should develop inclusive strategies, such as low-bandwidth alternatives or flexible scheduling, to ensure equity for marginalized learners. Finally, the study advocates for the integration of OREX with existing Learning Management Systems (LMS) and continued research into the long-term learning outcomes and stakeholder perceptions of digital oral assessments.

title: Flexible Learning for Dance Instruction in Higher Education Institutions at the National Capital Region, Philippines
abstract: This study addressed the lack of research on the use of flexible learning in dance in the Philippines. It investigated the experiences of dance teachers in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) in the National Capital Region (NCR) during the shift to flexible learning amid the pandemic, specifically from academic years 2020 to 2022. The study examined the different flexible learning approaches, methods and techniques used, and assessed their effectiveness in ensuring sustained effective delivery of dance instruction. It also examined the challenges encountered in using flexible learning. Questionnaires and in-depth interviews were used to collect data which were analyzed using descriptive analysis. Findings revealed that flexible learning, consisting of synchronous and asynchronous delivery modes, was the only suitable method during the Covid-19 pandemic. However, its adoption caused a lot of pressures and challenges among teachers, particularly in preparing lessons and teaching materials, including the lack of familiarity with using the appropriate technologies. Recommended steps to improve the use of flexible learning were gathered to provide readiness to dance teachers and students during times of restricted activities like the pandemic.
half:
This study investigated the implementation of flexible learning for dance instruction in Higher Education Institutions within the National Capital Region of the Philippines from 2020 to 2022. Using a mixed-methods approach, researchers collected data from 11 dance teachers across four institutions: the University of the Philippines Diliman, De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde, Guang Ming College, and the Asian Institute of Maritime Studies.

Findings indicated a shift from teacher-centered to student-centered learning, utilizing both synchronous and asynchronous modes. Learning Management Systems and communication tools like Zoom and Facebook Messenger were essential for content delivery. Significant challenges included technical issues like unstable internet and audio-visual lag, as well as pedagogical difficulties regarding the loss of tactile corrections and the difficulty of assessing musicality and artistic expression through a screen. Teachers also reported increased workloads and a lack of formal training in digital competencies.

Despite these hurdles, innovative strategies such as recorded lectures and video-based assessments proved effective, with most respondents successfully achieving course objectives. The study concludes that while flexible learning is a successful adaptation, the digital format cannot fully replace the tactile nature of traditional instruction. Researchers recommend that institutions provide specialized training in digital competencies and high-quality equipment. They also suggest developing specialized learning management systems designed specifically for the unique pedagogical requirements of dance instruction.
one:
This study investigated the implementation of flexible learning for dance instruction in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) within the National Capital Region of the Philippines from 2020 to 2022. The research addressed the challenges of transitioning performance-based, embodied disciplines from traditional studio settings to digital formats, specifically focusing on the difficulty of replicating physical presence, tactile feedback, and the "learn from the master" model through a screen.

Using a mixed-methods approach, the researchers collected data from 11 dance teachers across four HEIs: the University of the Philippines Diliman, De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde, Guang Ming College, and the Asian Institute of Maritime Studies. Data collection included a 5-point Likert scale questionnaire and semi-structured interviews conducted via Zoom, email, and Facebook Messenger. Analysis involved descriptive statistics and thematic analysis.

The findings showed that dance teachers shifted from teacher-centered to student-centered learning. Instructional delivery utilized a combination of synchronous and asynchronous modes. Synchronous sessions provided real-time interaction, while asynchronous activities allowed students to learn at their own pace. Learning Management Systems (LMS) like BigSky, Google Classroom, and Microsoft Teams, alongside communication tools like Zoom and Facebook Messenger, were essential for content delivery.

Several significant challenges were identified. Technical issues, such as unstable internet and audio-visual lag, were pervasive. Pedagogically, teachers struggled with the loss of tactile corrections and the difficulty of assessing musicality and authentic artistic expression through a two-dimensional screen. Additionally, teachers noted issues with student discipline and motivation, such as students turning off cameras, and reported feeling unprepared due to a lack of formal training in digital competencies and increased workloads.

Despite these hurdles, innovative strategies proved effective. Teachers successfully used uploaded course materials, online resource links, and recorded lectures. Video-based assessment emerged as a progressive tool, allowing students to observe their own movements and facilitate self-correction. Most respondents indicated they successfully achieved course objectives through these flexible methods.

The study concludes that while the transition was difficult due to the physical limitations of the medium and a lack of digital pedagogy experience, it was a successful and necessary adaptation. However, the digital format cannot fully replace the three-dimensional and tactile nature of traditional instruction. The researchers recommend that HEIs provide specialized training in digital competencies and support the acquisition of high-quality equipment like webcams and microphones. They also suggest that future research and institutional collaboration with IT experts should focus on developing specialized learning management systems designed specifically for the unique pedagogical requirements of dance instruction.
two:
This study investigated the implementation of flexible learning for dance instruction in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) within the National Capital Region (NCR) of the Philippines during the COVID-19 pandemic, specifically covering the academic years 2020 to 2022. The research addressed a significant gap in existing literature regarding how performance-based, embodied disciplines like dance transition from traditional studio-based settings to digital formats.

The problem centered on the inherent difficulty of replicating the energy, physical presence, and tactile feedback of a dance studio through a screen. Dance instruction traditionally relies on the "learn from the master" model, involving close observation, imitation, and physical corrections. The pandemic necessitated a shift to flexible learning—a pedagogical approach allowing for flexibility in time, place, and audience—which presented unique challenges for dance educators attempting to maintain educational standards and student engagement in a virtual environment.

To investigate this phenomenon, the researchers employed a mixed-methods approach, utilizing both qualitative and quantitative data. The study used purposeful sampling to select 11 dance teachers from four HEIs in the NCR: the University of the Philippines Diliman, De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde, Guang Ming College, and the Asian Institute of Maritime Studies. Data were collected through a researcher-designed questionnaire featuring a 5-point Likert scale and open-ended questions, supplemented by in-depth, semi-structured interviews conducted via Zoom, email, and Facebook Messenger. The analysis involved descriptive statistics for survey data and thematic analysis for interview transcripts.

The findings revealed that dance teachers shifted from teacher-centered to student-centered learning to better accommodate the unique needs and constraints of their students. Instructional delivery primarily consisted of a combination of synchronous (real-time) and asynchronous (delayed-time) modes. While synchronous sessions were valued for real-time interaction and monitoring, many teachers found it necessary to combine them with asynchronous activities to allow students to learn at their own pace. Learning Management Systems (LMS) such as BigSky, Google Classroom, and Microsoft Teams, along with communication tools like Zoom and Facebook Messenger, were essential for content delivery.

The study identified several significant challenges encountered by teachers. Technical difficulties, such as unstable internet connectivity and audio-visual lag, were pervasive. Pedagogically, teachers struggled with the loss of physical feedback, as they could no longer provide the tactile corrections essential to dance training. There were also difficulties in assessing students' musicality and authentic artistic expression through a two-dimensional screen. Furthermore, teachers faced issues regarding student discipline and motivation, noting that many students turned off their cameras, which hindered visual assessment. Finally, many educators reported feeling unprepared due to a lack of formal training in digital competencies and the increased workload required to prepare electronic teaching materials.

Despite these hurdles, the study found that many innovative strategies were effective. Uploading course materials, providing links to online resources, and using recorded lectures were highly rated by teachers. Recorded lectures, in particular, allowed students to review movements at their own pace. Video-based assessment emerged as a progressive tool, as it allowed students to observe their own bodies in motion and facilitated self-correction. Most respondents indicated that they successfully achieved their course objectives through these flexible learning methods, though they acknowledged the need for further refinement.

In conclusion, the study concludes that while the transition to flexible learning was difficult due to the lack of experience in digital pedagogy and the physical limitations of the medium, it was a successful and necessary adaptation. Dance teachers demonstrated resilience by adopting student-centered approaches and utilizing various digital tools to bridge the gap created by social distancing. However, the digital format cannot fully replace the physical, three-dimensional, and tactile nature of traditional dance instruction.

The implications of this research suggest a need for systemic support to sustain and improve online dance education. The authors recommend that HEIs provide dance teachers with specialized training in digital competencies and the use of appropriate technological tools. There is a call for institutions to support the acquisition of high-quality equipment, such as webcams, microphones, and lighting, to enhance the quality of instruction. Furthermore, the researchers suggest that future research and institutional collaboration with IT experts should focus on developing specialized learning management systems specifically designed to meet the unique pedagogical requirements of dance instruction.

title: Validity Testing of the Community of Inquiry (CoI) Survey as a Tool for Student Evaluation of Teaching and Learning in a Fully Online Philippine University
abstract: A Student Evaluation of Teaching (SET) is essential in any system of education. Not only does it provide vital information and feedback to enhance student learning outcomes, and thus, functioning as quality control and tool for teaching improvement (Holi Ali & Al Ajmi, 2013; Wright & Jenkins-Guarnieri, 2012), but it also serves as a platform for sharing of students’ experiences in their courses (Golding & Adam, 2016) while providing empirical evidence for faculty tenure and promotion. This study examined the validity of the Community of Inquiry (COI) Survey as a SET in a fully online university in the Philippines. A questionnaire incorporating the COI Survey was pilot tested among all students in the university who were enrolled in the first term of AY 2018-2019. The pilot testing and validation methods resulted in a four-factor, 31-item COI Survey that has mediocre to acceptable goodness of fit.
half:
In the study "Validity Testing of the Community of Inquiry (CoI) Survey as a Tool for Student Evaluation of Teaching and Learning in a Fully Online Philippine University," Roja Rivera and Rita Ramos investigate whether the CoI Survey is a suitable Student Evaluation of Teaching (SET) instrument for a fully online university. The researchers note that tools designed for face-to-face instruction often fail to capture the unique pedagogical nuances of online learning, where the instructor's role shifts toward facilitation.

Grounded in the CoI framework—which emphasizes cognitive, social, and teaching presence—the researchers conducted a pilot test with 714 students. Using Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), the study found that the original three-factor model did not fit the specific university context. The study titled "Validity Testing of the Community of Inquiry (CoI) Survey as a Tool for Student Evaluation of Teaching and Learning in a Fully Online Philippine University" by Roja Rivera and Rita Ramos investigates the suitability of the Community of Inquiry (CoI) Survey for use as a Student Evaluation of Teaching (SET) instrument within a specific educational context.

The researchers identify a significant problem in higher education: many university-developed SET instruments lack formal theoretical and psychometric rigor. Furthermore, conventional evaluation tools designed for face-to-face instruction often fail to capture the unique pedagogical, communicative, and structural nuances of online learning. In a fully online, open and distance learning (ODL) environment, the role of the instructor shifts toward facilitation and co-learning, and communication is often asynchronous and primarily written. Therefore, ODL institutions require evaluation tools that are psychometrically sound and specifically aligned with the constructivist nature of online instruction.

The study is grounded in the Community of Inquiry (CoI) theoretical framework, which posits that meaningful learning in online environments results from the synergy of three interrelated "presences": cognitive presence (the process of inquiry and learning), social presence (the ability to communicate and build interpersonal relationships), and teaching presence (the design and facilitation of the learning experience).

To address the research problem, the authors aimed to determine the applicability of the CoI Survey as a SET tool in a fully online Philippine university. The methodology involved a pilot test of a questionnaire incorporating the COI Survey among students enrolled in the first term of AY 2018-2019. The researchers collected 883 responses, which were screened down to 714 valid responses for analysis. The study employed Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) using Principal Axis Factoring and Oblimin rotation to determine underlying factors, and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) to test model goodness of fit. The researchers conducted three rounds of CFA to compare the original three-factor model against a four-factor model and a model with specific items removed.

The findings revealed that the original three-factor model of the COI Survey did not fit the specific context of the university. However, the EFA identified a four-factor structure: Cognitive Presence, Teaching Presence, Social Presence, and a newly emerged fourth factor, Design and Organization. The researchers noted that items 14, 15, and 28 exhibited cross-loading issues, meaning they did not clearly measure a single factor. Specifically, items related to getting to know participants and the value of online discussions loaded onto both Social Presence and Teaching Presence, suggesting these items might be influenced by the instructor's course design rather than purely by student social interaction. After removing these three problematic items, the four-factor model yielded satisfactory fit measures (CFI, TLI, and SRMR), although the RMSEA indicated a marginal fit. The four factors accounted for 75.5% of the overall variance, and the scale demonstrated high internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha coefficients ranging from 0.925 to 0.980.

The researchers conclude that a modified, 31-item version of the COI Survey—consisting of the four factors of Cognitive Presence, Teaching Presence, Social Presence, and Design and Organization—is an acceptable tool for evaluating teaching effectiveness at the university. However, they caution that the survey is most valid when applied to courses that actually function as a "true" community of inquiry. Because the university's general mode of instruction is "guided independent study" (where students work largely through pre-developed modules), some courses may lack the collaborative and reflective depth required for the COI framework to be a fair assessment tool.

The implications of this study are twofold. For institutions, it suggests that online universities should review their curriculum and faculty development programs to ensure they are fostering the three COI presences if they intend to use the survey for evaluation. For researchers, the study highlights the importance of considering the "cultural contingency" and specific instructional modes of an institution when validating international frameworks. The authors suggest that future research should explore the impact of the COI framework on different disciplines, conduct mixed-method studies to triangulate quantitative data with student and faculty perceptions, and investigate the effectiveness of the survey as a tool for faculty self-reflection.

title: Bridging the Gap: The Institutionalization of Reflective Practices in ODL Teacher Education in Tanzania
abstract: This study examines how reflective practices (RPs) are integrated within open and distance learning (ODL) pre-service teacher education in Tanzania, focusing on the Institute of Adult Education (IAE) and the Open University of Tanzania (OUT). Despite strong policy endorsement of learner-centered pedagogy, little empirical evidence exists on how reflection is enacted in ODL environments characterized by asynchronous interaction, limited supervision, and uneven digital access. Using a concurrent mixed-methods design, data were collected from second-year student teachers (n = 120) and institutional tutors (n = 8) through surveys, interviews, virtual observations, and curriculum analysis. Findings reveal that while RPs such as e-portfolios, peer feedback, journaling, and action research are formally present, their implementation is structurally fragmented and weakly institutionalized. Tutor commitment and student teachers’ engagement are evident; however, limited digital pedagogical training, inconsistent assessment frameworks, and inadequate institutional guidance constrain reflective depth, often reducing reflection to task completion rather than professional inquiry. The study argues that the challenge in Tanzanian ODL teacher education is not the absence of reflective practices but their under-institutionalization within curriculum, supervision, and assessment systems. These findings provide context-sensitive evidence for strengthening policy operationalization, tutor capacity, and structured reflective mechanisms in distance-based teacher preparation programs.

The study "Bridging the Gap: The Institutionalization of Reflective Practices in ODL Teacher Education in Tanzania" investigates the integration of reflective practices (RPs) within open and distance learning (ODL) at the Institute of Adult Education and the Open University of Tanzania. The research addresses a policy-practice paradox where national learner-centered policies are undermined by structural fragmentation, asynchronous interaction, and uneven digital access, which risks reducing transformative reflection to superficial, task-oriented exercises.

Using a mixed-methods design, the study collected data from 128 participants, including student teachers and tutors, through interviews, surveys, observations, and documentary reviews. Findings reveal that RPs are weakly institutionalized. While activities like e-portfolios and journaling are present, their integration is implicit and fragmented, lacking explicit policy guidelines, structured digital mentorship, and standardized assessment frameworks.

Tutors recognize the value of RPs but face hurdles such as inadequate training in digital pedagogy, which limits their ability to facilitate systematic reflection. Consequently, support often focuses on assignment feedback rather than transformative cycles. While 78.4% of students report active participation, many treat reflection as a task-oriented requirement for grades rather than authentic professional inquiry. The study concludes that RPs are under-institutionalized due to misalignments between curriculum, facilitation, and assessment. Recommendations include providing explicit guidelines, enhancing tutor training in digital pedagogy, standardizing reflective structures, and legitimizing low-tech alternatives to accommodate the digital divide.

The study "Bridging the Gap: The Institutionalization of Reflective Practices in ODL Teacher Education in Tanzania" investigates the integration of reflective practices (RPs) within open and distance learning (ODL) pre-service teacher education. The research focuses on two major Tanzanian institutions: the Institute of Adult Education (IAE) and the Open University of Tanzania (OUT).

The problem addressed by the author is a "policy-practice paradox." While Tanzanian national policies emphasize learner-centered and reflective pedagogy, the actual implementation within ODL environments is structurally fragmented. ODL settings present unique challenges, such as asynchronous interaction, limited direct supervision, and uneven digital access. These factors risk reducing deep, transformative reflection into superficial, "tick-box" exercises or mere task completion. There is a significant gap in empirical evidence regarding how reflective pedagogy survives the transition to distance modes in Global South contexts characterized by these specific digital and institutional constraints.

The context of the study is the rapid expansion of ODL in Tanzania as a primary method to address teacher shortages. The research is situated within the tension between the global push for digital teacher preparation and the local realities of technological infrastructure and tutor capacity. The study utilizes a concurrent mixed-methods design, adopting a pragmatic paradigm. Data were collected from 128 participants, including 120 second-year student teachers and 8 institutional tutors. The methodology employed four complementary data collection tools: documentary reviews of curricula, virtual semi-structured interviews, online surveys, and virtual classroom observations. The analysis was guided by Schön’s (1983) cyclical reflective practice framework, focusing on reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action.

The findings are categorized into three main areas: curriculum integration, tutor perceptions, and student engagement. Regarding the curriculum, the study found that RPs are present but weakly institutionalized. Activities such as e-portfolios, reflective journaling, action research, and peer feedback are included in various modules, but their integration is often implicit and fragmented. There is a lack of explicit policy guidelines, structured digital mentorship, and standardized assessment frameworks for reflection.

Tutor perceptions revealed that while instructors universally recognize the value of RPs for professional growth and adaptability, they face significant hurdles. Tutors expressed concerns regarding the feasibility of implementing deep reflection in virtual settings and noted that their ability to facilitate systematic reflection is limited by inadequate training in digital pedagogy. Consequently, tutor support often focuses on providing feedback on assignments rather than guiding students through iterative, transformative reflective cycles.

Student engagement was found to be high, with 78.4% of students reporting active participation in reflective activities. Students showed strong engagement with e-portfolios, collaborative teaching, and journaling. However, the depth of this engagement is a concern; qualitative data suggests that many students approach reflection as a task-oriented requirement for grades rather than a tool for authentic professional inquiry. There is also a noted tension between student autonomy and a heavy reliance on tutor validation.

The study concludes that while foundational conditions for reflective practice exist in Tanzanian ODL teacher education, the practice is under-institutionalized. The effectiveness of RPs is currently limited by a misalignment between curriculum design, tutor facilitation, assessment practices, and institutional support. Reflection is often treated as an ad hoc activity rather than a sustained mechanism for professional learning. The research highlights that the challenge is not a lack of reflective tools, but rather the lack of a coherent, structured system to support them.

The implications of these findings suggest a need for systemic reform in how ODL teacher education is structured in Tanzania. The author recommends several actions to bridge the gap. First, national and institutional policies should be operationalized to provide explicit, actionable guidelines for embedding RPs into curricula, including specific reflective tools and mentorship arrangements. Second, there is a critical need to enhance tutor professional capacity through targeted training in digital pedagogy and reflective facilitation. Third, the study suggests standardizing reflective structures, such as using structured e-portfolio templates and aligned assessment rubrics, to ensure consistency and transparency. Finally, the author recommends improving technological and pedagogical support by legitimizing low-tech reflective alternatives (like offline journals) to accommodate students facing digital divides, thereby fostering a more inclusive and robust reflective institutional culture.

title: Challenges and Opportunities in an Immersive and Gamified ODeL Course for Undergraduate Students
abstract: This study examined how a quest-based and immersive learning design shaped students’ experiences in an open and distance e-learning course. The intervention transformed one unit of an undergraduate instructional design course into a three-level Quest Mode that combined narrative framing, structured mechanics, and a Metaversal Quest built in FrameVR. Using a qualitative design that analyzed student reflection papers and a focus group discussion, the study explored how learners interpreted the opportunities and constraints of the quest-based environment. Participants reported that Quest Mode support engagement by organising learning into smaller scaffolded segments and by offering playful opportunities for exploration and paced progression. Several participants described reduced cognitive overload and sustained interest. Some learners also reported moments of social presence and peer collaboration within the immersive spaces. At the same time, technical instability, motion sickness, and interface complexity constrained participation for some students, and several indicated that reproducing regular course materials inside the metaverse limited the environment’s pedagogical affordances. These findings suggest conditions under which quest-based and metaversal elements can support persistence in ODeL, while highlighting the need to align mechanics, aesthetics, and content to the medium rather than rely on novelty alone.

Lexter Mangubat’s study, "Challenges and Opportunities in an Immersive and Gamified ODeL Course for Undergraduate Students," investigates how quest-based and immersive learning designs influence student experiences in open and distance e-learning (ODeL) environments. The research addresses the challenge of sustaining motivation and engagement in ODeL settings, where students often face isolation and cognitive overload. The study was conducted during the 2024–2025 academic year in an undergraduate instructional design course in Southeast Asia. The researcher implemented a "Quest Mode" consisting of three levels: narrative framing with an NPC, a Metaversal Quest in FrameVR using an escape-room style, and an "elixir" mechanic for rewards. Data were collected through 38 student reflection papers and one focus group discussion.

Findings revealed that students viewed the quest-based approach as approachable and motivating. Narrative cues and segmented content helped reduce the perceived burden of heavy readings, while the game-like interface served as a significant entry point for engagement. The metaverse environment facilitated spontaneous social connection and peer collaboration through informal chatting. However, challenges included technical instability, interface complexity, and physical discomfort like motion sickness. Students noted that virtual environments often merely replicated text-heavy materials rather than integrating content into the immersive experience. The study concludes that these elements can support persistence by redistributing cognitive load, provided there is meaningful integration of pedagogy with the medium.

The study titled "Challenges and Opportunities in an Immersive and Gamified ODeL Course for Undergraduate Students" by Lexter Mangubat investigates how quest-based and immersive learning designs influence student experiences within an open and distance e-learning (ODeL) environment.

The problem addressed is the persistent challenge of sustaining student motivation and engagement in ODeL settings. Because ODeL students often work independently, they face risks of isolation, heavy reading loads, and cognitive overload. While gamification and immersive technologies like the metaverse offer potential solutions to increase presence and interaction, there is a significant research gap regarding how quest-structured pathways and metaversal tasks interact within a full course sequence to influence pacing, social presence, and cognitive load.

The context of the study is an undergraduate instructional design course at an ODeL institution in Southeast Asia during the 2024–2025 academic year. The researcher implemented a "Quest Mode" for a single unit of the course, which was otherwise taught in a traditional ODeL format. This intervention transformed the unit into three sequential levels: Level 1 used narrative framing and an NPC named Pixel to guide students through introductory concepts; Level 2 utilized a Metaversal Quest built in FrameVR, where students navigated virtual rooms in an escape-room style to find codes; and Level 3 employed an "elixir" mechanic where students earned rewards by passing comprehension checkpoints.

The researcher employed a qualitative research design. Data were collected through 38 student reflection papers and one focus group discussion with five volunteer participants. The analysis followed reflexive thematic analysis, using the Mechanics, Dynamics, and Aesthetics (MDA) framework, Moore’s Theory of Transactional Distance, and the Community of Inquiry framework to interpret the findings.

The findings revealed several key themes regarding student perceptions. Regarding the Quest-Based Learning approach, students viewed it as an approachable and motivating format. The use of narrative cues and visual layouts helped them orient themselves, while the segmentation of content into checkpoints and pop-up questions helped reduce the perceived burden of heavy academic readings. Curiosity and the novelty of the game-like interface served as significant entry points for engagement.

In terms of engagement and satisfaction, students reported increased involvement due to the interactive nature of the tasks and the ability to repeat levels to achieve mastery. Interestingly, the metaverse environment facilitated spontaneous social connection and peer collaboration, as students encountered one another in the virtual space and engaged in informal chatting. Gamified rewards, such as elixirs and gates, provided satisfying indicators of progress. However, these benefits were tempered by significant challenges, including technical instability (lag and loading delays), interface complexity, and physical discomfort such as motion sickness.

Regarding specific opportunities and constraints, students identified the metaverse as a playful environment that could simulate real-world scenarios and encourage exploration. However, they also noted a constraint in pedagogical design: the virtual environment often merely replicated existing text-heavy materials rather than integrating the content into the immersive experience through redesigned tasks. Technical barriers remained a primary constraint that disrupted the learning flow.

The study concludes that quest-based and immersive elements can effectively support persistence in ODeL by redistributing cognitive load and providing structure. When designed well, these elements help students manage pacing and reduce the isolation typical of distance learning. However, the benefits are contingent upon platform stability and the meaningful integration of pedagogy with the medium. The researcher notes that the value of these tools lies not in their novelty, but in their ability to scaffold engagement when accessibility and pedagogical alignment are prioritized.

The implications of this research suggest several recommendations for educators and designers. First, gamification should be used to structure learning and clarify pacing rather than just as a decorative element. Second, immersive environments should be intentionally designed to foster social presence and collaborative interaction to combat ODeL isolation. Third, technical stability and ease of use must be foundational, as technical failures can negate the benefits of immersion. Finally, designers should move beyond the "aesthetic replication" of content and instead embed learning objectives directly into the mechanics and tasks of the immersive environment to ensure the medium supports deep application of knowledge.

title: Drop-Everything-And-Read-wRite-Research: Designing for Learning Presence in a Metaverse
abstract: This paper is a design case narrative seeking to capture, theorize and reflect on the process of redesigning a research course in which participants took part in a virtual research writing group or the Drop-Everything-And-Read-wRite-Research (D.E.A.R.) sessions within a metaverse and with learning presence in mind. Learning presence has been investigated through indications of self-regulation and co-regulation in the areas of forethought, planning and monitoring (Hayes et al., 2015). From the point of view of the co-faculty-in-charge-and-learning-designer, the design case narrative revealed a cyclical design thinking process for the course redesign process. It unfolded the D.E.A.R.’s ideation as a spin-off from the shared experiences of faculty members undertaking their dissertation writing during the pandemic, while its prototype was based on a synchronous writing group. Within a metaverse there are examples of learning presence worth sustaining to improve student research writing experiences. The paper recommends a case study to be undertaken in the future, to further investigate learning presence and its manifestations in research writing groups, capitalizing on the potential possibilities of the shared D.E.A.R. metaverse to harness learning alliance and community building among researchers in higher education. Further enhancements of the prototype are suggested to inform institutional support mechanisms for research student success.  Methodologically, the design thinking cycle revealed a story pattern through which a design case narrative can be told as a form of scholarship of teaching and learning in the context of online education.  The study likewise paves the way for further studies in support of a scholarship of online teaching and learning or SO2TL as research looking closely into instructional design models given that much of ‘online teaching’ happens through intentional design of learning content and the learning environment.
half:
In the article "Drop-Everything-And-Read-wRite-Research: Designing for Learning Presence in a Metaverse," Villanueva, Mangubat, Orbe, and Eacersall investigate the development of a virtual research writing group within a metaverse environment. The study addresses challenges such as academic workload and cognitive fatigue caused by traditional video conferencing. Using the Community of Inquiry framework and a five-phase design thinking process—empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test—the researchers sought to determine if a metaverse could foster "learning presence" through self-regulation and co-regulation.

The research team, consisting of a learning designer, a content expert, a metaverse custodian, and a student, transitioned "D.E.A.R." sessions from Zoom to the Frame VR platform to create a more immersive experience. Findings from the testing phase, gathered through meeting notes, digital artifacts, and chat transcripts, provided evidence of learning presence. Participants engaged in forethought, goal setting, progress monitoring, and strategic organization, such as using outlines.

The authors conclude that the D.E.A.R. Metaverse prototype demonstrates significant pedagogical potential. Unlike episodic video conferencing, the metaverse provides a persistent, shared space that supports focus and continuity. Digital avatars and virtual zones create "protected time," allowing researchers to work individually while maintaining peer awareness, which fosters accountability and community. The study suggests the metaverse is a viable environment for fostering learning presence and recommends using design thinking to develop innovative online learning experiences.

The context of the study is an open university setting where distance education is the norm. The researchers sought to leverage the "educational Metaverse" to move beyond transactional information exchange toward an embodied, relational, and persistent environment. The study is situated within the framework of the Community of Inquiry (CoI), specifically looking at how the metaverse can enhance learning alliance and community building through immersive, avatar-based co-presence.

Methodologically, the study employs a design case narrative, which the authors frame as a form of Scholarship of Online Teaching and Learning (SO2TL). This approach allows the researchers to tell a story of the instructional design process. The study utilized a cyclical design thinking process consisting of five phases: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test. The research team included a faculty-in-charge/learning designer, a content expert, a metaverse custodian, and a fellow user/student. Data collection included reviewing meeting notes, digital artifacts, and student chat transcripts from the metaverse sessions.

The findings are presented through the lens of the design thinking cycle. During the empathize and define phases, the team identified a need for research courses that support researcher identity and provide dedicated time for writing. This led to the ideation of the D.E.A.R. sessions, which were inspired by previous successful "drop-in-and-write" sessions held via Zoom. The prototype phase involved transitioning these sessions from video conferencing to the Frame VR platform, which allowed for a more immersive experience.

In the testing phase, the researchers documented initial evidence of learning presence through student chat transcripts. The findings revealed that participants engaged in forethought and planning (e.g., setting goals for reading specific documents), monitoring (e.g., tracking progress and refining research questions), and strategy use (e.g., using outlines to organize thoughts and cluster readings). These interactions suggest that the metaverse provides a unique space where self-regulation and co-regulation can be deliberately designed into the environment.

The authors conclude that the D.E.A.R. Metaverse prototype demonstrates significant pedagogical potential. Unlike traditional video conferencing, which often results in episodic, short-term meetings, the metaverse offers a persistent, shared space that supports focus and continuity. The use of digital avatars and specific virtual "zones" allows for a sense of "protected time" where researchers can work individually while remaining aware of the presence of their peers, thereby fostering accountability and community without the need for constant verbal interaction.

The implications of this study suggest that the metaverse can serve as a viable learning environment for fostering learning presence and community building in higher education. The authors recommend that the design thinking cycle be used as a formal instructional design model for developing innovative online learning experiences. Furthermore, they suggest that future research should include exploratory case studies to more deeply investigate how learning presence manifests in these spaces. They recommend using thematic analysis on chat transcripts and conducting focus group discussions to better understand how participants experience the virtual platform and the sense of "writing in the company of peers" through their digital avatars. Finally, the study suggests investigating how these immersive environments influence researcher identity and the development of research competencies.

title: Developing Micro-credentials in AI for Assessment in Asia and Europe
abstract:
The extreme transformation in education worldwide was driven by rapid technological advancements and an increasing demand for specialized skills. Microcredentials have emerged as smooth, skills-focused learning pathways, offering a flexible response to the evolving needs of the workforce and higher education. At the same time, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing educational practices, particularly in evaluation and assessment, by enabling personalized learning, enhancing efficiency, and providing data-driven insights. However, the widespread and ethical integration of AI in assessment faces significant challenges, including issues of bias, data privacy, and the need for strong quality assurance.
ASEF (Asia-Europe Foundation) for Higher Education and Innovative Laboratory is continuously conducting online training on AI for educators in Asia and Europe, focusing on two tracks: 1) Academic Paper track and 2) Developing a Micro-credential track. This paper is a documentation of the author’s involvement in that training program with the intent to learn and capacitate for personal and institutional development in the future. This paper will outline the path in development micro-credential course. It will examine the factors to consider before creating a micro-credential course that will focus on the use of AI for evaluation and assessment within the Asia-Europe context. It will present the rationale for such a course, explore the characteristics and benefits of micro-credentials, detail the applications and advantages of AI in assessment, and propose a curriculum designed to address the professional development needs of educators and administrators. A critical emphasis on navigating the complex ethical considerations and policy implications unique to Asia, advocating for transparency, accountability, and human oversight, will also be included.

The research proposes a three-step framework for developing micro-credentials focused on AI-supported assessment. The first step is a Contextual Needs Analysis and Scoping phase to define measurable competencies and align with industry standards. The second step is the Curriculum Structure phase, utilizing a modular, "bite-sized" design that progresses from foundational concepts to practical application and critical evaluation, including regional case studies on bias. The third step addresses Ethical Issues and Quality Assurance through expert reviews of data privacy and audits for systemic biases. The study concludes that modular, stackable micro-credentials offer a strategic, agile way to update pedagogical practices.

two:
The rapid advancement of technology has driven a global transformation in education, creating an urgent demand for specialized skills. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is currently revolutionizing educational practices, particularly in the realm of evaluation and assessment, by offering personalized learning, increased efficiency, and data-driven insights. However, the integration of AI into assessment faces significant hurdles, including potential bias, data privacy concerns, and the necessity for robust quality assurance. Furthermore, there is a notable disparity in technological maturity across Asia, ranging from hyper-connected urban centers to rural areas lacking basic connectivity. This creates a critical need for educators to achieve AI literacy—the ability to use AI effectively, ethically, and safely—to remain globally competitive and maintain academic integrity.

The context of this study is rooted in the 6th ASEF Higher Education Innovative Laboratory, organized by the Asia-Europe Foundation (ASEF). This intergovernmental organization facilitates knowledge sharing between Asia and Europe to tackle global challenges. The specific program, titled "University’s Role in Developing Skills for an AI-Powered Future," involved higher education professionals from both regions. The author participated in the "Developing a Micro-credential" track, which focused on drafting practical course frameworks to bridge AI knowledge gaps. This initiative aligns with broader regional efforts, such as the ASEAN Foundation's project to boost AI literacy across its ten member states.

To address the identified gaps, the author employed a conceptual Design-Based Research (DBR) approach. DBR is a methodology used in the learning sciences to simultaneously develop learning theory and the design of instructional interventions. Because this study focuses on the early stages of development, the conceptual DBR approach allowed for the systematic design of an educational intervention grounded in theory and contextual needs analysis prior to full-scale implementation. The research was guided by four primary questions regarding the current levels of AI literacy among educators, the specific competency gaps regarding AI-supported assessment, the design of a micro-credential to address these gaps, and the necessary considerations for making such a course culturally and ethically relevant.

The findings of the research process resulted in a proposed three-step framework for developing a micro-credential course focused on AI-supported assessment and evaluation. The first step involves a Contextual Needs Analysis and Scoping phase. This phase focuses on defining measurable competencies, such as designing AI-supported rubrics and interpreting predictive analytics, while engaging stakeholders from both Asia and Europe to ensure the skills addressed align with evolving industry standards. The second step is the Curriculum Structure phase. The proposed curriculum is designed to be "bite-sized" and modular, moving from foundational AI concepts to practical tool application and, finally, to critical evaluation. This structure includes authentic regional case studies, such as addressing bias against non-native English speakers in automated scoring, and experiential learning activities where participants develop their own AI-assessment modules. The third step focuses on Ethical Issues and Quality Assurance. This involves subjecting the curriculum to review by legal and ethical experts to address cross-border data transfer and student privacy, as well as auditing AI tools for systemic biases related to language, culture, or socioeconomic status.

The study concludes that developing micro-credentials in AI for educators is a strategic necessity rather than a luxury. Such programs provide the agility required to update pedagogical practices in months rather than years, offering a flexible, skills-based pathway for lifelong learning. The proposed framework balances technical competence with pedagogical design and ethical governance, providing a foundation for empowering educators to lead in an AI-driven educational landscape.

The implications of this work suggest that micro-credentials are an ideal vehicle for professional development because they are modular, stackable, and verifiable. They allow working professionals to upskill without the time commitment of a full degree and can be delivered online to reach diverse populations across different time zones. However, the author notes that as a conceptual study, the research is limited to the development of a framework rather than its empirical implementation. The study implies that future research must focus on piloting, testing, and iteratively refining these micro-credential programs across diverse institutional contexts to ensure they are effective in real-world settings. Ultimately, the integration of AI in education requires continuous collaboration between educators, technologists, and policymakers to ensure the technology is used in an equitable and socially responsible manner.

title: Innovations in Learning Design for Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL)
half:
This editorial for a special issue of the Center for Open and Digital Teaching and Learning (CODTL) at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) addresses the evolving landscape of Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL). The central problem identified is the necessity for intentional instructional design, the integration of emerging technologies, and the implementation of reflective practices to enhance engagement and community in distributed environments. As digital education expands, there is a critical need for pedagogical frameworks and tools that create inclusive and equitable learning experiences across diverse global contexts.

The collection features scholarly contributions from Asia, Africa, and Europe, providing a multifaceted examination of how different regions navigate online higher education. The research spans various levels of implementation, from individual student-centered perspectives to broader institutional strategies and new credentialing systems. Methods used include the validity testing of the Community of Inquiry (CoI) survey, qualitative examinations of e-portfolios and peer feedback, studies on immersive and gamified spaces like the metaverse, and research into the intersection of artificial intelligence and micro-credentials.

Key findings highlight several essential themes. In global collaboration, research emphasizes culturally responsive pedagogy and pragmatic discursive culture models. Regarding quality assurance, the validation of the CoI survey provides a reliable tool for evaluating teaching and learning in fully online settings. In Tanzania, findings suggest that institutionalizing reflective practices through digital tools like e-portfolios supports teacher professional development. Research into immersive and gamified courses and the metaverse examines how these spaces impact student agency and learning presence. Finally, the issue identifies emerging trends in the intersection of artificial intelligence and assessment through the development of micro-credentials in Asia and Europe.

The studies conclude that effective ODeL requires a shift toward reflective, learner-centered approaches where the integration of digital tools is purposeful and grounded in pedagogical frameworks. The common thread is the necessity of intentionality in instructional design to foster community and engagement. These findings suggest that practitioners should adopt culturally responsive and reflective practices; institutions should implement robust quality assurance tools and professional development; and the field must prepare for a future where the metaverse and AI provide immersive, flexible, and alternative pathways to recognition through micro-credentials. Collectively, these contributions advance the pursuit of equitable and innovative digital education practices globally

The editorial for this special issue of the Center for Open and Digital Teaching and Learning (CODTL) at the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) addresses the evolving landscape of Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL). The central problem addressed by the collective works in this issue is the need for intentional instructional design, the integration of emerging technologies, and the implementation of reflective practices to enhance learning, engagement, and community within distributed and online environments. As digital education expands, there is a critical requirement for pedagogical frameworks and digital tools that can create inclusive, meaningful, and equitable learning experiences across diverse global contexts.

The context of this collection is global, featuring scholarly contributions from educators and researchers located in Asia, Africa, and Europe. This international scope allows for a multifaceted examination of how different regions navigate the complexities of online higher education. The articles move through various levels of educational implementation, ranging from individual student-centered perspectives and specific pedagogical models to broader institutional strategies and the development of new credentialing systems.

The methods employed across the featured articles are diverse, reflecting the multidisciplinary nature of learning design. The research includes the development and validity testing of survey instruments, such as the Community of Inquiry (CoI) survey, to ensure quality assurance in online higher education. Other studies utilize qualitative and practical approaches, such as examining the use of e-portfolios, online journals, and peer feedback to support professional growth. Some research focuses on the implementation of immersive and gamified learning spaces, including the metaverse, to study student engagement and presence. Additionally, the collection includes studies on the development of micro-credentials, specifically focusing on the intersection of artificial intelligence and alternative credentialing.

The findings presented in the special issue highlight several key themes in modern ODeL. In the realm of global collaboration, research indicates the importance of culturally responsive pedagogy and a pragmatic discursive culture model when managing intercultural dimensions in global teams. Regarding quality assurance, the validation of the Community of Inquiry (CoI) survey provides a reliable tool for students to evaluate teaching and learning in fully online university settings. In the context of teacher education in Tanzania, findings suggest that institutionalizing reflective practices through digital tools like e-portfolios and peer feedback supports professional development.

Furthermore, the research explores student-centered engagement through innovative technologies. Studies on immersive and gamified courses, as well as research into the metaverse, examine how these spaces impact student agency and learning presence. Finally, the issue identifies emerging trends in the intersection of artificial intelligence and assessment, specifically through the development of micro-credentials in Asia and Europe.

The conclusions drawn from these various studies suggest that effective ODeL requires a shift toward reflective, learner-centered approaches. The integration of digital tools must be purposeful and grounded in pedagogical frameworks to be successful. Whether through the use of gamification, the implementation of reflective practices in teacher training, or the adoption of AI-driven micro-credentials, the common thread is the necessity of intentionality in instructional design to foster community and engagement in online spaces.

The implications of these findings are significant for educators, policymakers, and institutions worldwide. For practitioners, the research underscores the importance of adopting culturally responsive and reflective practices to support diverse learner populations. For institutions, the findings highlight the need for robust quality assurance tools and the institutionalization of professional development practices to maintain high standards in distance education. Finally, the exploration of emerging technologies like the metaverse and AI suggests that the future of ODeL will increasingly rely on the ability to design immersive, flexible, and technologically integrated learning environments that empower students and provide alternative pathways to recognition through micro-credentials. Collectively, these contributions advance the pursuit of equitable and innovative digital education practices on a global scale.
